title: ‘Everywhere there were pitifully injured people’: how a newly unearthed memoir captures the devastation of Hiroshima | Japan | The Guardian
description: In an exclusive extract from his memoir, Kiyoshi Tanimoto describes the terrifying trip across the city to locate his wife and child
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In an exclusive extract from his memoir, Kiyoshi Tanimoto describes the terrifying trip across the city to locate his wife and child
Content: The aftermath of the explosion in Hiroshima, 6 August 1945.Photograph: Anonymous/APView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the explosion in Hiroshima, 6 August 1945.Photograph: Anonymous/APJapan‘Everywhere there were pitifully injured people’: how a newly unearthed memoir captures the devastation of HiroshimaIn an exclusive extract from his memoir, Kiyoshi Tanimoto describes the terrifying trip across the city to locate his wife and child‘I didn’t want to be a victim of the bomb’:read an interviewwith Tanimoto’s daughter Koko KondoKiyoshi TanimotoSat 25 Jul 2026 06.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of the people of Hiroshima had neither seen nor heard any plane. They heard no sound of explosion. They had seen only a strange flash in open daylight, or merely felt the reflection of the flash. However, there had been a tremendous explosion.The parents of Mr Konda, one of our church members, had been waiting for a train at Yokogawa station, located 2km [one and a quarter miles] away from the centre of the bomb’s explosion. They saw a B-29 and a parachute dropping through the air. Before they had time to wonder at the sight, they fell unconscious. Afterward, they could not remember sensing any sound or light. When they regained consciousness, they found themselves lying on the ground, burned and without any clothing. The houses all around had been crushed to the ground. After getting to their feet, they ran toward the suburbs. Other people rushing along the Koi highway had the same experience.After crossing the Koi and Fukushima bridges, I reached a place about a kilometre away from the explosion. From the suburbs to this spot, houses were heavily damaged but somehow were still standing. However, the houses from here to the centre of the explosion were all flat on the ground, as if they had been toy buildings crushed by a hammer. Painful cries of “Tasukete!” – “Help! – could be heard from under smashed houses.View image in fullscreenHiroshima Nagarekawa church, where Tanimoto was minister, after the bombing. Courtesy of Koko KondoPeople seemed to be buried in the ground. I knew full well how hard a job it would be to pull out even one log from a collapsed house, because I had helped with the clearing of houses. Nothing whatsoever could be done, with the strength of only one person, to help the people beneath those houses. Yet there were people buried here and there – everywhere.After I had stopped to try to do something for these people, the thought that my wife and baby and neighbours must be in the same state flashed through my mind. I was the defence coordinator of my neighbourhood, and there were 120 lives entrusted to me. I had to hurry back to my post. I ran away in tears, saying, “Excuse me, I’m sorry, but excuse me!” I ran like a wild man. At Fukushima bridge, I saw Mr Matsuo, who had been with me when the atomic bomb exploded. He came running up, out of breath. “Mr Matsuo, please excuse me, for I have responsibilities,” I said, and ran on.double quotation markEverywhere there were pitifully injured people. They could no longer keep moving, so they were lying in the streetsI followed the riverbank of the Fukushima river, looking to find a place where the fire was not so furious. Then I came to Nakahiromachi, a northern neighbourhood, where there were many farm fields and not so many houses.Everywhere there were pitifully injured people. They could no longer keep moving, so they were lying in the streets. The further I moved into the city, the more wounded I saw. I grabbed my panama hat and threw it on the ground. In my heart I cried, “Forgive me!” because I felt no reason for why I had been left uninjured. I thought my wife and baby must be injured like these people and might be buried under our house. I asked their forgiveness for not being there to rescue them.The usual way home was to take the Misasa Bridge across the Ota River toward central Hiroshima and go out to Hakushima, but the foot of the bridge and the Hakushima district were in flames. Fortunately, the Ushita district, which was on the other side of the river, seemed to be unscathed by fire. If I could get past Ushita, my own neighbourhood of Noboricho would be within a stone’s throw.In a determined manner, I plunged into the river. It was not that I had confidence in my swimming ability, but there were no other means of reaching my goal. The Ota River varies in water level according to the tides. There was not much water, but the stream was swift. Naturally, I lost control of my limbs. I had already run continuously for about an hour and was dead tired.I began to swallow water, which ran into my nose and mouth. My body was heavy, and my head started to sink into the water. My gaiters became loose and dangled about my legs. One of my shoes came off. I thought I was drowning. I would not have resented being killed by American bombs, but it seemed regrettable to be drowned. I prayed while sinking, “Oh God, do help me. Protect my body until I can save my wife and child and my neighbours.” Then I calmed myself and became lighter by taking off my gaiters, coat and the other shoe. With all my remaining energy I swam through the water.Soon I reached shallow water about my height and was saved. When I got to the opposite bank, I could not move any longer and rested for some time with my head on the ground. After I regained some strength, I got on my feet and started walking toward Ushita. I was completely undressed and only differed from others by having no scars from burns.As the treasurer of my church lived nearby, I went to his house and saw that it was also crushed and deserted. Praying for his safety, I passed through Ushita. I saw no other residents and thought that everybody must have escaped by now.Mrs Tada’s house, where my wife often stayed overnight, was nearby, and I thought of dropping in. Although she usually was back home by half past six or seven o’clock in the morning, I wondered if she might have stayed until nine or 10 that morning at Mrs Tada’s place and thus would have been saved. Praying, I took a few steps toward the house, and, to my surprise, I found my wife carrying Koko in her arms, in a line of refugees. She was wearing a blood-stained chemise, her hair was hanging about her shoulders, and she had a ghostlike appearance.I called to her. She turned around, looked at me, and stood quietly with tears in her eyes. I looked away and asked, “What happened to you?”She said, “Just as I reached home, Mrs Takaki came for a visit. We were both talking at the door when we were buried.”“And what happened to Mrs Takaki?”With a miserable expression, she said, “I don’t know.”View image in fullscreenKiyoshi Tanimoto and his wife in a family portrait, with their daughter Koko on the right. Courtesy of Koko KondoI had not experienced the slightest pleasure seeing my wife and child safe. Rather, I was filled with indignation. It was unpardonable that a church member who was paying a visit to the parsonage should be killed during an air raid and the family of the pastor still be saved. Should not the wife of the pastor have died together with the church member? I was filled with accusatory feelings toward my wife.Afterward, I learned that my wife had been buried under the house in an instant and nearly crushed under the pressure of heavy wood. She could not breathe for a while and began to fall unconscious. However, she was brought to by the screams of Koko, who was still in her arms. She struggled with all her strength to save her baby. Calming herself, she noticed a small hole in the attic. Both of her arms were strongly pinned in the ruins, but she could move a bit and finally managed to stretch out one arm.She gradually made the small hole wider. Every time she struggled to move, broken pieces of roofing fell on her head. Koko continued to cry loudly. Struggling with all her strength, she enlarged the hole and was finally able to push out Koko. Then she did everything she could to free herself and managed to get out.By then, the house next door was on fire, and smoke was rising from it. She staggered along the alley with Koko in her arms. She thought of getting someone to help Mrs Takaki, but every house in sight was smashed and already deserted. The fire was spreading, and the smoke was getting thick. With the baby in her arms, she could not return to our house. Finally, she reached the Sentei gardens, after being pursued by the fire and smoke. However, her thoughts were with her neighbour.This is an edited extract from Hiroshima, 8:15: The Lost Memoir by Kiyoshi Tanimoto. It will be published by Ebury on 6 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: The AI jobs apocalypse probably isn’t coming anytime soon | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay
Content: ‘Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs.’Photograph: DragonImages/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs.’Photograph: DragonImages/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)The AI jobs apocalypse probably isn’t coming anytime soonEduardo PorterArtificial intelligence  may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to paySupported byAbout this contentSat 25 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.01 EDTShareIn March, Anthropic, the cutting-edge artificial intelligence business that gave us the chatbot Claude,published an analysison the impact of AI on employment, to help us assess the claim that intelligent robots were about to redefine human existence, ending demand for human labor.Last year in May, Anthropic’s co-founder, Dario Amodei, claimed AI could wipe out half of all entry-level jobs in one to five years. Last January,he told usAI would probably become a “general labor substitute for humans”. In Junehe saidwe risk “a world where the economic trade-off dial is stuck on the hypergrowth, hyper-inequality setting”.And yet, Anthropic’s report suggests that, so far, AI’s impact has fallen short of expectations: “We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022,” the report stated. Deployment of the technology “remains a fraction of what’s feasible”. Claude covers just 33% of all tasks in the computer and math category whereas theoretically it could take over nearly 100% of them.Forget the AI job apocalypse. AI’s real threat is worker control and surveillanceRead moreSpending on datacenters is going through the roof, for sure, butproductivityhas not been experiencing the galloping gains that the technorati’s epochal prognostications lead one to expect. Labor productivity was, in fact, slower in the first three years of our AI era than during the information technology boom that began in the mid 1990s.Even OpenAI’s Sam Altman, AI’s most public face, says he now doubts its job-killing potential. “I don’t think we’re going to have the kind ​of jobs apocalypse that some of the companies in our space advocate or talk about,”he said in May. As Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist David Autor noted: “A lot of people have noticed that the world is not changing as fast as they predicted.”This has opened the public conversation to a less cataclysmic narrative of the evolution of the technology. The emerging new story not only puts more emphasis on the complexity of the relationship between automation and human work across history. It is also raising doubts about the very feasibility of the threatened AI transformation of the universe. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index, which had been propelled almost exclusively by the rise of AI-related stocks, has fallen about 8% since its peak in early June.One strand of critique of the “AI-will-do-everything” story might be calledthe O-ring argument. It comes from the mid-flight explosion of the space shuttle Challenger 73 seconds into its flight on 28 January 1986. A lengthy investigation concluded that the demise of the multibillion dollar spaceship was causedby a rubber O-ringthat didn’t work at low temperatures.That cheap O-ring proved critical. The analogy suggests that as long as AI cannot perform every task perfectly, it will increase the value of the remaining tasks. Depending on whichthe AI takes over, it could increase the value of high skill workers who are relieved by AI of the low-end part of their job, or increase the opportunity of lower skilled workers by taking over the more expert tasks.Asone recent studynoted: “despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.”Things could change. As Jed Kolkopoints out, research on the labor market impact of artificial intelligence is still in its infancy. There are almost four years to go in Amodei’s one-to-five year window. And maybe devastation hits in year six. According to the Federal Reserve, adoption of AI isexpanding fastacross businesses.Moreover, Autor argues, AI is getting better. And its progress shows no sign that it will soon hit a ceiling. “Skepticism about thestochastic parrotis behind us,” he told me. The dystopian AI future – utopian, if you get to own and run the AI – is still on the cards.“Insiders are as gung ho as ever,” noted Daron Acemoglu, the Nobel prize-winning economist. “They still believe artificial general intelligence is around the corner.” Indeed, Elon Musk has not budged fromthe dream that“AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.”One may recall the quip by Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Solow in the early years of the computer revolution: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in theproductivity statistics.” It took another 10 years or so, as businesses reorganized around the new technology. But computers did eventually show up in the stats.Clouds are nonetheless gathering on the AI horizon. It’s not just that AI may not end all human work. AI may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay.The politics have decidedly soured on the project.Seven in 10 Americansoppose building AI datacenters in their area. While this has to do with their insatiable demand for energy, which drives up local electricity costs, AI’s unpopularity is no doubt related to the proposition that it will destroy society as we know it.There are other bumps in the road. Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs. “Not everything is a computational problem,” notes Autor. AI is good at replicating language, but it cannot connect language to the reality around it. Despite its progress, it still makes plenty ofcritical mistakes.Gig workers are endlessly exploited. AI could make more of us share their fateRead moreAnd then there are the impossible economics. Even if AI could eventually solve all our problems, the solution looks expensive. How much of GDP are we willing to invest in AI datacenters, 20%? 30%? 40%? According to some estimates, that is where we are headed. The International Energy Agency estimates that powerdemand from datacenterswill more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, more than the energy consumption of Japan.The economics look more fragile considering how fast the investment in AI depreciates, as new models overtake those developed just a few months ago. Companies developing AI models “are never going to make money”, Acemoglu said. “They are losing hundreds of billions of dollars every year.”One may discount Altman’s new modesty as a PR feint. Somebody may have told him that equating the AI revolution with mass joblessness was not smart politics. But misgivings about AI’s vaunted capabilities are more than a marketing twist. The grand, epochal promise may be in trouble. Maybe artificial intelligence can’t deliver at a price society is willing to pay.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedAnthropicOpenAIElon MuskUS work & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: What makes a woman a witch? Financial independence  | Women | The Guardian
description: Women aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but there is still risk and violence implicit in the label ‘witch’
Author: Lucianne Tonti
Headline: Women aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but there is still risk and violence implicit in the label ‘witch’
Content: ‘Historically it’s been dangerous for women to reach for financial independence and status’ … Lucianne Tonti travelled to places touched by the European witch trials that spanned the 15th to 18th centuries.Illustration: Ida Rentoul OuthwaiteView image in fullscreen‘Historically it’s been dangerous for women to reach for financial independence and status’ … Lucianne Tonti travelled to places touched by the European witch trials that spanned the 15th to 18th centuries.Illustration: Ida Rentoul OuthwaiteWomenWhat makes a woman a witch? Financial independenceWomen aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but there is still risk and violence implicit in the label ‘witch’Lucianne TontiSat 25 Jul 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Katherine Harrison’s husband passed away, she became the wealthiest woman in Wethersfield, Connecticut. Rather than wallow in her new status as a young widow she decided to run the farm she’d inherited on her own. She took up ranching and a slew of other hobbies including brewing ale, spinning yarn and beekeeping. She traded honey and beeswax for candles. She was by all accounts, headstrong, outspoken and clever.In many corners of the internet, Harrison’s interests are having a moment. Craft brewers have been spruiking classic ales for years, urban beekeeping is surging in popularity, and people are looking to textile-based crafts as ways to practise mindfulness.The rave secret: why middle-aged women are larging it – and seeing big health benefitsRead moreBut Harrison was a single woman and mother of three daughters who, in a notable contrast to today’s tradwives, felt she did not need a man. Her independence, wealth – and the fact that she practised astrology – make her hobbies seem less like those of a good wife and more like those of a good witch.Unfortunately, Harrison lived in the 17th century when fear and paranoia dominated the New England colonies. It was a time when a woman’s refusal to conform to puritanical, patriarchal norms made her vulnerable to accusations of witchcraft. In 1668, more than two decades before the Salem witch trials kicked off 200km north, Harrison was arrested and put on trial for witchcraft.View image in fullscreenA colonial-era house in Wethersfield, Connecticut.Photograph: Lucianne TontiIn 2024 I visited Harrison’s land in Wethersfield, one of the first stops I made on a research trip for my book Good Witch. Over three years, I spoke to dozens of experts, travelled from Connecticut to Massachusetts and then across the seas to Scotland, England, Denmark and the far north of Norway. Each place was touched by the European witch trials that spanned the 15th to 18th centuries, where 80% of the approximately 80,000 to 100,000 people tried were women.While there were many causative factors in the witch-hunts – patriarchy, economic hardship, and religious and political tensions, to name a few – a woman’s financial independence and power made her vulnerable. Sometimes this independence was realised through inheritance, sometimes her proficiency at work.Harrison’s initial charges were dismissed, but she was summoned before the court again the following year. The indictment alleged she had “familiarity with Satan … and by his help acted things beyond the ordinary course of nature”. The wide-ranging accusations included divination and healing; people said they’d seen her likeness appearing in their beds at night.double quotation markModern witchcraft has surfaced as a dreamy symbol of female intuition, but there is still risk and violence implicit in the labelIt was alleged she had asked for the devil’s help to make her work more profitable and to hinder the work of her neighbours. More than one witness mentioned being suspicious of her skills as a spinner, several men accused her of bewitching them to impede their trades as weavers and one tailor claimed she bewitched him to incorrectly sew sleeves on a jacket seven times in a row.During the trial, it was clear her neighbours’ accusations of witchcraft lacked evidence and were mostly based on petty grievances, jealousy and superstition. Although she was convicted the magistrate spared her life, citing weak evidence, and banished her from Wethersfield instead.Harrison’s case is emblematic of a pattern in the witch-hunts of colonial New England. In an analysis of the trials, the US historian Carol F Karlsen found that, although it was rare for women to inherit property, when they did, they were more susceptible to witchcraft allegations.Womenfrom families without male heirs (Harrison had three daughters) made up 64% of the females prosecuted, 76% of those who were found guilty, and 89% of those who were executed.The pattern reflects how “these women were aberrations in a society with an inheritance system designed to keep property in the hands of men,” writes Karlsen, in her 1987 book The Devil in the Shape of a Woman.That Harrison’s business endeavours are prevalent in her trial notes speaks to another pattern. “Like midwives, healers and female religious leaders, women who turned their traditional skills to profit placed themselves in competition with men – and in positions of vulnerability to witchcraft accusations,” writes Karlsen.View image in fullscreenThe remains of the church where Agnes Sampson and 100 other witches allegedly partied with the devil.Photograph: Lucianne TontiWomen’s work was a factor in witchcraft allegations in Europe too. ACambridge University studyby Dr Philippa Carter found that women’s employment options in the 16th and 17th centuries – healthcare, food preparation, dairy production and livestock management – all came with a higher risk of witchcraft accusations.Rather than relying on legal records, which painted a one-sided picture, Carter used the casebooks of a medical practitioner and astrologer, Richard Napier, who recorded at least 1,714 incidents of suspected bewitchment from 1597 to 1634. Work in dairying and medicine were naturally prone to spoilage and disease. These ordinary outcomes were viewed as corruption induced by bad magic: “corrupt blood made wounds rankle and corrupt milk made ill-scented cheese,” she writes.A woman’s daily tasks would often see her crisscrossing between homes, bakehouses and marketplaces, and thesefrequent interactions with neighbours also increased the chances of becoming embroiled in conflicts and labelled a witch.Across Europe, women’s work in medicine would be maligned as witchcraft by institutions – like the church and academia – too. Wise women once enjoyed prominence and reverence in their communities for treating ailments with herbal remedies and prayers, delivering babies, performing minor surgeries and setting bones. But in 1325, Pope John XXII wrote a letter to Bishop Stephen of Paris, warning him that women who were practising medicine without formal education were in fact practising witchcraft and asking him to forbid them from doing so.In the centuries that followed, regulations concerning who could legitimately study and practise medicine were tightened further. Since women were barred from academic institutions, they were effectively barred from the medical profession too.View image in fullscreenThe Scottish town of North Berwick, where Agnes Sampson’s witch trial took place.Photograph: Lucianne TontiEventually, the marginalisation of and attacks on female healers would culminate in witchcraft prosecutions, like in Scotland when the healer Agnes Sampson – another widow – was put on trial by King James VI in the North Berwick witch trials of 1590.She was accused of participating in a gathering of witches with the devil, where it was alleged they had cast spells to raise storms and sink the ships of King James as he sailed home from Denmark-Norway with his new bride, Princess Anne. James ordered that Sampson be tortured, and under immense duress she confessed. Of the 53 offences she was indicted with, over half focused on her practice as a healer.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Simon and SchusterWhat we see in Sampson’s case is evidence of how society maligned women’s labour as witchcraft and punished women for their feminine power. Accusations of witchcraft were wielded as threats against women like Harrison, who dared to defy the social structures that limited their participation in the workforce, and inheritance structures that kept property in male ownership.Historically it’s been dangerous for women to reach for financial independence and status. While modern witchcraft, from tarot cards to astrology, has surfaced in the zeitgeist as a dreamy symbol of female intuition and girlhood, there is still risk and violence implicit in the label.Women aren’t being burnt at the stake any more, but as we saw in June on thebillboards across Melbournedepicting Victorian premier Jacinta Allan in a black pointed hat, when people want to take a woman’s power away, they’ll still call her a witch.Good Witch: In Search of Our Lost Feminine Powerby Lucianne Tonti is available in Australia now through Simon & SchusterExplore more on these topicsWomenHistory booksWitchcraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more | Fiction | The Guardian
description: From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny Colgan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny Colgan
Content: Illustration by Zara PickenFictionThe perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and moreFrom a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny ColganSat 25 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 04.05 EDTShareItis important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiographyA Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it:Whistlerby Ann Patchett.For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time:This Is Where the Serpent Livesby Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon:Glorious Exploitsby Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago,The Guest,a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’sStrangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m:The Impossible Fortuneby Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello.Bonnes vacances!View image in fullscreenFreida McFaddenauthor of The HousemaidOne of my favourite reads of the year has beenTheCalamity Clubby Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.Caro Claire Burkeauthor of YesteryearInThe Shampoo Effectby Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.View image in fullscreenTaffy Brodesser-Aknerauthor of Fleishman Is in TroubleI broughtHere in the Darkby my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.Alice Osemanauthor of HeartstopperConvenience Store Womanby Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.Mick Herronauthor of the Slough House seriesBeaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’sCountry Peopleis a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.Nita Proseauthor of The MaidThe Paper Palaceby Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.View image in fullscreenLisa Jewellauthor of None of This Is TrueThe best page-turner I’ve read this year isIt’s Not What You Thinkby Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.André Acimanauthor of Call Me by Your NameLondon Fallingby Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.View image in fullscreenLucy Foleyauthor of The Guest ListThe Wedding Peopleby Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.Erin Kellyauthor of The Night StairsThe Pinnacleby Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.Leigh Bardugoauthor of the Ninth House seriesThe Last Baronby Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.View image in fullscreenMatt Haigauthor of The Midnight LibraryThe Infinite Sadness of Small Appliancesby Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.Florence Knappauthor of The NamesA will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. InNora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.View image in fullscreenRobert Harrisauthor of ConclaveGraham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particularThe Power and the Glory,The Honorary ConsulandThe Quiet American–perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.Rebecca F Kuangauthor ofYellowfaceI recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’sCloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.View image in fullscreenMike Gayleauthor of On We GoAn MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So beginsBody of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.Bella Mackieauthor of Claws Out!The Enchanted Aprilby Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.View image in fullscreenCurtis Sittenfeldauthor of American WifeCrash Into Meby Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.View image in fullscreenHarriet Tyceauthor of Witch TrialNonesuchby Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation forTime to Burnby Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.View image in fullscreenAbir Mukherjeeauthor of The Burning GroundsMy choice isThe Shadow Stepby Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.Abigail Deanauthor of The Death of UsI’d recommendMain Charactersby Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.Jennie Godfreyauthor of The Barbecue at No9This year,Dead Heatby Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.View image in fullscreenShari Lapenaauthor of Getting Away With MurderInFiveby Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.Nick Harkawayauthor of Karla’s ChoiceIf Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d getThere Is No Antimemetics Divisionby qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?Paula Hawkinsauthor of The Girl on the TrainFour Terrible Parentsby Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.Kate Mosseauthor of The Map of BonesRecently reissued,Fennyby Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.Adele Parksauthor of Just My LuckMad Mabelby Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.Claire Powellauthor of All InI couldn’t get enough ofSome Bright Nowhereby Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.To support the Guardian, order your beach reads atguardianbookshop.com/beach-reads

title: I grew up near Andy Burnham. This is what shaped the UK’s new PM | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century
Content: Burnham has recalled his upbringing as ‘modest’, but his family also ‘didn’t want for anything’.Composite: Guardian Design/PA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham has recalled his upbringing as ‘modest’, but his family also ‘didn’t want for anything’.Composite: Guardian Design/PA/Getty ImagesThe Saturday readAndy BurnhamI grew up near Andy Burnham. This is what shaped the UK’s new PMIn the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a centuryRichard PartingtonSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 03.28 EDTShareThe Cherry Tree pub is an unassuming local. On a busy road in the Cheshire village of Culcheth, it is a chain-run pub where four shots cost £8, every burger comes with a soft drink, and sport is shown all day on the big screens. It is also a favourite ofAndy Burnham, the new prime minister.Many of the drinkers have a story about – arguably – Culcheth’s most famous son.“I was at school with Andy,” says Mike Hodgson. “He went to our school, he likes the Smiths … He’s got a good northern sense of person, and he’s done a good job inManchester.”Janice Fox chips in: “I used to play with him when we were kids.”The Cherry is in the opening scene of Burnham’s book Head North. One night in April 1989, in its smoke-filled back room, the future leader of the country is recovering from about of “impostor syndrome”while home from Cambridge University. Panic, by the Smiths, is playing on the jukebox.It is also a place I know well: like Burnham, I grew up in this quiet Warrington suburb halfway between Manchester and Liverpool, I have spent many nights at the Cherry, and like many locals, I have my own story about him.View image in fullscreenThe Cherry Tree pub in Culcheth.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHere is mine: 15 years ago I met the then Labour MP for Leigh while drinking with mates in the Cherry. Labour had recently lost the 2010 election, and Burnham had recentlylost to Ed Milibandin the race to lead the party in opposition. Home from London for the weekend, I was struggling to get a job, so plucked up the courage for a chat.As the then shadow education secretary, he talked me through the impact of the Conservatives’ plan to cut Labour’sBuilding Schools for the Futureprogramme. That £55bn landmark New Labour policy turned cold, leaky 1960s prefab schools around the country into modern buildings of which teachers and pupils could be proud; it rebuilt my secondary,Culcheth high school.He gave me his mobile number and invited me for a cup of tea in parliament. I expected to be ghosted. But a few weeks later we were sitting in SW1 picking up the conversation over a brew in Portcullis House. Burnham told me Britain’s media and political landscape needed more northern accents like ours.On Friday, Burnham openedNo 10 North, in Manchester; a first step in his promise to rebalance power away from Westminster to deliver “good growth in every postcode”.This week I travelled back to WA3 to find out what people make of Burnham becoming the first northern prime minister since Harold Wilson 50 years ago. He has spoken with pride of his roots, and how reversing the decimation of Britain’s industrial communities under Margaret Thatcher is a top priority.Outside the Cherry, one group of friends say it’s at least nice that someone local is in No 10. One of the women lifts her sunglasses and we are transported back a quarter of a century: it’s my old geography teacher, Mrs Crinion.View image in fullscreenA group sat chatting outside the Cherry Tree in Culcheth, including Richard Partington’s former teacher Mrs Crinion (second from right).Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“I was quite proud seeing him walking down the street,” says one of her friends. “I felt a bit chuffed. I hope he does a good job.” But does having one of our own in high office change anything? “I very much doubt it,” says another.Earlier this month, Burnham recorded a video for social media arriving “home” from London at Warrington Bank Quay train station. It is far from the most beautiful spot on the railway, in the shadow of an old Unilever soap factory that is up for demolition.Once the diggers have finished here there are plans for an AI datacentre – a fact deployed byKeir Starmerlast month as a symbol of how a “left behind” community could reinvent itself.But this description elides much of Warrington’s character. The town has its difficulties – not least the boarded-up shops and crumbling, shuttered nightclubs on Bridge Street – but it is more affluent than many other “red wall” communities in this pocket of north-westEngland.View image in fullscreenThe Time Square development in Warrington town centre.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAs a postwar new town, there are miles of suburbia stretching into theCheshirecountryside. There are good transport links, affordable housing, and opportunities for work in high-paying sectors, such as technology and nuclear energy.This year, the Centre for Cities thinktank suggestedBritain could do with a few more towns like Warrington: local disposable incomes have galloped ahead here, growing 2.2 times faster than the UK average since 2013. Perhaps this could influence the Burnham economic blueprint?Still, many locals feel let down by Labour. Before Burnham replaced Starmer,Reform was predicted to sweep away the partyin Warrington’s two constituencies. But many say the new prime minister’s background could help change things.John Cross, whose family has run a butcher’s stall in Warrington market for five generations, is among them: “I’m made up. That we’ve got someone from the north, rather than someone from down south. There needs to be more balance, how we’re governed in this country. Don’t get me wrong; he’s got an absolute job in front of him. But I think it’s a good thing [that Burnham is prime minister].”View image in fullscreenButcher John Cross at Warrington market.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSupport is, however, far from uniform, including in Culcheth. Sitting outside McDee’s cafe, Tom says he has little time for politicians – “all a bunch of thieves”. Net zero, failure to invest in defence and prosecutions of British soldiers are his complaints. “It’sLabour, isn’t it? I don’t believe any of them will do anything different.”Inside the cafe, others are more positive. Veysel Hazar, the manager, seats me at the table where he has served Burnham and his mother, Eileen. He does not do politics, but says of the new prime minister: “Amazing person. I’m happy for Culcheth.”View image in fullscreenVeysel Hazar, manager at McDee’s cafe in Culcheth.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEating lunch on the table opposite, the Ollerton family are from nearby Golborne – where Burnham now lives and where coal mining once dominated. They have seen him out running in his retro Everton shirt, and are friends with his nextdoor neighbour on a road a few streets from his new Makerfield constituency.“You knew he was going to win. Makerfield would have voted Reform if it wasn’t for him,” says Marilyn Ollerton.“He’s very relatable, rather than just being somebody on the television; somebody from down south that you’ve probably got nothing in common with,” says Lianne Ollerton.Some places in Warrington – particularly the terraced streets near the town’s old wire factories – rank among the most deprived in England. Burnham’s former Leigh constituency, and his Makerfield one, are among them. Culcheth, though, is seen as “posh”.Where Burnham grew up, on Common Lane, many homes have gated driveways and easily sell for more than £1m. Locals jokingly call the area “Upper Culcheth” to distinguish it from the rest of the village, including the postwar social housing estate built for officers at the nearby Risley prison.View image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s Richard Partington being filmed in Culcheth, his and Andy Burnham’s home town.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThere is a golf course, parades of neat shops, a butcher, hair and beauty salons and pubs, as well as two Italian restaurants, both of which I worked in as a teenager.The presence of SUVs and flash cars has steadily increased – in part the spillover from Manchester’s economic renaissance. I do not remember Culcheth being this affluent. It was comfortable, but not in the same league as the footballer-belt Cheshire villages south of Warrington.But while it does not fit the media stereotype of Coronation Street-style terrace housing, flat caps and spoil heaps, it is still within touching distance of the industrial decline that has crushed this region.Growing up, the legacy of industry was obvious. I saw thedemolition of Parkside colliery’s concrete winding towers– the last deep mine in the Lancashire coalfield – from my bedroom window. A decade earlier, Burnham would pass here on his bus to school – St Aelreds Catholic technology college, now renamed Hope academy, in Newton-le-Willows – and bang on its window to show support to the picket line at the colliery gates during the 1984 miners’ strike.Born in 1970 at Aintree hospital in Liverpool, Burnham moved from Merseyside to Culcheth at about age one, after his father, Roy, was promoted to a job in Manchester. An engineer at the Post Office, he had once worked at a telephone exchange in the village – opposite the Cherry Tree – and liked the feel of the place.Raised Catholic, Burnham went to St Lewis primary school, a short walk down Mustard Lane from Croft primary, where I went. He recalls in Head North a “modest” upbringing. There were no holidays abroad. But his family also “didn’t want for anything”, and he went on to study at Cambridge, where he met his future wife, Dutch-born Marie-France van Heel.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, outside No 10 this week after he took office.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersBurnham is often in the village playing five-a-side football with his brothers, who are teachers, and their friends, including relatives of another famous son of Culcheth, Roger Hunt, the Liverpool striker and England 1966 World Cup winner.In the Lords of the North barbershop in Warrington town centre, hairdresser Nicole Egan tells me Burnham’s brother John taught her at school. “If he’s anything like his brother … 10 out of 10. Top family. I’m made up. He seems to be doing some great things already.”Egan’s mother, Cheryl Good, is cutting a boy’s hair. She says the prime minister went out with her old boss back “when he was a raver” in an Adidas tracksuit.“He went to a normal school. He wasn’t privately educated where they were told they were special or better than anybody else. So he’s started from the same starting point as everybody else, and he’s done really well for himself.”View image in fullscreenNicole Egan (left) and Cheryl Good at Lords of the North barbers in Warrington.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBoth are Green voters but see Burnham as moving in the right direction, despite hearing “alarm bells” over the rumours that he could allowmore North Sea oil and gas drilling. But first impressions matter: addressing the cost of living has cut through in a way that locals say has raised their hopes.“Working families are struggling,” says Egan. “So the things he’s done at the moment – the [cutting of the] tax on electricity bills,£2 cap on the fareson buses, and that’s only in his first couple of days. I’m very hopeful – what little we have left of that”Burnham was in Culcheth after a regular football game with his brothers, in his first fortnight as the mayor of Greater Manchester, when he was told of the Manchester Arena bombingon 22 May 2017. It was a moment that would become a turning point for the city,and for Burnham.People are full of praise for his ability to empathise. Three years ago, Burnham was at the candlelight vigil in his home villagefor Brianna Ghey, the 16-year-old transgender girl murdered in Culcheth Linear Park.They also credit him for the economic turnaround of the city along the M62. Manchester – and itsresulting “ism”– is central to Burnham’s political and economic blueprint for Britain; founded in the coordination of the private and public sector, and helped by new powers for local areas through devolution.View image in fullscreenShuttered shops in Warrington town centre.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianGrabbing power from Westminster and Whitehall resonates in these parts.In the market, Neil Kelly, who leads community engagement for the local rugby league team, Warrington Wolves, is having a coffee with his colleague Adam Leah. “There’s been a lot of fights with Whitehall all of the time. So I think devolution is going to work in that sense for Warrington.“You’ll see for Warrington what it means, and how it can have a real effect, particularly around on the streets and the towns, and the cultures and the communities.”There are, however, tensions and undercurrents. Warrington is among the most heavily indebted councils in England, with an outstanding pile worth more than £1.5bn. The town’s Labour leadership argues it needed to borrow to invest, to offset Tory austerity directed from Westminster. But critics fear handing over more powers might not be the right answer.The bus network in Warrington could also show the opportunities and difficulties of local power. Unlike most places, the town never lost control of its buses in the wave of 1980s privatisation.Buses have long been a Burnham preoccupation, after he overhauledthe network in Greater Manchester. The region’sBee Network, a system of joined-up, accessible transport, has brought buses under local control through franchising. In Warrington, the neon yellow fleet – close in colour to its Manchester equivalent – is fully electric, and locally controlled, but more expensive than many would like, at £5.90 for a day ticket.In Culcheth there will be tensions with Labour’s national priorities on housing development; in a semi-rural community ringed by green-belt land, many do not want to see more homes built, despite the climbing house prices pushing young people away.View image in fullscreenA Labour party meeting in Culcheth after Andy Burnham became prime minister.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianStill, at a Labour party branch meeting at Culcheth library, there is hope that Burnham can square the circle because he knows these issues. Margaret Webber, the branch chair, and Matt Smith, a local Labour councillor who was once my high school form tutor, say that where the person who leads Britain is from has an important bearing.“He’s got a lot of good will behind him, because he’s saying what a lot of people think.”

title: Blind date: ‘We were chatting as soon as we sat down’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Jacob, 27, a volunteer manager, meets Sophie, 28, a journalist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jacob, 27, a volunteer manager, meets Sophie, 28, a journalist
Content:
Composite: Antonio Olmos & Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Antonio Olmos & Linda Nylind/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘We were chatting as soon as we sat down’Jacob, 27, a volunteer manager, meets Sophie, 28, a journalistSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenJacob on SophieWhat were you hoping for?To meet someone who I could connect with and possibly go on further dates.First impressions?Sophie was very nice and upbeat.What did you talk about?Our conversation went all over the place, from both of us having connections to the US to her organising standup comedy nights.Most awkward moment?There were a couple of moments where the conversation stalled, but overall it flowed nicely.Good table manners?Yes.Best thing about Sophie?She was very funny and had me laughing out loud.Would you introduce Sophie to your friends?I don’t think we are at that stage.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Sophie in three wordsKind, authentic, humorous.What do you think Sophie made of you?I have no idea but I hope she enjoyed our conversation.Did you go on somewhere?No.And … did you kiss?No.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?I would have not arrived 15 minutes early. Multiple readings of a menu that I had already looked at online could have been avoided.Marks out of 10?7. She was a lovely person and I really enjoyed my time with her.Would you meet again?I enjoyed the evening but if we were to meet up again, it would be as friends.View image in fullscreenJacob and Sophie on their date.View image in fullscreenSophie on JacobWhat were you hoping for?To meet someone interesting, kind and fun.First impressions?Super easy to talk to from the get-go. We were chatting as soon as we sat down.What did you talk about?Why neither of us lives in the US any more. Being “Jew-ish”. How Londoners get a bad reputation (the city is more inviting than people think).Most awkward moment?Probably when we were leaving. I had to go on elsewhere, so we parted ways a bit abruptly.Good table manners?Very.Best thing about Jacob?He is really kind and genuine. He cares a lot about doing good in the world, and I find it admirable that he moved to London on somewhat of a whim.Would you introduce Jacob to your friends?He’s travelled a lot, so his geographic knowledge could come in handy at a pub quiz.Describe Jacob in three wordsFriendly, kind, open.What do you think Jacob made of you?Hopefully he thought I was funny!Blind date: ‘I made him take a few too many selfies…’Read moreDid you go on somewhere?No, unfortunately we were going in different directions.And … did you kiss?Just a hug.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?If I hadn’t made plans, we could have chatted for a little longer, or at least walked to the tube together.Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?As friends.Jacob and Sophie ate atGalvin Bistrot and Bar, London E1.Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid
Author: William Christou
Headline: Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid
Content: A fire in El Tiemblo, to the west of Madrid. Spain has declared a national emergency over the wildfires for the first time ever.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fire in El Tiemblo, to the west of Madrid. Spain has declared a national emergency over the wildfires for the first time ever.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresMore than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and SpainHundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in MadridWilliam ChristouSat 25 Jul 2026 12.23 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnrestrained wildfires in Spain andFrancehave forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes.About 70,000 people were evacuated from centralSpain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux.Spain declared a national emergency, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire. France’s evacuations constituted “probably” the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has ever seen, its interior minister said.Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance. In Spain, high winds were exacerbating the fires, and two of the three blazes merged on Friday.0:59Firefighters in Spain and France battle raging wildfires – videoFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said a huge military cargo plane, the Airbus A400M Atlas, was being deployed to join 18 other aircraft in the “long and very difficult” battle against wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France.The French government has called in the military to help,deploying 1,500 soldiers, and has rushed 1.5m face masks to help protect people from smoke inhalation. Fire crews have also been digging trenches, as well as using retardants, as winds were forecast to push the fires closer to Bordeaux.Wildfireswere reported to be about 20 miles west of the city.The French government ordered people in the path of the fire to evacuate, including those in Bordeaux’s western suburbs. Police went door to door to tell people to leave, with scenes of panic unfolding as residents fled their homes under a smoke-darkened sky.The Gironde regional prefect, Sophie Brocas, said on Friday that strong winds were driving the fire towards the Bordeaux metro area and that it had grown to “an unprecedented magnitude”.View image in fullscreenPeople who have been evacuated from their homes in the Bordeaux-Lac exhibition centre, which has been turned into a shelter for displaced people.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersOfficials said the sudden blazes caught residents and authorities off guard. Some people in France had to flee by boat when the flames headed towards coastal towns.The French prime minister, SébastienLecornu, said the fire in Gironde was so strong that it had begun generating its own winds.“The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” he wrote on X. “Our priority is clear: protecting human lives.” He urged people to obey evacuation orders “without delay”.The Spanish health minister instructed people in Madrid not to go outside over concern of the poor air quality.“Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” Monica Garcia said on X.On Saturday evening, Spain’s interior ministry said a man had died in a fire in Manises, in Valencia. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters on a support line between the villages of Lacanau and Saint-Hélène in the Bordeaux region.Photograph: Astrid Lagougne/EPAThe fire was a separate incident from the major blazes raging west of Madrid, which have so far not caused any reported deaths.The long, back-to-back heatwaves inEuropehave dried forests out, turning them into tinder for wildfires. Fires had already consumed 130,000 hectares (320,000 acres) of forest this year in Spain, about a third higher than the country’s annual average, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said on Saturday.In France, fires burned down more than 98,000 hectares, which France’s interior minister said was a “historic record”.Climate crisis-driven heat ‘sucking soils dry’ as extreme drought hits EuropeRead moreScientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading tothousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.Sánchez said that cooler weather on Saturday gave a “window of opportunity” for firefighters to help contain the blazes. “We are going to have some complex hours ahead because, although the temperatures have gone down, we do not know exactly how the wind will develop, how strong it will be,” he added.Other European countries were helping both countries fight the blazes, with Croatia, the Czech Republic, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Slovakia sending aid and water-dumping aircraft to France and Spain.The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised more help was on the way.“Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them. Five planes and two helicopters from the rescue fleet are now deployed in France and four planes are arriving in Spain today,” she said on X.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEuropeSpainFranceClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: One killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin Pride | Germany | The Guardian
description: Suspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Suspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’
Content: Emergency responders at work on Saturday after a car crashed into a crowd at Tiergarten park, Berlin.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersView image in fullscreenEmergency responders at work on Saturday after a car crashed into a crowd at Tiergarten park, Berlin.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersGermanyOne killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin PrideSuspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’Deborah Colein BerlinSat 25 Jul 2026 19.51 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to punish those responsible after a car struck people on the outskirts of Berlin’s Gay Pride celebrations, killing at least one person and wounding 16 others.A suspected ⁠perpetrator of the apparent attack on ⁠Saturday night has been ⁠identified as a member of the ⁠city’s “Islamist scene” but he ​has not ‌yet ‌been arrested, a Berlin police spokesperson said.The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and comes asGermanyremains on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks in recent years.Hours after the apparent attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle struck multiple ⁠people after charging into the city’s central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate.Police said those hurt “included several with life-threatening injuries”.The driver of a white van had swerved shortly before 10pm into the Tiergarten park, close to the route of the Pride march held earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree, police said.“[The vehicle] was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track ​down the perpetrator or perpetrators,” police said. Tabloid newspaper Bild cited a witness as saying that a man emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot.A manhunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.A Berlin fire department spokesperson, Dominik Pretz, said one person died and at least 16 others were injured.Emergency workers set up a helicopter landing pad near the Reichstag parliament building to transport the injured to hospitals.Merz said in a statement that he and the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, would “push to make sure this horrific act is fully investigated and punished”.Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a terrible day. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked.”Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in the German capital in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the pride parade.It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.Berlin mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a state election in September.The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “Taking a stand is hot” which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to queer people in Germany.More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest against the event.Before last year’s pride parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisationssounded the alarmthat attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat.Campaigners said a rise in hostility has accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.With Associated Press and ReutersExplore more on these topicsGermanyLGBTQ+ rightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea | Oil and gas companies | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Content: The Brent oilfield in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new oil drilling.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Brent oilfield in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new oil drilling.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyOil and gas companiesNew North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in seaExclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licenceGeraldine McKelvieSenior correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProduction at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.Andy Burnham’s new government isunder pressurefrom the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despiteopposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.Rosebank, located about 80 miles north-west of Shetland, was believed to be ready to generate oil before the end of the year, pending ministerial approval.Adura, the company responsible for Rosebank, now says it anticipates this will happen at some point in 2027. The field is projected to produce 300m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifespan, according to industry estimates.Some MPs believe enhanced domestic production of oil and gas would help tackle the cost of living, a central focus of the new prime minister, by improving energy security amid global instability, while green campaigners believe the impact on the UK economy of exploiting the fields would be minimal.However, delays at Rosebank mean production at the field will be unlikely to affect the UK’s energy supply over the winter months. Licences for Rosebank and another site, Jackdaw, were granted under the Conservatives but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups.Thenew energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on the fields’ future after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in August.North Sea oil industry urges Burnham to approve new drilling in UK watersRead moreEarlier this week, Adura told the BBC that the Jackdaw site, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could produce gas as early as October.However, preparations for oil production at Rosebank have been hindered by the rig incident, which occurred on 18 April. No workers were hurt, but two central pieces of drilling equipment, including a safety valve, were dropped 1,100 metres on to the seabed.The platform, hired by Adura from Norwegian company Odfjell Drilling, was taken to a shipyard in Bergen for repairs. It is now back at Rosebank but not yet operational.Odfjell Drilling said in internal documentation that the rig could be out of action for up to four months. The Guardian understands this means that some oil wells will be completed significantly behind schedule.Burnham is facing calls from trade unions and opposition parties to ramp up North Sea production. Some Labour MPs say the oil and gas industry, centred around Aberdeen, could face collapse without new investment.Sally Jameson, a Cabinet Office minister, has also argued that more domestic production of oil and gas would give Britain greater control over the cost of energy. Others fear it would have no real impact on bills, while wreaking untold damage on the climate.Mike Reader, part of the Labour Environment Campaign, said there was no evidence new drilling would save jobs in the long term.The Guardian revealed that only 27 direct full-time jobs would be created byJackdaw, one of the biggest gasfields remaining in the North Sea, according to anenvironmental impact assessmentfiled publicly by Adura.Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, previously described the Rosebank proposals as “climate vandalism” when Labour was in opposition. However, in recent weeks talks are believed to have taken place on how to allow new drilling without breaching Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitments, in which it pledged not to issue new licences but honour existing ones.Jackdaw gasfield would create only 27 direct full-time jobs, documents showRead moreSeveral environmental groups are understood to be considering whether they would have grounds to take legal action regarding any government decision to allow new drilling.Angeliki Papantoniou, a lecturer in environmental law at the University of Hull, said that, while a fresh challenge would be a “long shot”, it would be most likely to succeed if based on “substantive environmental matters” such as the disruption of ecosystems, pollution and potential health impacts.“It could be argued that those developments cannot reasonably be ignored when taking a decision with likely high environmental effects,” she said.“In theory, it could be hard for [Fahnbulleh] to claim that [the government] took all necessary precautionary measures without detailed risk assessments on the effects of drilling on the marine environment, climate and human health.”Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace, which challenged the original decision to grant licences, said approval for the fields would make “zero difference” to energy bills and generate few jobs.“Despite these meagre benefits, we would be prolonging a polluting industry that’s fuelling heatwaves while sending a disastrous signal to our international allies,” she said.Odfjell Drilling declined to comment. Adura did not respond to a request for comment.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
