title: Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Content: Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesNigel FaragePolice investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the GuardianScotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 electionGeraldine McKelvieSat 25 Jul 2026 15.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePayments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by theMetropolitan police.The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice.Scotland Yard is looking at two donations of £250,000 made to the party by Britain Means Business in the weeks before the 2024 general election.The Guardian revealed earlier this month thatFiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Businessshortly before the donations were made. About half of the funds were then passed to the party.Cottrell’s son, George, is a convicted fraudster with close links to Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage.The Guardian reported earlier this month thatFiona and George Cottrell have been interviewed under criminal cautionas part of the police investigation.In response to a query about the investigation from the BBC, Tice said: “This is the first I have heard of it – if true why are the Met police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties?“Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?”Fiona Cottrell also made two donations directly to the party, each worth £250,000, in May 2024. These are also within the scope of the Metropolitan police investigation.Tice, who was elected to parliament after the poll, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.He has previously confirmed that his company received donations from Fiona Cottrell but described reports about the money as a “politically motivated smear campaign”.The Guardian told how the transfer from Fiona Cottrell to Britain Means Business was reported to the National Crime Agency by bankers via a suspicious activity report.Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering.The Guardian understands that neither the NCA nor bankers have been able to trace the source of the original £1m sent by Fiona Cottrell to Tice’s company. The NCA is seeking help from a foreign partner in its attempts to understand where the money originated.Reform councillors told to call donations inquiry ‘establishment stitch-up’Read moreAReform UKspokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far.”Fiona Cottrell did not respond to the Guardian’s attempts to contact her about the donations to Britain Means Business.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreWhen asked about the developments by the BBC on Saturday evening, the Metropolitan police repeated a statement issued earlier this month.“An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election,” the force said.“Detectives from the Met’s special enquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.“Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.“An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageMetropolitan policeReform UKPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran war | US military | The Guardian
description: No press briefing has been held for months, as the defence department belatedly or inaccurately releases figures
Author: David Smith
Headline: No press briefing has been held for months, as the defence department belatedly or inaccurately releases figures
Content: The number of US troops killed in the war on Iran ​rose to 18 last weekend, while ‌roughly 430 US troops ​have been injured.Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenThe number of US troops killed in the war on Iran ​rose to 18 last weekend, while ‌roughly 430 US troops ​have been injured.Illustration: Guardian DesignUS military‘Shameful’: Pentagon accused of cover-up over US military casualties in Iran warNo press briefing has been held for months, as the defence department belatedly or inaccurately releases figuresDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.08 EDTShareThe Pentagon is taking a “shameful approach” to releasing information about US casualties in the Iran war,Leon Panetta, a former defence secretary and CIA director, has told the Guardian.The defence department hasnot held a press briefingfor two and a half months. Officials have faced accusations that they are engaged in a cover-up designed to hide the true cost ofDonald Trump’s war of choice in Iran, fearing a public backlash before November’s midterm elections.Panetta, who held weekly Pentagon briefings during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, criticised the department for failing to disclose how many people had been hurt in bomb attacks by Iran on US bases.“There’s a deliberate effort here to basically withhold information from the American people, and I think it represents in many ways a shameful approach to sharing the responsibility that we all have when it comes to fighting a war,”he said by phone.View image in fullscreenLeon Panetta at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois, on 22 August 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesA fragile ceasefire between the ​US and Iran collapsed earlier this month and both ​sides have been carrying out daily strikes against each other, prompting fears of a quagmire and a betrayal of Trump’s campaign promise to eschew “forever wars”.Pentagon list of service members killed in Iran war removes most recent fourRead moreThe number of US troops killed in the war on Iran ​rose to 18 last weekend, while ‌roughly 430 US troops ​have been injured. The Pentagon said on ​Monday that 100 service members had been injured since 7 July but that 96% had returned to duty. The department initially failed to disclose the figures, according toa New York Times newspaper report, only belatedly acknowledging the casualties in a social media post.Officials dismissed the Times’ article as “baseless and malicious” and contend that they are not strictly required to publicise injuries if service members are expected to return to duty. But questions intensified when another Times report said the Pentagon’s website had lowered the number of troop deaths from 18 to 14; Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesperson,blamed “a temporary data disruption”.Critics, however, say the information blackout is a calculated political strategy to hide a failing military intervention.Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations and former spokesperson for the state department, said: “This goes beyond a run-of-the-mill administration distrust toward and hostility against the press. This is more about shielding the American people from the true and total cost of this war.”The Pentagon versus the pressSince the war started five months ago, there has been a tension between the government’s desire for operational secrecy and the media’s demand for transparency on behalf of the public. Even during contentious, unpopular wars in Vietnam and Iraq, the lines of communication were kept more or less open. But since Trump’s return to power in January 2025, the Pentagon –restyled as the Department of War– has been restricting access.Almost immediately, it ousted major outlets including the New York Times, National Public Radio (NPR) and Politico from their long-held desks, supplanting them with Trump-friendly media such as Breitbart, One America News Network and the New York Post. In May, it imposed restrictions onthe free movement of reportersin much of the Pentagon building.In October, most news outlets turned in their access badges andwalked outof the Pentagon rather than agree to new rules that would leave them vulnerable to expulsion if they sought to report on information – classified or otherwise – that had not been approved by Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, for release. In December, the department helda three-day eventto usher in newly accredited media organisations, including pro-Trump podcasters and influencers.double quotation markWhat is happening at the Pentagon is unique in my 34 years in WashingtonMark Schoeff, National Press ClubIn March this year, the Pentagon introduced a rule that required journalists to be escorted on Pentagon grounds by authorised department personnel. In June, it said its press office wasnow a classified spaceinaccessible to journalists because it was used by speechwriters who “routinely handle classified material”. The ever-tightening limits have alarmed press freedom watchdogs.Clayton Weimers, the Washington director for Reporters Without Borders, said: “I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say this Pentagon has been more hostile to the news media than any other Pentagon in recent memory.”View image in fullscreenReporters carry their belongings from the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, on 15 October 2025, after news outlets declined to sign restrictive media rules and were stripped of their access credentials.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesMark Schoeff, president of the National Press Club, agrees that such hostility is a historical aberration, saying: “What is happening at the Pentagon is unique in my 34 years in Washington. We’ve not seen these kinds of restrictions on the media at the Pentagon. Even during Desert Storm [during the Gulf war] and the war in Afghanistan, I can’t recall a time when the Pentagon tried to shut down press access like this.”The current obfuscation is particularly jarring when contrasted with the administration’s earlier posture: in the opening days of the Iran war, Hegseth was a ubiquitous presence,delivering bombastic briefingsin which he crowed about annihilating the Iranian military with “no mercy” and restoring the US as a nation of “real warriors”.The Pentagon thenbanned photojournalistswhen images of Hegseth deemed “unflattering” appeared in the public domain. At one briefing, Hegseth compared reporters to the “Pharisees”, describing the media’s coverage of the war in Iran as an “endless stream of garbage”.View image in fullscreenReporters walk out of the Pentagon together on 15 October 2025.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesNow the bravado has been replaced by a vacuum. While there have been no briefings since May, Hegseth last week announced a screening programme for “testosterone deficiency” among troops, calling it necessary to allow them to operate at their “absolute best”. Such diversions raised suspicions that the war was spiralling out of control.Joel Rubin, a former deputy assistant secretary of state, said: “When you’re not able to communicate clearly what’s actually taking place on the ground, that means you’re likely not confident or comfortable with what is happening on the ground and how it will play politically and in the policy world here. It’s a pretty obvious thing that there’s a lot of concern about there being casualties in this war right now.”The cost of warThe war in Iran is already unpopular in the US due to rising gas prices and other inflationary impacts on people’s everyday lives. People who are paying attention know that 18 US service members have died, Price said. “But what they don’t know,” he added, “unless they’re really digging, is the full extent of casualties that our men and women in uniform have suffered as a result of this decision to take our country to war without clear objectives and certainly without a clear off-ramp.“This is not the sort of thing where a dozen or two dozen service members have suffered low-grade concussion. There are hundreds – by one count, some 500 US service members – who have suffered physically as a result of this war, and the administration probably rightly calculates that, if the economic costs were compounded with the full toll that this is taking on our service members, this war, which is already a politically losing proposition, would drag the administration down even further.”double quotation markIt raises questions about why they wouldn’t be reporting these casualties in a timely mannerJanessa Goldbeck, Vet Voice FoundationFor veterans and national security experts, the Pentagon’s handling of US casualties amounts to a shameful cover-up. “The Pentagon said 96% of those affected returned to duty but, again, a reminder that we know that modern warfare, like the impacts of an injury, might not be felt or seen until months or years later,” saidJanessa Goldbeck, chief executive of Vet Voice Foundation, a non-profit advocacy organisation. “We deserve to know exactly what’s happened and it raises questions about why they wouldn’t be reporting these casualties in a timely manner. My assumption is that it’s about controlling the political narrative before a major national election.”View image in fullscreenCarol Acevado being held by her sister, Judy Rachel, during the memorial service for her daughter, US army Sgt Angel S Rampersad, who died in an Iranian attack on a US army base in Jordan.Photograph: Dave Burns/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAlthough Hegseth has avoided the media, he was obliged to attend a hearing on Capitol Hill this week to defend a war that has already cost the US $37.5bn. During a combative Senate appropriations committee hearing on Tuesday, politicians from both sides of the aisle expressed deep frustration with the administration’s endless demands for money coupled with its refusal to provide straight answers or a coherent strategy.When the senator Gary Peters, a Democrat, called the administration’s approach a complete “failure”, Hegseth erupted in anger, snapping: “Shame on you and others who call this a quagmire and a failure.” Peters shot back: “You, sir, are the failure. You don’t have a strategy. You don’t have a long-term plan to actually win this war.”Steven Cash, a former intelligence officer and executive director of theSteady State– an advocacy group of more than 400 former national security officials – warns that the Trump administration and its Pentagon leadership do not view the public or the press as stakeholders to be informed, but as adversaries to be defeated.“Pete Hegseth and the president of the United States don’t see a real major role for the voters of America or the Congress, so why tell them anything? They’ve made it clear that they don’t see a role for you, the media. You are an enemy,” he said.double quotation markThey can dodge, bob and weave, and they can hide it but … in the end, the truth comes outLeon PanettaThe Pentagon denies that it is minimising reports of casualties.Sean Parnell, the chief spokesperson, said in a statement: “The Department of War and US Central Command has consistently provided comprehensive, real-time updates to the world on the United States’ strikes and operations in Iran.“President Trump andSecretary Hegsethhave been constantly providing updates directly to the media and the American people online, delivering clear, unfiltered insight into our objectives and decisive actions.”View image in fullscreenThe remains of Staff Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton and 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan during a dignified transfer at Dover air force base in Dover, Delaware, on 22 July 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAAlthough briefings have dried up, the news has not, and Pentagon beat reporters continue to work their sources and pursue information. Panetta said officials were “trying to tiptoe past the graveyard, so to speak, in the sense that they’re hoping that the less they say, the less controversy they’ll be involved in, but the reality is that the press will only operate that much more aggressively to find out exactly what’s going on.“In essence what they’re doing is challenging the press to find what’s really happening, and they will. They can dodge, bob and weave, they can hide it, but my experience is that no matter how much you try to hide it, in the end the truth comes out.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests | India | The Guardian
description: Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
Content: Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata party in Delhi celebrate after the resignation of Dharmendra PradhanPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of India's Cockroach Janata party in Delhi celebrate after the resignation of Dharmendra PradhanPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaIndia’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protestsDharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protestersHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiSat 25 Jul 2026 09.54 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has resigned after a week of mass demonstrations, handing a major victory to anew youth movementthat has posed an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.In a statement on Saturday afternoon, Pradhan said he had submitted his letter of resignation to the prime minister after student pressure.“Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and ‌across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation … I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister,” Pradhan wrote in a social media post.He said he had been “saddened by what unfolded over the last 10 days”, but added: “I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations ‌of the country’s youth.”During his 12 years in power, Modi has cultivated a strongman image and has maintained his ministers are not accountable to public pressure. This was the first time a mass uprising had forced one of his most loyal ministers to resign.The protests were organised by a newly formed youth political movement, the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which has escalated into a nationwide uprising of youth dissent this week.The core demand of the CJP and its supporters was the resignation of Pradhan over an exam leak scandal that has devastated the lives of millions of students and led to more than a dozen students taking their own lives.View image in fullscreenDharmendra Pradhan’s resignation marks the first time one of Narendra Modi’s ministers has been forced to step down due to public pressure.Photograph: Zuma/AlamyThe refusal by Modi to sack his minister over the scandal was widely seen as symbolic of the alleged lack of accountability of the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and its repeated failure to address the issues faced by young people, particularly in the country’s flawed education system.CJP organisers confirmed they had called off their demonstration after Pradhan’s resignation and a meeting with senior BJP ministers on Saturday afternoon.In a speech to the crowds gathered at the Delhi Jantar Mantar protest site, CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, saluted the “courage” of students who had turned out in huge numbers, even when they were subjected to police violence.“We have done it,” he said, to cries of “victory to India” and “long live the revolution”. But Dipke also emphasised Pradhan’s resignation was “just the beginning” in the movement’s push for systemic education reform and its fight for democratic rights.He also cautioned against people making a hero of him. “Do not make this mistake,” said Dipke. “The country has been ruined by making one person a hero.”Faria Asif, 26, a lawyer who was in the crowd, said: “I am extremely joyous. This is a huge victory, not just for the students, for the constitution and for the entire nation. Being part of this movement has been extremely empowering for all of us. I think it’s the beginning of change.”The news of Pradhan stepping down was met with ecstatic cheers by tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered in Delhi, who have been demanding accountability from the government.“This is one of the most historic days for our country,” said Rochelle Cope, 27. “For the first time in 12 years, someone from the government has been held accountable for wrongdoing. And it wasn’t political parties that did this; it was the people.“This is a movement of unity, love, solidarity, peace, justice and power. Being here has made me proud to be a citizen of India. This is only the beginning – this government will not be able to rule like it did before.”For many of those present, this week was the first time they had taken part in a political protest and the movement was described as a “gen Z political awakening” in India.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New DelhiAmong them was 16-year-old Kanishka Dabla, who said she hoped to become a doctor one day. “It’s wonderful that he has resigned,” she said. “It has made us all feel very powerful. And this also feels like justice for those students who committed suicide because of the exam leaks. It’s made me hopeful for my future again.”In a statement, the CJP said the resignation was a victory for democracy. “We have a free country where we are free to express ourselves, dissent, criticise the government we elect. We will never let anyone take that away from us,” it read.The statement added: “Remember, do not mess with cockroaches.”‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreSonam Wangchuk, the renowned Indian engineer and activist who had galvanised the movement as he went on a 26-day hunger strike, celebrated the “victory of democracy, straight from the streets”.The CJP demonstrations hadtaken a dramatic turn on Monday, when hundreds of thousands of young people and students took to the streets of Delhi in the largest youth-led protest seen in years. The police had hit back against the peaceful gatherings with brutality, including teargas and baton charges, leaving hundreds injured.Widespread anger erupted at the violent police response, prompting more people to come out in support of the movement. Throughout this week thousands had flocked to the CJP’s Delhi sit-in to chant slogans against the government and call for Pradhan’s resignation. Demonstrations also broke out across the country, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets in Kolkata and Mumbai.For weeks, the Modi government had ignored the CJP protesters, but as support grew into ahuge mass movement this week, the government agreed to have a dialogue.Modi had agreed to fast-track justice for the exam leaks, but had made no mention of the CJP’s core demand, the resignation of Pradhan, who was seen as one of his most important and loyal ministers.However, the CJP’s leadership had made it clear the resignation of Pradhan was a non-negotiable demand for the movement. As more protests erupted over the weekend and negotiations were at a deadlock, the BJP government appeared to be backed into a corner.Not all those who took part in the protests were gen Z. Annie Raja, 62, beamed as she looked out at the celebrating protesters. “I feel enthusiastic and happy,” she said.“The young people came out on the streets and they saved our democracy. Previously the government thought they had all the power, and the people were living only in fear. Now the Modi government is scared of us.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaNarendra ModiProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Madeleine McCann’s younger brother Sean finishes eighth in Commonwealth Games final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The parents of Madeleine McCann cheered on as their son, Sean, finished eighth in the 400m freestyle final on his Commonwealth Games debut for Scotland
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The parents of Madeleine McCann cheered on as their son, Sean, finished eighth in the 400m freestyle final on his Commonwealth Games debut for Scotland
Content: Sean McCann finished in eighth place in the 400m freestyle final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSean McCann finished in eighth place in the 400m freestyle final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Madeleine McCann’s younger brother Sean finishes eighth in Commonwealth Games final400m freestyle swimmer cheered on in Games debut‘I was certainly nervous with so many people watching’Sean Ingleat Tollcross International Swimming CentreSat 25 Jul 2026 14.35 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe parents of Madeleine McCann cheered with pride as their son Sean finished eighth in the final of the men’s 400m freestyle on hisCommonwealth Gamesdebut for Scotland.The 21-year-old, who studies at Loughborough University, was given a huge roar when he was announced to the crowd. But he was unable to match the pace set by Australia’s Sam Short, the 2023 world champion, who took gold in 3 mins 41.25 as he finished 12 seconds back.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead moreBut for McCann, reaching the final at all was a major achievement, especially as he was up against multiple Olympic and world medallists.“I’m buzzing,” said McCann, speaking after he qualified by finishing fourth in his morning heat. “It wasn’t really an expectation coming in, especially with how strong the field was, but I’m delighted to see I made it.“I wouldn’t say I felt the pressure but I was certainly nervous with so many people watching and I wanted to do well, not only for myself but Team Scotland as well. I was definitely nervous but I’m glad I produced a decent swim.“It was amazing, I could hear them the whole way through the race. They spurred me on to really give it my all down that last 100m.”McCann grew up in England, but qualifies for Scotland through his father, Gerry, who was at the Tollcross Swimming Centre, as was his mother, Kate, to support their son. He and his twin sister, Amelie, were two years old whenMadeleine, then aged three, went missingduring a family holiday in Praia Da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.View image in fullscreenKate and Gerry McCann (centre row), parents of Scotland’s Sean McCann, watch as he competes in the men’s 400m freestyle heats.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesMcCann started swimming seriously at Charnwood Triathlon Club when he was eight, and by the age of 10 had joined the high performance City of Leicester club. He has been part of the Scottish swimming programme since his teens.Asked about his motivation for wanting to swim, he said: “From a young age I really enjoyed competing. That makes all the hard hours in training worth it, coming out here in front of a crowd like this and swimming as well as I can really.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcCann is studying chemical engineering at Loughborough, where he is coached by Andi Manley, who is leading the England team in Glasgow. He will also compete in the 800m and 1500m freestyle and hopes it will be a launchpad to becoming an Olympian at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.“The Olympics is always that step even further so to be able to represent Scotland here is a good stepping stone,” he said. “Hopefully a couple of years of work will put my name in the mix.”Two other Australians completed the podium, with Elijah Winnington winning silver in 3:45.56, a hundredth of a second ahead of Benjamin Goedemans.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesSwimmingMadeleine McCannnewsShareReuse this content

title: Four types of thinker have been identified. Which one are you? | Consciousness | The Guardian
description: Investigation finds evidence of distinct groups, from big-picture thinkers to those who sweat the small stuff
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Investigation finds evidence of distinct groups, from big-picture thinkers to those who sweat the small stuff
Content: In the study, about 10% of thoughts centred on hobbies, games, play and art, with a similar amount focused on relationships.Illustration: Michael Parkin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn the study, about 10% of thoughts centred on hobbies, games, play and art, with a similar amount focused on relationships.Illustration: Michael Parkin/The GuardianConsciousnessFour types of thinker have been identified. Which one are you?Investigation finds evidence of distinct groups, from big-picture thinkers to those who sweat the small stuff.Illustrations by Michael ParkinIan SampleScience editorSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump toThe four types of thinkersThe worriersThe domesticsThe bodily thinkersThe work-hard, play-hardsAn investigation into what people think about has put the spotlight on the modern mind, revealing thoughts dominated by work, the need for coffee and a strong desire to go back to bed.It also found evidence for four distinct groups of thinkers who spend more time than most eitherworrying about the world; mulling on household chores and finances; focusing on the mind and body; or the work-hard, play-hard combination of career and pleasure.The groups are not definitive and people will move between them, but the finding shows how sampling people’s thoughts at random can provide a nuanced view of human thinking patterns, according to the researchers.Economists at Claremont Graduate University, in California, and Wuhan University, in Hubei, China, explored people’s conscious thoughts after finding a surprising dearth of work on the topic. “So much of what it means to be human is about what’s going on in our head,” said Dr Joshua Tasoff, a senior author on the study. “The fact that we haven’t really looked at that as economists is really quite extraordinary.”For the study, 258 volunteers aged 19 to 71 downloaded an app that beeped at eight random times per day for two weeks. On each beep, they were required to write down their thoughts, what they were doing and rate their happiness level.View image in fullscreenPart of the study tested an assertion by Marcus Aurelius: ‘The happiness of your life depends on the quality of your thoughts.’Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyAfter gathering more than 23,000 real-time responses, the economists saw that people’s thoughts flowed with the rhythms of the day, steered largely towards work in the day and entertainment in the evening. Roughly half of people’s thoughts were intentional, the rest being intrusive or accidental thoughts from mind wandering or reminders.Sensory information, including feeling tired and sleepy, and mental impressions, accounted for nearly a fifth of all thoughts. Next came work at 17% and food at 14%. About 10% of thoughts centred on hobbies, games, play and art, with a similar amount focused on relationships.When thoughts centred on what people wanted, nearly half involved food or drink, especially coffee. This chimed with thoughts that mentioned needs, with 29% seeking relaxation, and naps and sleep in particular.The mind was rarely blank, the study found, with only a fraction of a per cent of responses claiming no thoughts at all. However, even fewer thoughts appeared to be about sex, leading the researchers to suspect reticence. “There may be things people don’t want to share with us. You know: TMI [too much information],” Tasoff said. Perhaps related, a quarter of beeps went unanswered, according to apreprint of the study, which has yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal.Part of the study tested an assertion by the Roman emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius, who said: “The happiness of your life depends on the quality of your thoughts.” The researchers found that what people were thinking was more predictive of their happiness than anything else they looked at. “Maybe Marcus Aurelius was on to something,” they said.The authors cautioned against extrapolating the findings to the global population because the psychology of the volunteers, all classified as western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic – or Weird – could differ dramatically from other populations.The four types of thinkersThe analysis of people’s conscious thoughts showed they clustered into four groups, but the categories are tentative and people probably move between them. Tasoff said a longer study with more people was needed to confirm the results. The labels were designed to capture the “vibe” of each group, he added.The groups are based on common themes in people’s thoughts, but are not defined by a person’s background or what they do. People in different groups did similar activities and there were only minor differences in demographics, such as age, income and education, and socioeconomic status.The worriersView image in fullscreenWorriers thought about world events, politics and social issues about 60% more than average, their minds occupied with concerns over wars, the Covid pandemic when it was raging, and other major events. They thought about their safety and health about 50% more than average. Words that typically appeared in their thoughts included Covid, awake, lonely, pain, hunger and fatigue. Interestingly, the group thought about music nearly twice as often as average, possibly to mitigate the emotional toll of their other thoughts, the researchers speculated.The domesticsView image in fullscreenA group focused more on practical and household matters, domestics devote about 50% more thoughts than average to chores, the home, finances, but also stories through movies, books and TV. The words that often described their thoughts were highly variable, however, including solve, process, debate and document.The bodily thinkersView image in fullscreenNo other group thinks more about their senses, feelings and mental impressions of themselves and the world than this one. As a group, bodily thinkers are the youngest, with an average age of 32, and nearly two-thirds are women. They have the highest rate of unwanted, intrusive thoughts, at 28%. Words that appear frequently in their thoughts are therapist, ache and overwhelm. The group might exemplify how people can move from one pattern of thinking to another. The higher proportion of women in this group could be due to the effects of the menstrual cycle. It also reflects people who had physical or mental health issues during the study turning their thoughts towards their bodies, symptoms and care.The work-hard, play-hardsView image in fullscreenTheir minds are largely split between work and leisure, thinking about the job 50% more than average, while still thinking about hobbies, games and art about 25% more. The group has the highest income and happiness scores of all the groups and has slightly more males than females. Key words used to describe their thoughts include relaxation, presentation, flight, nail, project and gym.Explore more on these topicsConsciousnessNeuroscienceSleepHealthHealth & wellbeingPsychologyMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Really inappropriate’: teachers decry plan for humanoid robot in New York high school | New York | The Guardian
description: Robot from company that acquired sex doll maker to be introduced in school with large Native American population
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Robot from company that acquired sex doll maker to be introduced in school with large Native American population
Content: A Realbotix robot at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Realbotix robot at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesNew York‘Really inappropriate’: teachers decry plan for humanoid robot in New York high schoolRobot from company that acquired sex doll maker to be introduced in school with large Native American populationMichael SainatoSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA humanoid robot is being introduced as part of a pilot program, along with an AI teaching assistant, at Salamanca high school in Salamanca, New York,locatedon the Allegany territory of the Seneca nation.Teachers have criticized the program, deeming it “inappropriate” and claiming it dehumanizes the profession with the introduction of human-like robots. Some local Native American residents have also criticized the pilot program, citing its implementation as “culturally tone deaf”.The robot, named Sally, was purchased by the Cattaraugus county school district – which includes Salamanca high school – for $57,590. According to apresentationon the program, Sally will be a closed-loop system, but available virtually to students 24/7 for those with access, and offers personalized learning options.The district will be the first in the US to deploy a humanoid robot and AI teaching assistant, according to apress releaseby Realbotix.“The Salamanca pilot also includes deployment of a Realbotix M-Series humanoid robot, which uses natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences,” the press release states.Realbotix, formerly Tokens.com, a Toronto-based company,purchasedSimulacra, a Las Vegas-based company known for realistic sex dolls, for $16.7m in April 2024, marking a pivot for the company from crypto to humanoid robots.Realbotix has denied ties to the sex doll company, and denied any inferences that the dolls – manufactured by Abyss Creations, a subsidiary of Realbotix – are related to the pilot program.“The Salamanca teachers’ union as a whole is concerned about the background of the company of Realbotix. We’re very concerned about the security of the software that they’re implementing, and whether or not the data will be stored, how it will be gathered, are the recording capabilities,” said Lacey Pihlblad, president of Salamanca Teachers’ Association and a teacher at the high school.“We would like to see the school district pause implementing the robot, pause implementing the software aspect of this AI technology until we can have more individuals weigh in.”She saidNew Yorkstate is currently shifting away from too much technology in the classroom.“There’s a growing consensus that indicates our students should be exposed to less technology. Placing a humanoid robot into the classroom to interact with our children, I believe, is a massive step in the wrong direction, and I believe that the majority of our teachers feel the same.” she added. “If we’re going to do something of this magnitude, I feel we need to make sure that we do it the correct way, and I’m not sure that that’s currently what’s in place.”Pihlblad said the union was completing negotiations for a new union contract and intend to include protections around artificial intelligence.Melinda Person, president of the New York State United Teachers, theparent unionof the Salamanca Teachers’ Association, which represents teachers at the high school, told the Guardian that teachers across the state are concerned about the robot program.“Our members in Salamanca and educators across the state are sounding the alarm that this is really inappropriate,” said Person. “I would say our initial reaction is this is kind of creepy.”Person said it was “way out of the realm of what we should be doing in our schools”.“The answer to the challenges in education is not more screens, it’s not more algorithms, not more robots. What we need in our schools right now are more caring adults and more human connection,” she said.She said teachers were not anti-technology, but rather pro-child, and take positions based on whether something is beneficial for students.“Putting a lifeless machine in front of students is a bad idea,” she said. “I would say a machine that the intention of it is to simulate a human relationship with young people who are just learning those skills of how to interact, how to be with their peers, how to solve conflicts, and putting a robot that looks like a human that will lead to the dehumanization of the profession of education, is exactly the wrong thing for us to be doing.”Local residents have also criticized the selection of a high school with a significant Native American population to serve as the testing ground for humanoid robots in the classroom.Nearly 40%of the high school’s student body are Native Americans.The Seneca nation declined to comment to the Guardian.“Out of all the schools in New York state, let alone in the US, they chose to experiment on Native American children yet again,” said Sierra May Abrams, a substitute teacher at Salamanca high school and local resident. “Our culture is struggling to stay alive due to the impact of theNative American boarding schoolsand what they did to our elders. We live on the only reservation located in a city so it’s just absolutely insane that we’re the ones ‘testing it out’.”Alyson Brown, a community health specialist and local resident and Seneca nation member who graduated from Salamanca, said several students have connections to the traumas of Native American boarding schools.“Many students have connections to relatives who attended the Thomas Indian school located on our Cattaraugus territory. Many native families are viewing this pilot program as history repeating itself,” said Brown. “I see nothing positive to come from this being introduced in the classroom setting. I worry for the cognitive development of young minds in this exposure.”A spokesperson for Realbotix did not comment on criticisms from teachers and Native American residents or the call for a pause from the Salamanca Teachers’ Association.“Realbotix and Salamanca city central school district announced a limited pilot for fall 2026 involving Optio, an AI-powered educational assistant, and one new Realbotix M-Series humanoid unit,” the spokesperson said by email.“The program is intended to complement, not replace, teachers by giving students supervised access to emerging AI and robotics tools as part of the district’s existing Stem [science, technology, engineering and mathematics] curriculum. The partnership also gives educators an opportunity to evaluate these technologies in a controlled classroom environment under district oversight.”The Salamanca city central school district and superintendent Mark Beehler did not respond to multiple requests for comment.The assistant commissioner of public affairs for the New York state department of education, JP O’Hare, said the agency had been in contact with the school district regarding its purchase of a robot “and has raised serious concerns about student privacy, appropriate safeguards, and the risk that the robot could be used to perform functions that should remain the responsibility of trained, qualified professionals.“Technology can and should support educators and students, but it should not replace the human judgment or accountability essential to a safe and effective learning environment.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Lucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the case | US gun control | The Guardian
description: Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Content: Jane Coates, from Warrington, wants the UK government to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that her daughter, Lucy, was unlawfully killed.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJane Coates, from Warrington, wants the UK government to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that her daughter, Lucy, was unlawfully killed.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUS gun controlLucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the caseEighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen caseJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. Life could hardly get any better. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,”said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England.View image in fullscreenJane Coates, pictured here with Lucy for the final time, raised her daughter alone from the age of two.Photograph: Jane CoatesThat Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew toTexasto spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas.Lucy and Littler were due to fly home to the UK on 10 January 2025 when Coates received a knock on the door. It was Littler’s mother. Lucy had been shot, she said. She was dead.It was only later she learned that Kris Harrison had been holding the gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him, based on an investigation by local police.Eighteen months on, Coates is urging Andy Burnham’s government to encourage US authorities to reopen the case after a Cheshire coronerruledthat Lucy was unlawfully killed.Coates, a deputy head teacher, raised Lucy as a single parent from the age of two. The pair had an incredibly close bond and would talk about virtually everything. As a child, she was always outside exploring, climbing trees, riding her bike, before becoming engrossed in Harry Potter books – a “comfort blanket” she would turn to time and again into adulthood.By the age of nine, she was a devout Swiftie, performing a Taylor Swift song at her school leavers’ assembly and later going to three of her concerts. Anyone who knew Lucy knew her contagious laughter. “We call it like the Barbara Windsor belly laugh,” said Coates, 49.Like many young adults, Lucy went through difficult times. She struggled with the uncertainty of what she wanted to do with her life in her late teens, Coates said. She had counselling to help with the relationship with her father.But Lucy had never been happier than in 2024. She graduated from Manchester Metropolitan University with a degree in fashion buying and merchandising, began working at the retailer Boohoo and bought a home with Littler, her “soulmate”, five minutes from both of their mothers.“That final year of Lucy’s was the best year of her life,” Coates said. “She was such a high achiever and she just really wanted the best for herself.”She soaked up life, both good and bad. But that meant she would sometimes get upset about events happening thousands of miles away.View image in fullscreenLucy with her father, Kris Harrison, days before she was shot dead in Texas.Photograph: Jane CoatesThemurder of George Floydby a Minneapolis police officer in 2020 was one such event, Coates remembers. “She used to worry. She was an overthinker and used to cry a lot at different things. Sometimes it was with frustration because she was very passionate about things.”She was vehemently opposed to guns, an issue that caused tension with her father. Harrison, a telecoms executive originally from Liverpool, moved to Saudi Arabia for work when she was a child, later settling in Texas where he married Heather Harrison, an education recruiter, and had two daughters.Harrison had bought a pistol for $500 (£370) from a colleague two years before Lucy’s death. Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states.Her inquest inCheshirewas told that Lucy had expressed concern to friends about her two younger siblings being in the house with her father’s Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol.View image in fullscreenJane Coates said the US investigation was ‘not rigorous or thorough enough’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOn the morning of her death, Lucy and her father argued about sexual assault allegations against Donald Trump, who was about to start his second term as US president.Littler said Lucy had asked her father: “How would you feel if that was me and then the guy got away with it?”Harrison had replied that it “wouldn’t bother me that much” because his two younger daughters live with him, Littler said. Lucy “went into floods of tears and ran upstairs”, he added, and sent her father links to news articles about the Trump allegations, denied by the US president.Littler had been in a relationship with Lucy for five years by that point and had known her since they were 12. “This was the sort of stuff that happened on a regular basis,” Littler said. When he met Harrison in Prosper for the first time a year earlier, he told Lucy he did not want to go back. “You’d feel like you’re on eggshells.”View image in fullscreenLucy and her partner, Sam Littler, had just bought a house together.Photograph: Jane CoatesCoates is keen to stress that Lucy was not shot “because they’d had an argument about Trump”. Passionate debates were not uncommon between Lucy and her father: “It could have been an argument about anything.”Later that morning, the family were watching children’s television shows and preparing to go to the airport when Harrison took Lucy’s hand and escorted her to his bedroom.Harrison’s wife, Heather, looked at Littler in surprise and joked: “He never takes my hand like that.”“It was mysterious,” Littler said. “No one knew what was going on.”Then came the loud bang. Initially they thought it was a prank, then Harrison screamed for his wife. They ran into the room and saw Lucy on the floor. Harrison, in shock, could not say what had happened. The pistol was on the bed. He stammered: “I don’t know, I don’t know. Call an ambulance.”Bodycam footage shows Harrison telling officers he had shown his gun to Lucy when “it just went off”.“When I pulled it out, it went off,” he said.Despite an officer smelling alcohol on Harrison’s breath, he was not breathalysed. He initially denied drinking that day but later told police he had a drink problem and “keeps it going”, an admission an officer understood to mean that Harrison drinks throughout the day.CCTV obtained by police showed Harrison buying two 500ml cartons of wine earlier that day and discarding one of them outside a shop. He later admitted drinking that morning.1:21Bodycam footage shows Kris Harrison telling police he shot his daughter Lucy Harrison – videoDuring his police interview, a Texas ranger explained to Harrison that the “gun would only discharge if the trigger was pressed”, according to a report released to the UK inquest. “Kris said ‘OK’,” it noted. Yet authorities said they were unable to arrest Harrison because they could not prove intent.Coates said she had told a Texas ranger that Harrison must have been pointing the gun at Lucy and pulled the trigger, to which she said he had agreed, but argued: “We just can’t prove it.”On the same call in March 2025, a prosecutor said they were unable to conclude Harrison pointed the weapon at Lucy “because that implies intent”, Coates said. They told her the most they could say was that the “muzzle was aligned with Lucy’s chest and a trigger was pulled”.View image in fullscreenLucy had just graduated with first class honours from Manchester Metropolitan University.Photograph: Jane CoatesThe police case was handed to a grand jury in Collin County, Texas, which decided in June last year Harrison should not be prosecuted. Its reasoning, and the evidence it considered, has not been made public.Littler was also taken to the police station. While waiting to learn whether Lucy had survived, he said he heard a muffled conversation between officers in which they referred to the shooting as an “accident”.“The police just took Kris’s word for it,” said Coates. “The investigation was not rigorous or thorough enough.”She suspects the police would have treated Lucy’s death more seriously had it happened in a less “white middle-class prosperous area”.Of all the disturbing details they have learned, one of the most painful for Coates is that Lucy’s body was tested for alcohol and other substances – all with negative results – while Harrison was not even breathalysed. “That’s what we find absolutely incredulous,” Coates said. She and Littler have submitted formal complaints to Prosper police department.In February, the senior coroner for Cheshire, Jacqueline Devonish,ruledthat firing a pistol at Lucy from across the room was an act of gross negligence and that her death could not be considered accidental.View image in fullscreen‘There were no authorities supporting us as British nationals wanting justice for a British citizen who was killed by a British citizen,’ says Jane Coates.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianCoates said the family had been let down, not just by the Texas authorities but also by the British government. She was told the Foreign Office would not be able to help them because nobody had been prosecuted.Sarah Hall, theLabourMP for Warrington South, said the family did not have “adequate support” and called on the government to press the Texas authorities to re-examine the case.Coates hopes the new prime minister, who represents the nearby Makerfield constituency, will take up Lucy’s case with the US. She is keen to meet Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, to discuss how the government could better support the families of those killed abroad.“At the beginning, nobody was there for us apart from Sarah Hall,” she said. “We have got hope that this new cabinet and the foreign secretary will support us, [but] there were no authorities supporting us as British nationals wanting justice for a British citizen who was killed by a British citizen.”A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts remain with Jane and her family for the tragic loss they have suffered, and we will always look to learn lessons from cases such as this one to improve the consular support we offer to other families in the future.”Explore more on these topicsUS gun controlCheshireAndy BurnhamLabourUS policingViolence against women and girlsNorth of EnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Millions of people are losing weight using GLP-1s. How do the drugs affect their love lives? | Weight-loss drugs | The Guardian
description: Prescribing doctors often warn of the medications’ potential side-effects – but unexpected impacts on romantic relationships are less understood
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prescribing doctors often warn of the medications’ potential side-effects – but unexpected impacts on romantic relationships are less understood
Content: Joanna Wood and Bruce Hart have been in a relationship for 18 months. She was at first unwilling to reveal she takes a GLP-1, which he calls ‘a background issue’.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJoanna Wood and Bruce Hart have been in a relationship for 18 months. She was at first unwilling to reveal she takes a GLP-1, which he calls ‘a background issue’.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianWeight-loss drugsMillions of people are losing weight using GLP-1s. How do the drugs affect their love lives?Prescribing doctors often warn of the medications’ potential side-effects – but unexpected impacts on romantic relationships are less understoodMridula AminSat 25 Jul 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 22.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Jennifer, obesity was the obvious culprit for most of her problems.The litigation attorney told herself it was the reason why she wasn’t being invited to parties, and why she and her husband struggled with physical intimacy in their otherwise “solid” marriage.“If people excluded me, or if things weren’t going as I wanted them to, I often defaulted to, ‘Well, they don’t like fat people, they don’t want fat people at their event … they don’t want a fat person representing their brand,’” she says.Is a new weight-loss drug making people fall out of love?Read moreJennifer, who is 57 and asked to keep her surname private, had struggled with obesity since she was eight, when her parents divorced. In her 30s she underwent gastric sleeve surgery, only to put the weight and more back on. But that all changed in 2023 when she started using Mounjaro, a drug in the new class of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) weight-loss medications.Designed to manage type 2 diabetes by regulating blood sugar, slowing digestion and reducing appetite, GLP-1s are now taken by millions of people across the world for weight loss, with Australian prescriptionsincreasing almost 10-fold since 2020and use in the USmore than quadrupling.Jennifer’s husband had concerns about well-known potential side-effects, including abdominal pain, but ultimately agreed with her that it was a risk worth taking.Three years on – and with Jennifer 40kg (88lb) lighter – the drugs seem to have resolved her lifelong struggle to manage her weight. But while she had hoped weight loss might help with the niggling issues in her relationship, she’s now contending with its fallout on her 30-year marriage, something neither she nor her husband expected.“I’m glad I had five years of therapy before I started it,” she says. “I am not sure I would have been equipped for the psychological changes otherwise.”Prescribing doctors often advise patients they might experience well-known potential physical side-effects of GLP-1s, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation. What is not as well researched, or understood, are their effects on romantic relationships. Some patients in forums like Reddit and Facebook support groups have shared that they have experienced changes in desire, sexual function and emotional connection.Early researchsuggests the GLP-1s could suppress more than just hunger through their impact on brain pathways and hormones.“A potential unique mechanism with GLP-1s is their impact on the brain in regards to dopamine reward pathways,” says Dr Terri-Lynne South, a general practitioner specialising in obesity medicine. “We see this in regards to reducing the pleasure-seeking around alcohol, nicotine, and potentially sex drives.”Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe evidence surrounding changed sexual function is limited, and mixed.Some studiessuggest GLP-1 medications may improve testosterone levels, potentially benefiting sexual health, while a2025 analysisof US Food and Drug Administration data identified 185 reports of sexual dysfunction, particularly among men taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.A2025 Kinsey studyshowed that 18% of respondents said their sexual desire had increased on GLP-1s while 16% said it had decreased.8:01‘I’ve lost my butt’: how rapid weight loss can leave you with less muscle and more fat“Some of this we do need to tease out,” South says. “Is it weight loss? Is it GLP-1? Or is it some coexisting things that are happening at the same time? For example, a middle-aged perimenopausal female with reduced sexual function.”What is known is that experiencing major and rapid weight loss alone can significantly affect relationships – a2018 Swedish studythat analysed 1,958 patients who had bariatric surgery found there was an increased incidence of divorce or separation for those in couples, while there was a higher likelihood of a new relationship for those who were single.‘Maybe I hold him to a higher standard’Jennifer isn’t sure if the intimacy problems in her marriage are related to her age, or the weight-loss medication she’s on or the new identity she’s now embracing as a result of her changed body.While she was on a shopping trip, a man offered to take her grocery cart back to the bay for her. Before she lost weight, she says, that never happened. Meanwhile, in professional settings, people who don’t know she used to be heavier make comments about overweight colleagues that leave her stunned.double quotation markWhat we often say is that weight loss doesn’t cause relationship problems but it can reveal themGlenn Mackintosh, psychologistHer husband is the one who suggested couples therapy after 34 years together once Jennifer did not “magically become more physically demonstrative in the bedroom” after her weight loss. He also commented that she had become “meaner”.“I’m less afraid of our relationship failing, so maybe I hold him to a higher standard than I used to,” she acknowledges.Without her obesity to blame, Jennifer now realises that her marital problems were “always a two-person problem, but my weight was easy to point to because I felt so bad about it”.Relationship breakdown is complicated and rarely attributable to any single factor.“Human libido and relationships are complex at their core, so it would be very difficult to extrapolate what it is about these medicines specifically that would have an impact there,” says Dr Mark Mellor, a bariatric doctor and specialist GP who regularly prescribes GLP-1s and says research would be challenging.As people’s self-confidence soars, Mellor says, that could also play a role in “people perhaps thinking, ‘What am I doing here in this relationship?’”A grieving processGlenn Mackintosh, a psychologist and clinical director of Brisbane’s Weight Management Psychology Clinic, says couples who visit the clinic often mention disruption to their old lives before GLP-1s.“Say a couple who have a shared routine of finishing the day with Netflix and a pack of chips they share – if that eating is part of a shared routine, it will impact the relationship and so there’s a grieving process,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJoanna Wood: ‘I used to be a much bigger person and the story around that feels like a character defect rather than science.’Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianRenewed self-confidence and attention from others can also stir fear in partners.“It’s like, ‘OK, now my partner is getting more attention, are they going to leave me?’”These are issues that Mackintosh says he has seen resolved in secure, functioning relationships through communication and acceptance.“It can really cause friction. What we often say is that weight loss doesn’t cause relationship problems but it can reveal them.”Finding loveThe social penalties paid by people living with obesity in the dating world are well known. For some on GLP-1s, changes to their bodies can improve their self-confidence in approaching dating – but not without navigating psychological challenges.After 14 years of singledom, Joanna Wood started dating again last year after losing 25kg taking a GLP-1.The former Australian diplomat, who is 59, remembers feeling nervous before her date with Bruce Hart, a 63-year-old social worker. She felt all the natural vulnerability that comes with a first date but she also felt shame that she used a GLP-1.“I used to be a much bigger person and the story around that feels like a character defect rather than science,” she says.Is the growing use of GLP-1s reshaping ideas of Black beauty?Read moreAfter that initial date – which lasted eight hours – the relationship blossomed, as the couple started hiking together. When Wood finally revealed to Hart that she’d been on a GLP-1, it didn’t faze him.“To me, it was such a background issue,” Hart says. “I was more focused on what she was doing and her values and who she was as a person.”Dr Rebecca Puhl, a psychologist who studies weight stigma at the University of Connecticut and has previously consulted for Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Mounjaro, says people sometimes hide their GLP-1 use.“They’re worried that they’ll be viewed as cheating or lacking willpower by a potential partner,” Puhl says. “Even though obesity is recognised as a complex chronic disease ... for some people, internalization of weight stigma can persist even after losing significant amounts of weight.”Wood, who has heart disease, found the shame hard to shake even though her health has improved drastically.When she briefly stopped taking the medication,“food noise”returned. She regained 10kg and found herself hiding confectionery from Hart.She has since restarted the medication, accepting they are likely to be a lifelong treatment.Having retrained as a counsellor, Wood has developed a program for women over 50 on GLP-1s to navigate the psychological journey of using the drugs.Jennifer is also sure she’ll be on a GLP-1 for life.Her marriage is another commitment she expected to last a lifetime.“Things are stable for now,” she says. “We aren’t fighting and we continue to talk but we aren’t solving anything, either.”She isn’t sure whether the medication changed her marriage or simply stripped away the explanation she’d relied on for decades. The weight is gone but the questions it once answered are not.“We will adapt in some way – I am just not sure how yet.”Explore more on these topicsWeight-loss drugsHealth (Society)Health (Australia news)RelationshipsMarriageDatingAustralian lifestylefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine? | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
Author: James Risen
Headline: After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
Content: The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, sits with Laura Loomer on 23 July 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Ukrainian presidential press office/APView image in fullscreenThe Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, sits with Laura Loomer on 23 July 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Ukrainian presidential press office/APDonald TrumpAnalysisWhat’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?James RisenAfter a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winnerSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.02 EDTShareLaura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, buther sudden conversion to the Ukrainian causethis week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the secondTrump administration.The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days inKyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy forUkrainein its long war withRussia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda.Loomer – who has previously echoed Kremlin talking points to her 2 million followers on social media – has enjoyed direct access to Trump since the 2024 presidential campaign. During the early months after Trump returned to office, Loomer used her online presence to push for ideological purges of government personnel, including many in the national security arena.For a time, her power to break careers among foreign policy officials made her seem as if she wereTrump’s de facto national security adviser.It is unclear whether she still has that kind of pull inside the White House, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, certainly took her seriously when she arrived this week, holding a private meeting with her on Thursday.Maga influencer and de facto national security adviser Laura Loomer holds outsized sway on TrumpRead moreThree days earlier, Loomer posted about experiencing her first air raid, as Russian missiles pounded the Ukrainian capital“This is everyday for every Ukrainian,” she posting, adding she felt that she had been “an asshole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last 5 years”.“I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. There are people in Ukraine who have to run to a bomb shelter everyday and some of us had the audacity to say Russia wasn’t wrong because we believed the lie that Ukraine is a country full of Nazi sympathizers. We have been so propagandized by Russia and we don’t even realize it.”Before their meeting on Thursday, Zelenskyy’s office posted a statement saying: “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are.”Loomer’s change of heart is potentially important not only because she is close to Trump, but also because she has long served as a reliable barometer of Maga attitudes.Loomer has long been disdainful of Ukraine, adopting what could only be described as a pro-Russian perspective. Many in Maga circles have for years held positive views of the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, thanks to Russian propaganda that portrayed him as a bulwark against homosexuality and a defender of fundamentalist Christianity. They became convinced that the Russia-Ukraine war was a proxy fight between Russia’s fundamentalist Christianity and the EU’s western secularism.Loomer’s shift comes at a critical moment for Ukraine, which recently lost one of its strongest supporters in Washington with the death this month of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who had consistently pushed for increased sanctions on Russia to punish Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine.Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visitRead moreBut Loomer’s change also coincides with what appears to be an important recent shift in Trump’s own views on Ukraine.Trump returned to office openly hating Ukraine, at least in part because of the2019 impeachmentover his attempt to hold up aid to Ukraine in exchange for dirt on Joe Biden. Early in his second term, Trumphumiliated Zelenskyy in an Oval Office meeting, cut off direct the supply of US weapons and forced Ukraine’s European allies to buy American weapons for Kyiv instead.But Trump likes winners, and even without full support from Washington, Ukraine has been able to slow Russia’s advance. Kyiv has become a global leader in drone technology, and it has taken the war to Russia itself with long-range missile attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure, leading to an energy crisis in one of the world’s biggest oil-producing nations.Clearly impressed with Ukraine’s performance, Trump announced at the Nato summit in Turkey earlier this month that the US would license Patriot missile technology to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the advanced air defense missiles on its own.At the same time, Trump also supported a move in Congress, which had been backed by Graham, to impose new sanctions on Russia, while also seeming to back off an earlier insistence that Ukraine would have to agree to give up large swaths of territory in exchange for any US-brokered peace deal with Russia.Trump’s policy shifts were modest, but significant; it is possible that Loomer changed her position simply in order to stay in lockstep with Trump.But her about-face could be even more politically significant if it represents a broader thawing of Maga attitudes towards Ukraine and an awakening to the dangers of Russian propaganda.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationSocial mediaUS politicsUkraineRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: We discussed the pill on our first date, kissed on our second. By the third, I knew he was the one | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: In the 1960s, 19-year-old Anne Ring was set up with Ian and felt an immediate attraction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the 1960s, 19-year-old Anne Ring was set up with Ian and felt an immediate attraction
Content: ‘On the drive home, we sat close to each other on the bench car seats of the day, minus seatbelts’: Ann Ring and Ian in late 1961View image in fullscreen‘On the drive home, we sat close to each other on the bench car seats of the day, minus seatbelts’: Ann Ring and Ian in late 1961The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: We discussed the pill on our first date, kissed on our second. By the third, I knew he was the oneIn the 1960s, 19-year-oldAnne Ringwas set up with Ian and felt an immediate attractionFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesAnne RingSat 25 Jul 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 21.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was June 1961, I was 19, and innocently dating in the ways of that time – I’d had several boyfriends, had my heart broken once and had broken two.The moment I knew: I thought he was a handsome, arrogant colleague – then the tension between us brokeRead moreA platonic friend decided I should meet Ian, as we both liked to talk. So he invited Ian – who was 20 – and me to dinner. It was at our friend’s family’s home with Beethoven’s violin concerto playing in the background, and he was right. From the outset Ian and I were totally immersed in our conversation, and I felt an immediate connection and attraction to him. Driving me home, he asked me out the following Saturday.That first date was to an Indian restaurant in Sydney’s centre. Afterwards, we drove all the way to Palm Beach, about a 90-minute drive. There, we walked and talked until 4am about everything under the moon, including a pressing issue of the day, the pill. We had a lot of opinions in common despite our different backgrounds; my family as migrant Hungarian secular Jews coming from China, his as pioneer-stock Anglo-Australians who had lived in the same house since before Ian was born.It also turned out that, as we were then living in the same Sydney suburb, we had already noticed each other. Ian had seen me on the bus and had, he said, been much taken by my animated conversations and cheekbones. And I’d slid down in the driver’s seat of our car while driving past a young man – Ian, as it was – washing his car, hoping he wouldn’t see that I was in my dressing gown, worn as a dare by a friend living at the top of his street.View image in fullscreen‘My mother … was absolutely focused on us getting married eventually’: Ian and Anne cut their wedding cake in 1965Our second date, a week later, was a visit to one of my childhood homes in Wallerawang, almost three hours away, followed by a picnic in Lidsdale state forest. Walking hand in hand among the pine trees, we had our first kiss. And on the drive home, we sat close to each other on the bench car seats of the day, minus seatbelts.By our third date, when we’d talked and laughed about the movie that we had just seen – about complicated relationships, in Albert Finney’s Saturday Night and Sunday Morning – I knew that what we had was both uncomplicated and special, that what I felt for him was well beyond any boyfriend of the past. My parents always waited up for me after dates to debrief. When I got home that evening I told them I thought Ian could be the one. That was something that they hadn’t heard before. As loving parents, they were happy because I was so happy.Soon after that Ian wrote me a beautiful letter about how he felt. We became fully absorbed in our love, spending as much time together as we could, and making good use of the pill – helpfully provided by my enlightened father, a GP.As our relationship blossomed, Ian was keen on us living together without that “unnecessary piece of paper” but we were both busy studying for our respective degrees. My mother, meanwhile, was absolutely focused on us getting married eventually. During a holiday in the Snowy Mountains with my parents, when Ian was about to start his final year, she badgered my father into asking him – when the four of us were in his old Holden – what his intentions were. It was effectively a proposal, to which Ian said yes.View image in fullscreen‘We feel so lucky to have had 65 years and counting together’: the couple with their three daughters in 1987So that was that, and I never got the one on a bended knee. Instead, we chose a beautiful antique opal ring together, became engaged at the beginning of that year, and married after his final exams. To this day Ian is very glad he accepted my father’s proposal.We feel so lucky to have had 65 years and counting together, with our lives full of shared pleasures, adventures and challenges, and much travelling.
