We’ve mutually supported each other’s careers, his in public health and epidemiology, mine in social science research and writing, while having our three wonderful daughters and now, their families too.View image in fullscreen‘We don’t always see eye to eye but we always have each other’s back’: Anne and Ian on their 59th wedding anniversary in 2025We don’t always see eye to eye but we always have each other’s back, in our continuing romance based on love, trust and shared sense of humour.For Ian, Beethoven’s violin concerto is our song, and I also see it as the overture to our joyful life together.Dr Anne Ring is a health sociologist, freelance writer and author ofEngaging with Ageing: What matters as we grow older, available now through Halstead Press (A$34.95)Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? From quiet domestic scenes to dramatic revelations, Guardian Australia wants to hear about the moment you knew you were in lovePlease share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhere do you live?Tell us a bit about yourself (e.g. age and what you do for a living)OptionalTell us a bit about where and when your moment took place?Tell us a little bit about the moment itself?Are you comfortable with a journalist contacting you and your partner for this story?YesNoAre you comfortable sharing pictures for this story?YesNoEmail addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.Phone numberOptionalYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knewRelationshipsDatingMarriageFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Out of this world’: the best supermarket chocolate ice-cream, tasted and rated | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Who makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for you
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Who makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for you
Content: Simple pleasures: higher quality with fewer additives is the order of the day.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenSimple pleasures: higher quality with fewer additives is the order of the day.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.The FilterIce-cream and sorbetReview‘Out of this world’: the best supermarket chocolate ice-cream, tasted and ratedWho makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for youThe best supermarket dark chocolateTom HuntSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.There’s been a marked shift towards less-processed ice-cream sinceI tested vanilla ice-cream for this column last summer. Most ice-cream on the market used to be a cocktail of gums and emulsifiers, but now they’re of much higher quality and with fewer additives.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.All today’s chocolate ice-creams are sophisticated, rich and complex, with deep, dark flavours, and I scored them on taste and texture first (I favour denser, French-style, custard-based ice-creams). I also prioritised smoothness and mouthfeel.I awarded extra marks to products that are rich in cream, as well as for provenance and lower processing. Fewer additives were a plus, too. After all, a short and recognisable ingredients list rarely lies, and usually means more cream, better chocolate and a cleaner finish.The best supermarket chocolate ice-creamBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Santo Domingo chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£4.50 for 480ml at Waitrose (94p/100ml)★★★★☆Voluminous, super-rich, smooth and creamy (35% West Country whipping cream). Dark and deeply chocolatey, with complex flavour notes; quite sweet, though. Rainforest Alliance-certified Dominican Republic chocolate and free-range egg. Great Taste one-star award. Remarkably good, and no stabilisers.Best bargain:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 480ml at Sainsbury’s (73p/100ml)★★★★☆Rich, dense and very creamy, with a medium intensity. Made with British cow’s milk and (27%) double cream, while the Rainforest Alliance-certified cocoa produces a medium-dark chocolate custard with a sugary, toffee flavour. No stabilisers or emulsifiers beyond the soya lecithin in the chocolate.And the rest …Brickell’s all-natural craft chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£7.50 for 475ml at Brickell’s (£1.58/100ml)★★★★☆Out of this world: fudgy, rich and satiating. Very smooth and characterful, with a bittersweet, nutty, complex and strong caramel-molasses flavour from the dark brown sugar. Made with British milk from the family farm,Westcombe Dairy,Pump Street85%-cocoa Ecuadorian chocolate and free-range eggs. Additive-free, too, and this week’s best splurge.M&S 85% dark chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£5 for 500ml at Ocado (£1/100ml)★★★★☆Mousse-like, soft, silky and super-smooth. Clean but rich with West Country double cream and honey. The 85% chocolate is subtle and subdued by the milk and cream, but it still provides a bittersweet complexity. No stabilisers or emulsifiers.Häagen-Dazs Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£5.75 for 460ml at Tesco (£1.25/100ml)£6 for 460ml at Waitrose (£1.30/100ml)★★★★☆Interestingly textural, with 72%-cocoa dark chocolate shards dotted throughout the chocolate custard. Intensely rich (27.4% cream) and sweet, with a strong caramel flavour. Excellent quality, and the benchmark with which to compare other traditional ice creams.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesco Finest Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 480ml at Tesco (73p/100ml)★★★★☆Light, mousse-like and rich, and made with West Country whole milk, 24% double cream and small chocolate chips for textural crunch. Hits the sweet spot of sugar and fat, and dangerously addictive – it’s a bit like eating whipped frozen chocolate bars. Preservative and stabiliser free, bar the soya and sunflower lecithins in the chocolate.Morrisons the Best Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3 for 480ml at Morrisons (63p/100ml)★★★★☆Sophisticated and intensely chocolatey, with bitter cocoa notes dominating. Very sweet, with a smooth, mousse-like, airy texture. Made with Cornish milk and 26% cream. Refreshingly simple ingredients list.Lidl Deluxe Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£2.69 for 500ml at Lidl (54p/100ml), in store only★★★☆☆Luxuriously rich (24% British double cream), smooth, light and airy. Intensely chocolatey, with textural chunks of Rainforest Alliance chocolate. Contains several additives.Carte D’Or Indulgent chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.74 for 900ml at Asda (42p/100ml)£3.90 for 900ml at Tesco (43p/100ml)★★☆☆☆Airy and light, and made with a base of reconstituted skimmed milk, rather than whole milk or cream. Even so, surprisingly good, with a rich, bitter cocoa flavour (though it leaves a greasy feeling on the tongue and has a soya taste, too). Rainforest Alliance-certified milk chocolate pieces add texture. Contains several additives.Jude’s Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 460ml at Ocado (76p/100ml)★★☆☆☆Very airy and light, yet still rich and chewy. At 9.6% cream, it has less than you’d expect in a premium product, and coconut oil is used to boost the fat content. Very scoopable straight from the freezer, and smooth with no ice crystals. A dark and intense bitter cocoa flavour with added depth from vanilla, but a slightly synthetic flavour. Free-range eggs and Great Taste one star. Contains additives.For more, read thebest supermarket dark chocolateand thebest supermarket coffeeExplore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe FilterFoodChocolatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Treasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefacts  | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Content: The artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockHeritageTreasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefactsJewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological findsNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield.Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocallwearing earringsthat were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC.According to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer that owns the earrings, the gold medallion plaques are “attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-westIranin the late 1940s”. They were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, who mounted them with diamonds in yellow gold.View image in fullscreenGold plate showing a character fighting a lion from the Ziwiye Hoard exhibited at the Louvre Museum in Paris.Photograph: Lanmas/AlamyBut while the Mayfair retailer claims the jewellery celebrates “the remarkable artistry of ancient Persian goldsmiths” and encourages “wider appreciation of one of the world’s great artistic traditions”, academics take a different view.A petition has been launched calling for Barron London to publish the complete known provenance of the gold plaques, reveal the checks they undertook on the legality of the items, permit examination of the objects, and even suspend sale.Zendaya is used to the glare of camera lenses, but being the focus of academically qualified antiquarians is something else altogether.Dr Christos Tsirogiannis, an antiquities expert at the Swiss Federal Office of Culture, said: “Personally, after all these two and a half decades of continued scandals emerging everywhere about all sorts of illicit antiquities … I’m extremely surprised, negatively surprised, that no one among all these people that escort these celebrities said something to protect her.”‘Incredible’ Roman bathers’ gems lost 2,000 years ago found near Hadrian’s WallRead moreRomina Frohar, the founder of the Forensic Archive of Iran, an independent investigative archive documenting threats to Iran’s cultural heritage that set up the petition, said her concern was broader than Zendaya’s decision to wear the items.“Barron London has described the loan as a celebration of ancient Persian artistry, but cultural appreciation cannot substitute for provenance transparency,” she said. “If these objects are being publicly presented as Iranian cultural heritage, the evidence concerning their origin, export, ownership history and acquisition should be open to scrutiny.”Even if antiquities were authentic and lawfully possessed, ethical issues may still arise, said Frohar, a PhD researcher at the Glasgow School of Art. “Private custody can be responsible when it is transparent, conservation-led and attentive to public and scholarly access. But legal possession alone does not extinguish the cultural claims of the people whose history the object embodies.”The earrings’ odyssey from BC Iran to A-list actor involved a trip into the shadowy world of rare treasure trading – an industry in which priceless archeological finds are transformed into high-end luxury trinkets.Many of the collections of Mayfair dealers, auction houses and private homes would be at home in the glass cases of museums.Among items currently available to purchase from dealers online is an Egyptian mummy mask made of beads that dates from somewhere between 664BC to 332BC; Hellenistic gold earrings with garnet and agate dating back to the 3rd century BC, and a bronze dress pin with an end resembling an ibex that apparently comes from Iran and could be up to 3,000 years old. Their prices start at about £450.In parallel, auction houses have put astonishing antiquities under the hammer. In 2018, Christie’s sold a 3,000-year-old relief from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II, a neo-Assyrian king who ruled 800 years before the establishment of the Roman empire, fornearly $31m.Tsirogiannis is no stranger to such sales. His work has turned up evidence casting doubt on the provenance of numerous antiquities on the market. “About 90% of antiquities in the market one way or another, sooner or later, are proved to be illicit or lacking provenance, lacking documentation,” he said.If Zendaya’s earrings were authentic, they might also pose another moral conundrum: “Possibly they are coming from a burial. How does she feel that she is wearing an ancient dead woman’s earrings [that may have been] looted?” he said.View image in fullscreenThe Koh-i-noor diamond sits in a crown on the coffin of Britain’s late Queen Mother Elizabeth.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APProvenance and ownership of antiquities is an issue that has long passed beyond academia. Among the most notorious examplesis the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which was surrendered to Queen Victoria by the 10-year-old maharajah Duleep Singh in 1849 as part of the Treaty of Lahore, becoming part of the British crown jewels.The legalities around establishing who owns ancient items can be complex.“Most so-called source countries for antiquities now have state ownership laws in place to say that ancient objects discovered belong to the state,” said Simon Mackenzie, a professor of criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (Te Herenga Waka) in New Zealand. “So the act of discovery and looting is essentially a form of theft [from the government].”“In many countries, including Iran, these laws had been built up over time andwere not retroactive, so legal arguments could be made about what date exactly the theft rule applied from, he said.Despite the outrage, sprinkling some modern celebrity stardust on the treasures of millennia gone by is not always a bad thing. When bling attracts academic attention, a conversation about provenance can begin.When Kim Kardashian was snapped posing in a gold dress next to a gilded Egyptian coffin at the Met Gala in 2018, for example, experts in antiquities trafficking took notice.View image in fullscreenKim Kardashian’s appearance at the Met Gala in 2018 also sparked controversy.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe Met museum had acquired the 2,100-year-old coffin of a priest called Nedjemankh for $4m and made it the star of an exhibition. However,experts soon revealedit had been excavated by thieves in 2011 and smuggled out of Egypt to Dubai and then Europe, where it was restored and given false documents.The legal and ethical problems which came with Zendaya’s earrings may never be resolved, but there remains one conundrum that does not require a PhD to spot.As Tsirogiannis pointed out, the film star’s jewellery put the spotlight on Iran while promoting a film that had nothing to do with ancient Persia.Explore more on these topicsHeritageArchaeologyZendayaIranMiddle East and north AfricaCelebrityDisputed artnewsShareReuse this content

title: Euphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re together  | Television | The Guardian
description: I was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s drama
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s drama
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningTelevisionEuphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re togetherI was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s dramaRakel Clinton LucasSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t remember the exact moment when I started catching feelings for my friend Ellen. It might have been when she trusted me to cut her hair into a feathered bob, or when I noticed she’d taken to keeping my favourite tea at her parents’ house. But in the summer of 2019, a month before our final year of school together, I realised I was falling in love.We were 17 at the time and had been best friends since our first year of high school, both of us part of the same tight-knit group of girls. Ellen and I knew each other well and were quick to make each other laugh, but we were also very different. Whereas Ellen is reserved and gentle, I’m loud and loquacious. So my sudden attraction to her was confusing – especially since neither of us was openly queer.I had been raised in an accepting, liberal household in Stockholm, where queerness was never frowned upon. And yet, I had always assumed that I was straight. It was the default script that had been handed to me. So, each time Ellen greeted me with her one-dimpled smile, I tried to ignore the fluttering in my chest, thinking it would be too complicated, too daunting. Even as I sensed those feelings might be mutual, I didn’t dare act on them. I was worried it might damage our friendship.double quotation markIt was the first show I saw that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way tooThis all changed when I watched the first season of Sam Levinson’s television show Euphoria. Set in suburban California, the show (an adaptation of an Israeli series of the same name) follows a group of high-schoolers as they recklessly navigate adolescence. They abuse drugs, drink alcohol, have sex, watch porn and fall in and out of love.More specifically, it was the relationship between Rue (Zendaya), a recovering drug addict, and the town newcomer, a transgender girl named Jules (Hunter Schafer), that drew me in. The two meet after a party at the end of the first episode and quickly forge a connection. As their friendship deepens, Rue begins to fall for Jules.I recall watching the first few episodes at a friend’s house and being enthralled by Rue and Jules’s plotline, and how tender and complex it was. Even though my own world was far removed from the dark, gritty one of Euphoria, I related to the more innocuous parts of their story: the insecurities Rue has about her feelings toward Jules, that flicker of hope each time the line between platonic and romantic love is blurred. It all felt so similar to what I was experiencing.There was also something refreshing about the depiction of the characters’ sexuality. In the series, there are no major coming-out scenes, no need for Rue or Jules to explain their orientation. When Rue tells her mother she’s in a “relationship” with Jules, her mother simply responds by saying: “It may not matter what I think, but I really like her.” This is not to say that coming-out scenes in fiction aren’t important. But for me, Euphoria was the first show that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way too.Watching Rue and Jules open up to one another gave me the push I needed; when I finally did kiss Ellen, she kissed me right back. And as morning light filtered through the blinds of her bedroom, I knew I had made the right decision.We have been together for six years. We didn’t settle into a relationship right away; we needed time to figure out coupledom. But slowly, Ellen and I have managed to build a life, furnished with our mutual love of books, movie nights and laughter. She is my bulwark and the person who helps me decompress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI did try watching the later seasons of Euphoria. And while some viewers may have enjoyed thegrimmer tone, I couldn’t make it through the final run. Still, I’m grateful for that first season: it helped wash away my uncertainty and gave me the courage to make the first move. And truly, it was the greatest thing I ever did.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Andrew O’Hagan: ‘The worst thing anyone’s said to me? That I was the spitting image of David Cameron’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The author on an encounter with the CIA, an embarrassing moment in church, and longing to hold hands with David Attenborough
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The author on an encounter with the CIA, an embarrassing moment in church, and longing to hold hands with David Attenborough
Content: Andrew O’Hagan: ‘I wanted to be Albrecht in the classical ballet Giselle, dancing until I dropped dead.’Photograph: Premier ScotlandView image in fullscreenAndrew O’Hagan: ‘I wanted to be Albrecht in the classical ballet Giselle, dancing until I dropped dead.’Photograph: Premier ScotlandThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewAndrew O’Hagan: ‘The worst thing anyone’s said to me? That I was the spitting image of David Cameron’Rosanna GreenstreetThe author on an encounter with the CIA, an embarrassing moment in church, and longing to hold hands with David AttenboroughSat 25 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Glasgow, Andrew O’Hagan, 58, studied at the University of Strathclyde. In 1995, he published The Missing, a work of nonfiction. His debut novel, Our Fathers, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 1999; Be Near Me and The Illuminations were longlisted in 2006 and 2015. His recent novels are Caledonian Road and Mayflies. The latter was adapted for BBC television in 2022 and is now a play which will be performedat the Edinburgh fringefrom 7 to 30 August. O’Hagan is editor at large for the London Review of Books; he lives in London with his wife and has a daughter.What is your greatest fear?I can’t say it.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?My interest in Los Angeles.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Making people smaller than they are because of something they can’t handle in themselves.What was your most embarrassing moment?My first holy communion, where my trousers were too big for me and fell down, a circumstance which earned me both the instant contempt of the girls and the heightened interest of the priests. That’s just how it was in 1975.Ben Okri: ‘What happens when we die? We don’t die. We change realms’Read moreDescribe yourself in three wordsJust. Hanging. On.What makes you unhappy?Reform UK.What is your most unappealing habit?Deciding a TV drama is crap after 10 minutes of episode one, then building a case against it for the rest of the series.What do you most dislike about your appearance?My hands are tiny. I need both to lift a cupcake.Who would play you in the film of your life?Janette Krankie, I fear.Who is your celebrity crush?David Attenborough. We could just hold hands, like I was a baby orangutan.What did you want to be when you were growing up?Most days, I wanted to be Albrecht in the classical ballet Giselle, dancing until I dropped dead.What is the worst thing anyone’ssaid to you?Somebody once told me I was the spitting image of David Cameron.What is your guiltiest pleasure?Selling Sunset on Netflix.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat do you owe your parents?A debt of gratitude for a lifelong addiction to self-pity.What does love feel like?Like getting out of the right side of the bed every morning, even when you don’t.What has been your biggest disappointment?The internet. Such potential for good and for levelling up the world, but such a quagmire in reality.When’s the last time you changed your mind about something significant?The other day, when I decided that maybe I had been too harsh on mid-period Sting.What single thing would improve the quality of your life?For world capitalism to grind to a halt.What has been your closest brush with the law?The CIA once came after me with the accusation that I was keeping WikiLeaks secrets.How would you like to be remembered?As a good friend.Tell us a secret.According to sources, various young members of the royal family fully expect that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor will go to jail.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&AfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mexico’s avenging Mother Courage, an interview with the king of horror movies and why middle-aged women have rediscovered raving  |  | The Guardian
description: Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days
Content: Composite: Harol Bustos; Philip Cheung/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Harol Bustos; Philip Cheung/The GuardianSix great readsMexico’s avenging Mother Courage, an interview with the king of horror movies and why middle-aged women have rediscovered ravingNeed something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven daysSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.‘She was almost a Batman figure’: Mexico’s avenging Mother CourageView image in fullscreenIllustration: Harol BustosAfter her son disappeared, Isabel Miranda de Wallace swore she would bring the culprits to justice. She became a national hero. But did she go too far? Sam Edwards told the gripping story about one of Mexico’s most shocking miscarriages of justice of recent years.Read more2.‘Everything I know about evil I learned in that small town’: John Carpenter on terrifying the world with Halloween, The Thing and The FogView image in fullscreenJohn Carpenter.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The Guardiandouble quotation markIf you really want to know the truth about alien encounters, I think that my movies are more realistic about what will happen. Think of the settlers who came to the United States and their encounters with the Indians. It didn’t really go so well for the Indians, OK?Steve Rose interviewed the king of horror and sci-fi movies who, at 78, is as much of a rebel as ever. They discussed creativity, compromise, aliens and how he became addicted to movie-making.Read more3.The rave secret: why middle-aged women are larging it – and seeing big health benefitsView image in fullscreenDancing all night can be a panacea.Photograph: Posed by models; Dan Dalton/Getty Imagesdouble quotation markWhen you go into an inclusive dance space, you can enter a liminal space where time dissolves and everybody is treated as an equal. Doesn’t matter if you’re a CEO, a road sweeper, a woman or a man, if you’re 25 or 55, you can access that space, and that gives you a sense of belonging.For those who are burned out, perimenopausal, or both, dancing all night can be a panacea. It’s great exercise, lowers stress, boosts energy and provides connection. No wonder so many are doing it. Amy Fleming went clubbing till the small hours to re-experience raving.Read more4.‘I felt Holden was talking to me alone’: The Catcher in the Rye at 75View image in fullscreenJD Salinger.Photograph: Hoberman Publishing/Alamydouble quotation markAn older reader sees Holden’s isolation. Behind the teenage mouthiness is a roiling mass of neurosis. Jealous, insecure, frightened, frustrated, Holden has suffered terrible lossesJD Salinger’s wry, subversive classic inspired novelist Joseph O’Connor to be a writer. To mark the 75th anniversary of the novel’s publication, he reflected on why this story of a disaffected teenager remains as fresh and transgressive as ever, and how it alters its meanings depending on the reader’s age.Read more5.‘Liberate the lidos!’ Who will win the war over Italy’s private beaches?View image in fullscreenA lido beach at Miseno.Photograph: Gianni Cipriano/ The Guardian.Almost all of the sandy stretches on the country’s 8,000km of coastline are run for profit. Sometimes you have to walk for a mile or two before finding aspiaggia libera, a beach free of private lidos where bathers are allowed to put their towels on the sand and plant their own parasol. Those “free beaches” are invariably in the remote and less attractive areas, with no lifeguards or loos. Tobias Jones spoke to the “free beach” campaigners who are fighting back against the mafia, the military and those profiteering from sun loungers and cocktails.Read more6.‘It’s only going to get worse’: wildfires forcing firefighters to make impossible choicesView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackle the flames of the Vouzela wildfire in Portugal, in early July.Photograph: Paulo Cunha/EPAdouble quotation markIt’s not just about having more fires to fight, it’s the risk of operational collapse. When two or three fires break out simultaneously, we are forced to make immediate triage decisions.As the climate crisis fuels more intense blazes, pushing them to new parts of the world, those tackling them are forced to ration resources and decide which to fight. Ajit Niranjan and Caroline Davies reported on the shift from fighting all fires to picking battles.Read moreExplore more on these topicsSix great readsnewsShareReuse this content

title: From A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail
Content: Photograph: Olivia RichardsonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Olivia RichardsonGoing out, staying inCultureFrom A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trailSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaA Useful GhostOut nowWinner of best film at Cannes Critics’ Week, this tale of a woman reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner takes you to plenty of unexpected places, even when you discount the sort of unexpectedness suggested by the premise. Part Marxist thriller, part supernatural romance, and taking in foul-mouthed monks and drama with the in-laws along the way, Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke’s directorial debut is an oddball treat.On the SeaOut nowMade mostly outside the traditional funding mechanisms for UK film, this independent second feature from Helen Walsh is a lovely, graceful depiction of repression and queer desire in a Welsh mussel-harvesting community. Barry Ward gives a fine performance as the married man who finds himself drawn to a younger itinerant worker (Lorne MacFadyen).Aardman RetrospectiveCinemas nationwideIn the run-up to the release of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, look out for summer holiday rereleases of a plethora of Aardman classics in cinemas, including A Matter of Loaf and Death, The Curse of the Were-Rabbit and the film that first introduced woolly hero Shaun, A Close Shave.Pinocchio UnstrungOut nowDirector Rhys Frake-Waterfield was also behind Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey and its sequel. This new instalment in what the film-makers call The Twisted Childhood Universe features Robert Englund (Freddy Krueger) as the voice of Jiminy Cricket.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenBig country … Luke Combs goes next-level.Photograph: Dingena Mol/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesCamp BestivalLulworth Castle, nr Wareham,30 Julyto 2 AugustRob da Bank’s enduring family-friendly festival returns with its mix of kids’ activities – bee-keeping has been added this year, alongside skateboard ramp lessons and trampolining – and music from Bastille, Fatboy Slim, Self Esteem and more.Michael CraggElgar’s FirstRoyal Albert Hall, London,29 JulyThe English composer’s magnificent Symphony No 1 gets top billing, but this concert also features the first major world premiere of the BBC Proms season. The World’s Wife by Brett Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry and is performed by soprano Claire Booth and BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth.Flora WillsonLuke CombsEdinburgh,25 July; London,31 Julyto 2 AugustTheUS country music superstar, who scored a UK hit with his cover of Fast Car in 2023, steps up to stadiums. With six albums under his belt, including this year’s deeply personal The Way I Am, expect a setlist brimming with crowd-pleasing self-reflection.MCEdinburgh Jazz & Blues festivalVarious venues, 25 & 26 JulyThis event consistently embraces international and Scottish artists. Its closing weekend includes folk-inflected sax-led quartet Harben Kay (25 July), Joni Mitchell-inspired singer Michelle Willis (25 July) and multi award-winning jazz/hip-hop sax star Soweto Kinch (26 July).John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenBack to bedlam … Richard Dadd’s Bacchanalian Scene, 1862.Photograph: Oliver Cowling & RodTidnam/Tate ImagesRichard DaddRoyal Academy of Arts, London,25 Julyto 25 OctoberStep into a world of fairies and folklore in Beyond Bedlam, a look at the work of the Victorian artist. He remained forgotten by history until the 1960s, when his life in Victorian asylums became a source of inspiration for countless artists.Michael PinskyMidlands Arts Centre, Birmingham,25 Julyto 4 OctoberFor The Final Bid, Pinksy has filled this gallery with secondhand chairs, all hung from the ceiling, which visitors are invited to bid on. Each bid drives the chair higher up towards the ceiling, in a strange capitalistic ballet about value and detritus.Clare WoodsPitzthanger Manor, London,29 Julyto 8 NovemberThe exhibition, called Garden Without Seasons, sees meditative paintings and collages of the natural world in this Sir John Soane-designed country house, each work pushing the boundary between abstraction and figuration and asking viewers to slow down and contemplate.Susan HughesMAC, Belfast,30 Julyto 18 OctoberThis Belfast-based artist and fiddle player travelled around Ireland collecting stories about the mysteries, myths and collective power of traditional music. The result is this show filled with objects, songs and a stage for ad-hoc performances.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenDolly, pardon? … The World Is Full of Married Men.Photograph: Emmalisa PaulyThe World Is Full of Married MenThe Yard theatre, London,to 1 AugustThe great Yard theatre opens its doors after a huge refurb. Its opening season includes a reimagined King Lear with Ian McKellen as well as this brilliantly bizarre adaptation of Jackie Collins’s racy novel, set amid a series of doll’s houses – and performed by dolls.Miriam GillinsonMike Reiss25 July to 6 August; tour starts LondonAs part of The Simpsons’ original writing team – and co-showrunner during the programme’s early 1990s glory years – nobody is better placed to unpick the seminal cartoon’s ingenious comic tapestry than Reiss. This tour sees him spill all his Springfield-related secrets and take audience questions.Rachel AroestiMatthew Bourne’s The Car ManSheffieldLyceum,25 July;Sadler’s Wells,London,28 Julyto 29 AugustOne of Bourne’s steamiest dance shows is also one of his best dramas. Loosely based on Bizet’s Carmen, but transported to small-town 50s US, a gang of macho mechanics have their close-knit, closed-minded world interrupted when a stranger comes to town. Lust, betrayal, revenge, it’s all here.Lyndsey WinshipCherry OrchardThe Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon,to 29 AugustHelen Hunt, Bill Pullman and Kenneth Branagh star in Chekhov’s exquisite final play. The new version has been written by Laura Wade (Posh, Rivals) whose work always manages to be brilliantly entertaining but shot through with real darkness and political bite.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenMaking a killing … Scoot McNairy and Emmy Rossum in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyFuriousDisney+,27 JulyElizabeth Meriwether (New Girl, Dying for Sex) helms this thriller about an FBI agent whose first case happens to feature that rarest of beasts: a female serial killer. Emmy Rossum – who also came up with the show’s concept – stars as the detective who finds empathy for a devilish criminal.The RaptureiPlayer & BBC One, 26 July, 9pmAdapted by the performance artist Bryony Kimmings from Liz Jensen’s novel, this drama centres on a forensic psychologist treating a teenage girl with the ability to predict catastrophic events. If that doesn’t sound stressful enough, the whole thing takes place in a heatwave. Ruth Madeley, Iwan Rheon and Ruth Jones star.Ghosts AustraliaiPlayer & BBC Three,25 July, 10.30pmMost British comedies get lost in translation when franchised abroad, but this wildly original format is the exception. Following US, French, Greek and German versions, this Aussie spin sees a young couple haunted by an aerobics instructor, a biker, a gold rush miner and a socialite.Gomorrah: The OriginsNow & Sky Atlantic,28 July, 9pmRoberto Saviano’s acclaimed Italian mafia drama was described as a darker alternative to The Sopranos when it aired a decade ago. This similarly gritty prequel returns to the mean streets of 1970s Naples to recount the origin story of Camorra boss Pietro Savastano.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenChief concern … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: MicrosoftHalo: Campaign EvolvedPC, Xbox, out28 JulyA quarter-century on from the first Halo, the game has been revitalised with new visuals and the original voice actors re-recorded. No competitive multiplayer but you can play cooperatively with one local friend on console, or up to three online.Mistfall HunterPC, PS5, Xbox, out29 JulyTime to learn some new terminology, Gyldhunter. This dark fantasy PvPvE (player-v-player-v-environment) extraction ARPG (action role-playing game) has you (and optional friends) perfecting your weapon stances and combos to kill monsters in an ever-shifting battlefield beneath the Gyldenmist. Gyld luck!Jordan Erica WebberStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenWelcome to the Junglist … Nia Archives.Photograph: Iris LuzNia Archives – Emotional JunglistOut nowThe Brit-nominated “darling of jungle” follows up 2024’s Top 20 debut Silence Is Loud. Co-produced by her alongside James Ford (Arctic Monkeys) and Ethan P Flynn (FKA twigs), songs such as Boys in Blue expand on her sonic palette, pushing towards 90s electronica and indie.Baby Queen – I Hope You Don’t Remember MeOut nowInspired by a whirlwind relationship that ended with a ghosting, South Africa-born, London-based alt-pop star Bella Latham returns with a second album that channels emotional turbulence into galloping synthpop on Feel Something, and something far knottier on the frantic Word Vomit.The Strokes – Reality AwaitsOut nowHaving pulled off a surprising creative and commercial rebirth on 2020’s The New Abnormal, the Strokes return with this seventh album. Produced once again by bearded Zen master Rick Rubin, confounding recent single Going Shopping continues frontman Julian Casablancas’s obsession with Auto-Tune.Charli xcx – Music, Fashion, FilmOut nowDespite a recent pivot to acting, Charli returns with her second album of 2026. The follow-up to February’s excellent Wuthering Heights soundtrack dials up the guitars – see snarky lead single Rock Music – while keeping Brat’s potent mix of hedonism and existential dread.MCStaying in:Brain foodArmchair ExplorerPodcastJust in time for the summer holidays, this beloved travel documentary series features deep dives into global cultures and dream itineraries. Highlights include a road trip through Australia’s Northern Territory and a safari in Botswana wilderness.60 Second DocsInstagramPacking engrossing narrative and fascinating detail into one-minute shorts, this Instagram page is a treasure trove of bite-size curios. Topics range from spoon-playing musical maestros to the art of clay “hug pots” and green-screen tattoos.James Turrell: Master of LightBBC World Service,28 July, 4.32amAmerican artist James Turrell’s Skyspaces are large installations that play with natural light. For this edition of In the Studio, Julian May meets Turrell in Denmark as he prepares one of his most ambitious ones to date.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: ‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyChristopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epicCharlotte HigginsThere’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics?Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.42 EDTShareEveryone knows how dumb it is to be this person: the one who mourns the film adaptation of a favourite text because it misses out this scene, or misreads that particularly beloved character, or has a slightly “inauthentic” take on some detail. Of course I’m talking about Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of the Odyssey, a poem I have loved since I was a teenager. I enjoyed the movie, in common with a huge number of other people. It seems remarkable, even dizzying, that the adaptation of a nearly 3,000-year-old poemtook $264m(£196m) at the box office over its opening weekend, has sent translations of the Odysseysurging up the bestseller charts, and is sold out (for instance) at London’s BFI Imax screen deep into September. We are living in anOdyssey time, amid an Odyssey frenzy.There is no point trying to be a purist about a beloved classic text. Whoever reads the Odyssey, including Nolan, inescapably does so through the prism of their prejudices, informed by the conditions of their own place and time. Since the Odyssey is the result of decades, maybe centuries, of non-literate oral poets working with memory and improvisation, there’s no precise “original” place or time to return to, anyway. But what I can’t help doing is observe the choices Nolan has made and think about their consequences – because there are always divides in the road, paths not taken by any adapter.Nolan is brilliant at recreating one aspect of the original poem: its complicated structure. The poem tells the story of the decade-long return journey from the siege of Troy of its hero, Odysseus: the adventures he has along the way and how he reinstates himself as the head of his household once he’s home. There are monsters and witches and magic and storms at sea. And then he must infiltrate himself into his home disguised as a beggar, before a Tarantino-esque bloodbath of revenge. It is a story told not in sequence, but through parallel timelines and flashbacks. Nolan, as I had hoped of the creator ofInception,MementoandThe Prestige, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon (left, with bow) as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesBut his Odysseus, as filtered through Matt Damon’s performance, is a grim and agonised figure, not the loquacious, rhetorically able, charming liar that I see in the poem. Cinema is a visual medium – not a genre for wordy speeches – but nevertheless, Nolan’s hero is a notably laconic figure. He is also guilt-stricken and conscience-laden in a way that speaks more of a Judeo-Christian inheritance and Nolan’s sense of a war-weary world than anything in Homer. Where the poem has Odysseus inducting his son Telemachus into the life of a warrior, the pair fighting their domestic enemies together, the film finds a way to release the younger man from the burdens of a killer’s life.The Odyssey, though, is not an anti-war poem, though it is a post-war poem. Homer’s Odysseus is placed in a genealogy of warriors stretching back from the great veteran fighter Nestor and beyond (Nestor is absent from the film, so this layer of inheritance is lost) and forward to the next generation. War is, for the Odyssey, a fact of life – albeit one that is grievous and destructive. But the idea that Odysseus bears a moral burden for the destruction of Troy is pure Nolan. He has swamped the poem with his own preoccupations and anxieties, as all readers do in the end, and created an adaptation that is tamed and tuned to modern sensibilities. Had he cleaved closer to the source material, I’m not sure the movie accountants would be now totting up the money so gleefully. Would modern cinemagoers really queue up to see a row of enslaved women hanged, like doves caught in a trap (says the poem) their feet twitching as they are killed?Nolan has added, but of course he has also subtracted. He has removed not just dark and horrific moments like the hanging of the slaves, but also, by contrast, the epic’s lightness and wit. This is especially apparent in his treatment of female characters. Nolan’s resentful Helen, played by the excellent Lupita Nyong’o, is literally and metaphorically scarred, rather than poised and gleaming and elegant. His Circe is magnificent and strange (and given an extraordinary performance by Samantha Morton), but not funny or enticing. Because he has removed the Olympian gods from any meaningful role in the film, we miss a blissful moment in which the divine Calypso (played by Charlize Theron) rails to the god Hermes against the sexual double standard (it’s OK for gods to have sex with mortal women, she complains, but not for goddesses to sleep with men). The relationship between Zendaya’s Athena and Damon’s Odysseus lacks the flirtatious spark that’s so enjoyable in the poem.View image in fullscreenMia Goth as Melantho and Anne Hathaway as Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s adaptation.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesThere is no nervous young Nausicaa finding Odysseus battered and naked on the beach (a delicious scene), because Nolan has eradicated Nausicaa, and her enigmatic mother, Arete, too. Odysseus’s mother is also cut – and I would argue, his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), is also short of a couple of layers of complexity, her strange obliqueness gone. More or less removing the gods is an understandable decision, if you want to focus on human motivations and choices. It’s easier to imagine gods in a poem than to have them quivering awkwardly on a cloud in a film. I was reminded of novelist Colm Tóibíntelling mewhy there were no gods in his story House of Names, which also inhabits the world of the Trojan war: the novel is a deeply human form, he said, and the gods have no business in it. And for Nolan, at least, so is cinema. But why lose the sexual spark? I had a sneaking suspicion that by damping down Odysseus’s extramarital sexual adventures (and also Penelope’s ambivalence towards the men who are competing to marry her on Ithaca), Nolan has found another way to tame the Odyssey into modern moral acceptability.Read the poem. You won’t regret it. (If it feels forbidding, Mary Beard and I have apodcast seriesfor this.) And preorder Alice Oswald’s bookRhapsody: a Manifesto, which comes out in September and superbly draws out the qualities of Homer’s liquidness, the full wonder of his stories within stories, those Odyssean tales that peel back like layers of an onion to reveal further tales. She will show you the way the poem’s similes and apparently formulaic descriptions of characters are a form of time travel in which different, incompatible realities can coexist in a shimmering haze of poetic temporality that cinema, or at least this kind of cinema, cannot replicate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch things you will experience only if you engulf yourself in the poem. What you will learn in the film is about ourselves: about Nolan’s preoccupations, and about what modern sensibilities can stomach. Reading the poem turns the gaze outward – towards another reality that we recognise, but is at the same time foreign and wild and strange and delicious and disturbing and so different from our own. Watch the film, yes. Then open the pages of a book and disappear into a another world that no Imax cameras could ever summon.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyOpinionChristopher NolancommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t last | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President’s speech started well enough but quickly moved to the usual insults, taunts, jokes and grievances
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: President’s speech started well enough but quickly moved to the usual insults, taunts, jokes and grievances
Content: As often happens with his stump speeches these days, the president lost his audience.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APView image in fullscreenAs often happens with his stump speeches these days, the president lost his audience.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APThe US politics sketchDonald TrumpTrump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t lastPresident’s speech started well enough but quickly moved to the usual insults, taunts, jokes and grievancesRobert Taitin WashingtonSat 25 Jul 2026 04.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis time, at least, everyone got to finish their dinner.And any urge to hide under the table was driven not by the barking commands of Secret Service agents on alert against a marauding gunman, but by a desire to escape the tedium of a meandering speech fromDonald Trumpthat strayed quickly and wildly from the matter at hand into the weeds of his normal stump addresses.For more than two hours at Friday’s rescheduledWhite House Correspondents’ Association dinner, Trump was forced to play the good sport; smiling and applauding while awards were bestowed on journalistic foes he berates daily as purveyors of “fake news” and plaudits heaped on past presidents he loathes.But eventually something had to give. Trump had to be Trump, insults had to be hurled, some of them stale and familiar, a few of them funny, all of them grievously petty.As often happens with his stump speeches these days, the president lost his audience. Phones were gazed at, silence ensued. Never more so than when he embarked on a tiresome bigoted diatribe against the Democratic representative from Minnesota, Ilhan Omar, one of his frequent targets.Trump was finally getting to deliver his maiden speech as president to the association’s annual marquee gathering that a allegedwould-be assassin had denied himby trying to storm the original event in April, before being foiled by Secret Service agents.Both the association and Trump had decreed such an act of political violence could not be accepted as the final word. So a rescheduled dinner was arranged – but with significant adjustments.Instead of the vast auditorium at the Washington Hilton – the dinner’s venue for several decades and once the site of an attempt on the life of Ronald Reagan – the Astoria Waldorf was chosen to stage a drastically scaled-down dinner, with just 700 guests attending, compared with the 2,600 who were at the original event in April.Given the upheaval that unfolded then, the greater visibility of armed security personnel – even for a much smaller guest list – was unsurprising.Weijia Jiang, the outgoing WHCA president, vowed in advance that the restaged dinner would be “more intimate”.Trump, when he spoke – after being forcibly humbled by the dishing out of awards to a succession of journalists for their unflattering portrayal of his presidency – quickly established that humility would not feature strongly in his speech.His first comment on the changed venue was to observe that he had once owned it, when it was the Trump International Hotel.“This has not been an easy evening. All these awards. Do I have a say?” he asked. “But it’s great to be back at a place that I know very well because I built it, and I’m very proud of it because I built it for $2.9bn less than the Federal Reserve Building, which is a lot smaller, by the way.”To his credit, he quickly entered the intended spirit by invoking the episode that had caused everyone to be there in the first place.“Tonight we come back together to answer that heinous attack with unwavering resolve, and every one of us here this evening to show that in America we do not yield to political violence,” Trump said to applause. “So in this country, we believe in freedom of speech. We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate.”It seemed an apt response to Jiang’s appeal, based on the event’s theme of “celebrating the first amendment”, to respect and honor the media’s place in American life.“Many founders [of the US constitution] couldn’t stand the press … but they understood our access is restricted,” she said. “If the media faces government pressure or censorship, it’s the people who end up knowing less. There is a difference, though, an existential difference between criticizing the press and trying to undermine it.”But that was as high-minded and worthy as Trump was willing to allow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom there, it was on to the insults, taunts, jokes – and grievances. Some of it was amusing and drew laughter, notably when he jested at the expense of the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.“I hope that everyone finally got to enjoy their entire, very delicious beef tenderloins, very special beef,” he said. “And I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who’s right here, personally ran over the cow and he cut it up, and he brought it here for you to eat tonight. Bobby also suggested appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill, but we drew the line at that.”Adam Schiff, the Democratic senator for California and a particular Trump bete noire, was mocked as “watermelon head because he has the largest head I’ve ever seen with the smallest pencil neck”.Jimmy Kimmel, Jimmy Fallon and Stephen Colbert, all comedians who have mocked Trump unceasingly, were derided as “people without talent”.Trump said the speech was much more generous than the one he had planned to give in April before the gunman and would-be alleged assassin, Cole Tomas Allen, stole his thunder.But what could have been going through his mind as Wolf Blitzer, the veteran CNN anchor who famously witnessed the shooting scenes at the original dinner, announced that the Katharine Graham award for courage and accountability was going to a Wall Street Journal team who had reported on the president’s past relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.In the event, Trump shook hands with the team’s members, including one journalist whose home address had been disclosed in a $20bn suit he filed against the paper, forcing the reporter’s family to have to move home.“I hope you all know that I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room,” Trump told the gathering later, overlooking the fact that his administration had filedsubpoenasfor several New York Times reporters and their relatives after the paper had reported on security breaches on the new Air Force One jet, gifted by Qatar.“You people have no idea how lucky you are. When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke. There’s not going to be anybody to report on.”As he wound up, the sound system blared out YMCA by the Village People. By then, Trump had been talking for 65 minutes, paeans of praise to the founding fathers and journalistic bravery had been forgotten – and there seemed little doubt about whose event it really was.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe US politics sketchPress freedomfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Wealthy gen Xers stand in the way of a Burnham tax on the super-rich | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: If Andy Burnham wants to make the system fairer he will need to upset the professional classes with a land value tax
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: If Andy Burnham wants to make the system fairer he will need to upset the professional classes with a land value tax
Content: Queens Gate Terrace in London. Burnham has spoken in favour of a land tax, and he could phase in a scheme that replaces council tax and stamp duty.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/AlamyView image in fullscreenQueens Gate Terrace in London. Burnham has spoken in favour of a land tax, and he could phase in a scheme that replaces council tax and stamp duty.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/AlamyEconomics viewpointTax and spendingWealthy gen Xers stand in the way of a Burnham tax on the super-richPhillip InmanIf the prime minister wants to make the system fairer he will need to upset the professional classes with a land value taxSat 25 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTShareThe professional classes act like a Praetorian Guard for the super-rich.Having acquired some of the trappings of being rich, they defend the privileges of wealth – land, property and pensions. They do this as if they – company managers, lawyers, doctors, judges, senior civil servants, architects and chartered this and thats – were the main beneficiaries.Crucially, tax is a hill that many upper middle-income gen Xers and baby boomers are prepared to die on. That is, they will die at some point, and want to take as much money with them, whether as a sign of success, to secure their families financial security or to give to charity. Whatever the reason, they definitely don’t want democratically elected bodies – national or local – to have the money.It is true they pay a much higher proportion of the government’s tax receipts than they did 15 years ago, hence their reluctance to pay any more.It is an understandable stance, except that the tax system they now defend is one that is so complex and riddled with distorting incentives that it is slowly destroying the economy. And it allows the super-rich to escape almost all obligations to support the society that gave them huge wealth in the first place.The professional classes appear to care little that their defence of the current tax system undermines the incentive for work, and especially to work as a salaried employee, or that the current tax system deters business investment.They have calculated that their high level of wealth will be enough to cash out, hopefully as part of an early retirement package, live on the proceeds for the rest of their days and hand on the surplus to their favoured recipients.It might seem unfair to pick on a particular group, but wealthy gen Xers – those born from 1965 to 1980 (making them 46 to 61 years old) – and baby boomers born after the war and before the 1960s really began to swing, are the people in charge of pretty much everything; and, as such, are a powerful lobby against changes to the tax system.Sparks are about to fly because one of the battlegrounds inAndy Burnham’s first months in officewill be how to raise funds to support a wide array of measures he hopes will improve living standards.The new prime minister’s ability to borrow more funds will be limited, leaving his advisers with little option but to raise more tax.Taxing the rich will fit with his pledge to make the government “more Labour” to please the left flank of his party, which still flexes its considerable muscle despite Jeremy Corbyn’s expulsion.The tax change that would do more for the economy and would introduce a huge dose of fairness into the system would be a land value tax (LVT). Anyone who wants to read more about how we could ditch council tax and stamp duty – the two main taxes on property – in favour of an annual tax on the value of land can seethe latest discussion paperby Dan Neidle’s Tax Policy Associates.It replaces the £45.2bn raised by council tax and the £11.5bn from stamp duty with a flat LVT rate of 1.28%. Under the Neidle scheme, LVT raises £56.7bn. By his calculation, about 70% of homes pay less than their current council tax. These homes are mostly outside London and the south-east.The super-rich would be unable to dodge the tax because they cannot shift the land they own overseas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEconomists are almost uniformly in favour. One of the leading proponents, Fred Harrison, has written about how LVT was discussed in the highest circles during the early 19th century, just as wealth was being accumulated and largely untaxed, but defeated by lobbying from the newly minted professional classes.Burnham has spoken in favour of a land tax, and he could phase in a scheme that replaces council tax and stamp duty, setting England, and possibly the other countries of the UK if they follow suit, in an exciting new direction towards land being used more productively and not as a store of wealth.In the meantime, he needs extra cash. There are people close to the prime minister lobbying for a rise in capital gains tax (CGT) to match the thresholds for income tax. This would discourage taxpayers from accumulating wealth at the expense of income, which has been a trend for the last 40 years.Another, possibly complementary idea, focuses on thosefamilies with more than £100m in assets, which studies have shown can pay as little as zero tax and have an average tax rate at least half that paid by the bottom 80% of households.These wealthy families can sidestep CGT because they are so rich they do not need to sell assets and trigger a much higher CGT payout. These initiatives could raise £10bn-plus each.A tax commission that reported almost six years agorecommendeda one-off wealth tax that raised more than £300bn.Tackling the issue will not be for the faint-hearted. As long as the professional classes remain determined to protect their privileges and luck from 40 years of pension and property accumulation at the expense of economic growth, Burnham’s resolve will be tested.Explore more on these topicsTax and spendingEconomics viewpointEconomic growth (GDP)Andy BurnhamEconomic policyLabourCapital gains taxIncome taxcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup | Jacq Kelly | The Guardian
description: There’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every time, says Toronto-based writer Jacq Kelly
Author: Jacq Kelly
Headline: There’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every time, says Toronto-based writer Jacq Kelly
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyThe hill I will die onSaladThe hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownupJacq KellyThere’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every timeSat 25 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 13.39 EDTShareIrecently got into a row on X about the unlikely subject of salad. I want to acknowledge that arguing with strangers on social media is definitely for babies and I should know better by now, but I’m a work in progress. And so I mentioned that I had enjoyed how readily available salads had been at breakfast buffets while I had been travelling in Denmark and Sweden this year compared with the UK.Saladhas been a part of my breakfast for about a decade now, and I think a lot of people would benefit from it. It’s a pretty easy way of getting a couple of portions of fruit and veg before you have even left the house.All hell broke loose. Salad for breakfast is “not normal in a northern European climate”, according to one agitated typer in a response to my post about its availability at breakfasts there. In one of the towns we visited,Luleå, we were just 100km south of the Arctic Circle and the sea was still frozen in April. The hotel had an excellent breakfast buffet–a rotating assortment of freshly prepared salad items with fruit that hadn’t even been poured from a can. Someone should alert the authorities.“Only freaks eat salad for breakfast,” another wordsmith reported. What really took the rice-crispy cake was the person who explained: “It’s the uk [sic], our food is heavy and warm here. Cold island nation that had to be out in the fields with constant rain”, which was presumably typed on a precariously balanced laptop by someone driving a tractor somewhere on Shetland. Obviously the people I worked with in UK offices who I witnessed spooning sugary snack foods into their faces while staring at their computer screens are the outliers here.Don’t misunderstand me – I love a bowl of Coco Pops. Not as a morning food option but as an after-lunch-and-too-early-for-dinnerhangry-managementsolution. There’s no way I could get through an entire morning on a bowl of crispy rice dusted with cocoa sloshing around in semi-skimmed cow juice.View image in fullscreenA selection of Danish smørrebrød: ‘a pretty easy way of getting a couple of portions of fruit and veg before you even leave the house’.Photograph: Sofiia Popovych/ShutterstockI need sliced salted tomatoes, a generous handful of fresh assorted leaves, the crunch of a cucumber and, if I am being fancy, thinly sliced mangetout with a handful of finely chopped dill, mint or parsley to set me up for the morning, and ideally I want to have it sitting at a breakfast table. Whatever curveballs might come my way throughout the day, I can start it knowing I have done something for me and by me that was not only healthy but also delicious, and that made me sit down with a knife and fork to actually make time for at least one civilised meal.So no thanks to the people who told me I could go into a supermarket or McDonald’s and buy salad whenever I like. That sort of misses the point – I want to eat breakfast in the place where I am staying. I don’t want to pick wilted leaves from a plastic bowl with my fingers in the middle of the high street.Complain all you like, but I’m eating salad as part of breakfast whenever I can. There’s a reason those Scandinavians have colour in their cheeks and live long and healthy lives, and I want in on that. As for the person who responded to the photo of my breakfast of salad, garlic mushrooms and boiled egg on toast with a sophisticated total of three “being sick” emojis, thanks for proving my point – cereal for breakfast really is for babies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJacq Kelly is a Toronto-based writer and disability rights campaignerExplore more on these topicsSaladThe hill I will die onBreakfastFoodCereals and grainscommentShareReuse this content

title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
Content: ‘Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationStaff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious resultsArwa MahdawiA new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first termSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTShareDonald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates.According to anew reportcalled Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’snearly 150% higherthan the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”.High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretaryKristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as thePartnership for Public Servicenote in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far morestable.And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fuelinga power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king.“Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from thePartnership for Public Service writesin a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.”Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the presidentsaid in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,”he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.”Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helpedcreate, has been invaluable to him in this regard. InJuly 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme courtgave the president another gift:the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935rulingthat the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president.Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled inTrump v Cookthat the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile,wrote onTruth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”.I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who arebehind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there onpage 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere withelection administrationandweaponize the Department of Justiceagainst election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with.In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election.A bunch of losers are still complaining that the Odyssey isn’t white enoughElon Musk has been whining about Christopher Nolan casting Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy formonthsnow. This week, following rave reviews of the Odyssey, Muskannouncedthat his AI image and video generator Grok Imagine would create its own “historically accurate” version of the film. Perhaps Musk should listen to Colman Domingo, who recentlysaidon Jimmy Kimmel Live that he has a message for everyone upset about diversity in The Odyssey: “If you want to see a film with a cast of all white people who are cursed by the gods, the ‘Melania’ movie is currently streaming.”Record 384 World Cup-linked reports of domestic abuse in England and WalesThe data was collected as part of a strategy tobetter understand the linkbetween football tournaments and domestic abuse. A police chief citedextended pub opening hoursas one of the factors in the surge in violence.AOC is leading Kamala Harris in a new 2028 presidential poll by a long wayA University of New Hampshire poll has AOCleading the fieldwith 22% support while Pete Buttigieg has 21%. Harris only has 5%.Model scout for Jeffrey Epstein found dead at his home near ParisDaniel Siad, who was founddead at his home on Monday, compared his work trying to source women with fishing. “In This busyness I feel like fisherman some time I cache (sic) quick, some time no fish,”he wrotein an email to Epstein in 2014.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralian politician Pauline Hanson thinks domestic violence is a ‘two-way street’The senatoralso suggestedwomen experiencing abuse should simply “not put up with it”.Israeli rights groups warn of ‘mass pogroms’in occupied West BankWhile violence by Arabs is called “terrorism”, the media tends to downplay attacks by Jewish settlers in Israel by characterizing it as “settler violence”. This violence,enabledby the Israeli military and ignored by many in the US, has been intensifying.
