Following adeadly settler attack on Friday, Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem and 19 other Israeli human rights organisationscondemnedthe international community’s “silence and inaction” and called for “immediate action to stop Israel’s violence and prevent pogroms by settler militias”.Why middle-aged women are ravingWomen are putting the internalized ageism aside and realizing you’re never too old to go outclubbing.People are watching porn based on ICE raidsRule 34of the internet is that if something exists, there is porn of it. The dystopian machinations of the Trump administration are no exception. Wired has a disturbing pieceon the rise of Maga-themed porn.The week in pawtriarchyMeet Jimothy, who appears to be the internet’snew favourite racoon. Seattle-based Jimothy hasn’t won hearts and minds by passing outdrunk in a Virginia liquorstore like some of his compatriots. Rather, he has gone viral because of his distinctive body shape, which may be the result of a rare genetic condition called short spine syndrome. He looks a bit like afurry goblin, basically. I reckon Jimothy’s lack of a well-functioning backbone means he has a promising political career ahead of him. Perhaps Trump could make him Secretary of Trashury.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationThe Week in PatriarchyUS politicsDonald TrumpThe OdysseyElon MuskWorld CupAlexandria Ocasio-CortezcommentShareReuse this content

title: I tried so hard to become a salad eater. Now cyclospora is sending me back to burgers | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Between the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossible
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Between the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossible
Content: ‘The greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionFood safetyI tried so hard to become a salad eater. Now cyclospora is sending me back to burgersDave SchillingBetween the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossibleSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.43 EDTShareWhile war and conflict seem to be raging across the planet, the greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad – in the sense that fresh produce is now waging battle with our stomachs thanks to the cyclospora parasite. Cyclospora has infested an unknown amount of our food, causing thousands to suffer bowel movements that would make Pompeii look like a gender-reveal party.This is a tragedy for everyone except the fat cats at Big Toilet. Cyclospora may be spread through human feces getting into irrigation systems in the food supply due to poor worker hygiene. Itcan’t be killed through usual agricultural sanitation processes. The best we can do is throw all that cilantro away and start from scratch. The FDA is scrambling to find the source of the contamination as soon as possible, going as far as to finger the supplier Taylor Farms with a false positive test that they had to sloppily retract as fast as they declared it. I, for one, am trembling, and not because I’m seconds away from expelling parasitic eggs. I’m terrified because now I don’t know what to eat.A year-and-a-half ago, I was strongly recommended a diet by a kindly nutritionist that banished carbs and emphasized leafy greens. It brought down my cholesterol levels and blood pressure. I lost 40lbs. I’ve never felt less like a glistening slug, slithering through life trying to avoid getting stepped on by someone fitter than me during a vigorous jog.I’m not a healthy person, by nature. My son, who is addicted to McDonald’s chicken nuggets, caused me to indulge in fast food. If he’s going for yet another Happy Meal, why not a lovely Big Mac for Dad? When I wrote my first book, my only solace in the lonely days and nights of banging on a keyboard for hours was pizza delivery. Circumstances conspired to unlock my latent gluttony, causing every health marker on my chart to turn a sickly shade of red to denote “strong chance of every organ retiring from service all at once”. Personally, I’d like my body to keep working for another few years, so I took the advice from my nutritionist and gained all the benefits.Unfortunately, the very food I’m meant to eat to stay alive is now a potential threat. Sure, I could order a salad for lunch, but I also might have to move all my worldly possessions into the bathroom. I feel like I’ve stumbled into a Faustian bargain where, for the price of one prolonged bout of digestive emergency, I can have a summer beach body.I’d love to continue my journey toward dietary harmony, but as this outbreak continues, I’m starting to wonder if I should pivot back to my customary regimen of fried dough and cheese cones. If my food isn’t barbecued or dipped into hot grease, can I even trust it?Cuts to food safety programs at the federal levellast year certainly aren’t helping my belief in the propriety of what I put in my mouth. In 2025, a CDC program quietlytrimmed the number of foodborne illnesses it tracked from six to just two. One of the four illnesses axed from the program? Cyclosporiasis. Only salmonella andEcolisurvived the purge, which are at least two of the most famous illnesses. TheQ scorefor salmonella andEcolihas got to be Taylor-Swift-Rihanna levels at this point, making the term “going viral” almost literal.Yes, I know they are actually bacteria. But there’s an entire world of obscure microscopic bugs out there to contend with, and at least for now, we all need to eat food. Worse yet, we all need to eat good food, if such a thing even exists in our mass-produced, industrial culinary world. To match the voracious demand for sustenance and maximize profits, every step of the food-production process has been degraded. Who knows how many microplastics and pesticides are in my system right now, eager to wreak havoc on my internal systems at a moment’s notice? The answer to my food anxiety probably isn’t to subsist on Pop-Tarts and ranch dressing. The damage might be slower than bacteria would cause, but the bill will come due regardless.The problem isn’t with me or you or anyone else who relies on the safety of our food supply. It’s on the companies and the government agencies who manufacture and regulate what we eat. At this juncture, it feels less like my tax dollars go to securing our food and more like they’re going directly into my toilet.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsFood safetyOpinionHealthFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronze | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty has hit out at his critics after he was beaten into third place in the Commonwealth Games 100m breaststroke
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty has hit out at his critics after he was beaten into third place in the Commonwealth Games 100m breaststroke
Content: England's Adam Ramsay-Peaty on his way to finishing third in the men's 100m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEngland's Adam Ramsay-Peaty on his way to finishing third in the men's 100m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronzeRamsay-Peaty finishes third in 100m breaststroke‘People who comment … you don’t know who I am’Sean Ingleat Tollcross International Swimming CentreSat 25 Jul 2026 18.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 20.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdam Ramsay-Peaty has never been someone to mask his feelings. But defeat has never sounded as emotional or as raw as this. There were tears. Frustrations. Questions about why he kept putting himself through the 5.30am starts at the age of 31.And then came the crescendo in the form of a blistering attack on his critics on social media and the media. “You can’t hurt me,” he said, before telling them to “do better”. It was dramatic. It was powerful. And it was certainly heartfelt.This wasn’t the piece we came to the TollcrossSwimmingCentre to write. But then came a performance that no one – Ramsay-Peaty included – expected. He had believed he was in shape for gold after working hard in a heavy training block. Instead, at his best event, the 100m breaststroke, he had to settle for a bronze medal behind the Australian Sam Williamson and Jersey’s 18-year-old wunderkind Filip Nowicki.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead more“I’m not crying because it’s a bronze instead of a gold,” Ramsay-Peaty insisted. “I’m crying because I know that the swim could have been better, and I know I worked way better than that. Something isn’t hitting right. Whether it’s the pace, whether it’s the focus, I’m not sure. I feel like I couldn’t have really put more in.“And that’s where it hurts. I’m like: ‘What’s the point of all the 5.30am starts? What’s the point of being exhausted all the time? What’s the point of having to say no to family events because you’re training?’”Initially it seemed to be business as usual. Ramsay-Peaty arrived blowing kisses to the crowd. He then kept his rivals waiting as he took his pool coat off. Up to now this was classic Ramsay-Peaty. But when he launched into the pool, everything was off.At his best, the greatest breaststroke sprinter in history is able to power out of the blocks, establish a supreme dominance before the turn, and easily hold off any fast finishers. But he was in a fight from the start, and was only third at halfway.He scraped to the end, like all good fighters. But he was unable to catch Williamson, who won in 59.37sec, or Nowicki, who glided into second 0.17 back. Ramsay-Peaty’s finishing time of 59.65 was nearly three seconds off his world record.View image in fullscreenSam Williamson celebrates on the podium after winning the men’s 100m breaststroke final with Jersey’s Filip Nowicki and England’s Adam Ramsay-Peaty.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersAfter he collected his medal he kissed his wife, Holly, whose baby is due in December, on the belly. That recollection at least brought a smile. “She’s always going to be proud of me,” he said. “And as a father, it doesn’t matter if you come home with gold. As long as you come home with a teddy. That’s really what matters.“But I’m never going to be afraid to show weakness, because it’s so important for making stronger people, making stronger men, stronger fathers, husbands. And it’s a realisation of how much I do work. This cycle especially, I’m like: ‘Shit, how have I worked this hard at this age?’ And then you get a result like that, I’m like: ‘I’m better than that.’“And I can’t really put in where it went wrong. Maybe it’s just an off swim. Or maybe it is just because I’ve been two years out of the championships and heat semi-finals. But it does hurt.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThen came an attack on the media and snipers on social media, who have devoured every detail about the estrangement from one side of his family. Peaty said he had tried hard to focus hard on his job “without getting baited … and ignoring most of the rubbish you see online about me”, but then he addressed those who had attacked him directly.“You don’t know who I am,” he said. “And people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror. You can’t hurt me.“That hasn’t played a part in the sense of what I’ve experienced today, because I’m still happy with that result in some sense, but it has to stop. How many athletes, how many people, have to go through this until the media learn their lesson? You have to learn and do better.“I feel like I deserve more, to be honest. I know the shit I’ve been through. Which is no fault of my own, to be honest. But it does take a toll, you know?”Peaty still has another chance for a gold medal at these Commonwealths as he competes in the heats of the 50m on Sunday, with the final on Monday. But afterwards he suggested that maybe that 100m might no longer be on his longterm radar when it comes to the LA Olympics.“It’s too early to tell what I’m capable of at this age now,” he said. “But I’m a fighter. We’ve got two weeks until Europeans or just under, so we’ve got another opportunity to do it again. And yeah, I do enjoy a scrap, but I lost a scrap this time, and that is sport. But I feel like I deserve more, to be honest.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAdam Ramsay-PeatySwimmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Abi Martin snatches Commonwealth bronze for England in gymnastics team final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: England edged out Wales by 0.900 in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final, won by Australia, while Gabriel Langton is out of hospital after his fall
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: England edged out Wales by 0.900 in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final, won by Australia, while Gabriel Langton is out of hospital after his fall
Content: England's Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Shanna-Kae Grant, Alia Leat, Abi Martin and Ruby Stacey are all smiles after winning a bronze medal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenEngland's Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Shanna-Kae Grant, Alia Leat, Abi Martin and Ruby Stacey are all smiles after winning a bronze medal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Abi Martin snatches Commonwealth bronze for England in gymnastics team finalEngland pip Wales to secure medal by just 0.900ptsGabriel Langton discharged from hospital after fallYara El-Shabouryat Glasgow International ArenaSat 25 Jul 2026 16.58 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland held their nerve to claim bronze in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final after a tense final rotation enabled them to edge Wales by less than a point in Glasgow. The defending champions finished with 154.300 points, just enough to snatch third place from Wales, while Australia delivered a dominant display to win gold ahead of Canada.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two in picturesRead moreAustralia set the tone from the opening rotation, with Kate McDonald posting the highest uneven bars score of the day at 14.200 as the silver medallists from Birmingham 2022 established an early lead they would never relinquish. England made a solid start on vault through Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Ruby Stacey, Alia Leat and Abi Martin. However, the uneven bars proved costly. Amankwaah’s excellent 13.500 boosted England’s challenge, but Stacey fell during her routine and her score did not count, leaving England trailing Australia at the halfway stage.Heading into the final floor rotation, England trailed Canada by just 0.350 points in the battle for silver but also faced the threat of Wales, who watched on after they had set an impressive total earlier in the day.Amankwaah opened with a stylish routine before a music delay briefly interrupted Shanna-Kae Grant’sCommonwealth Gamesdebut, though that failed to unsettle her as she produced a superb routine, highlighted by a huge double Arabian, to keep England in medal contention. Leat’s 12.150 left England needing at least 12.350 from the final routine to overhaul Wales. Martin delivered under pressure, scoring 13.250 to spark celebrations as England secured bronze by just 0.900 points.Australia finished five points clear of Wales’ earlier total to reclaim Commonwealth gold, while Canada’s strong final vault rotation, led by Ellie Black’s impressive 13.950, secured silver. Wales were left agonisingly short of a first team medal since Glasgow 2014.Meanwhile, England’s Gabriel Langton has been discharged from hospital after scans determined no lasting damagefrom his fall during the men’s team finalon Friday. The 19-year-old landed head first off the high bar in the final apparatus. The competition was held up for 20 minutes as he was carried away from the arena on a stretcher.View image in fullscreenAbi Martin performs her floor routine which secured the bronze medal for England in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA“Gabriel was transferred to the hospital as a precautionary measure overnight and underwent multiple scans today, with very positive results,” Team England said in a statement. “Thankfully, he has been cleared of any serious injury complications and will be discharged to return to the team hotel this evening.“He is in good spirits and hugely grateful for the many messages of support and the excellent care provided by the medical teams. He is looking forward to being reunited with the team to celebrate his silver medal.”Earlier in the day, before the medals were decided, one of the loudest cheers inside the Glasgow International Arena was reserved for a gymnast who would compete for less than two minutes. Two years ago, Tiana Sumanasekera was a United States Olympic alternate, training at the famed World Champions Centre in Houston alongside Simone Biles and Jordan Chiles. Now she is representing Sri Lanka – the country of her parents’ birth – with the aim of making the finals at Los Angeles in 2028.Sri Lanka achieved a milestone at the Tokyo Olympics when Milka Gehani became their first gymnast to compete at the Games. Sumanasekera’s arrival represents another significant step forward with the 18-year-old boasting the talent to challenge for world championship and Olympic finals on balance beam and floor exercise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCommonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead moreSumanasekera is a multiple Pan American Games medallist who finished third on balance beam at the 2024 US Olympic Trials; she has long been regarded as one of the sport’s most promising gymnasts.“I started competing at the elite level when I was 13 years old when I was with Team USA,” she said. “I had been with them for about five years and in 2024 I became an Olympic alternate. It really shifted my perspective on my capabilities.“From when I was a little girl, I’ve always wanted to compete at the Olympics, so I thought the best decision was to represent my parents’ home country of Sri Lanka. I’m so proud and honoured to be here and doing so.”But the Commonwealth Games arrived at the wrong time. A shoulder injury forced her to abandon plans to compete in the all-around event. Instead, she entered women’s qualification on one apparatus – balance beam – hoping to make the final despite limited preparation.View image in fullscreenTiana Sumanasekera’s originality has made her a fan favourite.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianHer routine opened with a back dive to chest stand mount, displaying the originality that has made her a fan favourite, but her trademark back handspring layout series came up just short. She lost her balance, the one-point fall deduction ending her hopes.Rather than unravel, Sumanasekera reeled off a beautifully connected front aerial into a split jump before finishing with perhaps the best moment of the routine – a stuck layout full-twisting dismount that drew applause from the crowd.It was not enough to secure a place in the final, but Sumanasekera hopes she can build on this before LA 2028. “It was absolutely amazing being out here representing Sri Lanka on one of the biggest stages in the world. I was so grateful to compete.“It didn’t go my way, but things happen. You live and you learn and you move on, so I’m excited for what’s to come next.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesGymnasticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scotland’s Eilish McColgan pulls out in latest blow for Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Commonwealth Games has suffered yet another blow after Scotland’s star athlete Eilish McColgan became the latest big name to pull out
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Commonwealth Games has suffered yet another blow after Scotland’s star athlete Eilish McColgan became the latest big name to pull out
Content: Eilish McColgan has been suffering with a toe injury.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEilish McColgan has been suffering with a toe injury.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Scotland’s Eilish McColgan pulls out in latest blow for Commonwealth GamesHost nation’s star athlete is latest big-name withdrawal10,000m champion was due to defend title on MondaySean Inglein GlasgowSat 25 Jul 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Commonwealth Games has suffered yet another blow after Eilish McColgan, Scotland’s star athlete at these championships, became the latest big name to pull out. McColgan was due to defendher 10,000m titleon Monday, but on Saturday said: “Sadly, I won’t be competing at Glasgow 2026. After almost 10 weeks out following the London Marathon with my toe injury, it probably won’t come as a huge surprise.“The good news is I’m back running. The bad news is I’ve simply run out of time to get myself, and my toe, back into spikes. Having started the year stronger than ever, I know the fitness is there but having only taken my first run outdoors a couple of weeks ago, the clock was always against me.Commonwealth Games 2026: McColgan pulls out out plus day two updates – liveRead more“While these Games have come a few weeks too early for me, this isn’t the end of my season and I can’t wait to get back racing soon.”McColgan is the latest British track and field big name to be missing the home Games. On Thursday,Katarina Johnson-Thompson, the Olympic heptathlon silver medallist, pulled out with a calf injury, while other late withdrawals include the sprinter Dina Asher-Smith,Matt Hudson-Smith, the 400m Olympic silver medallist, andthe 2025 world indoor 400m champion, Amber Anning.England’sOlympic 800m champion, Keely Hodgkinson, has skipped the event to prioritise the European Championships. St Lucia’s100m Olympic champion, Julien Alfred, and Botswana’sOlympic 200m champion, Letsile Tebogo, are also missing, along with Canadian swimmer Summer McIntosh, who is instead favouring the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.Elinor Middlemiss, the TeamScotlandchef de mission, supported McColgan’s decision. “We’re sad Eilish won’t be competing at Glasgow 2026 as we know just how much it meant to her to defend her Commonwealth title in front of a home crowd,” she said.“Eilish is a legend of Scottish sport and her incredible 10,000m gold-medal victory in Birmingham will go down as one of the defining moments inCommonwealth Gameshistory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“She has worked tirelessly to give herself every opportunity to be on the start line, and we completely support her decision not to return before she’s ready to compete at her very best.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026AthleticsCommonwealth GamesScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Joshua knocked down twice but stops Kristian Prenga in round two | Boxing | The Guardian
description: The British heavyweight Anthony Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round but hit back to blast out the Albanian Kristian Prenga in the second
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The British heavyweight Anthony Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round but hit back to blast out the Albanian Kristian Prenga in the second
Content: Anthony Joshua (right) embraces Kristian Prenga after winning his fight by technical knockout in the second round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnthony Joshua (right) embraces Kristian Prenga after winning his fight by technical knockout in the second round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersBoxingAnthony Joshua knocked down twice but stops Kristian Prenga in round twoBriton on canvas inside 20 seconds and later in firstJoshua recovers to blast out Albanian in second roundDonald McRaeSat 25 Jul 2026 19.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Joshua cleared his final hurdle in the ring, before he fights Tyson Fury in November, but he was knocked down twice, shockingly, in the first round of his wild and chaotic bout with Kristian Prenga. In the early hours of Sunday morning in Jeddah, a devastating knockout in the second left Prenga crumpled in a heap on the canvas, wrapped up in the ropes, and rescued Joshua from humiliation.After the opening three minutes his extravaganza with Fury looked as if it was about to end in abject ruins but Joshua pulled himself out of a dark pit streaked with defeat to salvage his career – and his much-hyped fight with his British compatriot. This was a crazy firefight of a tune-up for Joshua, who was boxing for the first time since being injured in the car accident that took the lives of two of his closest friends, Sina Ghami and Latif Ayodele, last December.View image in fullscreenKristian Prenga surprises Anthony Joshua and knocks him down in the first round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/Reuters“He’s back” was emblazoned on the big screen behind the figure of Joshua as he walked at a steady, even sombre pace towards the ring. A booming Meek Mill track echoed around him while the faces of Ghami and Ayodele briefly filled the screen. Wearing a camouflage top and trunks, he then turned and quietly greeted Oleksandr Usyk, a new ally sat at ringside.Joshua had trained hard with Usyk and his team in the buildup to his arrival in Jeddah. Usyk remains the best heavyweight in the world and Joshua, having lost both his battles with the Ukrainian, had resolved with some humility that he needed to learn from his previous rival. With Usyk’s trainers in his corner, and coming into the ring lighter than he has been for years at 251lb, Joshua was apparently determined to resemble a much sharper and sleeker fighter against Prenga.After a fleeting prayer in his corner, Joshua stepped towards the centre of the ring and, within 20 seconds, the unheralded Prenga had floored him heavily with a crunching right uppercut. Joshua got up quickly, looking dazed. Halfway through the round, with his legs still unsteady, Joshua was rocking against the ropes. With 30 seconds left in the first Joshua was down again. He hauled himself up, shaking his head, with defeat closing in on him. It had been a disastrous round but Joshua fired back just before the bell.Fury must have been cursing as the biggest money-making contest in the history of British boxing looked on the brink of obliteration. But, Joshua came out in the second with real purpose and quickly hurt the strangely tentative Albanian, who was already backing away before the damaging punches landed. It was almost as if Prenga could not believe he had come so close to knocking out the feted former world champion.View image in fullscreenAnthony Joshua decisively knocks down Albania’s Kristian Prenga in the second round …Photograph: Ali Issa/APView image in fullscreen… and Kristian Prenga lies across the bottom rope.Photograph: Ali Issa/APWith 20 seconds left in the round, a jolting jab set up Joshua as he landed two heavy right hands. Sensing a seismic turnaround, Joshua unleashed a pulverising right which landed with brutal force and separated Prenga from his suddenly scrambled senses. It was immediately obvious that he would be counted out.Joshua celebrated exuberantly, climbing on the ropes and raising his hands in jubilation, but it was more telling to see how a shaken Usyk just drew in a deep breath of relief.A bizarrely uneven victory followed Fury’s contrastinglyroutine defeat of Mariusz Wach, a faded Polish journeyman, in Pattaya, Thailand, on Friday night. Fury dominated a one-sided scrap before Wach was rescued by his team after they decided he could not come out for the eighth round.Earlier in the week Fury had insisted that he would reject an invitation to fly to Saudi Arabia from Thailand to watch Joshua. He had even expressed doubts that his much-delayed battle with Joshua would ever happen and described his fellow British heavyweight as “a bottle-job flapper and a chinless wonder”. But it helps that he and and Joshua could each make close to $100m for a contest that should have happened eight years ago, when they were both close to their fighting prime. So it seems highly likely that they will meet in the ring later this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Hold on, wait a minute,” Joshua cried out when he was interviewed in the ring. “Have we got Tyson Fury in the room? Is he here or not?”When he was informed that Fury would not be joining him between the ropes, Joshua slipped into his best high-pitched whispery impersonation of Mike Tyson at his most unhinged as, jokingly, he said: “I am the meanest, most ruthless, most vicious champion. Nobody can stop me. He is no Alexander [the Great].” He also referenced Tyson’s claim that he would “eat the heart” of Lennox Lewis but it was all just a madhouse riff from Joshua as he delighted in his comeback.Tyson Fury defeats 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in warm-up for expected Joshua boutRead more“All jokes aside, there are two sides,” he continued. “One is the fighter and the other is respect. I respect everything [Fury] has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we’re here now. I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat.”The Fury-Joshua circus has been rolling for so many years that even the most optimistic members of boxing’s beleaguered fanbase have sometimes wondered if the two ex-world champions would ever fight each other. But, finally, as Joshua turned the prospect of a terrible defeat into a knockout win over Prenga, the shenanigans moved significantly closer to becoming a real showdown later this year.Explore more on these topicsBoxingAnthony JoshuanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pogacar set for Tour de France glory in shortened finale as Carapaz wins stage 20 | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar will take his fifth Tour sooner than planned after Sunday’s final stage was shortened to free up security forces to fight wildfires elsewhere
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar will take his fifth Tour sooner than planned after Sunday’s final stage was shortened to free up security forces to fight wildfires elsewhere
Content: Tadej Pogacar (left) and UAE teammate Isaac del Toro strike a pose as they cross the finish line on Alpe d'Huez.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar (left) and UAE teammate Isaac del Toro strike a pose as they cross the finish line on Alpe d'Huez.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APTour de France 2026Pogacar set for Tour de France glory in shortened finale as Carapaz wins stage 20Four-time victor holds huge lead after Alpe d’HuezFinal stage to be shortened due to wildfires elsewhereJeremy Whittleat Alpe d'HuezSat 25 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar’s likely victory parade on the streets of Paris will come sooner on Sunday after the final stage of theTour de Francewas shortened due to wildfires elsewhere in France. The stage will now be only 89km long and will start on the Champs-Élysées, where two laps of the avenue will be followed by the now traditional circuits of the Butte Montmartre.More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and SpainRead moreIn a joint statement with the prefecture police, the Tour organiser, ASO, said: “The ministry of the interior has decided to redeploy a portion of the internal security forces initially mobilised for the final stage of the Tour de France, in order to reinforce the response efforts inthe areas affected by the wildfires.”Wildfires around the Arcachon lagoon near Bordeaux and around Biscarrosse, in the Landes, have destroyed more than 36,000 hectares of forest. This is the third stage of the Tour to be subjected to prefecture intervention, due to wildfires or a heatwave, in this year’s race.Resources and the lack of them have also been a topic of debate sincePogacar’s astounding winon Alpe d’Huez on Friday. The four-time champion is now expected to secure a record-equalling fifth title in Paris on Sunday evening after Saturday’s 20th stage was won by Richard Carapaz.A day after setting a record time up the Alpe’s famous hairpin bends to extend his overall lead, Pogacar could afford to concede 39 seconds to his closest challenger, Remco Evenepoel, on Saturday and will start Sunday’s shortened stage into Paris ahead by six minutes and 26 seconds.However, there was significant fallout after Friday’s chaotic climb, largely due to the dangerous behaviour of some among the thousands at the roadside. Several incidents, which endangered both riders and fans, rebooted the debate over the safety of Tour stages on the Alpe.In-race motorbikes, blocked by the crowds, stalled an attack from Evenepoel, while a lack of crowd control led to the Movistar climber Einer Rubio abandoning the race after riding into the rear windscreen of a UAE team car. The crash, which led to Rubio being transported by helicopter to hospital in Grenoble, where he was given 20 stitches for facial injuries, was caused by an unruly spectator falling in front of the car, forcing it to suddenly brake.“If we had been using cars from 20 years ago, the accident wouldn’t have happened,” the race director, Thierry Gouvenou, said, apparently blaming the braking sensors in the car.View image in fullscreenRichard Carapaz, in the polka dot jersey, heads for his second win at this year’s race.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersMore footage of fans wrestling each other over gifts from thecaravane publicitaireand climbing over moving race vehicles – including the Guardian’s – further fuelled the notion of a race that was out of control. The French national champion, Romain Grégoire, said spectators were “so drunk that it was more like being slapped on the arse, than getting pushes”.Evenepoel’s Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe sports director, Klaas Lodewyck, said: “As long as they’re cheering on the riders and creating a good atmosphere, it’s fine. But when they start punching in side mirrors and banging on the windows, that’s crossing the line.”On Saturday’s final mountain stage, Pogacar the ogre, as L’Équipe called him, worked to protect the interests of his third-placed UAE teammate, Isaac del Toro. Carapaz, stage winner in Orcières-Merlette and third in Friday’s stage to Alpe d’Huez, was again one of the key animators, attacking on the first climb, the Col de la Croix de Fer, as he sought to consolidate his lead in the King of the Mountains classification.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTour de France 2026: stage 20 from Bourg d’Oisans to Alpe d’Huez – liveRead moreFatigue and frayed nerve endings also played their part in the Tour’s hardest mountain stage, and Ilan Van Wilder, 12th overall when the stage began, crashed out after falling on the descent of the Croix de Fer.But the spat between Carapaz and the French climber Lenny Martinez, who had been overtaken by Pogacar close to the finish of Friday’s stage to the Alpe, rumbled on into Saturday morning. The pair had engaged in a war of words after the Ecuadorian angrily accused the Frenchman of “cutting in front” of him on the final corner on Friday. Martinez seemed unconcerned.“I knew I had to be first through the corner,” Martinez said. “We’re not at Club Med – I’m not letting him go first.”Most of the real drama in the final mountain stage came on the narrow climb of the Col de Sarenne, where Paul Seixas lost ground on Pogacar, Del Toro and Evenepoel.Visma-Lease a Bike’s Sepp Kuss, descending towards a probable stage win on the Alpe, crashed on the exit of a tunnel and then, moments later, almost toppled into the void on a fast bend. The American came close to disappearing over a cliff edge, but was stopped by crash netting, mounted alongside the road.His mistake was enough to let the pursuing Carapaz speed past and, despite evident fatigue, the Ecuadorian held on to take his second stage win in three days and secured the polka dot jersey.Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris grabs F1 Hungarian GP pole while Hamilton and Antonelli are penalised | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris took pole for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who was then docked three places for impeding Oscar Piastri
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris took pole for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who was then docked three places for impeding Oscar Piastri
Content: McLaren’s Lando Norris indicates he’s No 1 after darting through to take pole position.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APView image in fullscreenMcLaren’s Lando Norris indicates he’s No 1 after darting through to take pole position.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APFormula One 2026Lando Norris grabs F1 Hungarian GP pole while Hamilton and Antonelli are penalisedDefending champion takes first pole of 2026 by 0.012secHamilton and Antonelli receive three-place penaltiesGiles Richardsat the HungaroringSat 25 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe margins were tiny and for a moment it seemedLewis Hamiltonhad finally found his edge in qualifying, only for the seven-time champion to be beaten by but a breath. The defending world champion, Lando Norris, pipped him to pole for the Hungarian Grand Prix in a thrilling, dramatic contest.Worse was to follow for Hamilton as his very real chance of converting a front-row start to a win in his hugely competitive Ferrari took a severe blow as he was penalised three grid places for impeding McLaren’sOscar Piastriduring their final laps. Hamilton will start from fifth place.Hungarian Grand Prix qualifying: Formula One – liveRead moreNorris took the top spot for McLaren by one-hundredth of a second from Hamilton’sFerrari, but the latter’s place on the front row remained in doubt, as he was under investigation by the FIA.Hamilton said he had been informed by the team that Piastri was closing on him only when theMcLarenwas already right behind him and that he did not know anyone was still on a hot lap behind him. Nonetheless, after qualifying, the stewards ruled he was at fault and imposed the grid penalty.“I was told when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming,” Hamilton said. “I thought everyone came out behind me. I was the first out so I thought everyone had finished their lap, and I think Charles was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn’t intentional.”Hamilton’s teammate, Charles Leclerc, was in third, with the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, in fourth for Mercedes, but the Italian was investigated for failing to slow under yellow flags and also given a three-place penalty. Antonelli leads Hamilton by 45 points and his teammate,George Russell, by 50 points in the championship.Piastri was fifth for McLaren, Max Verstappen sixth for Red Bull after he spun on his final lap, while Russell could manage only seventh and was told to pull his car off the track after his final lap with a water leak.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton was penalised for impeding Oscar Piastri.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe day belonged to Norris, who delivered a superb run for McLaren to claim pole. Given that the team had opened the season off the pace of Mercedes and Ferrari, their upgrades for Miami and further developments added in Canada have proved impressive and they are the first team to deny Mercedes the top spot this season.It is Norris’s second pole at the Hungarian GP and the 17th of his career, while for McLaren it is another strong result at the circuit. With Norris winning here last year and Piastri in 2024, they may well be in position to make it three in a row at a meeting where McLaren have a record 13 victories.On the opening laps in Q3 Verstappen made the running but was surpassed by Norris, yet Hamilton nailed his first lap to take provisional pole with a time of 1min 17.219sec, a tenth up on Norris in second, and a chance to take his first pole for Ferrari and a record 10th at the same track.The track had been steadily rubbering-in throughout the session, the times coming down as the grip increased and the final runs were crucial. Hamilton was sent out early but could not improve on his time and Norris, the last man on track, was on a quick run. Immense through the middle sector, there was nothing in it and he just edged out Hamilton by one-hundredth of a second with a time of 1:17.207.Given the track was evolving Hamilton felt the decision to send him out early had been an error. “I felt solid throughout qualifying, but for some reason we went out first, which I don’t think was the right call,” he said. “The grip wasn’t there for either Charles or I. We were quickest throughout, so it’s definitely one that got away.”Aston Martin brought their radically overhauled B-spec car to Hungary in the hope of turning round a disastrous opening to the season. The car was overweight and aerodynamically far from where they had expected to be, while their Honda engine is down on power and suffered from causing severe vibrations early in the season.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli, the championship leader, will start the Hungarian Grand Prix in seventh after a grid penalty.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAThe team principal and designer, Adrian Newey, admitted it had been an immensely difficult start. “These first races have been a complete nightmare,” he said. “Hopefully, we can get at least to a point of respectability now, that is the immediate goal.”In qualifying at least they made a step forward with Fernando Alonso putting an Aston into Q2 for the first time this season, no mean feat given they were two seconds slower than the Cadillacs in Belgium. Alonso ultimately finished in 16th.The success of the upgrade is considered to be key in persuading Alonso to stay for 2027, with a further development expected for Zandvoort when Honda will also bring their new engine.The return of the Malaysia to the F1 calendar could be confirmed as early as Sunday, with the meeting arranged after the cancellation of the races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier in the season. It will take place between the rounds in Baku and Singapore on 4 October. The race at the Sepang circuit near Kuala Lumpur is expected to be branded as the Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia, with Bahrain funding the event. The circuit last held an F1 meeting in 2017.F1 is also understood to be looking into the prospect of hosting the season finale at Imola if the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are unable to be held because of the conflict in the Middle East.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lando NorrisMcLarenFormula OneLewis HamiltonKimi AntonelliGeorge RussellnewsShareReuse this content

title: From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World Cup | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Norway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdle
Author: Natalie Tan
Headline: Norway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdle
Content: Erling Haaland carries his raccoon, Vozinha enjoys the moment, Merlin the duck, Scotland supporters enjoy Boston and Wonderwall by Oasis.Composite: Getty Images, Guardian designView image in fullscreenErling Haaland carries his raccoon, Vozinha enjoys the moment, Merlin the duck, Scotland supporters enjoy Boston and Wonderwall by Oasis.Composite: Getty Images, Guardian designWorld Cup 2026From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World CupNorway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdleNatalie TanandCalvin BurtonSat 25 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCuraçao’shistoric first goal“I played with him on my PlayStation, and now I’ve scored against him,” Livano Comenencia said after converting Curaçao’s first World Cup goal past Manuel Neuer in their opening match against Germany. The smallest nation ever to qualify for the World Cupwent on to lose 7-1but that goal – their only one of the tournament – will go down in history.‘Cablegate’Should Jude Bellingham’s first goal against Norway have been ruled out? Perhaps so given the ball appeared tohit an overhead cablein the buildup. Fifa insisted there had been no such intervention; Norway’s manager, Ståle Solbakken, was sure there had been. “Many on the bench reacted immediately … the ball fell down straight in front of us,” he said, furiously.Top 30: from half a million World Cup photos, why I love these the mostRead moreMarsch’s musings“I’d rather be us than them,” said Jesse Marschafter Canada were comprehensively beaten by Moroccoin the last 16. “It takes some nerve to say that when you lose 3-0,” said Morocco’s head coach, Mohamed Ouahbi, in response. Marsch also somewhat hilariously overestimated the capacity of BC Place after his side’s6–0 win over Qatar, saying: “There’ll be 60 million people that said they were here.”GlitteringGoldenBoot raceBetween 1978 and 2018, only the original Ronaldo had scored more than six goals at a single World Cup (eight in 2002). Lionel Messi and Kylian Mbappé had matched the Brazilian’s tally by the semi-finals this time around, with Mbappé winning the Golden Boot after scoring two goals against England inthe third-place playoff.Scotland fans take over BostonScottish supporters marked their return to football’s biggest stage in 28 years by taking over Boston, filling Fenway Park with songs and drinking their pubs dry. With the Tartan Army crowning some of the city’s most recognisable statues with bright orange traffic cones, the “Boston cone”was greeted byBoston’s mayor, Michelle Wu, upon its arrival from Glasgow last week. Scotland’s players may have made little impact in the US this summer, but their fans no doubt left a legacy.Ronaldo scores … andthen goes out with a whimper‘CR7’ finally ended his knockout goal droughtagainst Croatiaas Portugal squeezed into the last 16. However, joy soon turned to despair when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the next round. Ronaldo struggled to have any impact on proceedings, managing only 19 touches in what washis final World Cup match. “I gave it all, I gave it my best,” he said afterwards.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo scored against Croatia but could not prevent Portugal going out against Spain.Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockEmbolo’s mistaken identityThe mistaken identity rule was updated for this World Cup to cover situations where a player was booked but the offence was committed by the other team and well and truly took effectduring Argentina and Switzerland’s quarter-finalin Kansas City. The referee, João Pinheiro, initially issued Argentina’s Leandro Paredes a yellow card for his challenge on Switzerland’s Breel Embolo before the VAR called him to the monitor. Embolo was then ruled to have dived and was punished with a yellow card himself – it was the forward’s second of the game and he was duly sent off. “This rule destroyed the game today,” said Switzerland’s head coach, Murat Yakin, after his side’s 3-1 loss.Iran’s unprecedented tournamentCompeting against the backdrop of their country’s conflict with the US, Iran’s players faced incredible difficulties before a ball was kicked. With their training base abruptly switched from Arizona to Mexico before the tournament, the team were then only allowed to enter the US the day before their first two matches and had to leave immediately after. Despite that, they only narrowly missed out on the knockout rounds afterAustria and Algeria drew 3-3in the final round of the group stage to send them home on goal difference. “What these players have done should be written in history because the host country treated us very unfairly,” Iran’s head coach, Amir Ghalenoei, said.Erling Haaland: internet phenomenonSnapchat stories. Stuffed raccoons. Doing next to nothing against Brazil for 79 minutes and thenscoring twice in 11 minutes. It’s fair to say Erling Haaland made his mark at the World Cup. “When someone asks me what my biggest fear is but I can’t say being charged at by Haaland at full speed so I just say spiders,” reads a video that has racked up millions of views on Instagram, a reference to how Haaland chased down Iraq’s goalkeeper, Jalal Hassan, for his second goal of the tournament.Turkey are definitely not dark horsesTurkey were tipped to go far but, in the end, didn’t even make it out of the group stage. Indeed, they were the second country eliminated from the tournament following back-to-back losses to Australia and 10-man Paraguay. “We should have won these games … everybody’s sad, everybody’s crying,”said Arda Guler, Turkey’s wonderkid after his country’s less-than-wonderful showing.View image in fullscreenArda Guler (right) grimaces during Turkey’s defeat by Australia.Photograph: Lee Smith/ReutersEgypt outrage after controversial exit“I’m going home and won’t be watching any more games from the tournament,”said Egypt’s head coach, Hossam Hassan,after his side’s loss to Argentina in the last 16. “What happened to us wasn’t fair. We should have had a penalty, a goal was disallowed and I don’t know why.” Hassan was not alone in thinking crucial decisions had favoured the world champions in what was arguably the game of the tournament in Atlanta.The wonder of WonderwallIt started off as a standard submission for the World Cup’s official track list but was quickly adopted by England’s travelling support as the theme song of their tournament run, Oasis’s 1995 classic creating a genuinely uplifting bond between plays and fans. Harry Kane went as far as describing the post-match ritual of standing alongside his teammates, arms around each other’s shoulders, and facing a wall of happy, singing English faces as one of his “favourite ever moments in an England shirt”.Lamine Yamal’s brother becomes a starLamine Yamal had a great World Cup but not as great as his three-year-old brother, Keyne, whocaptured hearts worldwidewith his wide-eyed, big-grinned expressions of delight whenever his older sibling shone at the tournament. A young star was born on the back of another young star and both look here to stay.Mexico’s unofficial mascotMerlin the duck became a sensation after being spotted at Mexico’s post-game celebrations following their opening World Cup win over South Africa. Indeed, Merlin became so famous that he was granteda meeting with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. “We feel very honoured to be here with the president, it is an honour for us to stand before you and for the whole world to see the beautiful side of Mexico.” said Karla Gómez, Merlin’s owner. Sadly, Merlin wasunable to watch Mexico in the fleshdue to Fifa regulations.Death, taxesandMerino’s late winnersMessi, Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane … this has been a World Cup of goalscoring superstars well and truly coming to the fore, and thenthere has been Mikel Merino. The Spain midfielder came off the bench to score crucial winning goals against Portugal and Belgium in back-to-back knockout games. It was some contribution from the Arsenal player to his country’s World Cup triumph.View image in fullscreenMikel Merino races away after a late goal against Belgium.Photograph: Ringo Chiu/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAguirre meetsGordon“Gordon!” shouted Javier Aguirre at England’s left-sided forward during the first-half hydration break of an epic last-16 encounter at the Azteca, followed by something indistinguishable when Anthony Gordon turned back to look. Keen-eyed internet users later deciphered it as a very cheerful “fuck you!” from Mexico’s manager, with both men subsequently laughing with delight. “I’d just run the full-back down the line,” Gordon saidafter England’s 3-2 win. “So I took it as a bit of a compliment from him.”Vozinha’s star powerAfter being named player of the match in Cape Verde’sopening goalless draw with Spain, Vozinha teared up. “My mum didn’t manage to be here because of the visa,” said the 40-year-old goalkeeper. Two days later the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, announced that arrangements had been made to waive the cost of Ana Évora’s visa; she was subsequently in attendance as her son played in a2-2 draw with Uruguayand became one of the stars of the tournament.Penalty drama between Netherlands and MoroccoNeil El Aynaoui struck the crossbar. Justin Kluivert’s effort ricocheted off a post. Bart Verbruggen almost saved Soufiane Rahimi’s strike but helplessly watched it squirm under him and into the back of the net. At 2-2, Quinten Timber put his shot well wide, handing Morocco the advantage only for Achraf Hakimi to do the exact same thing. Standing bolt upright, Yassine Bounou saved from Crysencio Summerville before Ismael Saibari put an end to the rollercoaster of a trulyremarkable last-32 penalty shootout.Tuchel hits out at photographers“I’m begging Fifa to change the position of the photographers in the national anthem, because I could not see my team,” Thomas Tuchel said after England’sopening win against Croatia. “It was a very special moment, and I was standing in front of a wall of 50 photographers and I could not see one single player.” It wasn’t the first time at the tournament that England’s head coach made his frustrations clear.View image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel is not ready for his closeup.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesOpener smashes red-cardrecordMexico’s 2-0 win over South Africakicked off the World Cup and simultaneously almost equalled the 2022 tournament’s tally of red cards in a single match. Yaya Sithole capped off a terrible second half for South Africa by getting sent off just after the break before his teammate Themba Zwane and Mexican defender César Montes were shown red cards within eight minutes of each other.“Overturn this”With the vast majority of the football world rooting for them, Belgium reacted to the suspension of Folarin Balogun’s ban for the USA’s last-16 encounter with the Red Devils in Seattle with a ruthlessly commanding performance. Theybeat the co-hosts 4-1and marked the victory with a string of celebrations that made clear what they thought of thecontroversy surrounding’s Balogun’s presenceon the pitch, including an imitation of Donald Trump’s dance moves in the dressing room afterwards and a gleeful tweet from the team’s official account that simply read: “Overturn this.”Paraguay go from heroes to villainsThere was widespread delight whenParaguay eliminated Germany in the last 32with a show of togetherness and defiance but their popularity diminished during their subsequentdefeat by Franceon the back of a brutal display of the dark arts. Joe Hart brandished the South Americans an “absolute disgrace” while his fellow BBC pundit Micah Richards thought that the approach was wholly unnecessary, saying: “Paraguay are better than that. Defensively they were so good and they didn’t need to get into these antics.” The Uzbek referee, Ilgiz Tantashev, also faced intense criticism after inexplicably failing to book any Paraguay players.France players embrace DeschampsAfter Kylian Mbappé scored the first of his two goalsagainst Sweden, he and his teammates ran over to Didier Deschamps and hugged their head coach. The gesture was a response to Deschamps’ return to the touchline following the death of his mother. When asked about the embrace, Mbappé said: “That’s the DNA of this group. The coach has been through certain circumstances, and we’re all with him and will continue to support him.”View image in fullscreenDidier Deschamps is embraced by Kylian Mbappé as France take on Sweden.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesReferee stops play – with an injuryIn a bizarre twist, theUSA’s 2-0 victory over Australiain the group stages had to be stopped for, and not by, the referee, Felix Zwayer, after he collapsed with cramp in the dying minutes of the contest in Seattle. Australia’s midfielder Aiden O’Neill and the USA’s Balogun helped Zwayer stretch out the cramp amid ironic cheers from the crowd.Croatia goal disallowed by a hairCroatia had seemingly rescued their World Cup campaign from the jaws of defeat after Josko Gvardiol tapped in at the back post in the final stages of their last-32 encounter with Portugal in Toronto. But then VAR got involved and thegoal was ruled outafter Fifa’s sensor technology discovered that the cross to Gvardiol had taken the faintest touch off the head of Igor Matanovic. “It was very bad refereeing,” said Croatia’s manager, Zlatko Dalic. “I’m not saying that sometimes VAR can’t be of help, but it kills the emotions, it kills everything.”Jayden Adams tributesJayden Adams, who featured in all three of South Africa’s group games,passed away just days after returning homefrom North America. “Today, South African football mourn the loss of a talented player whose passion, dedication, and love for the beautiful game inspired many,” read a national team tribute. A minute’s silence was observed before all quarter-final matches, alongside an outpouring of touching tributes to the 25-year-old midfielder.Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Appeals court rejects Trump bid to curb mail-in voting in 23 states | US voting rights | The Guardian
description: Judge rejects administration’s request to lift injunction secured by several Democratic-led states on 25 June
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Judge rejects administration’s request to lift injunction secured by several Democratic-led states on 25 June
Content: Chester county, Pennsylvania, election workers process mail-in and absentee ballots at West Chester University in West Chester on 4 November 2020.Photograph: Matt Slocum/APView image in fullscreenChester county, Pennsylvania, election workers process mail-in and absentee ballots at West Chester University in West Chester on 4 November 2020.Photograph: Matt Slocum/APUS voting rightsAppeals court rejects Trump bid to curb mail-in voting in 23 statesJudge rejects administration’s request to lift injunction secured by several Democratic-led states on 25 JuneReutersSat 25 Jul 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal appeals court on Saturday declined to allow DonaldTrump’s administrationto implement in 23 states his executive order that aims to tighten rules for mail-in voting before the November elections that ⁠will decide control of Congress.The Boston-based ⁠first US circuit court ​of appeals rejected the administration’s request to lift an injunction several Democratic-led states secured on 25 June from a lower-court judge who concluded that key parts of the Republican president’s order were unconstitutional. In asking the court to ⁠pause the US district judge Indira Talwani’s ruling while it pursues an appeal, the Department of Justice argued that because government agencies had yet to finalize actions and policies to implement Trump’s directive, any lawsuit challenging his order was premature.The appeals court, ⁠in a 2-1 ruling, rejected that argument.“As the district court reasoned, the [executive order] lays out a clear set of rapidly approaching deadlines by which states must ​coordinate with federal officials and comply with new voting procedures – all while ‌the states must also ensure that their officials ‌and the public understand the evolving set of rules that would govern the upcoming September and November elections,” the judges wrote. “The Plaintiff States have no practical choice ‌but to respond to the [order] now.”Before Talwani ruled, a federal judge in Washington DC rejected a related effort by Democrats to block Trump’s order on similar grounds. The justice department warned that absent a ruling in its favor from the first circuit, it may be forced to ask the supreme court to intervene.Trump signed the executive order in March after years of calling for tighter rules on voting by mail and pushing the false claim that his 2020 election defeat was the result of widespread voter fraud. Under the US constitution, states are assigned the role ‌of administering federal elections.That order came on top of other efforts by Trump to overhaul elections. He has made winning approval in Congress of a divisive package of voting restrictions called the Save America Act a priority. Judges blocked an earlier ​executive order he signed requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and restricting the counting of mail-in ballots.The March order directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of confirmed US citizens eligible to vote in each state, derived from citizenship and naturalization records and other federal databases. Trump’s order also required the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on each state’s approved mail-in ballot list. USPS recently moved to implement Trump’s directive by ⁠issuing new proposed rules requiring states to provide the names and barcodes tied to their mail-in ballots.It also directed ​the DoJ to prioritize the investigation ​and prosecution of state and local election officials who ​issue federal ballots to people deemed “not eligible” to vote.But Talwani, in siding with a coalition of 23 states and ​the District of Columbia that was led ‌by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and ​Washington state, said the president lacked ​any authority to direct DHS to compile voter eligibility lists for each state to use and that USPS had no statutory authorization to adopt any binding regulations on mail-in voting.The judge, who was appointed by Barack Obama, said Trump also could not attempt through his order “to intimidate local election officials to use the necessarily incomplete confirmed citizenship lists as a resource, lest they face criminal prosecution”.Explore more on these topicsUS voting rightsLaw (US)Trump administrationDonald TrumpUS justice systemUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Japan avoid a Liz Truss-style shock as its PM embarks on a giant spending spree? | Japan | The Guardian
description: Sanae Takaichi’s blueprint to inject £1.7tn and double economic growth leaves many investors fearful
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Sanae Takaichi’s blueprint to inject £1.7tn and double economic growth leaves many investors fearful
Content: Sanae Takaichi, leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, puts a red paper rose on the name of an elected candidate at February’s general election.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenSanae Takaichi, leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, puts a red paper rose on the name of an elected candidate at February’s general election.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersJapanCan Japan avoid a Liz Truss-style shock as its PM embarks on a giant spending spree?Sanae Takaichi’s blueprint to inject £1.7tn and double economic growth leaves many investors fearfulPhillip InmanSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInternational investors are asking where Japan’s prime minister will find the ¥370tn (£1.7tn) of extra cash that she wants to invest in 17 industrial sectors by 2040.Such is the scale of spending by Sanae Takaichi’s coalition government that many in her own party fear she is about to blow up the Japanese economy, triggering aLiz Truss-style economic shock.Nerves are also jangling in financial markets, where investors are stunned by the plans of a usually sober Japanese government to rewrite previous budget rules and embark on a wide-ranging and unfunded shopping spree.The roots of Takaichi’s frustration date back to the financial crisis of 1991, when Japan’s property market bubble burst with spectacular effect. Tokyo had become the world’s most expensive place to live following the country’s export boom, but within months of the crash, banks behind much of the lending were bust.Before the turn of the century, a second slump brought more turmoil when some of Tokyo’s largest financial institutions, unable to cope with the hangover of bad debts from the first crash, went under.In the late 1980s, Japan’s government debts were equal to about 60% of national income, or gross domestic product (GDP). By the end of the 1990s, and after much of the financial sector had been bailed out, the debt to GDP ratio was 130%.Since the 2008 global financial shock, the economy has stagnated. In response, the government has regularly spent 10% more than it receives in tax receipts – much of it to cope with a rapidly ageing population – and debts have continued rising. By 2020, the debt-to-GDP ratio had reached 260% before tighter budgets and a modest improvement in economic growth brought it below 230% in 2025.Takaichi has said her investment plan will lift the productive capacity of the economy, keep Japan at the forefront of the AI revolution, and free the economy from its increasing dependence on trade with China.The stock market has reacted with a succession of downward steps ever since the proposals were unveiled in June, though the renewal of hostilities in the Middle East and the prospect of higher oil prices have not helped.Bank of Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high … of 1%Read moreMany investors sold up almost as soon as the government arrived in office, hitting the shares of the country’s biggest companies, among them Sony and Toyota Motor Corporation.Sony faces intense competition from rivals in South Korea and China while Toyota has stood out against all-electric cars, and now faces being crushed by aflourishing and highly subsidised Chinese car industry.Graph of Japanese interest rate rises from before 2024 and forecast beyond 2026Domestic and international lenders have pushed up the interest rate on Japanese government bonds (JGBs) to 2.8% in recent months, the highest in 29 years.Waning international support for Japan’s economic outlook has also hit the value of the yen. More recently it is Takaichi’s boldness, which like Truss’s is often characterised as recklessness, that has acted as a heavy weight on the currency, pushing it down to 163 to the US dollar, a four-decade low.Much of the blame for higher debt bills is connected to rising inflation, which has tracked upwards as the yen has fallen, largely because a low currency rate raises the price of imports of energy and raw materials.Although ​Japan’s core inflation has remained below the BoJ’s 2% target over the last four months, analysts a jump in the last quarter to the mid-2% ​range on higher oil prices following the Iran war.Kelvin Lam, an Asia specialist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, has said what the financial markets really fear is the lack of detail about where the fresh investment money will come from.“As long as you don’t say how you are going to finance your spending, you are on course for a Liz Truss moment,” he said, referring to the market response to the short-lived British prime minister’s plans for£45bn of unfunded tax cutsin September 2022.“The markets were already worried about Japan’s long term fiscal health and this plan hasn’t helped.”View image in fullscreenSanae Takaichi, third from right, at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, last month.Photograph: Thibault Camus/ReutersTakaichi’s conservative coalition secured victory last autumn with a slim majority that received a massive boost after shecalled February’s snap election, giving her a two-thirds majority in the lower house.A draft plan to revive the economy included forcing the Bank of Japan to walk in lockstep with the finance ministry and rewriting how government debt is calculated. A final submission agreed by the cabinet pledged to maintain central bank independence, but as a footnote.“To achieve a strong economy, it is very important for monetary policy to be conducted appropriately to see stable price rises,” it said.The damage was done, much as Truss found herself in an unrecoverable situation after going head to head with both the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility.Translated literally as big-boned policy, theHonebuto no Hoshininvestment scheme is aimed at injecting cash into 17 sectors over the next 14 years to more than double Japan’s economic growth to more than 1%.It will be a sharp ​break with previous leaders’ low-key policy blueprints and is in some respects reminiscent of Beijing’s grander five-year plans, which ​set national growth targets and direct industrial policy.View image in fullscreenPrecision machines for automotive parts in a factory at Kyowa Industrial Co, Takasaki, Japan.Photograph: Issei Kato/ReutersThe blueprint targets areas such as AI, semiconductors, biotech, defence, energy and shipbuilding to achieve a 1% growth rate “as early as possible”.The document emphasises “physical artificial intelligence” that combines AI with Japan’s strength in manufacturing hardware “to accelerate AI transformation in all sectors”.Forecasts by economists typically point to growth of 0.93% in 2027 and 0.85% in 2028, falling short of the 1% target, according to the Japan Center for Economic Research thinktank.In the background, successive governments have sought to disguise the country’s difficulties. Since 2022, the ministry of finance has spent about £160bn in efforts to limit the yen’s decline. It has also put pressure on the central bank to keep interest rates low amid a global drive to increase them to combat inflation after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.The BoJ has raised its policy rate to a 31-year high of 1%, but that is still low relative to its peers.Following the Covid-19 pandemic, all central banks financed government spending by buying government debt. While most have sought to reverse the situation in recent years, the BoJ is being encouraged to go further. Japanese pension funds are also feeling heat from the finance ministry, which expects them to buy government bonds out of a sense of patriotic duty.Takaichi said in a recent post on X that she spends all day and most of the night plotting Japan’s recovery, which is seen by many as an attempt to reverse last month’s 10-point poll rating decline.View image in fullscreenSanae Takaichi receives the award for buzzword of the year last December for her phrase ‘I will work, work, work, work, and work.’Photograph: Jiji Press/EPATakaichi is aware her project is fraught with danger now that financial markets have voiced their scepticism. Many are asking if an emphasis on manufacturing will prove successful as China seeks to produce more sophisticated goods, stepping into territory previously dominated by Japan, Germany and the US.The question is whether Tokyo has the resources to go up against Beijing and carve out a big enough niche to fund itself in the 2030s. Exports rose 20% year-on-year in June, but after taking into account the yen’s depreciation, the value of the rise was almost zero.Depreciating the currency every year to boost trade is not a sustainable policy. Maybe Takaichi’s investment plan will be.Explore more on these topicsJapanSanae TakaichiAsia PacificInvestmentsStock marketsLiz TrussEconomicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Southport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyer | Southport attack | The Guardian
description: Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
Content: Flowers and tributes outside the Atkinson Art Centre Southport after the attack on 29 July 2024.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenFlowers and tributes outside the Atkinson Art Centre Southport after the attack on 29 July 2024.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PASouthport attackSouthport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyerComment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospitalSammy GecsoylerSat 25 Jul 2026 06.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lawyer for the families of Axel Rudakubana’s victims has said the Southport killer is “trying to retraumatise the families from his cell” after it emergedhe had been transferred from prison to a psychiatric hospital.Rudakubana, now 19, was given a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.The Guardian revealed on Thursday thatRudakubana had been transferred to the high-security hospital Broadmoorfrom the category A prison Belmarsh after it was concluded that he could not be managed safely in jail.Next Wednesday marks two years since he carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024, which was followed by largely far-right riots that spread across the country.Earlier this week, the Ministry of Justice confirmed that Rudakubana had been transferred from prison to the psychiatric facility Broadmoor hospital.A spokesperson for the department stressed it did not alter the killer’s 52-year sentence.Chris Walker, who is representing the three bereaved families, told BBC Breakfast: “It’s a deep concern of mine that this is a pattern starting to develop by him trying to retraumatise the families from his cell, and it’s a deep concern that this is going to occur every anniversary.”He added that there was “no suggestion” that Rudakubana was under any form of “psychosis” when he carried out the murders.The families were informed of the decision in a letter on 22 July but were not given details on why the transfer happened.Walker said: “With the vacuum of information, the concern is that he’s manipulating the situation to his own benefit. For it to come out the week before the anniversary seems coincidental to us.“Whether that’s been poorly handled by the government, or whether it’s designed by him.”Sally Jameson, a housing minister and former prison officer, said on Friday that Rudakubana would be returned to prison “as soon as possible” but that she was not familiar with why the decision had been taken to move him.Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust previously confirmed Rudakubana had been under its care as a mental health patient between 2019 and 2023, when he “stopped engaging”. He was referred to them after taking a knife to school and later saying he had done so “to use it”.He was also referred to the UK’s counter-extremism programme, Prevent, because he had been researching school massacres on a computer at his next school, the Acorns.There were two other referrals to Prevent, but none were progressed as Rudakubana had no clear ideology behind his obsession with violence.Offenders who present an increased risk, and cannot be managed safely in a prison environment because of mental disorders, can be moved to secure psychiatric units.People in these units are treated as patients rather than prisoners.Broadmoor, in Crowthorne, Berkshire, is the oldest of England’s three high-security psychiatric hospitals. It has been used to hold some of the UK’s most notorious murderers including Peter Sutcliffe, the Yorkshire Ripper.Patients remain locked up, with conditions heavily regulated by strict physical security including locked wards, monitored by staff and 24-hour CCTV. They receive mandatory therapeutic and rehabilitative programmes. If offenders no longer require treatment in hospital, the 1983 Mental Health Act provides for a swift return to prison.Walker said: “When he did what he did, it was carefully planned, it was meticulous and it was designed to cause the maximum distress to society. There’s no evidence of any mental health disorder being a component of his crime. There’s no evidence of psychosis.“The families say, given that, he needs to serve a prison sentence, he should not be going to hospital. He needs to be in prison.”Explore more on these topicsSouthport attackSentencingPrisons and probationUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 75% of England’s riverbanks ‘off limits’ to public, figures show | Access to green space | The Guardian
description: Campaigners urge government to introduce right of access to water, particularly as heatwaves become more common
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Campaigners urge government to introduce right of access to water, particularly as heatwaves become more common
Content: People seeking relief from this summer’s heat in the River Avon near Bath.Photograph: Andrew Lloyd/AlamyView image in fullscreenPeople seeking relief from this summer’s heat in the River Avon near Bath.Photograph: Andrew Lloyd/AlamyAccess to green spaceAlmost 75% of England’s riverbanks ‘off limits’ to public, figures showCampaigners urge government to introduce right of access to water, particularly as heatwaves become more commonSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost three-quarters of riverbanks inEnglandhave no public access, according to data released by the Right to Roam campaign.Across the country, the public cannot use riverbanks or gain access to the rivers themselves in most of the river catchments from the west of Cornwall up to the Tweed, which flows through northern England and Scotland.Lewis Winks, an environmental social scientist from Right to Roam, who led the research, said: “Access to rivers should be a basic right, yet the vast majority remain off limits.
