As we continue to experience extreme heat, it’s vital the public are able to draw from the benefits that water brings.”The campaigners are calling on Angela Eagle, the new environment secretary, to launch a promised but long-delayed consultation on access –as part of an access to nature green paper– and introduce a right of responsible access to water and land in the next king’s speech.The research showed 71% of riverbanks along main rivers and tributaries in the 89 river catchments examined lacked any adjoining access to land or right of way within 100m of the water.The finding was consistent regardless of whether urban areas were included. There is also no defined statutory right to the water itself on 96% of rivers in England and Wales, which means activities such as swimming and paddling are often contested by landowners, and the vast majority of inland waters, including reservoirs and lakes, are treated as off limits.First of nine new river walks in England announced for north-westRead moreKate Rew, from the Outdoor Swimming Society, said in 20 years time she wanted to see living rivers across England, with people free to reach them to swim, paddle, walk and spend time by the water.“Being part of the natural world makes us healthier, happier and more alive,” said Rew. “But this is not only about what rivers can give us. We need to give rivers back some of the life we’ve taken out. People rarely fight for places they’re excluded from, and right now our rivers need people to fight for them. The work of restoring our rivers begins by reconnecting people with them.”Keir Starmer’s government committed to creating nine new national river walks, but Winks said the first of these, on the River Mersey, had not created any additional access.The fight foraccessible and swimmable waterwayshas become a major public issue, especially as record-breaking heatwaves prompt families and young people to seek free ways to cool down, although rescue services havewarned people to take carewhen entering cold water.The data published by Right to Roam revealed what it said were significant regional disparities in river access. In the Severn Middle Shropshire catchment, 90% of the riverbank had no right of access, while in the New Forest catchment, that figure was 49%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA barge on the River Severn in Worcester.Photograph: David Davies/PAThe lack of access is so widespread that many designated long-distance walking trails are named after rivers they cannot follow. These include the section of the Severn Way between Shrewsbury and Telford, which is almost entirely divorced from the river – diverting more than 800m away in some places, said Winks. The majority of the Test Way, a 44-mile (71km) walk named after the chalk stream, does not follow the river itself.A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said:“This government is focused on the things that matter most to the British public, including restoring nature so that we have pride in local communities and access to green spaces.“We are increasing access to nature and the countryside, delivering nine new national river walks, a coast-to-coast route in the north of England and the 2,700-mile King Charles III England coast path.”Explore more on these topicsAccess to green spaceRiversLand rightsEnglandEnvironmental activismEnvironment policyWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Lofty ambitions: can puffer jackets be made more sustainable? | Winter coats | The Guardian
description: As temperature dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying new
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: As temperature dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying new
Content: Given the price of padded jackets and how hard they are to recycle, experts recommend extending your puffer’s lifespan as much as possible.Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGiven the price of padded jackets and how hard they are to recycle, experts recommend extending your puffer’s lifespan as much as possible.Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty ImagesChange by degreesWinter coatsLofty ambitions: can puffer jackets be made more sustainable?As temperatures dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying newChange by degreesoffers life hacks and sustainable living tips each Saturday to help reduce your household’s carbon footprintGot a question or tip for reducing household emissions? Email us atchangebydegrees@theguardian.comSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockFri 24 Jul 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 02.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether you call it a parka, puffer or Tassie tuxedo, the insulated jacket has become a cold-weather closet staple.A 1920s version by Australian mountaineer George Finch was constructed from hot air balloon fabric and eiderdown, but most modern designs are amix of petroleum-based syntheticsas well as animal and plant fibres, with varying environmental and ethical impacts.Producing these materials, through agricultural or chemical processes, contributes 83% to the jacket’s overall carbon and water footprint, according toone life cycle study. The next largest contributor was water and energy usage during wear – with the average down jacket lasting seven years – followed by sewing and disposal. Natural fibres like down and wool also add animal welfare considerations.But, like all clothing items, the effects are multiplied across global production and consumption systems. The market for puffers is large and growing, with more than 100m jackets made in China annually. Some brands are even branching into new territory, with demand forpuppy pufferssoaring.Dr Carolina Quintero Rodriguez, a senior lecturer at RMIT University’s school of fashion and textiles, says advertising and social media are encouraging us to purchase more than we need.“That is incentivising or creating a need in the population for not only one jacket, but you need three jackets,” she says.A recentAdelaide University studyof nearly 600 people’s clothing habits found 89% of garments are bought new, with padded jackets one of the most expensive items that people own, but rarely wear, which provides a ready supply of secondhand puffers in great condition. That’s why it’s important to choose a good quality garment, from a responsible brand, and wear it and repair it for as long as possible.One jacket, many ingredientsJulie Boulton, a sustainable fashion consultant, says puffers usually consist of an inner and outer shell, a filler (“the stuff that makes it puff”), and notions like zips, snaps or buttons and thread.Setting store: how to keep woollen coats and puffer jackets packed away safelyRead moreShells are usually made from fossil fuel-derived materials, such as nylon or polyester, sometimes blended with cotton or wool.Jackets labelled “100% recycled” usually comprise polyesters made from plastic waste, such as water bottles or used textiles.The padding inside often consists of duck or goose feathers (called down), wool, or a synthetic fill, Boulton says. Some brands, like Pangaia, are moving to plant-based fluff, made from wildflowers, biopolymers and aerogel.According to the life cycle study, polyester fibre production, spinning, weaving, fabric dyeing and finishing are all high-energy consumption processes.Polyester is a petroleum-based fibre that has issues with greenhouse gas emissions and shedding microplastics, Quintero Rodriguez says. Natural down is biodegradable and a byproduct of the meat industry, she says, but can come with risks associated with animal welfare and supply chain opacity.Down is made by plucking the soft feathers of ducks or geese, usually after slaughter,according to the RSPCA, although a small percentage (1 to 2%) is still thought to be collected from live plucking, a practice the organisation says is a major welfare concern. Consumers are encouraged to look for the Responsible Down Standard, a voluntary certification that requires higher levels of animal welfare, traceability and prohibits live plucking.View image in fullscreenSome outdoor brands offer repair services or kits to help people patch and mend their puffer jackets.Photograph: Tatiana/Getty Images/iStockphotoWhen it comes to wool, Dr Natalie Roadknight, a senior scientific officer at the RSPCA, says the biggest welfare concern is a practice called mulesing, which involves cutting an area of skin near the tail. “It’s done while the lamb is completely conscious,” she says. “They’re able to feel the cuts”. Australia is one of the only countries where the practice is still legal, with the procedure banned in New Zealand and other countries.Consumers can choose to avoid wool products that involve mulesing, by asking the brand directly, or looking for the ZQ Merino or the Responsible Wool Standard.Re-wear and repairAustralians buy 1.5bn new items of clothing each year, and send 220,000 tonnes to landfill, areport by Seamless, Australia’s clothing stewardship scheme, has found.“If you’re thinking about getting a jacket, look secondhand, look from your friends,don’t think that you’ve got to go and buy new,” says Boulton.After that, the key is to keep it in service for as long as possible, she says. “While you’ve got it, use it, and wear it, wash it responsibly and take care of it and repair it.”Some outdoor brands offer repair services or kits to help people patch and mend their winter coats. About one in 10 items are repaired, the Adelaide University study found, even though mending extended a garment’s useful life by 2.5 years on average.Quintero Rodriguez says most garments don’t need to be washed as often as people think; sometimes, airing them out is enough. But if you do have to clean them, use cold water, she says, because heat can damage synthetic fabrics like nylons or elastane.Gentle washing can also extend the life of water resistant or repellentsurfaces in raincoats, with some finishes able to be reapplied or reactivated.Can puffers be recycled?Nationally, about half of unwanted clothes end up in landfill (53%), another 38% are reused locally or exported, and 9% are recycled.Textile recycling is a time and labour intensive process, Boulton says, partly due to a lack of infrastructure and also because the price of virgin polyester is so cheap. Someoutdoor brandsdo offer take back schemes,through places like Upparel.“It’s cheaper just to make a whole new [jacket] than it is to recover and repurpose, or deconstruct, recycle and put back into the system again, which is such a shame.”Quintero Rodriguez says: “My main message will be to extend the life of the item as much as possible. Care for the item as per the care instructions. And to make sure that you purchase [only] what you need.”Explore more on these topicsWinter coatsChange by degreesEthical and green livingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Home Office rejects Palestinian Jerusalemite woman’s UK visa but approves husband’s | Home Office | The Guardian
description: Officials not satisfied Therese Abdallah is a ‘genuine visitor’ and believe she would not leave after visit to son in London
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Officials not satisfied Therese Abdallah is a ‘genuine visitor’ and believe she would not leave after visit to son in London
Content: The Home Office had previously refused a visa application from Therese Abdallah in 2019, but she had previously travelled to the UK for academic visits with no problems.Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Home Office had previously refused a visa application from Therese Abdallah in 2019, but she had previously travelled to the UK for academic visits with no problems.Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesHome OfficeHome Office rejects Palestinian Jerusalemite woman’s UK visa but approves husband’sOfficials not satisfied Therese Abdallah is a ‘genuine visitor’ and believe she would not leave after visit to son in LondonDiane TaylorSat 25 Jul 2026 05.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Palestinian Jerusalemite who lives in London has been left devastated after a planned trip by his parents had to be cancelled when theHome Officeruled his mother was not a “genuine visitor” but granted his father a visa.Karim Abdallah, who has lived in the UK since 2019, was looking forward to hosting his parents, Therese Abdallah, 69, a retired English teacher, and his father, Ghassan Abdallah, a psychologist, for a few weeks.Both parents have previously travelled to the UK for academic visits without any visa problems, but in a rejection letter a Home Office worker said they could not be sure Therese would return home at the end of the trip.View image in fullscreen‘I was so looking forward to showing my parents places like Kew Gardens. The Home Office has ruined our summer holiday plans,’ Karim Abdallah said.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe decision was made all the more surprising by the fact that her husband of 40 years, who applied via the same process, had his visa approved.Palestinian Jerusalemites have a unique status. They are not Israeli citizens but have Israeli and Jordanian travel documents. As Karim’s mother needed separate visas for trips to London and to a family wedding in Ireland, she made one application with her Israeli travel document and the other with her Jordanian one.She had had a UK visa application refused in 2019 based on a technical issue about submitting her bank statement as proof of her financial means in Hebrew, according to Karim.But when Therese applied this time, the Home Office rejected her current visa application, stating: “I note that your UK ties out weight (sic) your home country ties.”The official was not confident she would leave the UK at the end of her visit. “I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that you are a genuine visitor,” they stated in the refusal letter. She was told she had no right to an appeal or administrative review of the decision.In fact, she only has one immediate family member living in the UK: her son. She has another son, an oncologist, who lives with his wife and children in East Jerusalem along with extended family members, friends and her wider community.Therese was born in East Jerusalem, has lived there for her whole life and, according to her son, would not want to lose her residency status, which would be at risk if she stayed away for too long.Karim said: “Both my parents applied for their UK visitor visa using the same invitation from my partner and me. We provided the same evidence for both of them about our financial means to support them during their visit. I have lived legally in the UK for the last eight years, work and pay my taxes and do not have access to any benefits in the UK. I am proud of my contribution here.”He added: “As well as the family wedding in Ireland I was so looking forward to showing my parents places like Kew Gardens, which is not far from where we live. The Home Office has ruined our summer holiday plans.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All visa applications are assessed on their individual merits and the evidence provided, including any declarations relating to previous visa refusals.”Explore more on these topicsHome OfficePalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK’s largest Muslim event goes ahead with added security as hate crime rises | Islam | The Guardian
description: Jalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authorities
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Jalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authorities
Content: The 2025 Jalsa Salana festival in Alton, Hampshire.Photograph: Ahmadiyya Muslim Community/PAView image in fullscreenThe 2025 Jalsa Salana festival in Alton, Hampshire.Photograph: Ahmadiyya Muslim Community/PAIslamUK’s largest Muslim event goes ahead with added security as hate crime risesJalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authoritiesAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity has been increased by several hundred additional staff at the UK’s largest Muslim convention, Jalsa Salana, alongside enhanced coordination with police, emergency services and local authorities, against a backdrop of growing anti-Muslim sentiment.Last month, another big Islamic gathering was forced to close earlyafter 12 people were arrested, including three on suspicion of conspiracy to murder, over a suspected far-right threat.Did Jalsa Salana’s organisers think twice about going ahead?“Not once. Not for a second,” said Rafiq Hayat, the head of the UK chapter of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, which organises the festival.View image in fullscreenRafiq Hayat, head of the UK chapter of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianNow in its 60th year, Jalsa Salana is expected to draw about 50,000 people from more than 100 countries to a temporary site inHampshirethis weekend. The convention opened on Friday with prayers, speeches – including an address from the community’s global leader, Hazrat Mirza Masroor Ahmad – and the raising of a union jack at the centre of the 208-acre site. MPs, bishops and other public figures are expected to attend.Hayat says the community has weathered hostility before. The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community has been in Britain for more than a century, having established itself in 1913, and built one of London’s first purpose-built mosques in 1926.“I personally have been in London since 1967, so I have been through all of the various rightwing movements: from skinheads, to the ‘rivers of blood’ speech by Enoch Powell to the British National party. We have seen it all,” Hayat said.During the construction of the movement’s mosque in Morden in the 1990s, hundreds of British National party supporters protested outside planning meetings, he added.But rather than withdrawing, Hayat said, the community deliberately invested in relationships with its neighbours.“We created a liaison group,” Hayat said. “We invited people from the church and from various local groups, from the local authority to the police. And we said we would hold a meeting every month at our mosque, and appointed a local councillor as the chair of the meeting.”He added that the first two meetings were “very heated”. But, 30 years later, “they will not do anything without us being involved”.For Hayat, that experience provides a useful lesson to how to respond to this current climate of rising anti-Muslim hatred. Latest figures show thatone mosque is attacked in Britain every five days, while anti-Muslim hate crime in England and Wales rose by 19% in the 12 months to March 2025.“One of the things that the community has been doing over the last 60 years is to bring people of all faith, all backgrounds, all ethnicities, everyone, together,” Hayat said. “The founder of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community reminded us that true Muslims should embody the teaching of the holy prophet Muhammad – that loyalty to the country in which you live is an integral part of your faith.”But hostility towards the Ahmadiyya community does not come solely from the far right. Ahmadis have long faced persecution from extremist Muslims, both abroad, particularly in Pakistan and, at times, in Britain.In 2016, Asad Shah, an Ahmadi Muslim man, was killed outside his shop in Glasgow by another Muslim in a religiously motivated murder.“The saddest part is that it is sometimes easier to deal with the rightwing than with some Muslim extremists,” Hayat said. “I grew up with lots of Muslims. Some of my closest friends are Muslims who are not Ahmadi. But there are some who have very extreme views.“But when we have these conferences, lots of Muslims come. When we had the big iftar at our large mosque, about 60% were young Muslims who weren’t Ahmadi.”Hayat said the community’s answer to threats was not to retreat from public life but to become more visible.“We say to our children that they must not be embarrassed about being Muslim in this country,” he said. “These misconceptions aboutIslamhave to be dealt with. And this is what I say to the larger Muslim community: please engage with people.”He didn’t minimise the level of threat facing the Muslim community, pointing to a recent incident in which one of their mosques was attacked, while hatred against Muslims had become increasingly visible online.Yet, he passionately believes that personal encounters remain the most effective antidote.Hayat recalled one visitor who admitted she had shared her live location with her husband before visiting the mosque, telling him that if he did not hear from her every 15 minutes, he should come to get her.Afterwards, she told Hayat she found warmth at the mosque and wanted to return with her family.“You don’t see my colour any more. You see the human being behind it. This is the key to peaceful coexistence,” Hayat said.Explore more on these topicsIslamIslamophobiaHampshireReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Proxy for Trump’ Milei tours Latin America to meet far-right leaders | Javier Milei | The Guardian
description: Tour comes amid Argentinian president’s declining popularity and far-right victories across Latin America
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Tour comes amid Argentinian president’s declining popularity and far-right victories across Latin America
Content: Javier Milei in Buenos Aires on 16 July.Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/ReutersView image in fullscreenJavier Milei in Buenos Aires on 16 July.Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/ReutersJavier Milei‘Proxy for Trump’ Milei tours Latin America to meet far-right leadersTour comes amid Argentinian president’s declining popularity and far-right victories across Latin AmericaTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArgentina’s president, Javier Milei, is not particularly fond of travelling to multilateral forums – it is not unusual for him to skip Mercosur summits, as he did a fewweeks ago.But on Saturday he begins a tour of Latin America to meet far-right leaders, starting inBrazilwith the launch of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign against the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, ahead of October’s election.Milei will then attendKeiko Fujimori’s inauguration in Peru on Tuesday, followed byAbelardo de la Espriella’s inauguration in Colombia on 7 August, from where he will travel to Ecuador to meet presidentDaniel Noboa.The self-styled libertarian hasjustifiedthe trips as those of “a president willing to open up to the world, seeking to triple the country’s trade”.But analysts point to the timing: amid hisdeclining popularityat home, the tour comes in the wake of a wave offar-right victoriesin presidential elections across Latin America.“As someone who has been in power for a little longer, Milei is trying to establish himself as a leader of that group,” said Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, a researcher and professor at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile.“I’ve never seen Milei take much interest in official visits to other countries,” said Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a sociologist and professor at Universidad Torcuato Di Tella in Buenos Aires. “What interests him are figures from the world ofbig techand the far right, but in neither case is there any real interest in opening trade negotiations,” he added.Benjamin Gedan, a senior fellow and director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said a constant in Milei’s trips has been his effort to remain “deferential to the US president, Donald Trump, and never trying to upstage him”.When Trump took office in January 2025, Milei faced relatively little competition for his affection in Latin America, where fewer than a dozen other far-right presidents were in office, most notably El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. Trump described Milei as his “favourite president”.Since then, however, rightwing or far-right candidates have won all seven presidential elections held in the region, with the US presidentaccusedof attempting to influencesome of them.Almost all of the winners alsointeractedwith Milei during their campaigns through public exchanges of praise or video calls but, according to Tokatlian, there is no doubt about whom they were really trying to please.“All these rightwing leaders see Milei as a kind of proxy for Trump, who is the one who is really in charge. They don’t want to be under any kind of Argentine leadership. It’s Milei who’s trying, but there’s no great eagerness for him,” he said.Tokatlian believes that any contest for Trump’s favour, if one exists at all, will be decided by “whoever gives the US the most on drug trafficking, migration, military cooperation and containing China’s influence”.The US has signed aseriesof military cooperation agreements with countries across the region. In March, Trump launched theShield of the Americas, a “counter-cartel coalition” made up exclusively of far-right leadersaligned with him. Notablyabsentwere key countries for drug production and trafficking in the region – Mexico, Brazil and Colombia – all of which are governed by leftwing administrations.After being elected, De la Espriella said that Colombia would join the initiative and establish a local Shield of the Americasoffice in Medellín.Ariel Goldstein, a researcher and professor at the University of Buenos Aires, believes Milei nonetheless remains ahead of the others in the race for Trump’s attention.“He has already spent the past two or three years building an intense relationship of friendship and subordination with the US,” he said.When Trump was re-elected, Milei travelled to Palm Beach to become thefirst foreign leaderto meet him after his victory.The Argentinian president has also emulated a number of policies from his US counterpart, includingwithdrawingfrom the World Health Organization and tighteningimmigration policies.Last year, Trump offered a $40bn US bailout that was widely seen ascrucialto the libertarian party’s victory in Argentina’smidterm elections.However, Milei’s path to re-election next year is far from looking smooth: although inflationhas fallen, purchasing power hasalso declined, while unemployment and informality have risen and his administration has been hit bycorruption scandals.Meanwhile, Goldstein believes that Milei and Trump are now heavily invested in winning the next major prize on the electoral calendar: Latin America’s largest country, Brazil.Besides attending the launch ofFlávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, the Argentinian president had hoped to visit the senator’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest after being convicted over an attempted coup, but the request was denied by a justice. Milei has never held a bilateral meeting with Lula.“A Bolsonaro victory would be hugely important to Milei and Trump because it would allow them to reorganise the whole region around an axis of subordination to the US,” said Goldstein.Explore more on these topicsJavier MileiArgentinaBrazilPeruColombiaEcuadornewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot wounds | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
Content: Police investigate the scene of the fatal house fire on 24 July 2026 in Grand Haven Township, Michigan.Photograph: Joel Bissell/Kalamazoo Gazette/APView image in fullscreenPolice investigate the scene of the fatal house fire on 24 July 2026 in Grand Haven Township, Michigan.Photograph: Joel Bissell/Kalamazoo Gazette/APMichiganEight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot woundsFirefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of childrenMarina DunbarSat 25 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA devastating tragedy has unfolded inMichiganafter emergency crews responding to a house fire found eight members of the same family, including six children, dead. At least some of the dead inside the home had gunshot wounds.Deputies with the Ottawa county sheriff’s office and firefighters from the Grand Haven fire department were dispatched at about 11.40am local time on Friday to a residence on Riverside Trail in Grand Haven Township.Once crews entered the smoke-filled home to extinguish the fire, they made the grim discovery.“Units made entry inside to battle the fire because there was smoke showing from the residence. When they got inside, they noticed that there were several people deceased inside the home,” Capt Jacob Sparks said at apress conference. “Some of the victims did have gunshot wounds to their bodies.”Officials confirmed the victims were two adults and six children aged five to 15. Their identities have not yet been released.Autopsies are scheduled to be completed over the weekend, according toABC News, as investigators continue working to determine exactly what happened.Authorities said they are not currently looking for any suspects from outside the home, though Sparks stressed the investigation is ongoing.“I don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point,” he said.Investigators with theMichiganstate police’s arson team have joined the investigation. Officials believe the fire originated inside the residence, but the exact cause and point of origin have not yet been determined.The home is located in Grand Haven Township, just outside the city of Grand Haven and about 20 miles (32km) south of Muskegon, Michigan.The investigation remains active, and authorities said additional information is expected after the victims’ autopsies are completed.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS crimeGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lou Koller, frontman of New York hardcore band Sick of It All, dies aged 59 | New York | The Guardian
description: Keller, who co-founded the celebrated band in 1986, had been battling cancer of the esophagus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Keller, who co-founded the celebrated band in 1986, had been battling cancer of the esophagus
Content: Lou Koller performs with Sick of It All in Copenhagen, Denmark, on 14 June 2023.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenLou Koller performs with Sick of It All in Copenhagen, Denmark, on 14 June 2023.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsNew YorkLou Koller, frontman of New York hardcore band Sick of It All, dies aged 59Koller, who co-founded the celebrated band in 1986, had been battling cancer of the esophagusGuardian staffSat 25 Jul 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLou Koller, the singer and co-founder ofNew Yorkhardcore band Sick of It All, has died after a battle with cancer, his bandmates announced. Koller was 59.In asocial media poston the band’s Instagram page, a statement paid tribute to Koller and his work and said: “The level of loss that we feel at this time is overwhelming.”It added: “We have lost a beloved friend and an iconic frontman. Lou had the power to raise everyone’s spirits at our shows with a smile and a sarcastic comment, and he won people over wherever we played, from every culture and every corner of the world.”Koller revealed in June 2024 that he was suffering from cancer of the esophagus, which had extended into his stomach. His illness forced the band to cancel a European tour while he underwent treatment. This year would have seen the band celebrate its 40th anniversary.After intensive treatment, including chemotherapy, Koller was declared cancer-free in May 2025, but the cancer returned shortly after.“His battle is over now and he can finally rest. Hopefully he can somehow still see and feel the beautiful, positive mark he left on the world,” the band’s statement said.Koller was born and raised in Queens, New York. He co-launched Sick of It All with his younger brother and drummer Armand Majidi in 1986 and become a key part of the city’s hardcore music scene. Sick of It All released 12 studio albums and became popular globally through many years of concert touring, winning a passionate audience for their work.This article was amended on 25 July 2026. Lou Koller’s name was originally misspelled in the headline as Keller.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkPunknewsShareReuse this content

title: How English-speaking Colombian islands have been caught up in Trump’s ‘drug war’ airstrikes | Colombia | The Guardian
description: At least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence said to have gone missing since January after US began attacking boats in Caribbean and eastern Pacific
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: At least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence said to have gone missing since January after US began attacking boats in Caribbean and eastern Pacific
Content: A beach on San Andrés island.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA beach on San Andrés island.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianColombiaHow English-speaking Colombian islands have been caught up in Trump’s ‘drug war’ airstrikesAt least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence said to have gone missing since January after US began attacking boats in Caribbean and eastern PacificTiago Rogeroand Daniela Díaz in San Andrés and ProvidenceSat 25 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficially, the islands of San Andrés and Providence belong toColombia– but the language spoken by most of the local Afro-descendant population is not Spanish.Walking among brightly painted wooden houses raised above the ground and lined with verandas – architecture more reminiscent of the Caribbean and the southern US – the language most commonly heard isCreole, a distinct variety of Caribbean English.Yet the same emerald waters that provide fish for local communities andattract touristsfrom around the world have become “mass graves” for local fishers.Because of the islands’ strategic location north-west of mainland Colombia between South and North America, young seafaring-skilled men have for years been recruited by groups moving cocaine produced in Colombia northwards, often as far as the US.They are members of the Raizal people, shaped by different waves of settlement over the centuries, but above all, defined by their African heritage.US military kills three people in boat strike in Pacific OceanRead moreAlthough the involvement of young Raizal men in drug trafficking is not new, residents agree it is growing and has acquired a dramatic dimension since the US began bombing speedboats allegedly carrying drugs in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific. The airstrikes havekilled 215 people since Septemberin what the UN hascondemned as “extrajudicial killings”.At least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence have gone missing since January, according to Edgar Jay Stephens, 58, the president of the main local association of fishers, I-Fish. He said some of them might have been carrying drugs, but “certainly” not all.The disappearances have also been a decades-long problem on the islands – whether because the men were killed, arrested by other countries or fell victim to harsh conditions at sea – but Stephens said the current pace was unprecedented.View image in fullscreenEdgar Jay Stephens puts the number of fishers from San Andrés and Providence to have disappeared this year at 16.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianA spokesperson for US Southern Command, which conducts the airstrikes, said it “does not comment on specific operational details”, but added: “We have no information of any strikes, operations, seizures, or arrests involving residents of San Andrés or Providence.”Given that the US hasrecently denied responsibilityfor other bombings in accounts that lawmakers, experts and academics have criticised as inconsistent, Stephens does not rule out the possibility it were involved.“How many people could have died without us knowing what happened to them?” he asked, echoing a frequent criticism made by human rights activists about the bombings: the US does not release information about the victims, making their identification a difficult task that has been accomplished inlittle more than a dozen cases, thanks mainly to the efforts oflawyersandjournalists.The sister of one of the 16 missing men said her brother had been trafficking drugs alongside two other Raizal men. “He accepted the job because it was easy money and he wanted to buy a plot of land and build a house,” said the sister, who asked not to be identified.When she saw the news ofa US airstrike on a speedboatcarrying three men near Costa Rica, she sent his documents to Colombia’s embassy in the neighbouring country, hoping he might be identified among the three. He was not.Meanwhile, Raizal fishers point to another consequence of the attacks: a direct impact on their livelihoods, as has happened in other traditional communities across the region.View image in fullscreenWith US airstrikes making the area more dangerous, fishers have changed their routes.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“We’ve changed our routines,” said Ling Jay Robinson, 38, explaining that there have been days when he chose not to go out to sea.“Those people [the US military] could mistake us for traffickers and bomb us. We’re living with fear,” said Robinson, who is the son, grandson, great-grandson and great-great-grandson of fishers. “It goes back through our ancestors.”The islands of San Andrés and Providence lie closer to the coast of Nicaragua – 260 miles (420km) away – than to mainland Colombia, which is 450 miles distant.After being initially claimed by Spain,they were permanently settled when English Puritans arrived in 1629.Pirates also passed through, and although Spain later reasserted control, it did not expel the English settlers. Enslaved Africans were subsequently brought to work on plantations, particularly cotton estates.View image in fullscreenSan Andrés and Providence are quite small, with populations of 56,000 and 6,000 respectively.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianFollowing Colombia’s independence, the islands agreed to become part of the new nation. But it was only from 1912 onward that the state began to exert significant influence, imposing Catholicism and Spanish as the official religion and language in place of Protestantism and Creole.To this day, however, many Raizales prefer to call Providence by its older name rather than the official Spanish one, Providencia.“I would say that the Raizal people are trilingual. We speak English, Spanish and Creole,” said the political scientist Sally Ann García Taylor, who was born in San Andrés and whose mother is from Providence.The Raizal people, she said, were the product of the interactions between all the peoples who had passed through the islands, although “Afro-descendant heritage is a major element in the formation of our identity”.Another profound change came in 1953, when the government declared San Andrés a freeport – exempting imported goods from taxes – and encouraged large-scale migration from mainland Colombia.The impact is still felt today in the island’s overcrowding. San Andrés, whose airport has daily flights to Bogotá and even Panama, covers 26 sq km (10 sq miles) and is home to 56,000 people. Providence, which has flights only to the neighbouring island, spans 17 sq km and has just 6,000 residents. Many local people say that, with its lack of hotels, fancy restaurants and duty-free shops, it is “like San Andrés 50 years ago”.The difference is also reflected in the islands’ ethnic makeup: while Raizales account for about 91% of Providence’s population, they now make up only 35% of San Andrés’s.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA house on Providence, which has largely preserved its traditional Caribbean architecture.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe contrast is also visible in the architecture. Providence, although still recovering fromHurricane Iota, which devastated more than 90% of its infrastructure in 2020, has largely preserved its traditional Caribbean architecture, while in San Andrés it is largely confined to the island’s southern areas, where most Raizales live.“If you ask how many Raizales own hotels in San Andrés, I don’t think there are even two or three,” said Jairo Rodriguez Davis, the secretary of the Raizal Council, the community’s main representative and deliberative body, adding that most of the money generated by the island’s tourism industry ended up in the hands of non-Raizales.To determine whether someone is Raizal, he relies on family trees tracing lineages back to the 1700s. “If they have a traceable root back then, you are considered Raizal,” he said.Davis’s office is located in what used to be the first and only Raizal university, created on the initiative of the community and a Baptist minister. The institution operated briefly – teaching in Creole – between the late 1990s and early 2000s, but closed for lack of government and private support. Today the building, stripped of most of its windows, railings and boundary walls, but facing the sea and surrounded by an endless grove of mango trees, serves as a community space for meetings and events.View image in fullscreenBooks have been abandoned in piles since the closure of the university.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian“We dream of having the university here again one day,” said Davis.Davis’s more immediate concern, however, is the violence. “Neither coca is grown here nor cocaine produced here, but many of our young people have been used by traffickers to carry drugs on those boats,” he said.Trafficking has passed through the islands since at least the 1970s: first marijuana heading north, then weapons moving south to fuel Colombia’s armed conflict; later cocaine flowing north again and, more recently, people attempting to reach the US.“Everyone has a relative who has been killed or disappeared at sea,” said Miguel Angel Castell Cano, San Andrés’s government secretary, who previously worked as a lawyer for Providence’s fishers’ association.His own father has been missing for 10 years after becoming involved in a drug-trafficking trip near Honduras. “It is neither something I am ashamed of nor proud of … But no one deserves to disappear, regardless of what they have done,” he said.View image in fullscreen‘Everyone has a relative who has been killed or disappeared at sea,’ said Miguel Angel Castell Cano.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianBeing missing does not necessarily mean being dead. Hooker Cabeza Ignacio Agenor, 40, was arrested by Costa Rican authorities in 2021 and sentenced to 10 years in prison for international drug trafficking. He has been eligible to apply for parole since February. His family has submitted a formal repatriation request to the Costa Rican government so that he can serve the remainder of his sentence in Colombia, but they have yet to receive a response.Families are often reluctant to speak out about their missing loved ones. “The islands are deeply religious. When people disappeared, even if they had simply been fishing, no one wants a relative to be subjected to moral judgment,” said the writer and lawyer Maríamatilde Rodríguez.Between the 1990s and 2000s, she led an investigation drawing on documents and interviews with dozens of relatives that arrived at the staggering figure of nearly 700 disappeared people across the two islands over the preceding 30 years. She said updating that count would require a similarly extensive effort. There is no official data from the Colombian authorities about it.“Our sea contains mass graves, and its beauty is matched only by the scale of the tragedies it has witnessed,” she said.View image in fullscreenIslanders have struggled to get help from the Colombian government.Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianRodríguez said the Colombian state did not treat the issue with the seriousness it deserved. “There is both ignorance and a tendency to minimise the issue – people assume that because the islands are small, the problems must also be small.”The government did not respond to requests for comment.Stephens said that if such a large number of people had gone missing anywhere else in the world, “that would set off alarm bells. Yet here nobody pays attention, and young men continue to disappear.”He believes that, despite the US bombings, the number of drug-trafficking trips in the region is increasing – many analysts have already argued that the airstrikes have hadlittle effecton the volume of drugs reaching the US – and this has led to greater recruitment of fishers.Beyond drug legalisation – “prohibition is what fuels the business” – the solution lies with the Colombian state, he argues. “We need more jobs for young people. Because they have so few opportunities here, some of them end up taking that path.”Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘People who commit heinous crimes can be victims’: Michael Mann on the provocative power of Manhunter at 40 | Michael Mann | The Guardian
description: As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworld
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworld
Content: Tom Noonan as serial killer Francis Dolarhyde in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesView image in fullscreenTom Noonan as serial killer Francis Dolarhyde in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesMichael Mann‘People who commit heinous crimes can be victims’: Michael Mann on the provocative power of Manhunter at 40As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworldMatthew AllanSat 25 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Mannhas shown time and again in films likeThief,Heat, Miami Vice andPublic Enemiesthat he is one of American film’s greatest explorers of the underworld. “It’s like a kind of cultural anthropology,” Mann tells me from his office in Los Angeles. “If you make films, you get to do that in a different place with a different subject every few years. For me, the exploration is the high.”With its unsettling atmosphere and soaring beauty, Mann’s 1986 film Manhunter reimagined how a thriller could look, sound and feel in an early high point for the director. To commemorate its 40th anniversaryManhunter: The Final Cut, a 4K restoration and director’s cut with three minutes of new footage, will see a theatrical release in New York and Los Angeles this weekend with a nationwide US rollout to follow.‘Maybe the best pumped-up sequel ever made’: James Cameron’s Aliens hits 40Read moreBased onThomas Harris’s bestselling horror novel Red Dragon, Manhunter follows FBI agent Will Graham (William Petersen), who has been lured out of retirement to hunt down an elusive serial killer before he performs another ritualistic killing on the night of the next full moon. Graham has been called on for his uncanny ability to access the methods and motives of killers by adopting their states of mind, though it has come with its own personal costs. When we meet Graham at his secluded beach house (rented to the film by pop artistRobert Rauschenberg) he’s recently returned from a stint in a psychiatric unit after a meltdown and a violent confrontation with the last prolific killer he captured but got too close to,Dr Hannibal Lecter(presented on screen for the first time here byBrian Cox).In a wounded and dreamlike fugue, Graham wanders through crime scenes late at night trying to psychically commune with the killer. Like the character he played, Petersen, who oscillates perfectly between dazed and hair-triggered here, had a hard time extricating himself from his work. “Your brain may know you’re acting, but your heart doesn’t,” Petersen said in a recent press release for The Final Cut. “Acting is a wonderful profession for giving you a rounded understanding of humanity. But you have to be careful not to get lost in it.” As soon as the film wrapped, Petersen shaved his beard and dyed his hair blonde to shake the role.Stephen Lang, who plays the ethically bankrupt tabloid reporter Freddie Lounds, remembers it as a challenging but rewarding shoot. “ I’ve worked with other directors who are considered within the business to be demanding,Jim [James] Cameronbeing one of them. And when asked the difference between the two, I have said that Jim and I discuss everything. We debate everything. When Michael says jump, I generally say: ‘How high?’ I don’t challenge Michael,” Lang says. “Michael could be tough and he could be short. But you also knew he was extremely generous as a director. He could be a lot of things. There’s a volatility to him, as there is in so many artists. Michael is not only a film-maker, he’s an artist. An auteur.”View image in fullscreenTom Noonan as Francis Dolarhyde with Stephen Lang as Freddie Lounds in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesIt’s hard not to see some of Mann himself in Graham. Known for an immersive pre-production process that leans heavy on investigation and research, Mann spent time with the FBI’s violent crimes and behavioral science units in preparation for Manhunter. He even corresponded for some time with an imprisoned murderer named Dennis Wayne Wallace, who would be the main inspiration for the film’s killer, Francis Dolarhyde (Tom Noonanin a career-defining role).“He’d write what he called ‘Jim Morrisonpsych-poetry’ to me, and tell me his whole story,” recalls Mann of Wallace. “ He had fantasized a love affair with Cinnamon Cindy, a go-go dancer at the Mellow Yellow in Gardena, California. Their song was In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida, which is why that’s used at the end of the picture. He also walked around wearing a hard hat with the Mad Magazine decal on it that said: ‘Support mental illness or I’ll kill you.’”In Wallace, Mann also saw how childhood abuse acted as a catalyst for brutality and used this insight to create a character that was at once evil and empathetic. “If Wallace soiled anything, shit was rubbed in his face,” says Mann. “He was literally leashed to a tree outside in the front yard. And that kind of abuse reduces self-esteem to some impossibly low level. You couple that with a strong ego and that’s how you get a Francis Dolarhyde.“I wanted to evoke that contradiction about killers. These people who commit heinous crimes who are at the same time victims themselves – how does one relate to that? Which is the dilemma for Graham.”View image in fullscreenJoan Allen in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesWe come to empathize most with Dolarhyde when he falls for Reba (Joan Allen), a blind woman he works with at a photolab in St Louis. Back at Dolarhyde’s place, they drink gin and tonics and, unbeknown to Reba, watch home movies of the family he plans to kill next. His eyes float between Reba and the bikini-clad woman in the home movie, a smiling mother playing with her child in a pool. There’s some shared humanity between this stranger on screen and the woman next to him that Dolarhyde appears to register. Later, they lie naked in bed together and Dolarhyde kisses sleeping Reba’s hand and weeps. You begin to see that maybe beneath the madness of this man, beneath his sense of godlike superiority over his victims, is some bottomless need for a love he never had. “To me that was evoking the Dolarhyde that had been there as an innocent child,” Mann says. “The person he could have evolved into had he not been the victim of such abuse.”Heat at 30: Michael Mann’s electric crime thriller is a film of fire and sadnessRead moreDespite the macabre content, Manhunter comes in as glossy and delectable a package as you can imagine. It’s got just enough juicy 80s B-movie DNA to offset everything vile unfolding on screen. Manhunter’s greatest achievement is its marriage of visual splendor and psychological depth. There’s a heightened, swooning quality to the look of the film that has never been replicated: all hypermodern, minimalist spaces flooded with alien light.The juxtaposition of Mann’s commitment to authenticity in research and writing with his complete disregard for it visually makes for a satisfying and hyper-real combination. Despite initial disappointment at the box office, Manhunter has continued to dig its claws into culture and has had a lasting influence few could have seen coming. Its icy synth-dominated score set the table for modern crime scores, particularly Cliff Martinez’s collaborations withNicolas Winding Refn. It’s hard to imagine the myriad of films and shows about criminal profiling existing without it.“It influenced a lot,” agrees Mann. “I was trying to find how I could push the medium forward, that was very much on my mind. How do I make it so expressive that you really feel you are in this place?”Manhunter: The Final Cut is out in the US now with a UK release on 25 September and an Australian release to be announcedExplore more on these topicsMichael MannBrian CoxHannibal LecterThomas HarrisCrime filmsThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Furious: this serial killer thriller is the most staggeringly feminist TV you’ll ever watch  | Television | The Guardian
description: The new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fans
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: The new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fans
Content: Murderess on the loose … Lola Petticrew as Catherine in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyView image in fullscreenMurderess on the loose … Lola Petticrew as Catherine in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyThe watcherTelevisionFurious: this serial killer thriller is the most staggeringly feminist TV you’ll ever watchThe new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fansRhik SamadderSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmale friend recently attended a Lily Allen show, and shakily described the experience to me. “I felt like a vegetarian fox at an armed chicken convention,” he said. An overwhelmingly female crowd were experiencing powerful catharsis, united in their anger at men and joy of bangers. I told him chickens couldn’t handle firearms, but I don’t think he heard me. He had tinnitus from the screaming.There isn’t much screaming in Furious, Disney+’s new detective series (from Monday, 27 July). Also missing are the standard tropes of murder dramas: mutilated female bodies, an absence of women’s agency generally. Furious is the cat and mouse story between junior FBI agent Alice Black (Emmy Rossum) and Catherine (Lola Petticrew), a serial killer who is bumping off male victims with calculated sadism. Catherine might be the least serial killer name imaginable, but that’s just one way this show rewrites the rule book. I’d say it’s the most feminist show I’ve ever seen – except that might lead some to write it off.The show’s ethos goes beyond having female leads. You can see it in the way Black and her FBI sex-crimes squad mentor Nora, played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine, interview victims. The clues and tells they notice, their knowledge of a system that fails women. Grimly fitted to Epstein-aware times, the show is interested in the way wealthy men buy legal immunity. Trafficking charges are hard to make stick, notes Nora, thanks to the vulnerability of female witnesses. “Once you accept money for sex, you are a criminal.”View image in fullscreenPsychology of killing … Emmy Rossum and Scoot McNairy in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyInjustice does not sit solely on the upper rungs of the social ladder. Black is forced to work the case alongside an abusive ex-partner from the NYPD. She never made a formal complaint against him, choosing to simply leave her police job. He’s brilliantly played by Jake Lacy, an actor I feel for. There’s something about his handsome, preppy face, instantly hateable in The White Lotus, that suits villainy. Something that screams “bro” louder than a reunion at a rowing club. Something about it that makes you think: “I want someone to punch you.” Can’t be easy.This isn’t a punching show, though. It’s more sophisticated, more weary. There is sisterhood, but it’s fraught. Black and Catherine share traumatic pasts; only one of them skilfully manipulates women and men alike to work through a kill list. Black chooses to swallow her PTSD, emotionally cauterising herself. Nora is jaded by decades of working in the dark. As part of her job, she has to watch child sexual abuse images, which she does in a locked room she compares to the entrance of Hades. “Why do you want to work in the basement on sex crimes, and crimes against children? Do you hate yourself?” she asks Black at their first meeting.In the half of the series I’ve watched, there are perhaps two men who aren’t at best chauvinists, and often coercive hypocrites. People might grumble about this. But it seems fair enough, given TV’s history of female representation. Plus you can’t critique a patriarchy-omelette without breaking some legs. I mean eggs. There’s no such thing as a vegetarian fox.One of the few nice ones is Black’s former partner Danny, played by Scoot McNairy. (He’s a work partner, not the violent romantic partner. The NYPD here clearly employ a good cop, bad cop, bad cop, bad cop strategy.) Danny believed Black’s story of domestic abuse and spoke out. His allyship has cost him the support of his male colleagues. Yet in an excruciating scene, we learn that Black has also stopped speaking to Danny; he reminds her of the past, her need to be rescued. This is a rare crime show equally interested in the psychology of victimhood as killing, and which values nuance and complexity over catharsis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFurious acknowledges its dark attraction to the damaged Catherine, whom Nora describes as “our avenging angel, our evil Fury, our murderess”, as she enacts a justice that otherwise never comes. Is it Catherine’s fury to which the show’s title refers? Nora herself, or Black? The childish anger of its weak men? Almost certainly, it speaks to its female audience. For fans ofKilling Eve,Promising Young WomanandLily Allen, it’s a must-see. I’m less sure if men will watch. Even the good ones, who know they should.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: hit British comedy Ghosts gets a fun new twist  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Scream for help … Ghosts Australia on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/© BBC Studios Productions Australia Pty Ltd, Network Ten Pty Limited, Network Ten All Access Pty Limited, Screenwest (Australia) Ltd 2024View image in fullscreenScream for help … Ghosts Australia on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/© BBC Studios Productions Australia Pty Ltd, Network Ten Pty Limited, Network Ten All Access Pty Limited, Screenwest (Australia) Ltd 2024TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: hit British comedy Ghosts gets a fun new twistThe Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Graeme Virtue,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 25 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGhosts Australia10.30pm, BBC ThreeBuy a mouldy flat with a toilet in the kitchen or move into the rundown mansion of a dead great-uncle? It’s a no-brainer for couple Kate and Sean in this Oz version of the hit British sitcom. But as fans of the original show already know, their home is riddled with ghosts, which only Kate can see after a near-death experience. A new batch of ghost characters add a fresh spin on a firm comedy favourite.Hollie RichardsonAlan Carr’s Picture Slam6.40pm, BBC OneThe new series of the picture quiz where contestants have to identify a range of snaps continues. Three teams are competing for the cash prize of £10k, including Alan Carr superfans Lucy and Sharon. They tell the comedian to “check the bins” when he gets home after the show. He looks scared.Priya ElanBonnie Tyler at the BBC8.30pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenI really need you tonight! … Bonnie Tyler at the BBC on BBC Two.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAThe husky-voiced powerhouse died earlier this month, so here are the belting songs that made her a Welsh legend over a five-decade career. Sing along to archive performances of hits from Lost in France to Loving You Is a Dirty Job and Holding Out for a Hero. But save your lungs for the Total Eclipse of the Heart finale.HRThe Sentinels9pm, BBC FourA double bill of the sombre French world war one drama about super-soldiers forced to put country over family. After losing a comrade, the remaining three Sentinels are ready to blow off some steam. Meanwhile, Irène’s investigations into dodgy military dealings point her toward the fleshpots of northern Paris.Graeme VirtueThe Staircase9.15pm, ITV1Colin Firth and Toni Collette’s true-crime drama first aired on Sky back in 2022. Michael Peterson called 911 to report finding his wife Kathleen’s body at the bottom of their stairs at home. But he immediately became a suspect, and the first episode shows flashbacks to what their relationship was really like.HRSchitt’s Creek11.45pm, BBC ThreeA triple bill of the much-loved Canadian sitcom that gave the late, great Catherine O’Hara a second wind. First up, Moira (O’Hara) and Johnny (Eugene Levy) go bargain hunting at an estate sale, while Alexis (Annie Murphy) tries to hide the fact that she can’t ride a bike.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceLurker, 6.15pm, Sky Cinema PremiereAt first sight, Alex Russell’s intense drama is about a pop singer stalked by an obsessive fan. Théodore Pellerin’s LA clothes shop worker Matthew talks himself into the entourage of the apparently easy-going Oliver (Archie Madekwe), a British musician on the up. As he sidles from obsequious gofer to would-be documentary profiler, Matthew’s neediness is embarrassing going on excruciating – but it also flatters Oliver. And as their relationship develops over weeks, the power balance between them shifts drastically.Simon WardellMonster, 10.25pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenHeartbreaking … Monster on BBC Four.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyJapanese film-maker Hirokazu Kore-eda has long been a brilliant illuminator of children’s fractured, often inarticulated lives. This 2023 Cannes winner is another compelling look into their inner worlds, framed as an episodic mystery. First, we see events from the point of view of Sakura Ando’s single mother Saori, who thinks her son Minato (Sōya Kurokawa) is being bullied by his teacher, Mr Hori (Eita Nagayama). But then we get Hori’s side of the story and, crucially, Minato’s; what emerges is a heartbreaking tale of friendship and difference.SWLive sportCommonwealth Games, 8.30am, TNT Sports 2Day two includes netball, boxing, artistic gymnastics and bowls.Men’s Tour de France , 10am, TNT Sports 1The penultimate stage, from Le Bourg-d’Oisans to Alpe d’Huez.World Matchplay Darts, 9pm, Sky Sports Main EventThe semi-finals in Blackpool.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #253: ​Once the season of surprise breakout hits, this summer’s TV has lost its heat | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited about
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited about
Content: Hot fail … Will Angus, Nicholas Duvernay and Jack Martin in Not Suitable For Work.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenHot fail … Will Angus, Nicholas Duvernay and Jack Martin in Not Suitable For Work.Photograph: DisneyThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #253: ​Once the season of surprise breakout hits, this summer’s TV has lost its heatIn this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited aboutGwilym MumfordSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in 2015, when I worked on the old print version of the Guide, weran a covercalling on readers to “Stay inside this summer”. Our argument went that, such was theamount of great TVairing in the months from June to August that year (True Detective,My Mad Fat Diary,Veepand, err, a show about Abz from the boyband 5ive’s new career in farming), you’d be a fool to head outside for some vitamin D.This wasn’t a contrarian viewpoint. Streaming’s sudden rise had broken down the walls that had previously left the summer a parched, desolate wasteland and kept the good TV penned into the more viewer-friendly periods of spring and autumn. Now, great new shows would arrive all year round. In the years that followed, some of the most talked-about scripted TV would debut around or after the solstice: Stranger Things, Yellowstone, Euphoria, I May Destroy You, The Bear, and plenty more besides.But, if the Guide magazine still existed in 2026, its equivalent cover would be very different.“Touch grass, not your TV remote”.This year’s summer televisual offering, in the UK and the US, has rarely been worth eschewing the sun for. There may have been a few big returnees (The Bear for its final season, Silo, House of the Dragon) and a couple of interesting curios (the BBC’s delicious premium trash series Two Weeks in August, or Apple TV’s fantastic For All Mankind spin-off Star City), but buzzy, agenda-setting new shows have failed to materialise. If you were feeling generous you might stretch the criteria to includeWidow’s Bay, which finished its much raved-about debut season on 17 June, but I’m not feeling generous: that was inarguably a spring sensation; its shivery, low-lit charms incompatible with a June heatwave. And, discounting that show, the cupboard is severely bare.There’s a major mitigating factor here, of course: a bigger-than-ever World Cup, one that, as well as taking over the TV schedules of BBC and ITV in the UK, had by virtue of happening in North American timezones, eaten into the US primetime period where you’d usually encounter big new summer series too. Still, I’m not sure that alone is enough to excuse the dearth of shows this summer, especially when plenty will have been seeking some non-football counter-programming. And the situation hardly seems to be improving now that the World Cup is over. I can see only two upcoming series in the entirety of August that might fall into the “big new show” bucket: Lanterns, an HBO superhero series that is mainly interesting for being Damon Lindelof’s first show since the excellent Watchmen; and The Shards, an FX Bret Easton Ellis adaptation from Ryan Murphy (and given Murphy’srecenttrack record, that has a more than slim chance of being a major disappointment).View image in fullscreenMaking the effort … Apple TV’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed.Photograph: Zach Dilgard/AppleWhere have the streamers – who don’t have to worry about such notions as “primetime” and “schedules” – been? Netflix, in particular, has endured a rotten summer so far, following on from a similarly miserable spring. Can you remember the last truly conversation-starting Netflix series? That inability to mint major new shows is said to be of serious concern to its higher-ups, according to Vulture’s TVindustry columnist, Joe Adalian. Amazon has hardly fared any better – its most-discussed show, the Legally Blonde prequelElle, has mainly prompted conversations over how wretched it is. Disney+ can only really point to the final season of The Bear as a qualified success this summer (Mindy Kaling’sNot Suitable For Workhaving been swiftly memory-holed), while HBO have produced little aside from the dreary House of the Dragon and a Larry David historical sketch show that landed with a thump. Only Apple TV seem to be at least making an effort this summer, with a regular drip-drip of programming: Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed, Star City, Lucky,Cape Fear, Silo,Sugar, and, next month, the returning Ted Lasso.Moreover, this isn’t a one-off aberration, 2025’s summer season was also something of a washout. The only debuting series that hasn’t been swiftly forgotten from that period was Alien: Earth. That suggests a larger tectonic shift away from the summer, and perhaps that’s the result of a greater emphasis on Emmy awards, which streaming services in particular are keen to hoover. Voting for the Emmys closes on 31 May, and in recent years there has been increasing eagerness to launch the best new series right before that cut off point. And why drop new shows in June, July and August when most viewers will still be catching up with the deluge delivered in late spring? (Something similar could be said to happen the UK, where the Bafta TV awards cut off point is 31 December, causing an autumnal glut of series.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt all means that TV-wise, summer is likely to be a washout for a while yet. Yes, you might have to go outside and enjoy the sunshine. Ghastly, I know.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterTelevisionnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘The rain in São Paulo makes everything so cinematic’: Simone Arruda’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The Brazilian photographer was drawn to the train passengers lost in their books on a soggy March evening
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The Brazilian photographer was drawn to the train passengers lost in their books on a soggy March evening
Content: Reading Through the Chaos, 2023, shot on Samsung Galaxy S20 FE.Photograph: Simone ArrudaView image in fullscreenReading Through the Chaos, 2023, shot on Samsung Galaxy S20 FE.Photograph: Simone ArrudaSmart shotPhotography‘The rain in São Paulo makes everything so cinematic’: Simone Arruda’s best phone pictureThe Brazilian photographer was drawn to the train passengers lost in their books on a soggy March eveningGrace HollidaySat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“São Paulo is a place that we love and hate,” says Simone Arruda of her Brazilian home city. “And anyone who knows it knows that when it rains, everything turns to chaos.”‘I wanted to show children playing under the open sky – and the joy of Sundays’: Monojit Dutta’s best phone pictureRead moreArruda took this shot at rush hour on a soggy March evening. She was heading home via Brás station, “a massive hub in a neighbourhood that is always extremely busy due to its intense commerce”, she says.Packed between tired, wet commuters, she observed those who had already secured a ride home through the train window. While the colours and contrast drew her eye, it was the human scene that made her lift her phone.“I love capturing people reading, because it represents a moment of introspection, a bit of peace amid all the hustle and bustle,” she says. “Also, the upwards glance of the woman on the right guides my eyes straight to the red light, signifying that the doors are closing. It’s as if she’s thinking, ‘Finally, this train is going to move,’ so there’s an element of solace here, too.”Arruda stayed true to the atmosphere of the scene when applying minor saturation and sharpness adjustments. “I always avoid exaggeration,” she says. “I never want to make things look artificial or alter their true essence. While the rain brings chaos, it also makes everything so cinematic. I’m proud of where I’m from.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT | Family | The Guardian
description: Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
Author: Jenny Kleeman
Headline: Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
Content: Video: Courtesy of Nicci Dhamu / Guardian DesignFamily‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPTAvtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?Jenny KleemanSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 10.45 EDTShareAs a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers.Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say.Your mum lives abroad.Avtar didn’t really pay any attention to it. “I thought, the neighbours are just making up stories.” But the stories were true: the woman raising Avtar was actually his grandmother. When he was too young to remember it, his father had emigrated to Canada to work as a teacher, leaving Avtar in the care of his paternal grandparents. His grandfather, a police officer, was a fearsome authoritarian, but his grandmother brought him up with tenderness, as if he were her own son. She called him by his nickname, Titu. He felt loved.When Avtar was around eight years old, he was told about his family in Canada: his dad, his mum and a little brother were waiting for him there, and he would soon travel to join them. Just after his ninth birthday, Avtar found himself sitting on a plane, dressed in a three‑piece suit and tie. He was travelling alone. He had never flown before. He didn’t speak a word of English. He landed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Christmas Eve, 1968; his family met him at the airport and took him home. “I didn’t know what to think,” Avtar, now 66, tells me in a video call from his home in Abbotsford, British Columbia. “Before I knew it, it was the first week of January, and I was put in school.”View image in fullscreenAvtar with his grandmother in the mid-60s in Amritsar, India (above), and (below) aged 10, in 1969, the year after he moved to Canada. Courtesy of Avtar SinghUnable to communicate with any of the other pupils, Avtar watched what they did and followed along, storing his snow boots in the cloakroom, standing up to sing the Canadian national anthem and God Save the Queen. But with his long hair tied in the topknot often worn by Sikh boys, he stood out. His parents offered to buy him a hockey stick and a pair of ice skates if he agreed to get his hair cut. He learned English. His nickname changed from Titu to the more Canadian “Tito”. He began to blend in.But Avtar didn’t fit in at home. He was much paler than everyone else – “the white sheep of the family,” he jokes. And they treated him like an outsider, an afterthought. When he was 14, his family went on holiday without him, leaving Avtar home alone for two weeks. He got on well enough with his father, but didn’t gel at all with his mother. “She didn’t have any of the warmth that my grandma had. She absolutely hated me.” She seemed much more like a stepmother than a mother.That feeling was confirmed when Avtar got married and his grandparents flew over to stay with him and his new wife, Rosey. His grandma “whispered into my wife’s ear” that Avtar was the product of his father’s first marriage. “She didn’t say what my mother’s name was. She just said, ‘Her family was from Africa, and she left the child with us and went back to Africa. She might have gone to live in the UK.’ That’s it.” It didn’t feel right to ask his grandparents for more information: this was clearly a family secret that no one wanted to discuss with Avtar.double quotation markThe thought of my mother didn’t leave my mind, everView image in fullscreenWhen his son was set a school assignment to complete his family tree, Avtar felt emboldened to approach his father. “I said, ‘Dad, you’ve got to tell me at least what my mother’s name was.’” His dad eventually relented: her first name was Savinder. But he would not give Avtar any more information, no matter how many times he asked. “I was stonewalled.” Avtar had no idea why his parents had split up. “All I really understood was that my mother’s family encouraged her to give up custody of me so it would be easier for them to remarry her.”He thought about his mother constantly. When Rosey was pregnant with their daughter, there were anomalies in some of the antenatal tests, and Rosey and Avtar were referred to a geneticist. Avtar was asked about his parents’ medical history. “I couldn’t tell them anything about my mother’s family history. It hit me right in the heart. That’s when I thought, I’ve got to do something.”He Googled and Facebooked, but there was almost nothing to go on; Savinder is a fairly common Punjabi Sikh name.
