In 2009, Avtar flew to London to visit the National Archives at Kew with the hope of finding immigration or marriage records that might lead him to his mother. “I couldn’t find anything at all.” On a later visit to London, he emailed Sunrise Radio, a British Asian station, asking if they could put out an appeal to find his mother, but they told Avtar they don’t do that kind of thing, out of respect for people’s privacy. That gave Avtar pause. “I thought, maybe I should just cool off. If my mother has some other family, I don’t want to disrupt her life.” Still, it niggled. Three or four years ago, he asked a British south Asian work colleague for advice; she suggested contacting the ITV show Long LostFamily. He watched a few episodes and decided it wasn’t for him. But he longed to know his mother. “The thought of her did not leave my mind, ever.”The one thing Avtar did not do was a DNA test. He is retired now, but he used to be a chartered accountant, and he knows enough about technology, data and privacy to be wary of giving up his genetic code to a corporation. “They can sell it. Not only that – if they see something in my DNA, that affects my kids. I don’t want that information up there.” He deactivated his Facebook account 12 years ago for similar reasons. “I don’t have faith that these companies have the proper safeguards.”double quotation markShe used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘my child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for herThen, on 8 May this year, Avtar and Rosey were on holiday in the south of France. Avtar had been battling cancer; their long-awaited trip to Europe came after he had finished his treatment. “It was early morning, and I had read all the news. I was bored. I had nothing else to do. I thought, I’ve tried Google and everything else, why don’t I give AI a shot?”View image in fullscreenSavinder Kaur in 1963. Courtesy of Nicci DhamuHe typed a prompt intoChatGPT, based on the little he knew, and what else he could infer. He assumed that his mother would be around the same age as his father (who died 10 years ago); he knew that Sikh women of her generation were generally given the middle name Kaur.AvtarCan you find any information about a Savinder Kaur?AvtarShe would be between 87 and 97 years old and would have lived in India and Africa and possibly in the UKChatGPTThe strongest match, based upon your clues, is this …ChatGPTSavinder Kaur Nagi, born in 1936 in Kisumu, Kenya, to Indian Sikh parents.ChatGPTThe article mentions family roots near Jammu and Kashmir in India and later migration connections to the UK.“I know that AI can just make up shit. So I thought, OK, that’snicesays Avtar. “But it actually referenced an article. I thought, I’ll look at that, at least. Just to see.”“I wrote it out of grief,” Nicci Dhamu tells me, in a cafe in west London. “Mummy never really had a voice, and that article was all about giving her one. I wanted to create a digital legacy for my mum.”Nicci is the jewellery designer behind the brand Sohavi. “Sohavi means beautiful in Gurmukhī, the Sikh script. I learned about making things beautiful from Mum.”Her article, published on both the Sohavi blog and the South Asian Heritage Month website, was a celebration of her mother’s creativity. “She suffered loss, and decisions were made for her when she young and wasn’t able to assert her own voice, like many south Asian women of her generation. But she lives on through me and the profound influences she had on me throughout my life,” Nicci wrote.Savinder Kaur Nagi died in her sleep in December 2024, aged 88. For the last five years of her life, she had dementia. Nicci, 58, had been her carer; they lived together and were very close. Nicci’s family moved to the UK from Kenya in 1973. She has an older sister and a younger brother, as well as three half-sisters from her dad’s first marriage; he was widowed before he met Savinder. “We grew up as one family. I didn’t know until I was about 10 or 11 years old that my sisters were my half‑sisters, and that was only because one of my sisters told me.” Theirs was a family that did not speak about the past.View image in fullscreenSavinder with Nicci Dhamu’s father, c1963. Courtesy of Nicci Dhamu“I remember once, Mum was in the kitchen making roti, and I asked her, ‘Mummy, you were, like, 25 years old when you got married to Dad. Wasn’t that a little old for somebody of your generation?’ I knew that something was different about our family, but I didn’t have the vocabulary to label it. My father never spoke to us about his wife who had died, and my mum never spoke about her life before him.”When Nicci was in her 40s, an older cousin casually revealed that Savinder had been married to another man before she met Nicci’s dad. “She was married off, very young. And it probably wasn’t what she wanted,” Nicci tells me. “My grandfather took her and her sisters out of school in Kenya and took them back to Punjab to a place called Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar.” Later in life, her mother would openly lament leaving school – she could read and write English, and loved studying – but never explained why she had been forced to give up her education. She did not discuss her first marriage. She never told her children they had an older half-brother.“My cousin told me in that conversation that she had a son.” Nicci’s eyes are bright at the memory. But she never felt able to ask her mother about him. “I couldn’t. There was intrinsic pain there.”There were times, Nicci says, when her mother would sink into a depression. “She would sit quietly, or take to bed because she was upset.” Nicci would bring Savinder her dinner, and encourage her to sit up and eat. “Towards the end of Mum’s life, she used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘My child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for her.”It was then – a couple of years before her mum’s death – that Nicci resolved to find the child her mother was crying for. But she did not know his name, and her mother was unwell so Nicci couldn’t ask her. Instead, she turned to her wider family.She began with her mother’s young brother, who lives in Birmingham. “He knew my mum’s child as a two- or three-year-old,” Nicci says. She picked his brains, and also her cousins’. She learned that her mother’s first husband was called Mohan Singh, a very educated man who taught at the Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school in Amritsar. Mohan’s father had been a police officer, and “quite a difficult man”. Savinder had told her father that her husband wasn’t treating her well. “I think my grandad thought, this is not a good place for my daughter to be. He went around and took his daughter back to his home, and she must have picked up her little boy, too.”Her mother raised the boy until he was three years old, Nicci was told. “As someone who is also divorced, I often reflect on the stigma my mother may have faced as a south Asian woman of her generation,” she tells me. “I think there was a lot of pressure from the family:let’s get her married. Somebody as young as her was going to have a very difficult life as a single mother. She was too young to be on her own. Her son’s family wanted him back. So they must have taken the child from her.”View image in fullscreenNicci Dhamu with Savinder in 2018. Courtesy of Nicci DhamuSavinder returned to Kenya, alone. At first, she stayed with her eldest brother. Nicci’s cousins have vivid memories of her time in their home. “She would take his baby clothes out and cry. She never forgot him.” She was soon introduced to Nicci’s father, a man 16 years her senior. “I think she carried that trauma throughout her life, but did a very good job of holding her head up high, making her life work, raising three more children.” Family in Kenya heard “through the grapevine” that Savinder’s first husband had moved to Canada, but they couldn’t tell Nicci when. And no one knew the name of Savinder’s little boy. They only knew his nickname: Titu.“No one’s going to call themselves Titu on LinkedIn, are they?” says Nicci with a deep laugh. That didn’t stop her trying to find him online, and his father and grandfather, too, Googling the names of teachers and police officers in Amritsar. “I didn’t capture anything. How do you find somebody without a name? It’s impossible.”Three or four months before her mother died, she submitted Savinder’s DNA to Ancestry.com. “I set up a profile for her, saying, ‘Profile managed by daughter, looking for her son, name is Titu, possibly living in Canada.’” She got some interesting titbits back about her mother’s ancestral roots in Kashmir, Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, which would explain her light complexion, but no useful matches.A month after her mother died, Nicci contacted friends who knew people who had worked for the magistrates court in Amritsar, in the hope of finding records of the divorce. “If there were divorce papers, there would be names – and maybe achild’sname.” But she was told that would be virtually impossible; a needle in a haystack.In April 2025, Nicci’s family took Savinder’s ashes to India. During her stay in Amritsar, Nicci hired a driver to take her to Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school, where Titu’s father had been a teacher. She spoke to the teachers and the security guard, but it was long after Mohan Singh’s time there, so no one knew of him or his son. All she wanted was a name for her half-brother, but no one could tell her. It felt hopeless.“I remember sitting there thinking, why doesn’t he just knock on the door? I knew that his father was an educated man – I was pretty sure that he must be educated, too. Why isn’t he looking for Mum?”Avtar blinked at the article ChatGPT had presented to him. Rosey was just waking up. He made her a coffee and showed her what he’d found, but she wasn’t convinced. After all, the article didn’t mention Savinder’s first marriage, divorce or long-lost son. “Rosey didn’t want me to be disappointed – she knows how hard I had looked for my mother.”Then he looked at the article again, and a picture stopped him in his tracks: not one of the many photos Nicci had posted of her mother – there was no flicker of instant recognition when he saw Savinder’s face – but an image of a certificate her mother had earned for dressmaking at a college in Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar, in 1962. (“She wassoproud of it,” Nicci beams. “She would talk about it quite often: ‘I went to college, I earned a certificate.’ I think that was her quiet victory.”)“This is two or three years after I was born, and it is in the exact city where I was born.” Avtar exhales deeply, as if he still can’t believe what he saw. He had to find out more. “This is the closest I’ve ever come. It would be a shame to just stop here.”At 8.36am that morning, he sent Nicci an email, thanking her for writing the tribute to her mother.AvtarWhat especially resonated with me was the part of her life connected to India. Reading about her journey raised many personal questions and reflections for me, and I found myself feeling there may be some distant family or community connections between us.AvtarI want to assure you that I am not reaching out for any business, financial, or other formal reason, only in the spirit of a friendly conversation.Nicci had spent the previous night praying at the gurdwara and watching Long Lost Familyon TV. Avtar’s email had arrived on the morning of what would have been her mother’s 90th birthday. “It waswild!” Nicci exclaims. “I just had a real sense of knowing. I can’t explain it. This is my mum’s son. It’sgotto be.”She agonised over how to reply, eventually adopting a similarly friendly but respectful tone.NicciI am equally intrigued to know if there might be a family connection. I would be happy to have a conversation with you.Her phone number was in her email signature. Avtar sent her a message on WhatsApp as soon as he saw it, asking when they could speak. Nicci scrutinised his WhatsApp profile picture. “He had a very distinctive nose. Everybody in my mother’s family has this prominent, distinguished nose.” She messaged back – she was free to talk there and then.It was barely two hours since Avtar had typed his prompt into ChatGPT. He was driving with Rosey to get some croissants for breakfast. He parked up, clicked on Nicci’s number and called her. There wasn’t much of a preamble. Avtar was too eager to have his questions finally answered.AvtarGood morning! This is Avtar SinghNicciHello AvtarAvtarHiNicciSo you live in CanadaAvtarWhen Is a good time to talkNicciI’m London based. As you probably know.NicciI’m free to talk nowAvtar 📞Voice call“Can you tell me a bit about your mother’s time in India?” he asked.“Mummy was married and divorced in India,” Nicci replied.“Did she have any children?”“Yes,” Nicci said. “She had a son.”Both Avtar and Rosey burst into tears.“Titu, is that you?” asked Nicci. “Are you Titu, my mother’s son?”“Yes,” Avtar replied. “That’s who I am. But I haven’t heard anyone pronounce my nickname that way since my grandma called me that, when I was a little boy.”“At that moment, time just froze,” Avtar remembers. “But I quickly recovered. I said, ‘You’re mysister. Holy shit – are there more of you out there?’ It had never occurred to me that my mother would have a family, and that I could actually meet them. That family, they knew aboutme– everybody knew about me, they just wouldn’t talk about it – but I had no knowledge aboutthemwhatsoever.”They spoke for two hours in that first phone call, until Avtar’s battery started to die. Nicci had assumed he must be in Canada; she couldn’t believe he was in France, so close by. “Why don’t you fly over?” she asked. Avtar’s head was spinning. They agreed to speak again later that evening, in a video call.AvtarThis was a dream of a lifetime!Nicci then gave Avtar a tour of the family photos displayed in the living room she used to share with their mother. “I was just sharing everything I could with him. And sobbing. And remembering Mum. All that grief about her yearning to see him again, and not meeting him. It’s like the universe just flung something at me – although I’ve lost my mum, I’ve gained a brother.”When Avtar told his son the news, he urged him to go to London and meet his newfound family. By the time he reached his daughter, she already knew: she had been using Avtar’s ChatGPT account and had seen his search history. “She said to me, ‘Dad, if you do not go see her now, you’re going to come back home and that’s all you’re going to think about. So go now.’”Within days, Avtar and Rosey were in London. Nicci shows me a picture of the first time they met, at a hotel near Heathrow. Their faces are flushed with joy. “I could see the raw emotion in her – she had been looking for me for so long,” Avtar says. “When I met her and hugged her tight, I thought, yes, this is my sister.” They went out for dinner and compared stories and timelines, piecing together the fragments that their families had given them.double quotation markEvery time I see Avtar, I just want to cry. That’s my brother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our livesView image in fullscreenNicci Dhamu.Photograph: Cian Oba Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAvtar Singh.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The GuardianThe following morning, Nicci took Avtar and Rosey to Birmingham, to meet their mother’s last-surviving sibling – their uncle – who had once shared a home with baby Titu. “He looked at me and said, ‘I remember you. I held you in my arms,’” Avtar tells me, his eyes awash with tears. “It was a great, great visit.”The next day, Avtar was introduced to his half‑brother – Nicci’s youngest sibling. He had been shocked when Nicci first told him she had found Avtar. “He said, ‘ButI’mMummy’s son,’” Nicci tells me, laughing. “I said, ‘Of course you are. Nothing’s going to change our family.’ When they finally met, Nicci says her younger brother shook Avtar’s hand. “I just knew it was going to be all right. My brother said, ‘I’ve always wanted a big brother.’”Avtar and Nicci both tell me they have no plans to confirm their relationship with a DNA test. There’s no need, they say.“I justknow,” Nicci tells me.“This world has a few billion people in it. And if somebody can randomly call me Titu … ” Avtar shakes his head. “I don’t think I need any more verification than that.”The joy at finally finding Titu is bittersweet for Nicci, because it came too late for her mother. “My biggest regret is that I didn’t talk to her about her son and let her cry about him, let her have a release,” she tells me. “It wasn’t her fault. It wasn’t anything that she did wrong. It just was a marriage that broke down.”“I grew up believing that she gave me up because it was the best thing to help her move on with her life. I was OK with that. I thought, I hope that she had a good life. I’m not the type of person to grieve or feel bad that I got abandoned or anything like that,” Avtar says. “Now I’ve heard from Nicci and other people in the family that my mum used to cry for me.That’s all I need to hear. It just feels so good to know that I was loved.”Plus, Avtar adds, there is “the treasure my mother left behind for me – I have all this family to get to know”. Word about Avtar is slowly spreading across the globe. He’s in a WhatsApp group for his maternal family, including cousins based in Kenya; they have seen each other on FaceTime. There’s discussion of a trip to Kenya so Avtar can meet them in the flesh, and see where Savinder once lived.double quotation markTechnology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be. There is a human touch to AI – look what happenedView image in fullscreenAvtar with Nicci in May during his first visit to the London home she shared with their mother.Photograph: courtesy of Avtar Singh“My cousins are so excited to meet him. He looks like them – same smiles, bald and bearded,” Nicci says with another throaty laugh. She whips out her phone to show me an AI-generated image Avtar has made of himself arm in arm with two cousins he’s yet to meet in person. Technology is bringing Savinder’s family together in ways she could never have envisaged, or even imagined.“We had a video call last night,” Nicci says. “Every time I see him, I look at him and I just want to cry. That’s mybrother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our lives.” She pauses. “Who would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.”Her half-brother sees things differently. “Right now, AI is still a glorified search engine. It is a piece of software that recognises a pattern in a string of characters, and it can look at millions of responses that match that character set and give you the highest probability best answer. What did it do? It looked at a couple of character strings that I typed in and found the best match. There’s no intelligence there.”Avtar remains as sceptical as ever about giving big tech his data, even though it was ChatGPT’s readiness to scrape blogs and give out personal information that led him to his maternal family. Had Avtar chosen to ask another AI, he might not have found Nicci at all. When he came back to Canada, he put the same prompt into Anthropic’s Claude, to see what it would say, just for fun. “It replied, ‘We don’t want to infringe on anybody’s privacy, so we don’t give out that information,” Avtar tells me. Then he shrugs. “I think that’s a good response.”

title: ‘We can see the boats that supply the restaurant’s lobsters from our seats’: a culinary tour of Gower, Wales | Wales holidays | The Guardian
description: On a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning scenery
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: On a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning scenery
Content: A selection of summer dishes at the View Rhossili on the Gower peninsula in south Wales.View image in fullscreenA selection of summer dishes at the View Rhossili on the Gower peninsula in south Wales.Wales holidays‘We can see the boats that supply the restaurant’s lobsters from our seats’: a culinary tour of Gower, WalesOn a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning sceneryFelicity CloakeSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf we take it as read that the better the view, the worse the cooking, then by rights south Wales’s Gower peninsula should be a culinary desert. The first time I visited almost 15 years ago, I was unprepared for its loveliness – back in 1956, Gower (nevertheGower, as locals were quick to correct me) was thefirst place in the UK to be designated an area of outstanding natural beauty, and though the peninsula abuts the country’s second city, Swansea, it still feels profoundly rural. Crisscrossed by narrow lanes flanked by towering hedges and ancient churches, it’s a great place to cycle, to drive, and above all to walk up an appetite.Indeed, it’s been a long-held ambition of mine to hike the 43 miles of the Welsh Coast Path from Mumbles to Loughor. Sadly, it remains just that because on this latest trip I spent considerably more time chomping than yomping … though in fairness I was on a research mission for a walking trip with a friend here later in the summer, because as a food writer and semi-professional glutton, I never like to head anywhere unprepared.View image in fullscreenWith this in mind, and another friend on hand as a chauffeur, Wilf the dog and I began our investigations in Mumbles, where Swansea thins into a pretty seaside village of colourful Victorian villas culminating in a magnificent, privately owned pier. (A few years ago, a visiting Prince William observed to owner Bert Bollom, the third generation of his family to run it, that this was an unusual career choice. Bert shrugged that he’d inherited the job from his dad. “Tell me about it,” he recalls the prince sighing.)Though the pier is undergoing restoration work, there’s a good view of the “crown of the Bristol Channel” from another Bollom enterprise,On the Rocks, a steak restaurant with a terrace jutting over the foreshore that’s no doubt a terrific place for a sundowner. But, I tell myself sternly, when you’re starting a walk you need to put one foot in front of the other, not sit around drinking, especially as the friend I plan to come back with later in the summer is happily, if rather inconveniently, pregnant.View image in fullscreenCrab sandwich at the Gower Seafood Hut in Mumbles.There’s thus not much point in returning to theGower Brewery Taproom, despite the warm welcome and dog biscuits we receive on this occasion – I’ll probably suggest we stop instead atJoe’s, the local cult masquerading as an ice-cream parlour. (Vanilla, freshly churned in-house daily, is the only move here. Unless you’re under the age of 10, do not waste your time on other flavours.) Thankfully, the expectant one is past the nauseous stage, so I can also steer her in the direction of the crab sandwiches (local sourdough and deliciously saltyShirgar butter) at theGower Seafood Hutwith a clear conscience – depending on the time of day, it might also feel appropriate to fortify ourselves with a helping of fried whitebait or cockle popcorn before joining the coast path, particularly as Chris Price, who mans the stoves, has, according to co-owner Sarah Kift, already walked much of it himself.That said, I reckon I’ve got the fuelling part of the route covered; for a start, there’s another ice-cream parlour,Fortes, just round the headland in Limeslade Bay. From the neat beach huts of Langland to the golden sands of Three Cliffs Bay, however, the sites are more prehistoric than edible (tasty as theBacon Hole cavesounds, the nearest it gets to cured meat is its hoard of ancient narrow-nosed rhinoceros and straight-tusked elephant bones, now 200 miles away in the British Museum). Take a brief detour into the village of Southgate though, and you’ll happen upon a brilliant Greek cafe – I didn’t anticipate tucking into a sugar-dustedbougatsacustard pie and a punchy little coffee inThe Gower Deli, but this place is full of surprises.double quotation markI didn’t anticipate tucking into a sugar-dusted bougatsa custard pie in The Gower Deli, but this place is full of surprisesSometimes they come too thick and fast even for my boundless appetite: just 20 minutes inland from Three Cliffs, if you follow the lazy meandering waters of the Pennard Pill past the ruins of a Norman castle, sits theGower Heritage Centre. Clustered around a 12th-century water mill, it boasts a cider press, organic community agriculture project, sauerkraut producer, jewellery designer and bike shop plus – and the jewel in its crown as far as I’m concerned – the superbLittle Valley bakery, whose traditional Gower loaf is produced using the mill’s barley flour. They also make ridiculously flaky pasties, focaccia sandwiches, huge cookies and excellent viennoiserie – in short, a rambler’s dream.View image in fullscreenThe Beach House restaurant in Oxwich on the Gower.From Three Cliffs, it’s about another five miles along the coast to Oxwich. If you make one reservation for your Gower trip, make it at theBeach Housethere. Admittedly, given its Michelin star, one might not want to wander in directly from the path in quick-dry hiking sandals, but our welcome couldn’t be warmer, despite Wilf’s rather over-effusive manner (the terrace is dog-friendly, as is one table inside, which you can bet your boots I will be booking well in advance).View image in fullscreenA Michelin-star dish at the Beach House restaurant in Oxwich.From our seats, we can see the two boats that supply the restaurant with lobster. “They belong to Paul and Jim,” says chef Hywel Griffith. “Every morning, I text them what we need that day.” The lamb is from the North Gower salt marsh; the seaweed in the laverbread rolls (a clever play on the traditional puree) from Selwyn’s in Pen-clawdd; and the dessert, a malted mousse with wood sorrel and fermented pine syrup, is the single most delicious thing I’ve eaten since Sarah Kift’s crab sandwich.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFive more miles brings us to Port Eynon, whose chief attraction on this visit is the tiny, genuinely artisanGower Gin Company– having enjoyed one solo guided tasting with my designated driver and the teetotal terrier, I’ll pass on another with a reluctant abstainer. It’s six more miles to Rhossili, once, somewhat absurdly, declared the “ninth best beach in the world” by TripAdvisor. What’s not up for debate is that it’s 3 miles long and stunning.View image in fullscreenSunrise over Mumbles lighthouse and privately owned pier.Photograph: leighcol/Getty ImagesThanks to the National Trust, it’s also untouched by the grubby hand of commercialism, so should you be peckish, pause at the aptly namedView cafebefore you descend the cliff. Offering colourful vegan “power bowls” (popular with the surfing crowd apparently) and homemade falafel alongside the rarebit and bara brith, the only packaged food in sight is a bag of locally produced dog treats I’m bullied into buying for my elderly companion who, despite a brisk trot down to the Worms Head Coastwatch station beforehand, is in no mood to obey the house rule that “shouting is not permitted”.The key to an unforgettable holiday? Just focus on the food | Felicity CloakeRead moreTurn the corner on to the north coast, and you’re faced with Whiteford Sands, yet another broad expanse of golden gorgeousness with great cooking attached in the form of theBritannia Innin Llanmadoc, where the salt marsh lamb croquettes at the bar drive the tiny diner under the table to distraction.Fortunately, I don’t have to test Wilf’s restraint on the living, bleating thing on this occasion, as the remaining seven miles of the route – through the marshes to Pen-clawdd, – will have to wait till next month. When we finally get there, however, I will insist on stopping at the Gower Brewery to toast our achievement. I’ve even road-tested their Zero beer in preparation. As I said, I like to plan ahead.Explore more on these topicsWales holidaysEurope holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysFood and drinkFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegan recipe for cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and lime | Noodles | The Guardian
description: This globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kick
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: This globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kick
Content: Meera Sodha's cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut coriander and lime.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha's cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut coriander and lime.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.The new veganNoodlesMeera Sodha’s vegan recipe for cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and limeThis globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kickMeera SodhaSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan a person in a heatwave ever have too many cold noodle dishes? I’d wager no – hence today’s recipe. It started life as one of my favourite meals, the mighty spaghetti pomodoro, but then packed its bags and travelled through the Middle East, picking up some tahini along the way, then on to Indonesia for some heat (sambal oelek), and then hopped over to Vietnam for a final hurrah of fresh lime, coriander and peanuts. The result is a creamy but perky tomato sauce that can live in the fridge for up to a week for the too-hot-to-cook days.Cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and limeI’ve said “light” tahini and agave syrup (over “dark”), but if the jar or bottle doesn’t say which it is, don’t worry. Ramen noodles are available in larger supermarkets; you’ll need to go farther afield (or online) for sambal oelek, a bright Indonesian chilli sauce, but it’s worthwhile. It’s a very easy-to-use and versatile condiment. You can make the tomato sauce ahead of time and add the cooked noodles and topping when you’re ready to serve.Prep10 minCook30 minServes4250g ramen noodles3½ tbsp neutral oil(eg, rapeseed or sunflower)3 garlic cloves, peeled and finely minced1½cm x 2cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated400g tin finely chopped tomatoes(AKA “polpa”)1¼ tsp fine sea salt1 tbsp sambal oelek2 tbsp light tahini1½ tbsp light soy sauce1½ tbsp toasted sesame oil2 tsp light agave syrup75g roasted salted peanuts, finely chopped to breadcrumb size1 lime, zest finely grated, then juiced to get 1 tbsp15g fresh coriander, finely choppedCook the noodles according to the packet instructions. Just before the end of the cooking time, take out a small mug of the cooking water, then drain the noodles and rinse them under the cold tap until cold. Gently and with clean hands, mix in a tablespoon of oil, then leave to drain.To make the sauce, put two tablespoons of oil in a large saucepan or deep saute pan on a medium heat. When hot, add the garlic and ginger, cook for a couple of minutes until sticky and golden, then add the tinned tomatoes. Fill the empty tin a quarter-full of water (to get the last bits), then tip this into the pan, too, along with a teaspoon of salt and the sambal oelek.Cook for eight to 10 minutes, until the bubbles are thick and the sauce reduced. Mash away any lumps of tomato with a potato masher, then take off the heat and stir through the tahini, soy sauce, sesame oil and agave.For the topping, put the peanuts, lime zest, a quarter-teaspoon of salt and half a tablespoon of oil in a small pan on a medium to low heat, and stir frequently until the peanuts take on a deep, brown colour. Stir in the tablespoon of lime juice, leave that to dry off, then take off the heat and leave to cool for five minutes.Stir the coriander through the topping mix. Add the noodles to the cooled sauce, toss to coat, then tip on to a platter and sprinkle over the topping.Explore more on these topicsNoodlesThe new veganVegetablesFoodTomatoesSummer food and drinkSauces and graviesMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: Summer holiday car hire: drive a great deal and avoid hidden fees | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Unclear terms and expensive extras can turn what seemed like a cheap rental into a costly one
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Unclear terms and expensive extras can turn what seemed like a cheap rental into a costly one
Content: Booking directly with a car hire company doesn’t necessarily guarantee the best deal, so shop around online first.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyView image in fullscreenBooking directly with a car hire company doesn’t necessarily guarantee the best deal, so shop around online first.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyConsumer affairsSummer holiday car hire: drive a great deal and avoid hidden feesUnclear terms and expensive extras can turn what seemed like a cheap rental into a costly oneShane HickeySat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is not too late to get a good deal on your holiday car rental, even if you have booked already and are travelling soon. But there are many pitfalls to avoid so that you do not end up paying over the odds.A survey fromWhich? found that one in eight peoplewho had hired a car in the past two years had ended up paying more than they were first quoted.“Booking car hire should be straightforward, but hidden fees, unclear terms and costly add-ons still make it difficult for travellers to compare prices and know who is really offering the best deal,” says Guy Hobbs, a travel expert at the consumer group.“Too often we hear from holidaymakers who have faced poor customer service and unexpected charges that turn a seemingly cheap rental into an expensive one.”BookingBooking directly with a hire company will not necessarily give you the best deal, so check out as many aggregator and broker websites as possible.Those such as Carrentals.co.uk, Skyscanner, Kayak and Zest Car Rental cover holiday destinations around the world.When comparing offers, it is vital that you are clear about what you are getting for the price. A cheaper deal may not be offering everything you want.One of the most important things to look out for is free cancellation. Many providers offer this and the period often runs up to 48 or 72 hours before the booking starts.As rental prices fluctuate all the time, watch out for the best deals and switch if you come across something that is better value.Figures from iCarhireinsurance showed European hires for the same holiday week went down in price by 16% in July compared with January last year. This means a week-long rental in places such as Nice and Crete could be £100 cheaper if you cancel and rebook.When booking, aim for a deal with unlimited mileage – otherwise you will be charged for every mile that you go over the limit. And pick a deal where you return the car full of fuel, rather than returning it empty, to avoid the often high price of rental firms’ petrol and diesel.When overseas, it is worth refilling your car a short distance away from the airport, as prices near the terminal can be higher than elsewhere.Look at the customer rating applied to the provider, which is often attached to search rankings. It is worth paying more and getting a reliable provider, than going with a poorly rated one that is cheap.View image in fullscreenWhen you pick up your car the rental firm will often try to sell ‘extra’ or ‘top-up’ insurance but this is often bad value.Photograph: Stephen Barnes/Travel/AlamyCollectionAll rentals in the UK and Europe will come with a level of insurance. If there is an accident, or damage is caused to the vehicle you have rented, you will typically have to pay an excess, and the insurance will cover the rest. But this excess can be hundreds – and sometimes thousands – of pounds.When you pick up your car, the rental company will often try to sell you “extra” or “top-up” insurance to cover that excess.This is usually bad value. Instead, buy your own policy before you travel. If there is an accident, then you pay the excess to the rental company and claim it back off your policy.You can compare these car hire excess policies using aggregator sites such as MoneyMaxim. Which? scores the Cover4Rentals silver plan highest. You can buy single, or multi-trip policies. It charges £30.50 a year for one driver hiring cars on multiple trips to Europe.The excess and other deposits will be authorised on your credit card – a debit card will usually not be accepted.Make sure you have enough credit available and that the credit card is in the name of the person who made the booking. Also make sure you take your driving licence.Once you have the keys, check the car thoroughly for any damage, and take time-stamped pictures and a video of any scrapes, scratches or other problems. Report back straight away anything that is different from the details in the hire documents that the company sent you. If it is too dark to do an inspection, do it the next day, make a note and inform the rental company. Make sure the fuel tank is full.If you are collecting your car late at night, you may be charged extra for “out of hours” pickup.For example, Hertz at Dublin airport charges €30 (£26) after midnight for a “late service fee”. Other rental companies may charge similar fees, though the amount will vary. Check the terms and conditions of the rental carefully.View image in fullscreenWhen you hand the keys back stay for the inspection, and once home keep an eye on bank statements.Photograph: Eric Audras/Getty Images/OnokyDrop-offAfter refilling the car at a garage, take it back and stay for the inspection. Try to get the paperwork completed there and then. If there has been an accident, ensure you keep all documents and receipts for a later claim on your excess insurance.If you are delayed and are going to return the car late, you may be charged an extra day of rental fees. Companies will often have a grace period, typically 29 minutes after the car is due to be returned, for you to bring it back without penalty, but these can vary.Once home, keep an eye on your card statements to make sure that any money ringfenced on your credit card has been returned.If you have a problem and have not got a resolution through the car rental company’s complaints procedure, you can lodge a complaint with theEuropean Car Rental Conciliation Service.However, the ECRCS only covers companies signed up to the scheme and in Europe. They are Alamo Rent A Car, Avis Budget, Budget, Dollar, Enterprise, Europcar, Hertz, National Car Rental, Sixt, Thrifty and Firefly.In the UK, theBritish Vehicle Rental and Leasing Associationhas a conciliation service.If you have a problem with a rental in the US, complain to the company first, then ask your bank whether you can raise a chargeback against the company.The UK International Consumer Centre, a government-funded body, can help with advice.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsMotoringCar insuranceInsuranceConsumer rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK savings deals: the heat is on as banks offer up to 8% | Savings | The Guardian
description: Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts say
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts say
Content: You can currently get easy-access accounts that pay up to 5% interest, while the average one-year fixed-rate bond pays 4.22% – the highest since November 2024.Photograph: Viktoria  Rodriguez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYou can currently get easy-access accounts that pay up to 5% interest, while the average one-year fixed-rate bond pays 4.22% – the highest since November 2024.Photograph: Viktoria  Rodriguez/Getty ImagesSavingsUK savings deals: the heat is on as banks offer up to 8%Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts sayRupert JonesSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is shaping up to be a decent summer for savers as fierce competition among providers pushes up interest rates and increases choice.You can currently get instant- and easy-access accounts that pay up to 5% interest, and fixed-rate savings bonds that pay almost that much. Meanwhile, those looking for a regular savings account can now get up to 8%.So if you have cash languishing in a savings, or current, account that is earning no interest, or only giving you a paltry return, now is the time to move it to a better-paying home.“Things are looking promising – the choice is really good, but it’s all about being proactive and switching, and making the most of these products while they are there,” says Rachel Springall at the financial data providerMoneyfacts.This month, the number of “live” savings accounts paying more than the Bank of England base rate – currently 3.75% – rose to 1,385, the highest figure for more than six years, says Moneyfacts. That figure represents more than half of the total number. (Though it is based on the interest rate paid on a balance of £5,000.)With the cost of living still a big issue, many savers will be keen to keep their cash close at hand where they can get at it if needed. The average non-Isa easy-access account rate is now the highest it has been for almost a year, at 2.53%.The top-paying easy-access accounts offer quite a bit more.Revolut, the fast-growing fintech that is now a fully fledged bank, recently launched a “market-leading” savings rate offer for new UK customers. If you open one of its instant-access savings accounts between now and 4 August, you can benefit from a rate of 5% until 4 December this year. This will apply on balances up to £25,000. After 4 December, the interest will revert to the rate determined by your plan. So if you are on Revolut’s free standard plan, or its £3.99-a-month Plus plan, for example, it will fall to 2.9%.Chase, the British retail arm of the US bank JP Morgan, has an easy-access account called Chase Saver that pays new customers 4.5%. That rate is boosted by a 2.25% interest bonus that lasts for 12 months – the account’s standard rate is 2.25%. It lets people stash away up to £3m – however, a (free) Chase current account is required.Fixed-rate savings bonds offer some of the highest rates. You typically have to tie up your money for between six months and five years, and they provide a clear, guaranteed return.One-year fixed-rate bonds have been “very popular”, says Springall, as many people do not want to tie up their cash for too long. The good news is that this month, the average one-year fixed bond rate rose to 4.22% – its highest since November 2024.However, at the time of writing you could get more than that: for example, Marcus by Goldman Sachs had a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 4.9%. Up to £250,000 can be paid into this online account. And Atom Bank has a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 4.8%.Regular savings accounts often offer eye-catching interest rates. With these, you put aside some money each month for a limited period. Often, you have to have a current account with the bank offering the product, and in many cases the headline rate only lasts for a year.Lloyds launched a new instant-access regular savings account earlier this month called Monthly Saver. The account pays an impressive 8%. There is also a version available for customers of Halifax and Bank of Scotland, although the Halifax one (called Regular Saver) does not let you access your savings during the 12-month term. In all cases you can save from £25 to £250 a month by standing order or bank transfer, and your interest is paid 12 months after you open the account.Santander also has a regular savings account paying 8% for 12 months. It lets you save up to £200 a month from its current accounts.But watch out for the savings interest “tax trap” if you are putting a large-ish sum of money into a decent-paying non-Isa account.Interest earned outside an Isa is subject to tax once you go over yourpersonal savings allowance. This is £1,000 for basic-rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers, and up to £5,000 if you earn less than £17,570 a year.Explore more on these topicsSavingsSavings ratesBanks and building societiesBankingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: my dog has post-traumatic sheep disorder | Family | The Guardian
description: There is nothing woolly about the sheep awareness training a Kent farmer subjects our dog to
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: There is nothing woolly about the sheep awareness training a Kent farmer subjects our dog to
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: my dog has post-traumatic sheep disorderThere is nothing woolly about the sheep awareness training a Kent farmer subjects our dog toTim DowlingSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s another scorching day, maybe the ninth or tenth in a row. Work is impossible – I spend the afternoon wandering the house in search of the coolest place to stand. I’m busy interrupting a faint breeze at the foot of the stairs when my wife rings.“This is ridiculous,” she says. “I’m standing still.”“Me too,” I say. “Where are you?”“On the M25,” she says. “In traffic.”“Where have you been?” I say.“Sheep awareness training,” she says.“Oh yeah,” I say. “How was it?”“Brilliant,” she says. “She’s absolutely traumatised. I’ll tell you about it, if we ever get home.”Our old dog, unfailingly obedient and chicken-hearted, never troubled sheep. At two years old, the new dog has had almost no direct experience of livestock but has never met an animal it did not want to chase: foxes, squirrels, Canada geese. It was hard to imagine a first encounter going well.double quotation markWe can hear bleating from both sides of the valley. As soon as the dog hears the sound, it gets back in the carWhen my wife heard about a farmer in Kent who would cure your dog of any interest in sheep in an afternoon, she made an appointment.“Is this because of the thing that happened in the Archers?” I’d said.“No,” she’d said. “I signed up before all that.”My wife arrives home 90 minutes later, trailing a hint of car air conditioning. The dog comes into the kitchen behind her and immediately flattens itself against the cool floorboards.“She’s got post-traumatic sheep disorder,” my wife says.“What was it like?” I say.“So he’s a real farmer,” she says. “In farmer’s clothes.”“OK,” I say.“And you start out in a tiny pen, half the size of this kitchen, with two sheep and the dog on a short lead,” she says. “Predictably, the dog is going nuts.”“Predictably,” I say.“Barking, straining, trying to get at the sheep. And the farmer has this plastic bottle full of pebbles, which he shakes. And shouts at the same time. The shouting is important.”“Of course,” I say.“Anyway, within five minutes she’s just sitting there, trying not to make eye contact with the sheep.”“Then what?” I say.“Then you move to a bigger pen, with more sheep, and you do it again. By this point she won’t leave my side. And he’s still shaking the bottle whenever she even starts to look at the sheep. She’s hating every minute of it.”“And that’s it?” I say.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Oh no,” my wife says. “After that we graduate to an actual field full of sheep, with two collies driving the flock right at us, over and over. By now, she’s completely freaking out and is trying to pretend there are no sheep.”“Huh,” I say.“The whole thing took half an hour.”“How much?” I say.“Forty pounds,” she says.The place where we happen to be spending the following weekend is surrounded by fields. On arrival there are no sheep to be seen, but when we get out of the car we can hear distant bleating from both sides of the valley. As soon as the dog hears the sound, it gets back in the car.“So our dog now has a sheep phobia,” I say. “We’ll have to go back to London.”“We can’t,” my wife says. “I need to do reinforcement training.”“Here?” I say, looking at the baked fields.“Where else?” she says. “First, I need to fill this bottle with pebbles.”Up the hill and along a track we eventually come to a gate. On the other side a flock of black sheep is gathered under a tree. My wife opens the gate and the dog, now on a long lead, reluctantly steps through.“Really?” I say.“Come on,” my wife says, heading towards the sheep.The sheep seem larger than I expected, and rather more prepared to stand their ground – only when we’re very close do they give way, resentfully stepping further up the slope to let us pass. The dog, ears tucked back, is giving them as wide a berth as the lead will allow.“Wow,” I say. “It really works.”One lone sheep has gone downhill instead, separating itself from the rest. The dog does not see it through the tall grass as she walks toward it. No more than 10 yards separate the two animals when the dog finally senses movement, and looks up. For a brief moment the sheep and the dog regard one another with wary respect.“Hyah!” my wife screams, slamming down her bottle of pebbles.The dog jumps in terror, and so do I.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Young country diary: Beetles, newts and ‘scorpions’, all in my simple river trap | Insects | The Guardian
description: Norfolk: I check it every day to see what I get. This time all the creatures started fighting so I had to quickly put them back
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Norfolk: I check it every day to see what I get. This time all the creatures started fighting so I had to quickly put them back
Content: Hal emptying his river trap.Photograph: Family handoutView image in fullscreenHal emptying his river trap.Photograph: Family handoutYoung country diaryInsectsYoung country diary: Beetles, newts and ‘scorpions’, all in my simple river trapNorfolk:I check it every day to see what I get. This time all the creatures started fighting so I had to quickly put them backSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlive near theRiver Bureand I like to go there every day to watch the wildlife. Recently, I made a trap out of a large plastic bottle and put it in some shallow ditches to see what I could get. I cut off the top of the bottle and stuck it inside the bottom bit upside-down. That way, creatures can come in through the top but can’t escape because it’s pointing inwards. I found two bamboo poles, stuck them in the ditch and put the trap between them. It was filled halfway with ditch water.The next morning, I found aEurasian water scorpion, a small beetle, a newt, some leeches and a few sticklebacks in the trap. The scorpions are not venomous but you can’t handle them because they’ll give you a nasty bite.View image in fullscreenA young water scorpion (Nepa cinerea) in shallow water, Norfolk.Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockThey’re called water scorpions because they have a long whip-like tail which they use to breathe under water, four skinny legs to walk on and two dagger-like claws to catch prey. They’re not related to scorpions.When I looked in the trap, the beetle was attacking the water scorpion. The water scorpion managed to fling the beetle to the other side, where the newt was. Then this beetle clung on to the newt’s neck and tried to bite it and this caused a fight. The newt was 10 times bigger than the beetle and flung it off, but the beetle just went back on the newt again. I opened the trap and quickly put all of the creatures back in the ditch before any of them got killed.Hal, eightRead today’s other YCD, by Jess, 10: ‘A jellyfish party around our surfboards’. title: Young country diary: A jellyfish party around our surfboards | Marine life | The Guardian
description: North Devon: The cool water was full of them – and we found out later that one of them, the compass jellyfish, should be avoided
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: North Devon: The cool water was full of them – and we found out later that one of them, the compass jellyfish, should be avoided
Content: A compass jellyfish. ‘It was amazing to watch and hard to fear these beautiful creatures.’Photograph: The Marine Conservation Society/Peter Bardsley/PAView image in fullscreenA compass jellyfish. ‘It was amazing to watch and hard to fear these beautiful creatures.’Photograph: The Marine Conservation Society/Peter Bardsley/PAYoung country diaryMarine lifeYoung country diary: A jellyfish party around our surfboardsNorth Devon:The cool water was full of them – and we found out later that one of them, the compass jellyfish, should be avoidedSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a scorching hot day, my friend and I went surfing at my local beach. We partnered up to carry the boards down to the water – mine coral-coloured, his blue – and we clambered across the dunes, with the sand burning the soles of our feet. As we jumped into the cool water, we realised we were not alone. At first, we saw one or two, but by the point we were knee-deep, we realised we were surrounded. Jellyfish of all shapes and sizes were floating around us, purple-y ones, brown ones.We later learned that the beautifulmoon jellyfishis recognisable by its dome shape and the fact it’s completely translucent apart from purple circles across the centre. These are harmless and are commonly washed up on UK beaches.View image in fullscreenJess at her local beach. ‘We rescued two jellyfish and returned them back to the ocean.’Photograph: Family handoutWe think the others werecompass jellyfish, which come out from May to October. These are also translucent but have yellowy-white and brown markings on top of the bell and can give a nasty sting. I read that their sting is quite mild, a bit worse than a stinging nettle. At first, I wasn’t too bothered about them, enjoying watching them bobbing around me, until my friend told me that they can be dangerous if you’re not careful. So, after that, I tried as hard as I could to avoid brushing against them.As we enjoyed the surf, the relentless waves brought many more jellyfish to join the party around our boards. It was amazing to watch and hard to fear these beautiful creatures. Eventually, we headed in, but not before we had rescued two beached jellyfish and returned them to their home, the ocean.Jess, 10Read today’s other YCD, by Hal, 8: ‘Beetles, newts and ’scorpions’, all in my simple river trap’. title: ‘Without us, they are doomed’: volunteers save fish from French rivers drying up in heatwaves | France | The Guardian
description: Fish being moved to oxygenated flowing water further downstream as water levels drop across country
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Fish being moved to oxygenated flowing water further downstream as water levels drop across country
Content: A dried-up branch of the Loire, in Loireauxence, last week.Photograph: Sebastien Salom-Gomis/Sipa/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA dried-up branch of the Loire, in Loireauxence, last week.Photograph: Sebastien Salom-Gomis/Sipa/ShutterstockFrance‘Without us, they are doomed’: volunteers save fish from French rivers drying up in heatwavesFish being moved to oxygenated flowing water further downstream as water levels drop across countryKim WillsherSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlong the Odet River in Brittany, fisher Mathieu Le Bouter and a dozen volunteers are catching hundreds of trout and young salmon – not for sport but to save them.They are only a few miles from the source of the river, which springs from the Black Mountains in Finistère and runs for about 40 miles (65km) into the Atlantic Ocean, but the water is barely up to their knees.“The situation is catastrophic, far worse than we thought,” said Le Bouter, of the Finistère fishing federation. Once they catch the fish, he and his team transfer them to tanks of oxygenated water then release them 10 or 12 miles downstream where the rivers are joined by tributaries, raising the water level.View image in fullscreenDead trout stranded in a residual pool on the bed of the Source River, near Chatillon-sur-Seine, in Burgundy.Photograph: Konrad K/Sipa/Shutterstock“The fish are under a great deal of stress. When you combine very high temperatures with low levels of dissolved oxygen, problems arise,” Le Bouter said.“What’s really scaring us is that the 10-day forecast suggests there won’t be any rain, and temperatures will generally be high. The fish, particularly trout and young salmon, need water with a current and oxygen, so these conditions become lethal for them.”While thefires raging across forestsin France are a dramatic reminder of three successive heatwaves in as many months,the state of the country’s rivers provides another, no less worrying insight into the impact of extreme heat supercharged by the climate crisis.The Loire, France’s longest river, is at a historical low, with the flow of some branches, including through the city of Orléans, reduced to a trickle between sandbanks. Two weeks ago, 16% of French rivers were reported to have dried up. A quarter of small streams were stagnant or had disappeared altogether, according to the national low water observatory. There has been little rain since.View image in fullscreenA branch of the Loire in Loireauxence in western France.Photograph: Sebastien Salom-Gomis/Sipa/ShutterstockThe Dive River, at Rom in the western Deux-Sèvres department, is dry, and all that is left of the Mignon further north is a dusty bed. Normally at this time of year, water levels would be between 40cm and 70cm.The Seine, which divides Paris and supplies drinking water to the city, is now “on life support”, declaredLe Monde, with half of the river’s flow being drawn from reservoir lakes upstream and its tributaries in Champagne and Burgundy, a measure that would not normally be needed for another month. In Vernon, Normandy, the flow of the Seine has dropped from an average of 200 cubic metres per second in July last year to 110.Despite a rainy winter that caused flooding, the sweltering heat this summer and low rainfall since April has created an extreme drought,sucking rivers across Europe dry.In France, 99 out of the country’s 101 departments are under water restrictions, and a state of emergency has been declared in 58 of them. In a statement, the ministry for ecological transition said almost a third ofriver monitoring stationshad recorded the lowest levels in 20 years anda quarter of smaller waterwayshad dried up. It noted a rise “in the death of fish linked to the rise in water temperature”.“The situation is very worrying,” it added.An emergency agriculture bill passed by the French parliament on Tuesday, which facilitates the construction of water storage tanks for crop irrigation and livestock farms, has raised concerns over the equitable sharing of water resources and fears that farmers are being prioritised.Claude Roustan, the president of the national fishing federation, said rivers were suffering not just from the drought and climate change but “excessive extraction” of water to irrigate scorched crops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are the first line of observation of the state of the waters across France; we act as first responders and what we are seeing is that some areas are in great difficulty,” he said. The agriculture bill, he added, ran counter to conservation efforts.‘It’s only going to get worse’: wildfires forcing firefighters to make impossible choicesRead moreLe Bouter said water levels in the Odet and nearby Isole River, where Atlantic salmon spawn and the young fish develop before migrating to the ocean, always drop in summer, but never this early. He described the current situation as “a vicious circle”.The drop in river levels causes a rise in water temperature, which kills the aquatic vegetation. Other plants grow back, particularly filamentous algae, further reducing oxygen levels for the fish.“As the days go by, the environment becomes increasingly suffocating for them. Without doing what we are doing, those that remain are doomed,” Le Bouter said. “We’re in a crisis situation.”Le Bouter says he and his volunteers will keep wading through the Odet and Isole for as long as necessary.“We seem to be the only ones who are concerned about the fish. Unlike birds, deer and foxes, which are more visible, they tend to get forgotten.”He added: “It’s the holidays, and we’d rather be doing something else, but at the moment we’re the only ones out there carrying out these rescues and systematically raising the alarm.”Explore more on these topicsFranceRiversDroughtFishExtreme heatEuropeClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reclaiming stolen childhoods: swimming classes resume in Gaza after three years of war | Gaza | The Guardian
description: In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives
Content: A group of children relax after their swimming class.  Photograph: Amjad Tantesh/The GuardianIn sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily livesBySeham Tanteshin Gaza andEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem; photographs by Amjed TanteshSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwimming classes have started again inGazaafter three years of war, with hundreds of children learning to float, doggy paddle and take their first strokes in five makeshift sea pools built from sandbags and rubble.The lessons allow a few hundred girls and boys to reclaim their childhood for a few hours in a place where there are no playgrounds, no formal education and children live in fear of continuing Israeli attacks. A UN survey in March found that 96% of children felt death was imminent.View image in fullscreenActivity on the Gaza seafront“Swimming gives me a chance to escape the war, and the worries I live with,” said Alma Shabat, 13, who saw her mother killed in an Israeli strike in May.After three weeks of classes, her favourite stroke is freestyle, she has made new friends and she is no longer afraid of the waves and open sea. “Coming to the beach is a beautiful and enjoyable experience,” she said.Swimming classes begin again in Gaza – loopAmjed Tantesh, who founded Gaza’s first swimming academy more than two decades ago, has mobilised dozens of volunteers this summer to create the string of pools on the beaches of central Gaza, with tarpaulins providing some shade from the fierce Mediterranean sun.There is very little heavy machinery left in Gaza so they did everything by hand, moving tonnes of rubble and filling sandbags to build walls, then excavating sand to deepen the pools.View image in fullscreenChildren take part in a swimming classIn the morning they hold free classes for children whose parents were killed in Israeli attacks. In the afternoon, the pools are open to everyone and constantly filled with delighted children splashing in the warm water.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTulin Al-Othmaneh, 10, and Aseel Al-Kafarna“Its a rare chance to enjoy, relax and reclaim part of their stolen childhood,” said Tantesh, who has also worked as a journalist for the Guardian and other outlets. His niece, Seham Tantesh, reports for the Guardian from Gaza. “The pools attract children from all along the beach like huge magnets”.Most Palestinian children have endured years of extreme trauma. There is the loss and maiming of loved ones, with one in ten of the prewar population killed or injured in Israeli attacks. Thousands more are thought to be buried under the rubble.View image in fullscreenA big group of the children pose for a photo on the beachView image in fullscreenChildren form a chain before getting into the waterGaza has the highest concentration of child amputees in the world. “Disability among Palestinian children has ceased to be an individual medical condition and has now become a defining demographic reality,” a UN commission said in a report on Israel’s targeting of Palestinian children.The human-made famine caused by Israel’s siege last year will leave some children with lifelong mental and physical stunting.View image in fullscreenInstructor Ali Al-Attar with a group of the childrenThere has been no formal schooling for three years, and almost all school buildings have been damaged or destroyed. There are nearly 700,000 school-age children in Gaza, and only a minority have access to the makeshift tent schools run by aid groups.Survivors are crammed into crowded, hot and noisy tent camps in just a third of the prewar Gaza without adequate water or sanitation.View image in fullscreenAmjed Tantesh takes a selfie while a swimming class takes place behind himSwimming classes are a desperately needed escape from this grim reality, physically and mentally. “Being here allows me to train, play and breath fresh air, away from the tents,” said Maryam al Musri, 10, who lost her father in the war.Laila Qahman, 14, who lost her seven-year-old brother when a mosque near where he was playing was bombed and who dreams of becoming a pharmacist, said swimming gave her the chance to relax, cool down and forget about life in a tent.View image in fullscreenLaila Qahman“I come here every other day because it makes me feel like I’m living my life and enjoying my time, instead of staying in the tent listening to the sounds of shelling and living with fear and sadness,” she said.“Before I learned how to swim, I was a little afraid of the sea and did not have the courage to go into the water. Now, I feel much more confident and no longer feel afraid when I swim.”So far 700 children have attended six weeks of classes, and Tantesh hopes to teach thousands more over the summer if he can get funding to pay teachers, who are currently all working for free, and cover other basic expenses.The joy of these young swimmers has been healing for him as well, as he mourns his older brother Bahjat, a karate champion killed in an Israeli attack last year as the brothers fled their family home under Israeli evacuation orders.“Bahjat was the one that taught me swimming in the first place, then inspired me to pursue sporting excellence as a young man,” he said. “To have him die in my arms was the worst thing imaginable.”View image in fullscreenA group of children sitting on the beach after their swimming classThe original academy was inspired in equal measure by hope and tragedy.Palestinemade its Olympic debut at the Atlanta Games in 1996, giving athletes from Gaza the first chance to compete on the world’s biggest stage, and Tantesh a new mission.“I wanted to be at the Olympics, but I started as a professional swimmer at a very late age. So I decided to achieve my dream through a new generation,” he said.Closer to home, each summer brought deaths by drowning at sea. Families would flock to the beach to relax, splash around and cool off but few people could swim and there were no lifeguards at his local beach. Swimming lessons would make children safer and they could train future lifeguards, he decided.View image in fullscreenKamal Taha, 12, being interviewed by a local TV channelHis biggest challenge when the classes first launched was persuading parents to sign up their children. “People were terrified by water, the sea looked like a monster to them as it consumed dozens of people annually,” he said.For the first few years children learned to swim in Gaza’s port, where breakwaters protected children from the waves. Then he constructed a series of pools along the coast for classes, where about 11,000 people learned to swim.The biggest, built with rubble from homes bombed by Israel in 2014, was more than 1,000 square metres. Israeli attacks since 2023 razed all the pools, killed tens of swimming students and at least six coaches, and injured countless more.Restarting classes seemed almost impossible. “I only had the sea, but the sea is dangerous even during summer. You have jellyfish, you have high waves, strong currents, rocks,” he said.So he came up with the plan for new pools, for the sake of Gaza’s children and as a tribute to his brother. Seeing the children leave the horrors of war behind for a brief period, when they dive into the sea, has also been healing for him.“Actually the first person I helped with this project was myself,” he said. “It has given me a great feeling of happiness and recovery. I am alive again.”You can find more about the swimming pool projecthereExplore more on these topicsGazaIsrael-Gaza warChildrenMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Herbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical maker | Herbicides | The Guardian
description: Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease
Content: Paraquat, a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries, has been produced by the Swiss company Syngenta for decades, but has long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.Photograph: Arnd Wiegmann/ReutersView image in fullscreenParaquat, a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries, has been produced by the Swiss company Syngenta for decades, but has long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.Photograph: Arnd Wiegmann/ReutersHerbicidesHerbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical makerSyngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s diseaseGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerSat 25 Jul 2026 00.59 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSyngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has beenlinked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemicalannounced by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in June.A global threat for millennia: experts warn Australia’s nuclear submarine legacy will be weapons-usable uranium cacheRead moreParaquat has been produced by the Swiss company for decades, buthas long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.It is banned in more than 70 countries and has been prohibited in the European Union since 2007.It cannot be used in domestic settings in Australia, but is still widely used in agriculture, particularly broad-acre cropping like grains, sugarcane and cotton. The APVMA assessed that the weight of evidence does not show that paraquat exposure through approved uses increases the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease.But it did impose new restrictions to address acute exposure and risks to animals.The company said the decision to pull the products followed a commercial review carried out in the wake of the APVMA’s rules.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailSyngenta ANZ’s managing director, David Van Ryswyk, said the company will manage the phase-out of its paraquat products in strict alignment with the APVMA’s designated sell-out and use-by timelines.“Regulatory constraints, combined with a highly complex and increasingly expensive supply chain, have made the paraquat herbicide products commercially unviable,” Van Ryswyk said.The new restrictions on the herbicide required that backpack sprayers be phased out, mandate additional personal protective equipment for users and set a much lower maximum rate of application per hectare.At the time of the APVMA’s decision,Syngenta saidthe pesticide “does not cause an unacceptable environmental impact” and that the regulation would limit its use in a significant number of crop use cases.The company had planned to continue supplying through a third-party manufacturer, but on Friday it said the new regulations and an increasingly expensive supply chain had made the product unviable.Generic paraquat products will still be available for local farmers.Last month, the Melbourne neurologist Associate Prof Wes Thevathasan told the ABC that there has been “global consensus” in his field that exposure to paraquat was linked to the development of Parkinson’s disease.“There are now multiple epidemiological studies or real-world exposure studies that have suggested that paraquat increases the risk of Parkinson’s disease by around threefold,” Thevathasan said.Grain Producers Australia spokesperson Andrew Weidemann said Syngenta’s decision created uncertainty for local growers.“Its withdrawal leaves some important questions about what happens next,” he said.“Australia is a relatively small market, and decisions like this call future investment into question.“If companies cannot see sufficient value in maintaining products here, growers risk being left with fewer choices at the same time we urgently need more tools to manage herbicide resistance.”Explore more title: One killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin Pride | Germany | The Guardian
description: Suspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Suspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’
Content: Emergency responders at work on Saturday after a car crashed into a crowd at Tiergarten park, Berlin.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersView image in fullscreenEmergency responders at work on Saturday after a car crashed into a crowd at Tiergarten park, Berlin.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersGermanyOne killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin PrideSuspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’Deborah Colein BerlinSat 25 Jul 2026 19.51 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to punish those responsible after a car struck people on the outskirts of Berlin’s Gay Pride celebrations, killing at least one person and wounding 16 others.A suspected ⁠perpetrator of the apparent attack on ⁠Saturday night has been ⁠identified as a member of the ⁠city’s “Islamist scene” but he ​has not ‌yet ‌been arrested, a Berlin police spokesperson said.The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and comes asGermanyremains on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks in recent years.Hours after the apparent attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle struck multiple ⁠people after charging into the city’s central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate.Police said those hurt “included several with life-threatening injuries”.The driver of a white van had swerved shortly before 10pm into the Tiergarten park, close to the route of the Pride march held earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree, police said.“[The vehicle] was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track ​down the perpetrator or perpetrators,” police said. Tabloid newspaper Bild cited a witness as saying that a man emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot.A manhunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.A Berlin fire department spokesperson, Dominik Pretz, said one person died and at least 16 others were injured.Emergency workers set up a helicopter landing pad near the Reichstag parliament building to transport the injured to hospitals.Merz said in a statement that he and the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, would “push to make sure this horrific act is fully investigated and punished”.Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a terrible day. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked.”Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in the German capital in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the pride parade.It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.Berlin mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally.
