Berlin will hold a state election in September.The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “Taking a stand is hot” which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to queer people in Germany.More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest against the event.Before last year’s pride parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisationssounded the alarmthat attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat.Campaigners said a rise in hostility has accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.With Associated Press and ReutersExplore more on these topicsGermanyLGBTQ+ rightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: France and Spain race to control wildfires as more than 250,000 evacuated – as it happened | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Meanwhile, in the UK, a blaze in the Cairngorms national park has been described as ‘very serious’ by Scotland’s first minister
Author: Hamish Mackay
Headline: Meanwhile, in the UK, a blaze in the Cairngorms national park has been described as ‘very serious’ by Scotland’s first minister
Content: 07.33 EDTTotal number evacuated in France and Spain is now 267,000The number of people evacuated inFrancein Spain has now passed 250,000, according to authorities in both countries.The French government said that 197,000 people were evacuated because of wildfires near Bordeaux, in southwest France.The Spanish interior ministry said a total of 70,000 people were evacuated from villages west of Madrid.Both countries are facing unprecedented blazes that are spreading unchecked despite the efforts of many hundreds of firefighters backed by water-dropping aircraft.Share

title: More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid
Author: William Christou
Headline: Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid
Content: A fire in El Tiemblo, to the west of Madrid. Spain has declared a national emergency over the wildfires for the first time ever.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fire in El Tiemblo, to the west of Madrid. Spain has declared a national emergency over the wildfires for the first time ever.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresMore than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and SpainHundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in MadridWilliam ChristouSat 25 Jul 2026 12.23 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnrestrained wildfires in Spain andFrancehave forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes.About 70,000 people were evacuated from centralSpain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux.Spain declared a national emergency, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire. France’s evacuations constituted “probably” the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has ever seen, its interior minister said.Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance. In Spain, high winds were exacerbating the fires, and two of the three blazes merged on Friday.0:59Firefighters in Spain and France battle raging wildfires – videoFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said a huge military cargo plane, the Airbus A400M Atlas, was being deployed to join 18 other aircraft in the “long and very difficult” battle against wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France.The French government has called in the military to help,deploying 1,500 soldiers, and has rushed 1.5m face masks to help protect people from smoke inhalation. Fire crews have also been digging trenches, as well as using retardants, as winds were forecast to push the fires closer to Bordeaux.Wildfireswere reported to be about 20 miles west of the city.The French government ordered people in the path of the fire to evacuate, including those in Bordeaux’s western suburbs. Police went door to door to tell people to leave, with scenes of panic unfolding as residents fled their homes under a smoke-darkened sky.The Gironde regional prefect, Sophie Brocas, said on Friday that strong winds were driving the fire towards the Bordeaux metro area and that it had grown to “an unprecedented magnitude”.View image in fullscreenPeople who have been evacuated from their homes in the Bordeaux-Lac exhibition centre, which has been turned into a shelter for displaced people.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersOfficials said the sudden blazes caught residents and authorities off guard. Some people in France had to flee by boat when the flames headed towards coastal towns.The French prime minister, SébastienLecornu, said the fire in Gironde was so strong that it had begun generating its own winds.“The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” he wrote on X. “Our priority is clear: protecting human lives.” He urged people to obey evacuation orders “without delay”.The Spanish health minister instructed people in Madrid not to go outside over concern of the poor air quality.“Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” Monica Garcia said on X.On Saturday evening, Spain’s interior ministry said a man had died in a fire in Manises, in Valencia. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters on a support line between the villages of Lacanau and Saint-Hélène in the Bordeaux region.Photograph: Astrid Lagougne/EPAThe fire was a separate incident from the major blazes raging west of Madrid, which have so far not caused any reported deaths.The long, back-to-back heatwaves inEuropehave dried forests out, turning them into tinder for wildfires. Fires had already consumed 130,000 hectares (320,000 acres) of forest this year in Spain, about a third higher than the country’s annual average, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said on Saturday.In France, fires burned down more than 98,000 hectares, which France’s interior minister said was a “historic record”.Climate crisis-driven heat ‘sucking soils dry’ as extreme drought hits EuropeRead moreScientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading tothousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.Sánchez said that cooler weather on Saturday gave a “window of opportunity” for firefighters to help contain the blazes. “We are going to have some complex hours ahead because, although the temperatures have gone down, we do not know exactly how the wind will develop, how strong it will be,” he added.Other European countries were helping both countries fight the blazes, with Croatia, the Czech Republic, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Slovakia sending aid and water-dumping aircraft to France and Spain.The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised more help was on the way.“Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them. Five planes and two helicopters from the rescue fleet are now deployed in France and four planes are arriving in Spain today,” she said on X.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEuropeSpainFranceClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine? | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
Author: James Risen
Headline: After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
Content: The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, sits with Laura Loomer on 23 July 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Ukrainian presidential press office/APView image in fullscreenThe Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, sits with Laura Loomer on 23 July 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Ukrainian presidential press office/APDonald TrumpAnalysisWhat’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?James RisenAfter a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winnerSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.02 EDTShareLaura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, buther sudden conversion to the Ukrainian causethis week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the secondTrump administration.The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days inKyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy forUkrainein its long war withRussia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda.Loomer – who has previously echoed Kremlin talking points to her 2 million followers on social media – has enjoyed direct access to Trump since the 2024 presidential campaign. During the early months after Trump returned to office, Loomer used her online presence to push for ideological purges of government personnel, including many in the national security arena.For a time, her power to break careers among foreign policy officials made her seem as if she wereTrump’s de facto national security adviser.It is unclear whether she still has that kind of pull inside the White House, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, certainly took her seriously when she arrived this week, holding a private meeting with her on Thursday.Maga influencer and de facto national security adviser Laura Loomer holds outsized sway on TrumpRead moreThree days earlier, Loomer posted about experiencing her first air raid, as Russian missiles pounded the Ukrainian capital“This is everyday for every Ukrainian,” she posting, adding she felt that she had been “an asshole for minimizing the struggle of Ukrainians for the last 5 years”.“I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. There are people in Ukraine who have to run to a bomb shelter everyday and some of us had the audacity to say Russia wasn’t wrong because we believed the lie that Ukraine is a country full of Nazi sympathizers. We have been so propagandized by Russia and we don’t even realize it.”Before their meeting on Thursday, Zelenskyy’s office posted a statement saying: “It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are.”Loomer’s change of heart is potentially important not only because she is close to Trump, but also because she has long served as a reliable barometer of Maga attitudes.Loomer has long been disdainful of Ukraine, adopting what could only be described as a pro-Russian perspective. Many in Maga circles have for years held positive views of the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, thanks to Russian propaganda that portrayed him as a bulwark against homosexuality and a defender of fundamentalist Christianity. They became convinced that the Russia-Ukraine war was a proxy fight between Russia’s fundamentalist Christianity and the EU’s western secularism.Loomer’s shift comes at a critical moment for Ukraine, which recently lost one of its strongest supporters in Washington with the death this month of Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina who had consistently pushed for increased sanctions on Russia to punish Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine.Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visitRead moreBut Loomer’s change also coincides with what appears to be an important recent shift in Trump’s own views on Ukraine.Trump returned to office openly hating Ukraine, at least in part because of the2019 impeachmentover his attempt to hold up aid to Ukraine in exchange for dirt on Joe Biden. Early in his second term, Trumphumiliated Zelenskyy in an Oval Office meeting, cut off direct the supply of US weapons and forced Ukraine’s European allies to buy American weapons for Kyiv instead.But Trump likes winners, and even without full support from Washington, Ukraine has been able to slow Russia’s advance. Kyiv has become a global leader in drone technology, and it has taken the war to Russia itself with long-range missile attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure, leading to an energy crisis in one of the world’s biggest oil-producing nations.Clearly impressed with Ukraine’s performance, Trump announced at the Nato summit in Turkey earlier this month that the US would license Patriot missile technology to Ukraine, allowing Kyiv to produce the advanced air defense missiles on its own.At the same time, Trump also supported a move in Congress, which had been backed by Graham, to impose new sanctions on Russia, while also seeming to back off an earlier insistence that Ukraine would have to agree to give up large swaths of territory in exchange for any US-brokered peace deal with Russia.Trump’s policy shifts were modest, but significant; it is possible that Loomer changed her position simply in order to stay in lockstep with Trump.But her about-face could be even more politically significant if it represents a broader thawing of Maga attitudes towards Ukraine and an awakening to the dangers of Russian propaganda.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationSocial mediaUS politicsUkraineRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘No time to waste’: Greece bids for Mount Olympus to be included on Unesco list of world heritage sites | Greece | The Guardian
description: Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation
Content: Hikers walk in the direction of Stefani peak, also known as the throne of Zeus, at sunrise on Mount Olympus. The mountain’s popularity has soared over the past decade, with about 500,000 visitors recorded last year.Photograph: Angelos Tzortzinis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHikers walk in the direction of Stefani peak, also known as the throne of Zeus, at sunrise on Mount Olympus. The mountain’s popularity has soared over the past decade, with about 500,000 visitors recorded last year.Photograph: Angelos Tzortzinis/AFP/Getty ImagesGreece‘No time to waste’: Greece bids for Mount Olympus to be included on Unesco list of world heritage sitesOfficials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designationHelena Smithin LitochoroSat 25 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than four decades have elapsed since Evangelos Geroliolios made his first ascent to the home of the ancient gods. At the top of Mount Olympus, on the rocky peak of Greece’s highest mountain, he felt unalloyed awe.“I’ve never forgotten that unique moment, that unique feeling up there on the throne of Zeus,” recalled Geroliolios, who as mayor of Dion-Olympus now spends a great deal of his time administering the area around the site.Described by Homer as the “seat of the immortals”, its craggy summit – where Zeus, the father of the gods, is said to have held court – rises 2,918 metres above the sea.“You get this incredible sense of place, fused by myth, beauty and the weight of history – all of which we want to share and hope will be recognised internationally,” he said.Greek officials have long lobbied for Mount Olympus to be included on theUnescolist of world heritage sites; soon champions of the cause will learn if the site will finally be granted the coveted designation.The World Heritage Committee is scheduled to begin discussing the nomination on Sunday at its 48thsession, now under way in Busan, South Korea. The annual meeting ends on 29 July.Greece first proposed the mountain’s inclusion on the list of places considered by Unesco to be “of outstanding value to humanity” in 2014, citing both its cultural and environmental significance.The area was declared a national forest – the country’s first – in 1938, in tribute to the uniqueness of terrain covered not only by verdant forest but alpine fields, gorges, ravines and springs, all within close proximity of the sea.Litochoro, the nearest town to the mountain, lies three miles (5km) away from breathtaking beaches practically at the foot of the mountain.In recognition of its abundance of flora and fauna, Unesco designated Olympus a biosphere reserve in 1981. Further environmental protection came in the form of a presidential decree, when the mountain was declared a national park, in 2021.“But,” says Geroliolios, “becoming a world heritage site would not only be important for Greeks. It would speak to the entire planet. Olympus is up there with the Parthenon and it’s vital that we safeguard this environment of myth and history. For us, protection is the alpha and omega.”View image in fullscreenA butterfly perches on a wildflower on Mount Olympus. In recognition of the site’s abundance of flora and fauna, Unesco designated it a biosphere reserve in 1981.Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/APLast year, the committee inscribed 26 new properties on Unesco’s World Heritage list, bringing the total number of sites to 1,428 across 170 countries. Of the 21 in Greece, only two have been inducted as mixed cultural and natural world heritage sites.Under an international treaty overseen by Unesco, the treasures, which include landmarks such as the Great Wall of China, the Egyptian Pyramids and the Taj Mahal, automatically become protected zones.Increasingly the designation is regarded as a bulwark against the depredations of development and overtourism. Like much of Greece, the mountain’s popularity has soared over the past decade, with about 500,000 visitors recorded last year.It is a number that is widely predicted to rise on the back of revived interest in the ancient world after the 17 July release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. The record-breaking blockbuster, inspired by Homer’s epic, was partially filmed in Greece, which also helped subsidise the movie.“We’re happy to have tourists but more of them will mean more risks,” said Dimitris Pappas, the deputy director of the Olympus national park management agency.“There’s no doubt that if the area is declared a Unesco world heritage site it will help contribute to the mountain’s protection. If we lose what we have it will be a catastrophe.”Pappas said by far the biggest threat to the site was forest fires exacerbated by climate breakdown.“They could be averted with extra funds to improve fire protection measures, including clearing walking paths and building shelters. River bridges and roads could be upgraded, too.”View image in fullscreenA wild goat is seen on Mount Olympus. The biggest threat to the site has been identified as forest fires exacerbated by climate breakdown.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesWorld heritage sites are provided with technical support and financial assistance from Unesco, which also gives expert advice to help preserve the monuments.Tourists visiting the site this week said the designation was not only deserved, but overdue. “It’s not just a good idea, it’s the best idea,” enthused Lenka Hotmarova, 62, from the Czech Republic. “There’s room for improvement along the trails and it would help raise awareness about the need for preservation. It should have happened earlier.”Greece has also highlighted the region’s religious significance, citing the discovery of an open-air sanctuary, on one of the mountain’s lowest peaks, in its nomination file.The sanctuary is believed to have been described by Plutarch, the philosopher historian, in the second century AD in connection with animal sacrifices made to Zeus.Mount Olympus is thought to be home to the highest altitude chapel in the Christian Orthodox world with Byzantine monasteries and other places of worship built into its folds and peaks.The bid’s outcome is still far from certain. Advisory bodies from the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS) and International Union for Conservation of Nature are reported to have recommended further details with the draft agenda of the Unesco meeting in Busan suggesting the nomination will be referred back to Greece – prolonging the quest further.At a time of soaring tourism, that worries Geroliolios. “It’s all about balance,” he says. “Olympus’s carrying capacity has reached its limit.”Designation as a world heritage site would “place greater responsibility on our part to protect the environment”, he said, adding: “But even if we don’t succeed, there’s no time to waste. Further protective measures have to be taken.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceUnescoMountainsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate | Houthis | The Guardian
description: Saudi air defences intercept ballistic missiles as Iran reports first night without US strikes in two weeks
Author: William Christou
Headline: Saudi air defences intercept ballistic missiles as Iran reports first night without US strikes in two weeks
Content: Saudi Arabia struck the port city of Hodeida in Yemen in response to Iranian-backed Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.Photograph: Khaled Abdullah/ReutersView image in fullscreenSaudi Arabia struck the port city of Hodeida in Yemen in response to Iranian-backed Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.Photograph: Khaled Abdullah/ReutersHouthisIran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalateSaudi air defences intercept ballistic missiles as Iran reports first night without US strikes in two weeksWilliam ChristouSat 25 Jul 2026 08.28 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 22.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week.Iran, meanwhile, reported no strikes overnight on Saturday for the first time after two weeks of US attacks. The Iranian health ministry spokesperson, Hossein Kermanpour, said: “Iran had a peaceful night” in a post on X. Tensions, however, remain high.A memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June seemed to break down two weeks ago, after Iranian attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz prompted US strikes on Iran, which led to Iranian retaliation against US allies in the region.The MoU was meant to reopen the strait after its closure by Iran during the war and pause hostilities for 60 days to give room for negotiations, but active fighting has prevented progress in talks. Much of the current fighting has centred on the strait, a transit point for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas prior to the war.Donald Trump had threatened expanded strikes on Iran, meeting top national security advisers on Friday to decide whether the administration should escalate attacks.But by Saturday evening, the US president had reportedly, at least for now, set aside plans for an escalated assault, according to the New York Times.Iran issued warnings to citizens of Gulf countries hosting US military sites to stay away from bases to protect themselves from future attacks.On Saturday night, a spokesperson ⁠for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said ⁠that ​Britain would become ⁠a “definite and legitimate target” if it ⁠supported the ​US ‌in any ‌war with Tehran, ‌according to the Iranian state broadcaster, Irib.The spokesperson said any country, ‌including Britain and Gulf states, ​that backed the US in a conflict ⁠would be considered ​a legitimate ​target, adding ​that US ​bombers ‌had recently ​used ​British airfields.Trump insisted on Friday that, despite the fighting, negotiations with Iran were going well, calling them “by far the most serious that we’ve seen”.The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the “American approach” was preventing peace talks from proceeding, while vowing Iran was “neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure”.Tensions over the strait continued, with the US firing on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman which it said was violating its blockade of Iranian ports, while the UK maritime agency reported an incident between a tanker and military forces on Friday, without specifying the responsible parties.View image in fullscreenA screen grab of video footage posted on social media showing smoke rising after strikes on the Saudi Aramco refinery in Jizan.Photograph: UGC/UNKNOWN/AFP/Getty ImagesAir defence systems inSaudi Arabiaintercepted two ballistic missiles from Yemen on Saturday, Reuters reported. The attacks targeted oil refineries in Yanbu on the Red Sea, while the Saudi civil defence also issued warnings for the port city of Jizan, close to the border with Yemen.A video circulating on social media showed dark clouds rising above a refinery in Jizan belonging to Aramco, the Saudi oil giant. A Yemeni security source told Agence France-Presse a naval base in Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were targeted by Saudi Arabia on Friday. TheHouthissaid the attacks were a “dangerous escalation”.The Iran-aligned Houthi movement, which controls northern and western Yemen, declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last week after the kingdom struck the airport in Sana’a. TheHouthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea on Thursday, prompting Trump to threaten a “major military punishment” for Tehran and the Houthis.Oil passes $100 a barrel again and shares slide as Middle East conflict escalatesRead moreThe naval blockade threatens to further upend global energy markets, as Saudi Arabia has been avoiding the closure of the strait by diverting millions of barrels of oil to the Red Sea. Oil prices pushed past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, while the cost of shipping insurance through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies.Araghchi said on Saturday that there was no military solution to the Saudi-Houthi conflict and that it was “rooted in old disputes”.“We believe that there is no military solution to the issue of Yemen,Bab al-Mandab and other regional issues,” Araghchi said in an interview with an Iranian newspaper. He called for further dialogue between the two sides.Mediators have tried to keep talks alive amid the escalating fighting, Pakistan and Qatar delivering messages between the US and Iran over the last two weeks. The New York Times reported that Iraq had delivered a ceasefire proposal to Tehran, which was promptly rejected – a report disputed by Iraq.Pakistan has also reportedly been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after a diplomatic initiative by China explored new dialogue. Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, visited Istanbul this week to discuss the topic, reports said.Explore more on these topicsHouthisUS-Israel war on IranYemenSaudi ArabiaUS foreign policyStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Treasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefacts  | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Content: The artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockHeritageTreasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefactsJewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological findsNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield.Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocallwearing earringsthat were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC.According to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer that owns the earrings, the gold medallion plaques are “attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-westIranin the late 1940s”. They were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, who mounted them with diamonds in yellow gold.View image in fullscreenGold plate showing a character fighting a lion from the Ziwiye Hoard exhibited at the Louvre Museum in Paris.Photograph: Lanmas/AlamyBut while the Mayfair retailer claims the jewellery celebrates “the remarkable artistry of ancient Persian goldsmiths” and encourages “wider appreciation of one of the world’s great artistic traditions”, academics take a different view.A petition has been launched calling for Barron London to publish the complete known provenance of the gold plaques, reveal the checks they undertook on the legality of the items, permit examination of the objects, and even suspend sale.Zendaya is used to the glare of camera lenses, but being the focus of academically qualified antiquarians is something else altogether.Dr Christos Tsirogiannis, an antiquities expert at the Swiss Federal Office of Culture, said: “Personally, after all these two and a half decades of continued scandals emerging everywhere about all sorts of illicit antiquities … I’m extremely surprised, negatively surprised, that no one among all these people that escort these celebrities said something to protect her.”‘Incredible’ Roman bathers’ gems lost 2,000 years ago found near Hadrian’s WallRead moreRomina Frohar, the founder of the Forensic Archive of Iran, an independent investigative archive documenting threats to Iran’s cultural heritage that set up the petition, said her concern was broader than Zendaya’s decision to wear the items.“Barron London has described the loan as a celebration of ancient Persian artistry, but cultural appreciation cannot substitute for provenance transparency,” she said. “If these objects are being publicly presented as Iranian cultural heritage, the evidence concerning their origin, export, ownership history and acquisition should be open to scrutiny.”Even if antiquities were authentic and lawfully possessed, ethical issues may still arise, said Frohar, a PhD researcher at the Glasgow School of Art. “Private custody can be responsible when it is transparent, conservation-led and attentive to public and scholarly access. But legal possession alone does not extinguish the cultural claims of the people whose history the object embodies.”The earrings’ odyssey from BC Iran to A-list actor involved a trip into the shadowy world of rare treasure trading – an industry in which priceless archeological finds are transformed into high-end luxury trinkets.Many of the collections of Mayfair dealers, auction houses and private homes would be at home in the glass cases of museums.Among items currently available to purchase from dealers online is an Egyptian mummy mask made of beads that dates from somewhere between 664BC to 332BC; Hellenistic gold earrings with garnet and agate dating back to the 3rd century BC, and a bronze dress pin with an end resembling an ibex that apparently comes from Iran and could be up to 3,000 years old. Their prices start at about £450.In parallel, auction houses have put astonishing antiquities under the hammer. In 2018, Christie’s sold a 3,000-year-old relief from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II, a neo-Assyrian king who ruled 800 years before the establishment of the Roman empire, fornearly $31m.Tsirogiannis is no stranger to such sales. His work has turned up evidence casting doubt on the provenance of numerous antiquities on the market. “About 90% of antiquities in the market one way or another, sooner or later, are proved to be illicit or lacking provenance, lacking documentation,” he said.If Zendaya’s earrings were authentic, they might also pose another moral conundrum: “Possibly they are coming from a burial. How does she feel that she is wearing an ancient dead woman’s earrings [that may have been] looted?” he said.View image in fullscreenThe Koh-i-noor diamond sits in a crown on the coffin of Britain’s late Queen Mother Elizabeth.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APProvenance and ownership of antiquities is an issue that has long passed beyond academia. Among the most notorious examplesis the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which was surrendered to Queen Victoria by the 10-year-old maharajah Duleep Singh in 1849 as part of the Treaty of Lahore, becoming part of the British crown jewels.The legalities around establishing who owns ancient items can be complex.“Most so-called source countries for antiquities now have state ownership laws in place to say that ancient objects discovered belong to the state,” said Simon Mackenzie, a professor of criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (Te Herenga Waka) in New Zealand. “So the act of discovery and looting is essentially a form of theft [from the government].”“In many countries, including Iran, these laws had been built up over time andwere not retroactive, so legal arguments could be made about what date exactly the theft rule applied from, he said.Despite the outrage, sprinkling some modern celebrity stardust on the treasures of millennia gone by is not always a bad thing. When bling attracts academic attention, a conversation about provenance can begin.When Kim Kardashian was snapped posing in a gold dress next to a gilded Egyptian coffin at the Met Gala in 2018, for example, experts in antiquities trafficking took notice.View image in fullscreenKim Kardashian’s appearance at the Met Gala in 2018 also sparked controversy.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe Met museum had acquired the 2,100-year-old coffin of a priest called Nedjemankh for $4m and made it the star of an exhibition. However,experts soon revealedit had been excavated by thieves in 2011 and smuggled out of Egypt to Dubai and then Europe, where it was restored and given false documents.The legal and ethical problems which came with Zendaya’s earrings may never be resolved, but there remains one conundrum that does not require a PhD to spot.As Tsirogiannis pointed out, the film star’s jewellery put the spotlight on Iran while promoting a film that had nothing to do with ancient Persia.Explore more on these topicsHeritageArchaeologyZendayaIranMiddle East and north AfricaCelebrityDisputed artnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reclaiming stolen childhoods: swimming classes resume in Gaza after three years of war | Gaza | The Guardian
description: In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives
Content: A group of children relax after their swimming class.  Photograph: Amjad Tantesh/The GuardianIn sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily livesBySeham Tanteshin Gaza andEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem; photographs by Amjed TanteshSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwimming classes have started again inGazaafter three years of war, with hundreds of children learning to float, doggy paddle and take their first strokes in five makeshift sea pools built from sandbags and rubble.The lessons allow a few hundred girls and boys to reclaim their childhood for a few hours in a place where there are no playgrounds, no formal education and children live in fear of continuing Israeli attacks. A UN survey in March found that 96% of children felt death was imminent.View image in fullscreenActivity on the Gaza seafront“Swimming gives me a chance to escape the war, and the worries I live with,” said Alma Shabat, 13, who saw her mother killed in an Israeli strike in May.After three weeks of classes, her favourite stroke is freestyle, she has made new friends and she is no longer afraid of the waves and open sea. “Coming to the beach is a beautiful and enjoyable experience,” she said.Swimming classes begin again in Gaza – loopAmjed Tantesh, who founded Gaza’s first swimming academy more than two decades ago, has mobilised dozens of volunteers this summer to create the string of pools on the beaches of central Gaza, with tarpaulins providing some shade from the fierce Mediterranean sun.There is very little heavy machinery left in Gaza so they did everything by hand, moving tonnes of rubble and filling sandbags to build walls, then excavating sand to deepen the pools.View image in fullscreenChildren take part in a swimming classIn the morning they hold free classes for children whose parents were killed in Israeli attacks. In the afternoon, the pools are open to everyone and constantly filled with delighted children splashing in the warm water.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTulin Al-Othmaneh, 10, and Aseel Al-Kafarna“Its a rare chance to enjoy, relax and reclaim part of their stolen childhood,” said Tantesh, who has also worked as a journalist for the Guardian and other outlets. His niece, Seham Tantesh, reports for the Guardian from Gaza. “The pools attract children from all along the beach like huge magnets”.Most Palestinian children have endured years of extreme trauma. There is the loss and maiming of loved ones, with one in ten of the prewar population killed or injured in Israeli attacks. Thousands more are thought to be buried under the rubble.View image in fullscreenA big group of the children pose for a photo on the beachView image in fullscreenChildren form a chain before getting into the waterGaza has the highest concentration of child amputees in the world. “Disability among Palestinian children has ceased to be an individual medical condition and has now become a defining demographic reality,” a UN commission said in a report on Israel’s targeting of Palestinian children.The human-made famine caused by Israel’s siege last year will leave some children with lifelong mental and physical stunting.View image in fullscreenInstructor Ali Al-Attar with a group of the childrenThere has been no formal schooling for three years, and almost all school buildings have been damaged or destroyed. There are nearly 700,000 school-age children in Gaza, and only a minority have access to the makeshift tent schools run by aid groups.Survivors are crammed into crowded, hot and noisy tent camps in just a third of the prewar Gaza without adequate water or sanitation.View image in fullscreenAmjed Tantesh takes a selfie while a swimming class takes place behind himSwimming classes are a desperately needed escape from this grim reality, physically and mentally. “Being here allows me to train, play and breath fresh air, away from the tents,” said Maryam al Musri, 10, who lost her father in the war.Laila Qahman, 14, who lost her seven-year-old brother when a mosque near where he was playing was bombed and who dreams of becoming a pharmacist, said swimming gave her the chance to relax, cool down and forget about life in a tent.View image in fullscreenLaila Qahman“I come here every other day because it makes me feel like I’m living my life and enjoying my time, instead of staying in the tent listening to the sounds of shelling and living with fear and sadness,” she said.“Before I learned how to swim, I was a little afraid of the sea and did not have the courage to go into the water. Now, I feel much more confident and no longer feel afraid when I swim.”So far 700 children have attended six weeks of classes, and Tantesh hopes to teach thousands more over the summer if he can get funding to pay teachers, who are currently all working for free, and cover other basic expenses.The joy of these young swimmers has been healing for him as well, as he mourns his older brother Bahjat, a karate champion killed in an Israeli attack last year as the brothers fled their family home under Israeli evacuation orders.“Bahjat was the one that taught me swimming in the first place, then inspired me to pursue sporting excellence as a young man,” he said. “To have him die in my arms was the worst thing imaginable.”View image in fullscreenA group of children sitting on the beach after their swimming classThe original academy was inspired in equal measure by hope and tragedy.Palestinemade its Olympic debut at the Atlanta Games in 1996, giving athletes from Gaza the first chance to compete on the world’s biggest stage, and Tantesh a new mission.“I wanted to be at the Olympics, but I started as a professional swimmer at a very late age. So I decided to achieve my dream through a new generation,” he said.Closer to home, each summer brought deaths by drowning at sea. Families would flock to the beach to relax, splash around and cool off but few people could swim and there were no lifeguards at his local beach. Swimming lessons would make children safer and they could train future lifeguards, he decided.View image in fullscreenKamal Taha, 12, being interviewed by a local TV channelHis biggest challenge when the classes first launched was persuading parents to sign up their children. “People were terrified by water, the sea looked like a monster to them as it consumed dozens of people annually,” he said.For the first few years children learned to swim in Gaza’s port, where breakwaters protected children from the waves. Then he constructed a series of pools along the coast for classes, where about 11,000 people learned to swim.The biggest, built with rubble from homes bombed by Israel in 2014, was more than 1,000 square metres. Israeli attacks since 2023 razed all the pools, killed tens of swimming students and at least six coaches, and injured countless more.Restarting classes seemed almost impossible. “I only had the sea, but the sea is dangerous even during summer. You have jellyfish, you have high waves, strong currents, rocks,” he said.So he came up with the plan for new pools, for the sake of Gaza’s children and as a tribute to his brother. Seeing the children leave the horrors of war behind for a brief period, when they dive into the sea, has also been healing for him.“Actually the first person I helped with this project was myself,” he said. “It has given me a great feeling of happiness and recovery. I am alive again.”You can find more about the swimming pool projecthereExplore more on these topicsGazaIsrael-Gaza warChildrenMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests | India | The Guardian
description: Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
Content: Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata party in Delhi celebrate after the resignation of Dharmendra PradhanPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of India's Cockroach Janata party in Delhi celebrate after the resignation of Dharmendra PradhanPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndiaIndia’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protestsDharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protestersHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiSat 25 Jul 2026 09.54 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 06.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has resigned after a week of mass demonstrations, handing a major victory to anew youth movementthat has posed an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.In a statement on Saturday afternoon, Pradhan said he had submitted his letter of resignation to the prime minister after student pressure.“Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and ‌across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation … I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister,” Pradhan wrote in a social media post.He said he had been “saddened by what unfolded over the last 10 days”, but added: “I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations ‌of the country’s youth.”During his 12 years in power, Modi has cultivated a strongman image and has maintained his ministers are not accountable to public pressure. This was the first time a mass uprising had forced one of his most loyal ministers to resign.The protests were organised by a newly formed youth political movement, the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which has escalated into a nationwide uprising of youth dissent this week.The core demand of the CJP and its supporters was the resignation of Pradhan over an exam leak scandal that has devastated the lives of millions of students and led to more than a dozen students taking their own lives.View image in fullscreenDharmendra Pradhan’s resignation marks the first time one of Narendra Modi’s ministers has been forced to step down due to public pressure.Photograph: Zuma/AlamyThe refusal by Modi to sack his minister over the scandal was widely seen as symbolic of the alleged lack of accountability of the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and its repeated failure to address the issues faced by young people, particularly in the country’s flawed education system.CJP organisers confirmed they had called off their demonstration after Pradhan’s resignation and a meeting with senior BJP ministers on Saturday afternoon.In a speech to the crowds gathered at the Delhi Jantar Mantar protest site, CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, saluted the “courage” of students who had turned out in huge numbers, even when they were subjected to police violence.“We have done it,” he said, to cries of “victory to India” and “long live the revolution”. But Dipke also emphasised Pradhan’s resignation was “just the beginning” in the movement’s push for systemic education reform and its fight for democratic rights.He also cautioned against people making a hero of him. “Do not make this mistake,” said Dipke. “The country has been ruined by making one person a hero.”Faria Asif, 26, a lawyer who was in the crowd, said: “I am extremely joyous. This is a huge victory, not just for the students, for the constitution and for the entire nation. Being part of this movement has been extremely empowering for all of us. I think it’s the beginning of change.”The news of Pradhan stepping down was met with ecstatic cheers by tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered in Delhi, who have been demanding accountability from the government.“This is one of the most historic days for our country,” said Rochelle Cope, 27. “For the first time in 12 years, someone from the government has been held accountable for wrongdoing. And it wasn’t political parties that did this; it was the people.“This is a movement of unity, love, solidarity, peace, justice and power. Being here has made me proud to be a citizen of India. This is only the beginning – this government will not be able to rule like it did before.”For many of those present, this week was the first time they had taken part in a political protest and the movement was described as a “gen Z political awakening” in India.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New DelhiAmong them was 16-year-old Kanishka Dabla, who said she hoped to become a doctor one day. “It’s wonderful that he has resigned,” she said. “It has made us all feel very powerful. And this also feels like justice for those students who committed suicide because of the exam leaks. It’s made me hopeful for my future again.”In a statement, the CJP said the resignation was a victory for democracy. “We have a free country where we are free to express ourselves, dissent, criticise the government we elect. We will never let anyone take that away from us,” it read.The statement added: “Remember, do not mess with cockroaches.”‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreSonam Wangchuk, the renowned Indian engineer and activist who had galvanised the movement as he went on a 26-day hunger strike, celebrated the “victory of democracy, straight from the streets”.The CJP demonstrations hadtaken a dramatic turn on Monday, when hundreds of thousands of young people and students took to the streets of Delhi in the largest youth-led protest seen in years. The police had hit back against the peaceful gatherings with brutality, including teargas and baton charges, leaving hundreds injured.Widespread anger erupted at the violent police response, prompting more people to come out in support of the movement. Throughout this week thousands had flocked to the CJP’s Delhi sit-in to chant slogans against the government and call for Pradhan’s resignation. Demonstrations also broke out across the country, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets in Kolkata and Mumbai.For weeks, the Modi government had ignored the CJP protesters, but as support grew into ahuge mass movement this week, the government agreed to have a dialogue.Modi had agreed to fast-track justice for the exam leaks, but had made no mention of the CJP’s core demand, the resignation of Pradhan, who was seen as one of his most important and loyal ministers.However, the CJP’s leadership had made it clear the resignation of Pradhan was a non-negotiable demand for the movement. As more protests erupted over the weekend and negotiations were at a deadlock, the BJP government appeared to be backed into a corner.Not all those who took part in the protests were gen Z. Annie Raja, 62, beamed as she looked out at the celebrating protesters. “I feel enthusiastic and happy,” she said.“The young people came out on the streets and they saved our democracy. Previously the government thought they had all the power, and the people were living only in fear. Now the Modi government is scared of us.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaNarendra ModiProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian celebrities fiercely criticised for silence on Cockroach protests | India | The Guardian
description: Bollywood stars accused of ‘cowardice’ as hundreds of thousands of young Indians take to the streets to challenge government
Author: Amrit Dhillon
Headline: Bollywood stars accused of ‘cowardice’ as hundreds of thousands of young Indians take to the streets to challenge government
Content: Protesters shout slogans during a demonstration demanding educational reforms as part of the Cockroach Janata party's ongoing protest movement in Mumbai, India on Thursday.Photograph: Rafiq Maqbool/APView image in fullscreenProtesters shout slogans during a demonstration demanding educational reforms as part of the Cockroach Janata party's ongoing protest movement in Mumbai, India on Thursday.Photograph: Rafiq Maqbool/APIndiaIndian celebrities fiercely criticised for silence on Cockroach protestsBollywood stars accused of ‘cowardice’ as hundreds of thousands of young Indians take to the streets to challenge governmentAmrit Dhillonin DelhiSat 25 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBollywood stars and other Indian celebrities have faced fierce criticism for staying silent in the face of some of the biggest protestsIndiahas seen in years.Hundreds of thousands of young Indians took to the streets this week as part of a new youth movement that calls itself theCockroach Janata party(CJP), demanding accountability over exam paper leaks in an unprecedented challenge to prime minister Narendra Modi’s government. Many vented their anger against what they saw as “cowardice” from India’s biggest celebrities.“We are the ones who made them famous and wealthy by turning up and paying for their films and matches,” said Vijay Rai, 24, who travelled more than 2,000km from Chennai in south India to the site. “Now when it’s our turn for a little help, we get nothing.”View image in fullscreenActor Salman Khan told students to go back home and not make their ‘parents worried for them’.Photograph: Prodip Guha/AlamyCJP organisers and protesters have been sleeping on the ground, enduring scorching sunshine, monsoon downpours and the misery of sweltering humidity since they began their indefinite sit-in protest on 20 June in the capital.The mass demonstrations have led tothe resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Prasad – a central demand from the CJP over a paper leak in May that forced 2 million students to resit an important exam and led to more than a dozen student suicides. In the 12 years the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) has been in power, it was the first time one of Modi’s most loyal ministers has been forced into resigning due to public pressure.On Monday, the mass peaceful student protest was met with police brutality, including the use of batons, teargas and, allegedly, pellet guns.Protesters were scathing about how celebrities had commented on global tragedies or injustices but turned a blind eye to the grievances of people at home, even when their most devoted fanbase were being baton-charged and teargassed by the police.“Just a few words on social media to express their moral support for our demands would have been welcome,” said Seema, who works cleaning homes in Delhi.View image in fullscreenBollywood actor Anupam Kher warned the protesters about ‘political opportunists’, echoing comments made by BJP ministers.Photograph: Deepak Sharma/APIn recent years Bollywood, which was once seen to be outside politics, is widely believed to have been co-opted by the far-right politics of Narendra Modi, leading to a surge of hyper-nationalist films accused of promoting the political agenda of the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) government.Many of Bollywood’s biggest stars are Muslims, and are seen to have to tread very carefully to ensure their films do not attract boycotts by powerful Hindu right-wing groups. Indian actor and film-maker Aamir Khan was viciously trolled in 2015 when he said, against a backdrop of Muslims being lynched, that his wife felt unsafe and wondered if they should leave India.‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreThose few superstars who did eventually comment this week mostly refrained from directly criticising the government, and were condemned for their non-committal remarks.This included one of Bollywood’s most famous actors, Salman Khan, who in a statement told students to go back home and not make their “parents worried for them”, insisting that Modi had the situation under control.Anupam Kher, another Bollywood actor, said in a comment that he understood the “restlessness and anger” of students, but also warned about “political opportunists” and people with their “own agenda” taking control of the movement – echoing comments made by BJP ministers.As the CJP protests gathered momentum, Aamir Khan was also criticised after he claimed that his 2009 hit film Three Idiots was not based on Sonam Wangchuk, the engineer and activist, which had been widely accepted film-lore for more than 15 years.Wangchuk went on a 26-day hunger striketo support the Cockroach movement and many saw it as an attempt by Khan to distance himself and his career from the protests.Top cricketing stars such as Virat Kohli and his wife, actor Anushka Sharma, were also trolled for lacking a “spine”.In a post on X, cricketer Sachin Tendulkar posted a vague statement, simply saying that “we must create a culture where hard work is rewarded, honesty is encouraged, and merit wins”.Influencer Alexander Balakrishnan, 29, said he realised that some celebrities might be reluctant to antagonise the government for fear of damaging their careers by losing contracts and endorsements. “But the big ones are so famous, their fame gives them protection and even they haven’t spoken.”Notable exceptions were veteran actors Naseeruddin Shah, 76, who was damning of Bollywood’s silence, and Shabana Azmi, who was among those who travelled from Mumbai to Delhi to take part in the protest. She told The Times of India: “Why can’t they listen to them? We need to build their hope, not crush their spirit.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of missing Rohingya footballer fear he is among 500 believed dead in Myanmar shipwrecks | Global development | The Guardian
description: ‘I can’t tolerate this life,’ said the 24-year-old in his last voice message to his relatives. Attacked by the military, a rebel army and criminal gangs, Siraz Ullah risked all for a better future
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: ‘I can’t tolerate this life,’ said the 24-year-old in his last voice message to his relatives. Attacked by the military, a rebel army and criminal gangs, Siraz Ullah risked all for a better future
Content: Siraz Ullah, centre, clung on to a dream of being a professional football player.View image in fullscreenSiraz Ullah, centre, clung on to a dream of being a professional football player.Global developmentFamily of missing Rohingya footballer fear he is among 500 believed dead in Myanmar shipwrecks‘I can’t tolerate this life,’ said the 24-year-old in his last voice message to his relatives. Attacked by the military, a rebel army and criminal gangs, Siraz Ullah risked all for a better futureSupported byAbout this contentKaamil AhmedSat 25 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fear was audible as he spoke, recording a message to his family, asking for their prayers. After pressing send, 24-year-old Siraz Ullah boarded a boat he hoped could deliver him from the violence and persecution surrounding him at home inMyanmar.Instead, Siraz is among 500 Rohingya refugees who havevanished at sea after setting sail forMalaysia in late June.“Please pray for me and for all the passengers. We are risking our lives, but there is nothing else we can do,” he said in the voice message. “I can’t tolerate this life.”Siraz had hoped that inMalaysiahe might be able to pursue his dream of playing football professionally. But a month on, the boat is feared lost.Siraz’s last message showed he was aware of the dangers of a journey that thousands of Rohingya have taken this year – in April,250 Rohingya died on a boatthat capsized in the Andaman Sea.Decades of persecution and military violence have left an estimated550,000 Rohingya remaining in Myanmar– from a population thought to be about 1.4 million a decade ago.More than 1 millionRohingya are now living as refugees in Bangladesh, confined to heavily policed camps.Criminals have been luringRohingyafrom both places with promises of better lives in Malaysia, often subjecting people to abuse and extortion before cramming them on to boats ill-equipped for rough seas.View image in fullscreenSiraz Ullah, right, with his nephew Mumtaz.According to Mumtaz Ullah, Siraz’s nephew, the last time anyone in the family spoke to him was on 22 June. It was around that time that a boat first attempted to leave but had to turn back, departing again a few days later.“We don’t know whether he’s alive. Like many others, we are living in fear and uncertainty,” he said. “It feels as if we’ve been torn into pieces.”In recent days, there have been rumours that the boat may have been hijacked by rival traffickers but there has been no other news.It seems likely that Sirazwas on board one of two boats the UN believescapsized off the Myanmar coast, carrying 250 and 280 people respectively.He travelled willingly but a human rights researcher, who was not cleared by their organisation to speak to media, told the Guardian that other families say their relatives were kidnapped from parts of Myanmar andBangladeshand held in detention camps until their families agreed to pay a ransom to the traffickers.Since the early 2000s a vast criminal network has operated between the Bay of Bengal and Malaysia, profiting from Rohingya desires to escape conditions in Myanmar and Bangladesh.View image in fullscreenNewly arrived Rohingya refugees are stranded on a boat as they were denied permission to land, Pineung, Aceh province, Indonesia, November 2023.Photograph: Amanda Jufrian/AFP/Getty ImagesThe mostly Muslim minority group was stripped of citizenship by Myanmar in 1982 and has faced several rounds of expulsion, mostly to Bangladesh. Once there, Rohingya face restrictions on their movement and have limited access to work or education.Ullah first left Myanmar in 2017, when a military campaign of violence expelled 700,000 Rohingya to Bangladesh. He lived there with his nephew Mumtaz.“We studied together, we played together. We were more like brothers than uncle and nephew,” says Mumtaz. “Since he was a child, his biggest dream was to become a professional football player. He held on to that dream despite all the difficulties we faced.”How paragliding soldiers carrying bombs rain destruction on Myanmar’s villagesRead moreSiraz won awards as a footballer, playing as a striker for Rohingya teams, but found it difficult to pursue his passion from Bangladesh’s refugee camps where there was little space for games.He first attempted to reach Malaysia in 2022. That boat got caught in a storm and its passengers ended up in the hands of the Myanmar authorities, who routinely imprison Rohingya who leave their villages without permission.View image in fullscreenSiraz with other Rohingya in 2022.His family had to pay 2.9m Myanmar kyat (£1,000) for his release.Conditions in Myanmar have deteriorated again in the past 24 months,with more than 150,000 Rohingya arriving in Bangladeshbecause offighting between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, a rebel group drawn from the Rakhine ethnicity.Both sides have been accused ofkilling Rohingyaandforcing them into labour and fighting.For young men like Siraz, the risk of a sea crossing can seem their only option.“We begged him not to go because we knew how dangerous it was but he believed he had no other choice … this isn’t just the story of Siraz, it’s the story of many other Rohingya families,” said Mumtaz. “We still hope that Siraz is alive, we pray that one day he will come home.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRohingyaMyanmarRefugeesMigrationBangladeshMalaysianewsShareReuse this content

title: Evacuated villagers in Cairngorms allowed home after wildfire threat lifts | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Scottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fire
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Scottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fire
Content: A firefighter tackling the major wildfire, which started in the Cairngorms on Wednesday 15 July.Photograph: RSPB Scotland/PAView image in fullscreenA firefighter tackling the major wildfire, which started in the Cairngorms on Wednesday 15 July.Photograph: RSPB Scotland/PAWildfiresEvacuated villagers in Cairngorms allowed home after wildfire threat liftsScottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fireKevin RawlinsonandNadeem BadshahSat 25 Jul 2026 18.08 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 05.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleResidents of Nethy Bridge have been told they can return to their homes after a large fire broke out in the Cairngorms national park.Supt Judy Hill of PoliceScotlandsaid: “Thanks to the efforts of fire crews, gamekeepers, contractors, partners and many others over the past 24 hours, there is no longer the immediate threat which prompted the evacuation of properties in Nethy Bridge.“We are grateful to the community for their support and understanding in what has been a period of concern and disruption.”Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, welcomed the news, saying: “Efforts to tackle the wildfire in the Cairngorms are in their 10th day, and changeable weather conditions have presented a range of challenges for those on the ground. I praise their resilience and tireless efforts to bring it under control.“With residents in Nethy Bridge now able to return to their homes, Police Scotland have lifted the major incident declaration.“I want to stress, however, that the Scottish government, the emergency services and all relevant authorities will continue to treat this wildfire, as has been the case since its onset, with the utmost seriousness and necessary resources until the last flames are out.”Earlier in the day Swinney had asked for military aid from the UK government as more than 500 firefighters alongside specialist wildfire appliances, all-terrain vehicles, helicopter water-bombing operations and partner agencies tackled the fire that had raged in the Cairngorms national park for the past 10 days and forced the evacuation of homes in the remote region.UK in ‘firewave’ as extreme heat provides ideal conditions for wildfires, experts warnRead moreResidents of Nethy Bridge were taken to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore hotel. Access roads were closed amid fears the fire was heading for the village. Just before 11pm on Saturday residents were told they could return home.Swinney had said earlier in the day that changing wind conditions had “intensified the pace of spread of the wildfire, adding that the Scottish fire and rescue service (SFRS) was focusing its resources on creating a firebreak.View image in fullscreenChanging wind conditions have intensified the pace of spread of the wildfire.Photograph: SFRSView image in fullscreenMore than 500 firefighters were mobilised over the course of the incident to deal with the blaze alongside specialist services.Photograph: SFRSThe wildfire, which broke out near the village of Glenmore on 15 July, led to residents and campsites being evacuated. It covered an area of about 6 sq km (2.3 sq miles) of heather and small trees at its height and its smoke drifted as far as Aberdeen, about 60 miles (97km) from where the fire started.Claire Montague, 65, a retired GP, and her family were evacuated from their home on Friday.She said: “We could see the smoke rising and when the wind changed direction we could see the flames – it was pretty scary and felt pretty close although it was still a few kilometres away.“We could see lots of smoke today when we popped back home, masses coming from a very large area. It is not contained by any means.“It was absolutely terrifying, nothing like I’ve felt before. TheDava Moor fire last summerwas farther away from us.“Thankfully they have managed to put in a firebreak.”Montague added: “Where the fire started is the original area of the Caledonian forest, a desperately important ecosystem, which they were trying very hard to preserve and expand.“The whole land had to be bulldozed for the firebreak, which is desperately sad.”View image in fullscreenFirefighters tackling a major wildfire, which started in heathland near Glenmore.Photograph: RSPB Scotland/PASenior emergency service officials said that firefighters “continue to work across a vast and challenging landscape alongside Forestry and Land Scotland, the Cairngorms national park authority, landowners, estate gamekeepers and emergency service partners. Their expertise, local knowledge and support have been instrumental in helping crews respond to this complex and dynamic incident.”On Saturday, the SFRA warned residents in Tomintoul – about 10 miles (16km) to the east of Nethy Bridge – to keep windows and doors closed because of the smoke from the wildfire.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresScotlandScottish politicsClimate crisisExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Content: Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesNigel FaragePolice investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the GuardianScotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 electionGeraldine McKelvieSat 25 Jul 2026 15.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePayments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by theMetropolitan police.The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice.Scotland Yard is looking at two donations of £250,000 made to the party by Britain Means Business in the weeks before the 2024 general election.The Guardian revealed earlier this month thatFiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Businessshortly before the donations were made. About half of the funds were then passed to the party.Cottrell’s son, George, is a convicted fraudster with close links to Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage.The Guardian reported earlier this month thatFiona and George Cottrell have been interviewed under criminal cautionas part of the police investigation.In response to a query about the investigation from the BBC, Tice said: “This is the first I have heard of it – if true why are the Met police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties?“Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?”Fiona Cottrell also made two donations directly to the party, each worth £250,000, in May 2024. These are also within the scope of the Metropolitan police investigation.Tice, who was elected to parliament after the poll, is the sole director of Britain Means Business.He has previously confirmed that his company received donations from Fiona Cottrell but described reports about the money as a “politically motivated smear campaign”.The Guardian told how the transfer from Fiona Cottrell to Britain Means Business was reported to the National Crime Agency by bankers via a suspicious activity report.Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering.The Guardian understands that neither the NCA nor bankers have been able to trace the source of the original £1m sent by Fiona Cottrell to Tice’s company. The NCA is seeking help from a foreign partner in its attempts to understand where the money originated.Reform councillors told to call donations inquiry ‘establishment stitch-up’Read moreAReform UKspokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far.”Fiona Cottrell did not respond to the Guardian’s attempts to contact her about the donations to Britain Means Business.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreWhen asked about the developments by the BBC on Saturday evening, the Metropolitan police repeated a statement issued earlier this month.“An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election,” the force said.“Detectives from the Met’s special enquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.“Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.“An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageMetropolitan policeReform UKPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea | Oil and gas companies | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Content: The Brent oilfield in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new oil drilling.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Brent oilfield in the North Sea. Andy Burnham’s government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow new oil drilling.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyOil and gas companiesNew North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in seaExclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licenceGeraldine McKelvieSenior correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProduction at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.Andy Burnham’s new government isunder pressurefrom the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despiteopposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.Rosebank, located about 80 miles north-west of Shetland, was believed to be ready to generate oil before the end of the year, pending ministerial approval.Adura, the company responsible for Rosebank, now says it anticipates this will happen at some point in 2027. The field is projected to produce 300m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifespan, according to industry estimates.Some MPs believe enhanced domestic production of oil and gas would help tackle the cost of living, a central focus of the new prime minister, by improving energy security amid global instability, while green campaigners believe the impact on the UK economy of exploiting the fields would be minimal.However, delays at Rosebank mean production at the field will be unlikely to affect the UK’s energy supply over the winter months. Licences for Rosebank and another site, Jackdaw, were granted under the Conservatives but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups.Thenew energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on the fields’ future after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in August.North Sea oil industry urges Burnham to approve new drilling in UK watersRead moreEarlier this week, Adura told the BBC that the Jackdaw site, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could produce gas as early as October.However, preparations for oil production at Rosebank have been hindered by the rig incident, which occurred on 18 April. No workers were hurt, but two central pieces of drilling equipment, including a safety valve, were dropped 1,100 metres on to the seabed.The platform, hired by Adura from Norwegian company Odfjell Drilling, was taken to a shipyard in Bergen for repairs. It is now back at Rosebank but not yet operational.Odfjell Drilling said in internal documentation that the rig could be out of action for up to four months. The Guardian understands this means that some oil wells will be completed significantly behind schedule.Burnham is facing calls from trade unions and opposition parties to ramp up North Sea production. Some Labour MPs say the oil and gas industry, centred around Aberdeen, could face collapse without new investment.Sally Jameson, a Cabinet Office minister, has also argued that more domestic production of oil and gas would give Britain greater control over the cost of energy. Others fear it would have no real impact on bills, while wreaking untold damage on the climate.Mike Reader, part of the Labour Environment Campaign, said there was no evidence new drilling would save jobs in the long term.The Guardian revealed that only 27 direct full-time jobs would be created byJackdaw, one of the biggest gasfields remaining in the North Sea, according to anenvironmental impact assessmentfiled publicly by Adura.Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, previously described the Rosebank proposals as “climate vandalism” when Labour was in opposition.
