However, in recent weeks talks are believed to have taken place on how to allow new drilling without breaching Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitments, in which it pledged not to issue new licences but honour existing ones.Jackdaw gasfield would create only 27 direct full-time jobs, documents showRead moreSeveral environmental groups are understood to be considering whether they would have grounds to take legal action regarding any government decision to allow new drilling.Angeliki Papantoniou, a lecturer in environmental law at the University of Hull, said that, while a fresh challenge would be a “long shot”, it would be most likely to succeed if based on “substantive environmental matters” such as the disruption of ecosystems, pollution and potential health impacts.“It could be argued that those developments cannot reasonably be ignored when taking a decision with likely high environmental effects,” she said.“In theory, it could be hard for [Fahnbulleh] to claim that [the government] took all necessary precautionary measures without detailed risk assessments on the effects of drilling on the marine environment, climate and human health.”Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace, which challenged the original decision to grant licences, said approval for the fields would make “zero difference” to energy bills and generate few jobs.“Despite these meagre benefits, we would be prolonging a polluting industry that’s fuelling heatwaves while sending a disastrous signal to our international allies,” she said.Odfjell Drilling declined to comment. Adura did not respond to a request for comment.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: Southport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyer | Southport attack | The Guardian
description: Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
Content: Flowers and tributes outside the Atkinson Art Centre Southport after the attack on 29 July 2024.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenFlowers and tributes outside the Atkinson Art Centre Southport after the attack on 29 July 2024.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PASouthport attackSouthport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyerComment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospitalSammy GecsoylerSat 25 Jul 2026 06.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lawyer for the families of Axel Rudakubana’s victims has said the Southport killer is “trying to retraumatise the families from his cell” after it emergedhe had been transferred from prison to a psychiatric hospital.Rudakubana, now 19, was given a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.The Guardian revealed on Thursday thatRudakubana had been transferred to the high-security hospital Broadmoorfrom the category A prison Belmarsh after it was concluded that he could not be managed safely in jail.Next Wednesday marks two years since he carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024, which was followed by largely far-right riots that spread across the country.Earlier this week, the Ministry of Justice confirmed that Rudakubana had been transferred from prison to the psychiatric facility Broadmoor hospital.A spokesperson for the department stressed it did not alter the killer’s 52-year sentence.Chris Walker, who is representing the three bereaved families, told BBC Breakfast: “It’s a deep concern of mine that this is a pattern starting to develop by him trying to retraumatise the families from his cell, and it’s a deep concern that this is going to occur every anniversary.”He added that there was “no suggestion” that Rudakubana was under any form of “psychosis” when he carried out the murders.The families were informed of the decision in a letter on 22 July but were not given details on why the transfer happened.Walker said: “With the vacuum of information, the concern is that he’s manipulating the situation to his own benefit. For it to come out the week before the anniversary seems coincidental to us.“Whether that’s been poorly handled by the government, or whether it’s designed by him.”Sally Jameson, a housing minister and former prison officer, said on Friday that Rudakubana would be returned to prison “as soon as possible” but that she was not familiar with why the decision had been taken to move him.Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust previously confirmed Rudakubana had been under its care as a mental health patient between 2019 and 2023, when he “stopped engaging”. He was referred to them after taking a knife to school and later saying he had done so “to use it”.He was also referred to the UK’s counter-extremism programme, Prevent, because he had been researching school massacres on a computer at his next school, the Acorns.There were two other referrals to Prevent, but none were progressed as Rudakubana had no clear ideology behind his obsession with violence.Offenders who present an increased risk, and cannot be managed safely in a prison environment because of mental disorders, can be moved to secure psychiatric units.People in these units are treated as patients rather than prisoners.Broadmoor, in Crowthorne, Berkshire, is the oldest of England’s three high-security psychiatric hospitals. It has been used to hold some of the UK’s most notorious murderers including Peter Sutcliffe, the Yorkshire Ripper.Patients remain locked up, with conditions heavily regulated by strict physical security including locked wards, monitored by staff and 24-hour CCTV. They receive mandatory therapeutic and rehabilitative programmes. If offenders no longer require treatment in hospital, the 1983 Mental Health Act provides for a swift return to prison.Walker said: “When he did what he did, it was carefully planned, it was meticulous and it was designed to cause the maximum distress to society. There’s no evidence of any mental health disorder being a component of his crime. There’s no evidence of psychosis.“The families say, given that, he needs to serve a prison sentence, he should not be going to hospital. He needs to be in prison.”Explore more on these topicsSouthport attackSentencingPrisons and probationUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the case | US gun control | The Guardian
description: Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Content: Jane Coates, from Warrington, wants the UK government to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that her daughter, Lucy, was unlawfully killed.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJane Coates, from Warrington, wants the UK government to reopen the case after a Cheshire coroner ruled that her daughter, Lucy, was unlawfully killed.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUS gun controlLucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the caseEighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen caseJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSat 25 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. Life could hardly get any better. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,”said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England.View image in fullscreenJane Coates, pictured here with Lucy for the final time, raised her daughter alone from the age of two.Photograph: Jane CoatesThat Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew toTexasto spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas.Lucy and Littler were due to fly home to the UK on 10 January 2025 when Coates received a knock on the door. It was Littler’s mother. Lucy had been shot, she said. She was dead.It was only later she learned that Kris Harrison had been holding the gun. He was never arrested and a grand jury chose not to indict him, based on an investigation by local police.Eighteen months on, Coates is urging Andy Burnham’s government to encourage US authorities to reopen the case after a Cheshire coronerruledthat Lucy was unlawfully killed.Coates, a deputy head teacher, raised Lucy as a single parent from the age of two. The pair had an incredibly close bond and would talk about virtually everything. As a child, she was always outside exploring, climbing trees, riding her bike, before becoming engrossed in Harry Potter books – a “comfort blanket” she would turn to time and again into adulthood.By the age of nine, she was a devout Swiftie, performing a Taylor Swift song at her school leavers’ assembly and later going to three of her concerts. Anyone who knew Lucy knew her contagious laughter. “We call it like the Barbara Windsor belly laugh,” said Coates, 49.Like many young adults, Lucy went through difficult times. She struggled with the uncertainty of what she wanted to do with her life in her late teens, Coates said. She had counselling to help with the relationship with her father.But Lucy had never been happier than in 2024. She graduated from Manchester Metropolitan University with a degree in fashion buying and merchandising, began working at the retailer Boohoo and bought a home with Littler, her “soulmate”, five minutes from both of their mothers.“That final year of Lucy’s was the best year of her life,” Coates said. “She was such a high achiever and she just really wanted the best for herself.”She soaked up life, both good and bad. But that meant she would sometimes get upset about events happening thousands of miles away.View image in fullscreenLucy with her father, Kris Harrison, days before she was shot dead in Texas.Photograph: Jane CoatesThemurder of George Floydby a Minneapolis police officer in 2020 was one such event, Coates remembers. “She used to worry. She was an overthinker and used to cry a lot at different things. Sometimes it was with frustration because she was very passionate about things.”She was vehemently opposed to guns, an issue that caused tension with her father. Harrison, a telecoms executive originally from Liverpool, moved to Saudi Arabia for work when she was a child, later settling in Texas where he married Heather Harrison, an education recruiter, and had two daughters.Harrison had bought a pistol for $500 (£370) from a colleague two years before Lucy’s death. Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states.Her inquest inCheshirewas told that Lucy had expressed concern to friends about her two younger siblings being in the house with her father’s Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol.View image in fullscreenJane Coates said the US investigation was ‘not rigorous or thorough enough’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOn the morning of her death, Lucy and her father argued about sexual assault allegations against Donald Trump, who was about to start his second term as US president.Littler said Lucy had asked her father: “How would you feel if that was me and then the guy got away with it?”Harrison had replied that it “wouldn’t bother me that much” because his two younger daughters live with him, Littler said. Lucy “went into floods of tears and ran upstairs”, he added, and sent her father links to news articles about the Trump allegations, denied by the US president.Littler had been in a relationship with Lucy for five years by that point and had known her since they were 12. “This was the sort of stuff that happened on a regular basis,” Littler said. When he met Harrison in Prosper for the first time a year earlier, he told Lucy he did not want to go back. “You’d feel like you’re on eggshells.”View image in fullscreenLucy and her partner, Sam Littler, had just bought a house together.Photograph: Jane CoatesCoates is keen to stress that Lucy was not shot “because they’d had an argument about Trump”. Passionate debates were not uncommon between Lucy and her father: “It could have been an argument about anything.”Later that morning, the family were watching children’s television shows and preparing to go to the airport when Harrison took Lucy’s hand and escorted her to his bedroom.Harrison’s wife, Heather, looked at Littler in surprise and joked: “He never takes my hand like that.”“It was mysterious,” Littler said. “No one knew what was going on.”Then came the loud bang. Initially they thought it was a prank, then Harrison screamed for his wife. They ran into the room and saw Lucy on the floor. Harrison, in shock, could not say what had happened. The pistol was on the bed. He stammered: “I don’t know, I don’t know. Call an ambulance.”Bodycam footage shows Harrison telling officers he had shown his gun to Lucy when “it just went off”.“When I pulled it out, it went off,” he said.Despite an officer smelling alcohol on Harrison’s breath, he was not breathalysed. He initially denied drinking that day but later told police he had a drink problem and “keeps it going”, an admission an officer understood to mean that Harrison drinks throughout the day.CCTV obtained by police showed Harrison buying two 500ml cartons of wine earlier that day and discarding one of them outside a shop. He later admitted drinking that morning.1:21Bodycam footage shows Kris Harrison telling police he shot his daughter Lucy Harrison – videoDuring his police interview, a Texas ranger explained to Harrison that the “gun would only discharge if the trigger was pressed”, according to a report released to the UK inquest. “Kris said ‘OK’,” it noted. Yet authorities said they were unable to arrest Harrison because they could not prove intent.Coates said she had told a Texas ranger that Harrison must have been pointing the gun at Lucy and pulled the trigger, to which she said he had agreed, but argued: “We just can’t prove it.”On the same call in March 2025, a prosecutor said they were unable to conclude Harrison pointed the weapon at Lucy “because that implies intent”, Coates said. They told her the most they could say was that the “muzzle was aligned with Lucy’s chest and a trigger was pulled”.View image in fullscreenLucy had just graduated with first class honours from Manchester Metropolitan University.Photograph: Jane CoatesThe police case was handed to a grand jury in Collin County, Texas, which decided in June last year Harrison should not be prosecuted. Its reasoning, and the evidence it considered, has not been made public.Littler was also taken to the police station. While waiting to learn whether Lucy had survived, he said he heard a muffled conversation between officers in which they referred to the shooting as an “accident”.“The police just took Kris’s word for it,” said Coates. “The investigation was not rigorous or thorough enough.”She suspects the police would have treated Lucy’s death more seriously had it happened in a less “white middle-class prosperous area”.Of all the disturbing details they have learned, one of the most painful for Coates is that Lucy’s body was tested for alcohol and other substances – all with negative results – while Harrison was not even breathalysed. “That’s what we find absolutely incredulous,” Coates said. She and Littler have submitted formal complaints to Prosper police department.In February, the senior coroner for Cheshire, Jacqueline Devonish,ruledthat firing a pistol at Lucy from across the room was an act of gross negligence and that her death could not be considered accidental.View image in fullscreen‘There were no authorities supporting us as British nationals wanting justice for a British citizen who was killed by a British citizen,’ says Jane Coates.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianCoates said the family had been let down, not just by the Texas authorities but also by the British government. She was told the Foreign Office would not be able to help them because nobody had been prosecuted.Sarah Hall, theLabourMP for Warrington South, said the family did not have “adequate support” and called on the government to press the Texas authorities to re-examine the case.Coates hopes the new prime minister, who represents the nearby Makerfield constituency, will take up Lucy’s case with the US. She is keen to meet Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, to discuss how the government could better support the families of those killed abroad.“At the beginning, nobody was there for us apart from Sarah Hall,” she said. “We have got hope that this new cabinet and the foreign secretary will support us, [but] there were no authorities supporting us as British nationals wanting justice for a British citizen who was killed by a British citizen.”A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts remain with Jane and her family for the tragic loss they have suffered, and we will always look to learn lessons from cases such as this one to improve the consular support we offer to other families in the future.”Explore more on these topicsUS gun controlCheshireAndy BurnhamLabourUS policingViolence against women and girlsNorth of EnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passed | US news | The Guardian
description: Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
Content: A person receives food aid bags at the Young Family YMCA in Atlanta, Georgia, 6 November 2025.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/EPAView image in fullscreenA person receives food aid bags at the Young Family YMCA in Atlanta, Georgia, 6 November 2025.Photograph: Erik S Lesser/EPAUS newsMore than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passedAnalysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026Marina DunbarSat 25 Jul 2026 15.07 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a million children across the US have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) food benefits since Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to a new report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP).Theanalysisfound that more than 4 millions Americans were removed from Snap from July 2025 to March 2026, marking a significant decline in participation in the federal food assistance program.Arizonarecorded the largest drop in enrollment after the bill became law. The legislation tightened eligibility rules for food assistance and increased state screening requirements. State data through May shows that more than 450,000 Arizonans have come off Snap, cutting overall participation within the state in half.According to the CBPP analysis, children make up a significant portion of those losing benefits, with more than 1 million children across the 19 states studied no longer receiving Snap assistance.InLouisiana, nearly one in four children receiving Snap benefits lost assistance.MassachusettsandTexaseach saw close to one-fifth of children enrolled in the program removed from Snap.The report comes as participation in the programcontinues to fallnationwide followingmajor reductionsto the federal food assistance program under the Trump administration.Snap, commonly referred to as food stamps, provides monthly benefits to low-income and no-income households to help pay for groceries and remains the country’s largest food assistance program.The report says the steep decline in participation is likely tied in large part to the 2025 Republican reconciliation law, also known as theOne Big Beautiful Bill Act, which shifted a substantial share of Snap benefit costs to states based on their payment error rates.The CBPP warned that the situation would continue to deteriorate unless Congress intervenes. “Without immediate congressional action to delay this cost shift for all states, the unfolding emergency will only worsen as more children are cut off from the food assistance their families need to afford nutritious food,” the CBPP said.Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive Democrat fromMinnesota, pointed to the outcomesduring a speechon the House floor earlier this month. Omar had introduced an amendment aimed at reversing the Snap cuts, but the proposal was rejected by the Republican majority.The latest figures also prompted action from the US Conference of Mayors. On Monday, the nonpartisan organization representing cities with populations of at least 30,000 senta letterto the Senate signed by more than 200 mayors calling for lawmakers to reverse the Snap cuts amid the US’s “deepening food security crisis”.“Snap remains the nation’s most effective and efficient anti-hunger program. It reduces poverty, supports local economies, and provides an automatic stabilizer during economic downturns,” the letter said. “Hunger is not a partisan issue, and efforts to address food insecurity should rise above political divisions.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsChildrenPovertyHungerTrump administrationSocial exclusionUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scorching US heatwave to hit 70 million people with third ‘heat dome’ in month | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Temperatures of 95-105F (35-40C) are expected, spanning Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwest
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Temperatures of 95-105F (35-40C) are expected, spanning Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwest
Content: Families seek refuge in the pool at the North Hollywood recreation center in Los Angeles, California, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Chris Torres/EPAView image in fullscreenFamilies seek refuge in the pool at the North Hollywood recreation center in Los Angeles, California, on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Chris Torres/EPAExtreme heatScorching US heatwave to hit 70 million people with third ‘heat dome’ in monthTemperatures of 95-105F (35-40C) are expected, spanning Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwestOliver Milmanand agenciesSat 25 Jul 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 70 million people in the US are set to face excessive heat advisories as dangerously hot temperatures scorch much of the country’s southern and central states.The third major “heat dome” event to hit the US in the past month is gathering strength over the weekend, spanning a vast swathe of the country, from the Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwest.Temperatures of 95-105F (35-40C) areexpected, with some areas of the south-western US desert potentially reaching 120F (48C). The elevated heat is expected to linger into the coming week, held in place by the heat dome, which is when a high-pressure atmospheric system acts as a sort of lid, trapping heat in place over a region for days or even weeks.View image in fullscreenA man rests in the shade in Los Angeles on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Chris Torres/EPAView image in fullscreenLying by the pool in Los Angeles on 20 July 2026.Photograph: Chris Torres/EPAWhile heatwaves are nothing new to American summers, the regularity and severity of such events is worsening due to the human-causedclimate crisis. The release of heat-trapping gases due to the burning of fossil fuels has caused global temperatures to escalate above anything previously experienced during human civilization.It has already been a sweltering summer for many people in the US, with a huge heat dome event in early July causing some Independence Day events to be canceled in the east of the country. Another heatwave hit further west after that, causing 115F (46C) heat in Montana and temperature records to tumble.The latest heat dome event could potentially break records in the Denver area, while the National Weather Service has issued an extreme heat warning for western Nebraska, where weekend temperatures are forecast to reach 108F (42C).Heat is the deadliest weather phenomenon in the US, with elevated temperatures throughout the nighttime and high humidity in the latest heatwave set to provide no respite for people affected. Older people, pregnant people, young children and people with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat.View image in fullscreenPeople hit the beach in Santa Monica, California, on 21 July 2026.Photograph: Chris Torres/EPADangerously hot conditions are also currently gripping much of Europe, with 250,000 peoplefleeingwildfires in Spain and France. A separate Juneheatwaveresulted in an estimated 5,700 deaths in France, officialshave estimated.Parts of the UK are alsoburningin the wake of hot, dry conditions that have primed the landscape for fire. Across the US, 88 fires are presently beingtackledby firefighters.“We are experiencing exactly what the climate models in the 1990s said we should experience now,” said Andy Pershing, chief program officer at Climate Central, a climate change communications non-profit.“That is, more frequent, more severe heatwaves, bigger temperature anomalies, more humidity, higher overnight temperatures. These are all part and parcel of the climate story.”The Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatUS weatherClimate crisisExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Cecilia Vega of 60 Minutes says she felt pressure from CBS to add ‘political bias’ | CBS | The Guardian
description: Vega made remarks to ABC’s John Quiñones at National Association of Hispanic Journalists conference
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Vega made remarks to ABC’s John Quiñones at National Association of Hispanic Journalists conference
Content: Cecilia Vega, then of ABC News, asks Donald Trump a question on 1 October 2018.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenCecilia Vega, then of ABC News, asks Donald Trump a question on 1 October 2018.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPACBSCecilia Vega of 60 Minutes says she felt pressure from CBS to add ‘political bias’Vega made remarks to ABC’s John Quiñones at  National Association of Hispanic Journalists conferenceUwa Ede-OsifoSat 25 Jul 2026 14.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCecilia Vega, the former 60 Minutes correspondent, said on Thursday she felt pressured byCBSNews’s executives to incorporate “political bias” into segments for the broadcast program.Vega made the remarks during an onstage interview with John Quiñones, the ABC News correspondent, at the National Association of Hispanic Journalists’ annual conference in New Orleans. Her comments were first reported byStatus.“I’ve gone head-to-head with editors for 25 years in this business,” Vega said, according to theNew York Times. “But never in my career, until now, have I felt that those edits, that those suggestions, came from a place of misinformation or politics.”As she was wrapping up a segment on the deadly federal immigration operations in Minnesota, during which Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents fatally shot two American citizens, Vega said, she was instructed to include footage of protesters attacking ICE agents,MS Nowreported.The footage did not exist, according to Vega.She also was questioned on why she did not interview JD Vance for a segment on poverty in West Virginia. The piece was centered on the Trump administration’s slashes to Snap benefits, according to MS Now.Vegaalso saidshe was asked to report on comments from the Minneapolis mayor, Jacob Frey, suggesting he wanted local police to fight federal immigration agents in the state, despite no evidence of such comments.A spokesperson for CBS News did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Vega’s remarks.When Vega was fired from the network this spring, she expressed concern for the flagship Sunday newsmagazine’s future, which has seen a leadership shakeup sinceBari Weisswas appointed as CBS News’s editor-in-chief last October by Paramount’s CEO, David Ellison, a Trump ally. Weiss, who has no background in broadcast news, founded media startup the Free Press, which was acquired by Paramount, and is known for her critiques of liberal institutions and what she has deemed “cancel culture”.“In recent months, my producing teams and I have experienced efforts to insert political bias into our stories. Reporting teams have held back on submitting story pitches about important news topics out of fear of the internal repercussions,” Vega saidin a statementin May. “Let’s call this what it is: censorship, both imposed and self-driven. It is dangerous for the show and dangerous for democracy.”“We respect Ms Vega and her contributions, but her claims are not based in reality,” a CBS spokesperson said at the time.Weiss received scrutiny late last year aftershe delayed a segmentabout the federal government deporting hundreds of Venezuelans to a notorious El Salvador prison, citing a need for further reporting. The segment’s correspondent, Sharyn Alfonsi, called the decision “a political one”.There has been a wave offiringsat 60 Minutes since Weiss assumed the network mantle.Veteran correspondent Scott Pelley blasted the cuts at the network, accusing Weiss in a tense meeting with 60 Minutes’ staffers of “murdering” the show. “She does not love this place. She was brought in to kill it and is doing exactly that,” he said then. Pelley wasfiredfollowing the clash.Explore more on these topicsCBSBari WeissUS television industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary race | Maine | The Guardian
description: Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
Content: Troy Jackson acknowledges supporters at the Maine Democratic nominating convention on 25 July 2026 in Bangor, Maine.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenTroy Jackson acknowledges supporters at the Maine Democratic nominating convention on 25 July 2026 in Bangor, Maine.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APMaineTroy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary raceProgressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegationsShrai Popatin Bangor, MaineSat 25 Jul 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a race defined by scandal, withdrawals and a frantic hunt for a replacement candidate, Maine Democrats hit reset on their chaotic Senate primary on Saturday as Troy Jacksonofficially securedthe party’s nomination.He took the stage at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to rapturous applause, a standing ovation and Noah Kahan’s Northern Attitude blaring over the speakers.“This is the absolute honor of my life,” Jackson said. “If you’ve ever been ignored, underestimated, pushed around or told that you have to wait your turn while the rich cut the line, I’m asking you to stand with us in this campaign.”Jackson’s win amounted to a coronation for the progressive fifth‑generation logger and former state senate president, who faced no real opposition at the special convention after every major rival stepped aside. Their exits cleared the path for Jackson to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman and marine veteran who ended his campaign amid mounting controversies that culminated in a sexual assault allegation he has denied.Platnerdropped outdays after Politico reported that a woman he dated five years ago said he forced her to have sex despite repeated objections. His withdrawal triggered a breakneck scramble inside the Maine Democratic party to devise a process for selecting a new nominee before the state’s 27 July deadline to select a replacement for the general‑election ballot.“I know many of you poured your hearts into building this movement way before I ever entered this race,” Jackson said on Saturday before the official vote. “But the hope that you built never belonged to anyone campaigning. It belongs to every Mainer who knows that healthcare is a human right, belongs to every worker fighting for a union, a living wage and a dignified environment.”Jackson, who finished third in the ranked‑choice gubernatorial primary, won the snap convention by a vote of 566-5 on Saturday. But his victory was all but assured once a majority of Mainers who won county‑level delegate elections last weekend pledged to back him before the convention. The remaining delegates come from the state party committee.By Sunday, as Jackson’s nomination became inevitable, all of his major challengers bowed out of the hastily assembled contest. That included fellow gubernatorial contenders – former Maine CDC director Nirav Shah and the Maine secretary of state, Shenna Bellows – as well as Jordan Wood, the former congressional candidate who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic primary for Maine’s second district.“The easy solution”, said the Maine Democratic party chair, Charlie Dingman, would be to let the state committee select the new nominee. “Instead, we responded to the growing grassroots movement in our state to build power for ordinary working people,” he said.However, some Democratic voters said the convention process was still not representative of the more than 200,000 voters who turned out in the primary to elect Platner in June.Jackson will now face the five‑term Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, in one of the most closely watched races of the midterm cycle – for a seatDemocratsview as central to their audacious plan to retake the Senate. They need four pickups nationwide in November, and Maine is integral to that strategy. Collins is also the only Republican in the upper chamber seeking re-election in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024.Democrats are aiming at Maine for a Senate seat. But will the state give up Susan Collins?Read more“For 30 years, she’s told us that she’s ‘concerned’. But look, concern is not courage,” Jackson said on Saturday, as supporters waved “Retire Susan” placards in the audience. “What she says in Maine does not erase what she does down in Washington.”Preliminary polling from the University of New Hampshire shows Jackson witha slight edgeover Collins, a moderate GOP senator who has beenpolitically untouchablefor the past three decades. And while Jackson is well-known in Maine political circles, his nascent campaign will have to accelerate quickly to match Collins’s fundraising lead and the momentum Platner built after months of statewide travel, town halls and a grassroots surge strong enough to force the term‑limited governor, Janet Mills, out of the Democratic primary in April.Jackson, whobegan his political careeras a Republican and once opposed abortion and gay marriage, is now staunchly progressive and campaigned alongside Platner’s economic‑populist platform, even earning Platner’s endorsement during his own unsuccessful run for governor. Both points are likely to feature prominently in the efforts by Collins and conservative groups to undermine his political acumen in the months ahead.Shortly after Platner exited the race, Jackson tried to distance himself from the turmoil – telling MS Now that Platner assured him there was “nothing in his past that I had to worry about”.“He lied to me. And he lied to a lot of us,” Jackson said in an interview after Platner posted an 11‑minute video announcing his withdrawal. In Bangor on Saturday, the new nominee insisted the chaos that has consumed the Democratic race was in the rearview mirror without naming Platner.“Today we turn the page. Today this becomes a general election campaign, and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November,” Jackson said.A number of delegates said that Jackson’s proximity to Platner’s messaging shouldn’t be off-putting. “It never was about the person, but about the policies,” said Lydia Stone, 31, who lives in North Yarmouth and works for a company that sells forestry supplies. “I think what Graham said he was, I think Troy Jackson actually is.”Many people in Bangor noted that it was crucial for Jackson to be meeting voters as much as possible in the 101 days until the election.“It’s going to be difficult because there’s a short window window of time, but I would say to get out there as much as he can into especially those rural communities like where he’s from, and actually be there,” said Lisa Marin, 69, who lives in Jonesport and chairs the Washington county Democratic committee.Marin added: “That was one of the things in the Platner campaign that I think was really helpful for Graham – he was out there and really meeting people where they are. And I know Troy wants to do that, and as much as he can, I feel like that’s what he needs to do.”Explore more on these topicsMaineDemocratsUS SenateUS midterm elections 2026US CongressUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot wounds | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
Content: Police investigate the scene of the fatal house fire on 24 July 2026 in Grand Haven Township, Michigan.Photograph: Joel Bissell/Kalamazoo Gazette/APView image in fullscreenPolice investigate the scene of the fatal house fire on 24 July 2026 in Grand Haven Township, Michigan.Photograph: Joel Bissell/Kalamazoo Gazette/APMichiganEight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot woundsFirefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of childrenMarina DunbarSat 25 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA devastating tragedy has unfolded inMichiganafter emergency crews responding to a house fire found eight members of the same family, including six children, dead. At least some of the dead inside the home had gunshot wounds.Deputies with the Ottawa county sheriff’s office and firefighters from the Grand Haven fire department were dispatched at about 11.40am local time on Friday to a residence on Riverside Trail in Grand Haven Township.Once crews entered the smoke-filled home to extinguish the fire, they made the grim discovery.“Units made entry inside to battle the fire because there was smoke showing from the residence. When they got inside, they noticed that there were several people deceased inside the home,” Capt Jacob Sparks said at apress conference. “Some of the victims did have gunshot wounds to their bodies.”Officials confirmed the victims were two adults and six children aged five to 15. Their identities have not yet been released.Autopsies are scheduled to be completed over the weekend, according toABC News, as investigators continue working to determine exactly what happened.Authorities said they are not currently looking for any suspects from outside the home, though Sparks stressed the investigation is ongoing.“I don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point,” he said.Investigators with theMichiganstate police’s arson team have joined the investigation. Officials believe the fire originated inside the residence, but the exact cause and point of origin have not yet been determined.The home is located in Grand Haven Township, just outside the city of Grand Haven and about 20 miles (32km) south of Muskegon, Michigan.The investigation remains active, and authorities said additional information is expected after the victims’ autopsies are completed.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS crimeGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: LeBron James’ final act in Philadelphia is about more than basketball. It’s about time | LeBron James | The Guardian
description: LeBron James’ move to Philadelphia isn’t about nostalgia or money. It’s about confronting basketball mortality and chasing one last meaningful title
Author: Claire de Lune
Headline: LeBron James’ move to Philadelphia isn’t about nostalgia or money. It’s about confronting basketball mortality and chasing one last meaningful title
Content: LeBron James said he seriously contemplated retirement after last season before deciding to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.Photograph: Joshua Gateley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeBron James said he seriously contemplated retirement after last season before deciding to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.Photograph: Joshua Gateley/Getty ImagesLeBron JamesLeBron James’ final act in Philadelphia is about more than basketball. It’s about timeClaire de LuneThe NBA superstar’s shock move to the Philadelphia 76ers isn’t about money or legacy. It’s about confronting the end of a career and making the most of whatever remainsSat 25 Jul 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 14.11 EDTShareThe most enormous celebrities, those larger-than-life characters with immense cultural impact, occupy a kind of hard-to-quantify space in the zeitgeist. They’re human, of course; that’s what makes them compelling. But they often come to represent something beyond themselves. In LeBron James’ case, for me, he’s become a measure of the passing of time. An aide-mémoire of my own mortality. Yes, his defiance of the aging process has been heartening proof that while Father Time comes for us all, the pace isn’t fixed. But the growing number of gray hairs in his beard, the players born after he was drafted who now meet him in transition, are persistent reminders that time marches on.LeBron James going to the Philadelphia 76ers is perfectly in characterRead moreOn the one hand, as anyone who has experienced it can attest, aging is exhausting. Battles once worth fighting no longer seem worth the effort. An extra 30 minutes of quiet solitude starts to feel like life’s greatest luxury. So perhaps that instinctive understanding clouded all of our assumptions about where LeBron would choose to finish his career. Surely,by now, he had to be tired. Why not golf with Stephen Curry in northern California while playing probably meaningless (but highly entertaining) basketball? Why not head back to Miami, where Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo could shoulder the defensive burden, allowing James to hand over the offensive keys and spend whatever time remained by the pool? Or why not end it in Cleveland, where he’s already beloved, where the stakes are lower, where the narrative is clean and tidy? Wouldn’t that beeasier?But something else comes with aging and the passing of time: the growing sharpness with which the fleeting nature of life comes into view. James may have served as a metaphor for time’s relentless forward march for everyone who watched him. But in his own life, it was moving just as fast, if not faster, as it does for the rest of us.That, it seems, was the real motivator of his decision to shock the league and sign with the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday. In a statement releasedvia his own X account, James said he was grappling with his basketball mortality at the end of his 2025-26 campaign, which marked the end of his eight-year stint with the Los Angeles Lakers – the longest continuous stint of his career. “I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game,” James said. “I was honest at that last press conference [after the Lakerswere eliminated by Oklahoma City] when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give.”James went on to explain that the decision wasn’t motivated by money – a claim easily corroborated by the two-year, $8m veteran’s minimum contract he signed – nor by family, who are currently split between Los Angeles, Tucson and Akron. The deciding factor? A new challenge, fresh excitement and one last good-faith shot at the ultimate prize. “What am I really playing for at this point?” James said in the statement. “I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning a championship.”View image in fullscreenLeBron James (left) talks with the 76ers’ VJ Edgecombe after a game last season in Philadelphia.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APAcquiring a player of LeBron James’ caliber – even at 41 years old – on a minimum contract simply doesn’t happen. But after seriously considering retirement, James’ freedom to choose virtually any destination came at the cost of a massive pay cut. Sticking it to his former employer was, of course, a fringe benefit: it’s been widely reported that James felt disrespected by the Lakers’ brass. Even to an outside observer, it was clear the franchise was eager to turn the page, building around 27-year-old Slovenian wunderkind Luka Dončić after pulling off thesports heist of the century. So even after James dragged an injury-depleted Lakers roster beyond the first round of the playoffs in April, the divorce felt inevitable. And like any middle-aged man going through a divorce, it appeared to elicit some genuine introspection.‘Maybe he’s a ‌racist’: Donald Trump takes bizarre swipe at NBA great LeBron JamesRead moreThe decision to sign withPhiladelphiamakes sense when viewed through that prism. That of a man who knows his time playing the game he loves, that which has defined his life, is rapidly coming to a close. A man forced to ask whether the juice is still worth the squeeze and, if it is, to what end. In some ways, signing with the Sixers is risky proposition: it’s a brand new city and team, with a lot of big names and personalities (in addition to Process™ holdover Joel Embiid, there’s All-NBA guard Tyrese Maxey, last season’s Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe and newly acquired Twitch-streaming NBA finals MVP Jaylen Brown). And then there’s the health issues, which have plagued Embiid and the franchise at large for years. But that’s also what makes the opportunity compelling. Delivering Philadelphia its first NBA championship in more than four decades would instantly become one of the defining achievements of James’ career. And with one of the league’s most talented starting lineups, the Sixers offer him the one thing he appears to have spent the summer searching for: a genuine chance to win one last title.One thing I often find myself pondering when considering the passing of time is the idea of alternate timelines – parallel realities where a single decision changes everything. The twilight of LeBron James’ career is full of them. What if he had stayed in Cleveland in 2018? What if the Lakers had never landed Dončić, extending James’ stay in Los Angeles? And perhaps most intriguing of all: what if the New York Knicks hadn’t won the championship this year? Had they fallen short, Madison Square Garden would have offered James perhaps the most irresistible final act in basketball. Win, and he’d deliver the Knicks the title they had chased for more than half a century. Lose, and he’d at least have the chance to write the ending himself. According to his agent, Rich Paul, that alternate reality came remarkably close to becoming this one. On the Game Over podcast, while reviewing anow-infamous whiteboardof potential destinations with co-host Max Kellerman, Paulpaused on New York. If they hadn’t hoisted the Larry O’Brien in 2026, Paul said, “there would be no board. He’d be going to the Knicks.”Instead, a different timeline prevails. One that’s intriguing, suspenseful and even bizarre: LeBron James, at age 41, is a 76er. In Philadelphia, he can attempt to do what no NBA player has ever done: win a championship with a fourth different team. He can have fun playing basketball, free from the enormous shadow the past version of himself casts in somewhere like Miami or Cleveland. He can grapple with his basketball mortality while trying, in equal measure, to stave it off. He can try and make the most of what’s left of his time.Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesPhiladelphia 76ersPhiladelphiaLos Angeles LakerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Joshua knocked down twice but stops Kristian Prenga in round two | Boxing | The Guardian
description: The British heavyweight Anthony Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round but hit back to blast out the Albanian Kristian Prenga in the second
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The British heavyweight Anthony Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round but hit back to blast out the Albanian Kristian Prenga in the second
Content: Anthony Joshua (right) embraces Kristian Prenga after winning his fight by technical knockout in the second round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnthony Joshua (right) embraces Kristian Prenga after winning his fight by technical knockout in the second round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersBoxingAnthony Joshua knocked down twice but stops Kristian Prenga in round twoBriton on canvas inside 20 seconds and later in firstJoshua recovers to blast out Albanian in second roundDonald McRaeSat 25 Jul 2026 19.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Joshua cleared his final hurdle in the ring, before he fights Tyson Fury in November, but he was knocked down twice, shockingly, in the first round of his wild and chaotic bout with Kristian Prenga. In the early hours of Sunday morning in Jeddah, a devastating knockout in the second left Prenga crumpled in a heap on the canvas, wrapped up in the ropes, and rescued Joshua from humiliation.After the opening three minutes his extravaganza with Fury looked as if it was about to end in abject ruins but Joshua pulled himself out of a dark pit streaked with defeat to salvage his career – and his much-hyped fight with his British compatriot. This was a crazy firefight of a tune-up for Joshua, who was boxing for the first time since being injured in the car accident that took the lives of two of his closest friends, Sina Ghami and Latif Ayodele, last December.View image in fullscreenKristian Prenga surprises Anthony Joshua and knocks him down in the first round.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/Reuters“He’s back” was emblazoned on the big screen behind the figure of Joshua as he walked at a steady, even sombre pace towards the ring. A booming Meek Mill track echoed around him while the faces of Ghami and Ayodele briefly filled the screen. Wearing a camouflage top and trunks, he then turned and quietly greeted Oleksandr Usyk, a new ally sat at ringside.Joshua had trained hard with Usyk and his team in the buildup to his arrival in Jeddah. Usyk remains the best heavyweight in the world and Joshua, having lost both his battles with the Ukrainian, had resolved with some humility that he needed to learn from his previous rival. With Usyk’s trainers in his corner, and coming into the ring lighter than he has been for years at 251lb, Joshua was apparently determined to resemble a much sharper and sleeker fighter against Prenga.After a fleeting prayer in his corner, Joshua stepped towards the centre of the ring and, within 20 seconds, the unheralded Prenga had floored him heavily with a crunching right uppercut. Joshua got up quickly, looking dazed. Halfway through the round, with his legs still unsteady, Joshua was rocking against the ropes. With 30 seconds left in the first Joshua was down again. He hauled himself up, shaking his head, with defeat closing in on him. It had been a disastrous round but Joshua fired back just before the bell.Fury must have been cursing as the biggest money-making contest in the history of British boxing looked on the brink of obliteration. But, Joshua came out in the second with real purpose and quickly hurt the strangely tentative Albanian, who was already backing away before the damaging punches landed. It was almost as if Prenga could not believe he had come so close to knocking out the feted former world champion.View image in fullscreenAnthony Joshua decisively knocks down Albania’s Kristian Prenga in the second round …Photograph: Ali Issa/APView image in fullscreen… and Kristian Prenga lies across the bottom rope.Photograph: Ali Issa/APWith 20 seconds left in the round, a jolting jab set up Joshua as he landed two heavy right hands. Sensing a seismic turnaround, Joshua unleashed a pulverising right which landed with brutal force and separated Prenga from his suddenly scrambled senses. It was immediately obvious that he would be counted out.Joshua celebrated exuberantly, climbing on the ropes and raising his hands in jubilation, but it was more telling to see how a shaken Usyk just drew in a deep breath of relief.A bizarrely uneven victory followed Fury’s contrastinglyroutine defeat of Mariusz Wach, a faded Polish journeyman, in Pattaya, Thailand, on Friday night. Fury dominated a one-sided scrap before Wach was rescued by his team after they decided he could not come out for the eighth round.Earlier in the week Fury had insisted that he would reject an invitation to fly to Saudi Arabia from Thailand to watch Joshua. He had even expressed doubts that his much-delayed battle with Joshua would ever happen and described his fellow British heavyweight as “a bottle-job flapper and a chinless wonder”. But it helps that he and and Joshua could each make close to $100m for a contest that should have happened eight years ago, when they were both close to their fighting prime. So it seems highly likely that they will meet in the ring later this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Hold on, wait a minute,” Joshua cried out when he was interviewed in the ring. “Have we got Tyson Fury in the room? Is he here or not?”When he was informed that Fury would not be joining him between the ropes, Joshua slipped into his best high-pitched whispery impersonation of Mike Tyson at his most unhinged as, jokingly, he said: “I am the meanest, most ruthless, most vicious champion. Nobody can stop me. He is no Alexander [the Great].” He also referenced Tyson’s claim that he would “eat the heart” of Lennox Lewis but it was all just a madhouse riff from Joshua as he delighted in his comeback.Tyson Fury defeats 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in warm-up for expected Joshua boutRead more“All jokes aside, there are two sides,” he continued. “One is the fighter and the other is respect. I respect everything [Fury] has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we’re here now. I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat.”The Fury-Joshua circus has been rolling for so many years that even the most optimistic members of boxing’s beleaguered fanbase have sometimes wondered if the two ex-world champions would ever fight each other. But, finally, as Joshua turned the prospect of a terrible defeat into a knockout win over Prenga, the shenanigans moved significantly closer to becoming a real showdown later this year.Explore more on these topicsBoxingAnthony JoshuanewsShareReuse this content

title: San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan to be limited in camp after serious car crash | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan sustained a concussion and multiple fractures in a car crash earlier this month and will miss the start of training camp
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan sustained a concussion and multiple fractures in a car crash earlier this month and will miss the start of training camp
Content: Kyle Shanahan has a 91-72 record in the regular season and playoffs for the 49ers.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenKyle Shanahan has a 91-72 record in the regular season and playoffs for the 49ers.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APSan Francisco 49ersSan Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan to be limited in camp after serious car crashShanahan suffered concussion in 14 July crashAssistant Chris Foerster to lead practicesTeam expects coach back before openerAgenciesSat 25 Jul 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSan Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan suffered a concussion and other injuries in a car crash earlier this month that will limit his participation at the start of training camp, the team announced Saturday, when camp opened.The two-car accident happened on 14 Jily in Palo Alto, leading to Shanahan being taken to the hospital. The other driver was not hospitalized. Palo Alto police lieutenant Nicholas Martinez said there was no evidence that either driver was impaired and that both cooperated with police. No one was cited in the collision.Niners general manager John Lynch said Shanahan sustained a concussion, along with a broken nose, broken ribs and an injured hand.“Kyle is doing good,” Lynch said Saturday. “He’s got some bumps and bruises. He did suffer a concussion in the accident, has some lingering effects from that concussion.”Lynch said Shanahan is going through the same type of protocol that players undergo after a concussion and that doctors would determine when he will be able to be back at full speed.Lynch said Shanahan might be on the practice field when drills start on Sunday but won’t run practice or team meetings until he is recovered.“He’s a tremendous head coach, but this is bigger than that,” Lynch said. “This is about his well-being. We’re going to take the time necessary. And I think we’re very equipped to do that.”The Niners will conduct their first practice on Sunday with assistant head coach/offensive line coach Chris Foerster running the team, along with coordinators Klay Kubiak, Raheem Morris and Brant Boyer.Foerster has been on the 49ers’ staff since 2019 and also worked under Shanahan in Washington as an offensive line coach when Shanahan was offensive coordinator.Lynch didn’t give a timeline for Shanahan’s return but did say the team anticipates he will be back well before the season opener on 11 September in Australia against the Los Angeles Rams.Rams coach Sean McVay, who worked on the same staff as Shanahan in Washington from 2010-13, said he has talked to Shanahan since the crash and was thankful everyone involved was OK.“I think any time that something like that happens, it shakes you up a little bit,” McVay said. “But most importantly, I’ve talked to him, my thoughts and prayers are with his family, and I know he’s got an incredible perspective on it all. Kyle is a stud. I have as much respect for him as anybody, and he’s a friend of mine and I love him, and I’m hoping that he’s going to have a great recovery.”Shanahan is entering his 10th season as 49ers coach and is one of the most highly regarded coaches in the game for his offensive acumen. San Francisco has made two trips to the Super Bowl under his watch following the 2019 and 2023 seasons and made two additional appearances in the NFC title game in the 2021 and ‘22 seasons.Shanahan has a 91-72 record in the regular season and playoffs for the 49ers, ranking third in franchise history in wins behind George Seifert (108) and Bill Walsh (102).The team overcame significant injuries last season to finish 12-5 in the regular season and win a playoff game as Shanahan finished fifth in voting for the APNFLCoach of the Year.Explore more on these topicsSan Francisco 49ersNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Jordan Devey, former Patriots guard and Super Bowl winner, dies by suicide aged 38 | NFL | The Guardian
description: Jordan Devey, a former NFL offensive lineman who won Super Bowl XLIX with the Patriots, has died at 38 after what a GoFundMe for his family said was suicide
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jordan Devey, a former NFL offensive lineman who won Super Bowl XLIX with the Patriots, has died at 38 after what a GoFundMe for his family said was suicide
Content: Jordan Devey played 44 games over eight seasons.Photograph: Timothy T Ludwig/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan Devey played 44 games over eight seasons.Photograph: Timothy T Ludwig/Getty ImagesNFLJordan Devey, former Patriots guard and Super Bowl winner, dies by suicide aged 38Ex-NFL offensive lineman dies at age 38GoFundMe says Devey took his own lifeDevey played 44 games in eight seasonsAgenciesSat 25 Jul 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan Devey, a retiredNFLoffensive lineman who won a Super Bowl with the New ⁠England Patriots, died at age 38.According to a GoFundMe page started to benefit his wife, ⁠Linsey, and their four ⁠young children, ​Devey “took his own life”. As of Saturday morning, the fund had collected more than $92,000 of its $200,000 ⁠goal.Devey was the rare NFL player who didn’t play high school football, giving up the sport after junior ⁠high. Afflicted by a disease that causes knee inflammation and pain in ​children and teens, Devey ‌played tuba in the ‌school band.After a two-year mission with the Church of Latter Day ‌Saints, he enrolled in Snow College in Ephraim, Utah, and played two years of football since his knee issue had lessened. He transferred to Memphis for his final two seasons, then signed with the Baltimore Ravens after being unselected in the 2013 NFL ‌draft.The Patriots signed the 6ft 7in Devey to their practice squad that September and promoted him to the active ​roster in 2014 – the same season New England defeated the Seattle Seahawks to win Super Bowl XLIX.He played with the San Francisco 49ers in 2015, appearing in a career-high 15 games (nine starts), then followed ⁠with stops with the Kansas City Chiefs, then-Oakland Raiders and ​Buffalo Bills through ​the 2020 season. In ​all, he played in 44 NFL games (21 starts).Following his ​career, he volunteered ‌as a coach ​of his ​kids’ teams and coached high school football coach in Idaho.In an interview with Fox 13 in Salt Lake City, Leslie Devey said she believed the brain injury CTE contributed to her son’s death on Tuesday.In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsNFLNew England PatriotsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris grabs F1 Hungarian GP pole while Hamilton and Antonelli are penalised | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris took pole for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who was then docked three places for impeding Oscar Piastri
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris took pole for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who was then docked three places for impeding Oscar Piastri
Content: McLaren’s Lando Norris indicates he’s No 1 after darting through to take pole position.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APView image in fullscreenMcLaren’s Lando Norris indicates he’s No 1 after darting through to take pole position.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APFormula One 2026Lando Norris grabs F1 Hungarian GP pole while Hamilton and Antonelli are penalisedDefending champion takes first pole of 2026 by 0.012secHamilton and Antonelli receive three-place penaltiesGiles Richardsat the HungaroringSat 25 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe margins were tiny and for a moment it seemedLewis Hamiltonhad finally found his edge in qualifying, only for the seven-time champion to be beaten by but a breath. The defending world champion, Lando Norris, pipped him to pole for the Hungarian Grand Prix in a thrilling, dramatic contest.Worse was to follow for Hamilton as his very real chance of converting a front-row start to a win in his hugely competitive Ferrari took a severe blow as he was penalised three grid places for impeding McLaren’sOscar Piastriduring their final laps. Hamilton will start from fifth place.Hungarian Grand Prix qualifying: Formula One – liveRead moreNorris took the top spot for McLaren by one-hundredth of a second from Hamilton’sFerrari, but the latter’s place on the front row remained in doubt, as he was under investigation by the FIA.Hamilton said he had been informed by the team that Piastri was closing on him only when theMcLarenwas already right behind him and that he did not know anyone was still on a hot lap behind him. Nonetheless, after qualifying, the stewards ruled he was at fault and imposed the grid penalty.“I was told when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming,” Hamilton said. “I thought everyone came out behind me. I was the first out so I thought everyone had finished their lap, and I think Charles was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn’t intentional.”Hamilton’s teammate, Charles Leclerc, was in third, with the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, in fourth for Mercedes, but the Italian was investigated for failing to slow under yellow flags and also given a three-place penalty. Antonelli leads Hamilton by 45 points and his teammate,George Russell, by 50 points in the championship.Piastri was fifth for McLaren, Max Verstappen sixth for Red Bull after he spun on his final lap, while Russell could manage only seventh and was told to pull his car off the track after his final lap with a water leak.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton was penalised for impeding Oscar Piastri.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe day belonged to Norris, who delivered a superb run for McLaren to claim pole. Given that the team had opened the season off the pace of Mercedes and Ferrari, their upgrades for Miami and further developments added in Canada have proved impressive and they are the first team to deny Mercedes the top spot this season.It is Norris’s second pole at the Hungarian GP and the 17th of his career, while for McLaren it is another strong result at the circuit. With Norris winning here last year and Piastri in 2024, they may well be in position to make it three in a row at a meeting where McLaren have a record 13 victories.On the opening laps in Q3 Verstappen made the running but was surpassed by Norris, yet Hamilton nailed his first lap to take provisional pole with a time of 1min 17.219sec, a tenth up on Norris in second, and a chance to take his first pole for Ferrari and a record 10th at the same track.The track had been steadily rubbering-in throughout the session, the times coming down as the grip increased and the final runs were crucial. Hamilton was sent out early but could not improve on his time and Norris, the last man on track, was on a quick run. Immense through the middle sector, there was nothing in it and he just edged out Hamilton by one-hundredth of a second with a time of 1:17.207.Given the track was evolving Hamilton felt the decision to send him out early had been an error. “I felt solid throughout qualifying, but for some reason we went out first, which I don’t think was the right call,” he said. “The grip wasn’t there for either Charles or I. We were quickest throughout, so it’s definitely one that got away.”Aston Martin brought their radically overhauled B-spec car to Hungary in the hope of turning round a disastrous opening to the season. The car was overweight and aerodynamically far from where they had expected to be, while their Honda engine is down on power and suffered from causing severe vibrations early in the season.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli, the championship leader, will start the Hungarian Grand Prix in seventh after a grid penalty.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAThe team principal and designer, Adrian Newey, admitted it had been an immensely difficult start. “These first races have been a complete nightmare,” he said. “Hopefully, we can get at least to a point of respectability now, that is the immediate goal.”In qualifying at least they made a step forward with Fernando Alonso putting an Aston into Q2 for the first time this season, no mean feat given they were two seconds slower than the Cadillacs in Belgium. Alonso ultimately finished in 16th.The success of the upgrade is considered to be key in persuading Alonso to stay for 2027, with a further development expected for Zandvoort when Honda will also bring their new engine.The return of the Malaysia to the F1 calendar could be confirmed as early as Sunday, with the meeting arranged after the cancellation of the races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier in the season. It will take place between the rounds in Baku and Singapore on 4 October. The race at the Sepang circuit near Kuala Lumpur is expected to be branded as the Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia, with Bahrain funding the event. The circuit last held an F1 meeting in 2017.F1 is also understood to be looking into the prospect of hosting the season finale at Imola if the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are unable to be held because of the conflict in the Middle East.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lando NorrisMcLarenFormula OneLewis HamiltonKimi AntonelliGeorge RussellnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pogacar set for Tour de France glory in shortened finale as Carapaz wins stage 20 | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar will take his fifth Tour sooner than planned after Sunday’s final stage was shortened to free up security forces to fight wildfires elsewhere
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar will take his fifth Tour sooner than planned after Sunday’s final stage was shortened to free up security forces to fight wildfires elsewhere
Content: Tadej Pogacar (left) and UAE teammate Isaac del Toro strike a pose as they cross the finish line on Alpe d'Huez.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar (left) and UAE teammate Isaac del Toro strike a pose as they cross the finish line on Alpe d'Huez.Photograph: Mosa’ab Elshamy/APTour de France 2026Pogacar set for Tour de France glory in shortened finale as Carapaz wins stage 20Four-time victor holds huge lead after Alpe d’HuezFinal stage to be shortened due to wildfires elsewhereJeremy Whittleat Alpe d'HuezSat 25 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar’s likely victory parade on the streets of Paris will come sooner on Sunday after the final stage of theTour de Francewas shortened due to wildfires elsewhere in France. The stage will now be only 89km long and will start on the Champs-Élysées, where two laps of the avenue will be followed by the now traditional circuits of the Butte Montmartre.More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and SpainRead moreIn a joint statement with the prefecture police, the Tour organiser, ASO, said: “The ministry of the interior has decided to redeploy a portion of the internal security forces initially mobilised for the final stage of the Tour de France, in order to reinforce the response efforts inthe areas affected by the wildfires.”Wildfires around the Arcachon lagoon near Bordeaux and around Biscarrosse, in the Landes, have destroyed more than 36,000 hectares of forest. This is the third stage of the Tour to be subjected to prefecture intervention, due to wildfires or a heatwave, in this year’s race.Resources and the lack of them have also been a topic of debate sincePogacar’s astounding winon Alpe d’Huez on Friday. The four-time champion is now expected to secure a record-equalling fifth title in Paris on Sunday evening after Saturday’s 20th stage was won by Richard Carapaz.A day after setting a record time up the Alpe’s famous hairpin bends to extend his overall lead, Pogacar could afford to concede 39 seconds to his closest challenger, Remco Evenepoel, on Saturday and will start Sunday’s shortened stage into Paris ahead by six minutes and 26 seconds.However, there was significant fallout after Friday’s chaotic climb, largely due to the dangerous behaviour of some among the thousands at the roadside. Several incidents, which endangered both riders and fans, rebooted the debate over the safety of Tour stages on the Alpe.In-race motorbikes, blocked by the crowds, stalled an attack from Evenepoel, while a lack of crowd control led to the Movistar climber Einer Rubio abandoning the race after riding into the rear windscreen of a UAE team car. The crash, which led to Rubio being transported by helicopter to hospital in Grenoble, where he was given 20 stitches for facial injuries, was caused by an unruly spectator falling in front of the car, forcing it to suddenly brake.“If we had been using cars from 20 years ago, the accident wouldn’t have happened,” the race director, Thierry Gouvenou, said, apparently blaming the braking sensors in the car.View image in fullscreenRichard Carapaz, in the polka dot jersey, heads for his second win at this year’s race.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersMore footage of fans wrestling each other over gifts from thecaravane publicitaireand climbing over moving race vehicles – including the Guardian’s – further fuelled the notion of a race that was out of control. The French national champion, Romain Grégoire, said spectators were “so drunk that it was more like being slapped on the arse, than getting pushes”.Evenepoel’s Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe sports director, Klaas Lodewyck, said: “As long as they’re cheering on the riders and creating a good atmosphere, it’s fine. But when they start punching in side mirrors and banging on the windows, that’s crossing the line.”On Saturday’s final mountain stage, Pogacar the ogre, as L’Équipe called him, worked to protect the interests of his third-placed UAE teammate, Isaac del Toro. Carapaz, stage winner in Orcières-Merlette and third in Friday’s stage to Alpe d’Huez, was again one of the key animators, attacking on the first climb, the Col de la Croix de Fer, as he sought to consolidate his lead in the King of the Mountains classification.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTour de France 2026: stage 20 from Bourg d’Oisans to Alpe d’Huez – liveRead moreFatigue and frayed nerve endings also played their part in the Tour’s hardest mountain stage, and Ilan Van Wilder, 12th overall when the stage began, crashed out after falling on the descent of the Croix de Fer.But the spat between Carapaz and the French climber Lenny Martinez, who had been overtaken by Pogacar close to the finish of Friday’s stage to the Alpe, rumbled on into Saturday morning. The pair had engaged in a war of words after the Ecuadorian angrily accused the Frenchman of “cutting in front” of him on the final corner on Friday. Martinez seemed unconcerned.“I knew I had to be first through the corner,” Martinez said. “We’re not at Club Med – I’m not letting him go first.”Most of the real drama in the final mountain stage came on the narrow climb of the Col de Sarenne, where Paul Seixas lost ground on Pogacar, Del Toro and Evenepoel.Visma-Lease a Bike’s Sepp Kuss, descending towards a probable stage win on the Alpe, crashed on the exit of a tunnel and then, moments later, almost toppled into the void on a fast bend. The American came close to disappearing over a cliff edge, but was stopped by crash netting, mounted alongside the road.His mistake was enough to let the pursuing Carapaz speed past and, despite evident fatigue, the Ecuadorian held on to take his second stage win in three days and secured the polka dot jersey.Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal make shock approach to sign Vinícius Júnior from Real Madrid | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta is keen to bring in the Brazil forward who has one year left on his contract at Real and may be open to leaving after the arrival of José Mourinho as manager
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mikel Arteta is keen to bring in the Brazil forward who has one year left on his contract at Real and may be open to leaving after the arrival of José Mourinho as manager
Content: Vinícius Júnior scored four goals for Brazil in the World Cup.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Allstar Picture Library Ltd/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior scored four goals for Brazil in the World Cup.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Allstar Picture Library Ltd/SportsphotoArsenalArsenal make shock approach to sign Vinícius Júnior from Real MadridBrazil forward has one year left on contract at BernabéuVinícius future at Real uncertain after Mourinho arrivalPA MediaSat 25 Jul 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal are exploring a shock deal to signVinícius Júniorfrom Real Madrid. Arsenal have inquired about the Brazil international, who has one year remaining on his contract at the Bernabéu.It is believed any move for Vinícius – who scored 22 goals for Real last season and four for Brazil at the World Cup – is at a formative stage as Mikel Arteta seeks a marquee signing to build on theclub’s first Premier League titlein more than two decades.Premier League: club-by-club guide to transfer business so far – and what they still needRead moreThe 26-year-old Vinícius fits that bill, with Atlético Madrid’s Julián Álvarez, RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomande and Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain also on their radar.Arsenal bolstered their attacking options with the £34msigning of Christos Tzolisfrom Club Brugge this week.
