Morgan Rogers had also been identified as a target, but it is believed Arsenal were not prepared to pay more than £80m for the England international, who hasjoined Chelsea in a £117m deal– a British record fee.Vinícius’s future at Real is uncertain after José Mourinho’s return and the club could cash in on the player, rather than risk losing him for nothing in a year’s time.Mourinho, who hassigned a three-year deal at the Bernabéu, was criticised for comments he made after Vinícius accused Benfica’s Gianluca Prestianni of racially abusing him during a Champions League tie in February. Mourinho, Benfica manager at the time,said “something happens, always”in matches where Vinícius plays. Prestianni wasbanned for six matchesafter he admitted to using homophobic language towards Vinicius.Tzolis followed Piero Hincapié – who turned his temporary deal into a full-time switch – and the goalkeeper Illan Meslier, who was out of contract at Leeds, as Arsenal’s third addition.Bruno Guimarãescould also move to the Emirateswith Arsenal keen on signing the Brazil international. After Newcastle’s 1-1 pre-season draw at Gateshead on Saturday, Eddie Howe said: “We don’t want to lose our best players. I’ve spoken to him [Guimarães] as I would do. Bruno is just a fantastic person. We’ve had some really good conversations, both before the World Cup, during the World Cup and after the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t know what’s going to happen with Bruno’s future. That’s for other people to speculate about.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalVinícius JúniorReal MadridTransfer windowJosé MourinhonewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘What the hell just happened?’: Ryan Fox on his Open triumph and famous sporting family | The Open | The Guardian
description: New Zealander has returned home with the Claret Jug in tow after stepping out of his father’s shadow
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: New Zealander has returned home with the Claret Jug in tow after stepping out of his father’s shadow
Content: Ryan Fox with the Claret Jug in front of the Royal Birkdale clubhouse after his one-shot victory over Cameron Young.Photograph: Oisin Keniry/R&A/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRyan Fox with the Claret Jug in front of the Royal Birkdale clubhouse after his one-shot victory over Cameron Young.Photograph: Oisin Keniry/R&A/Getty ImagesThe OpenInterview‘What the hell just happened?’: Ryan Fox on his Open triumph and famous sporting familyEwan MurrayNew Zealander has returned home with the Claret Jug in tow after stepping out of his father’s shadowSat 25 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe curse of the iconic sporting parent. Accidental, yet real. Decades of evidence show how difficult it is for the offspring of those who have scaled the greatest heights in sport to replicate those achievements. Until Sunday and a stunning finale at Royal Birkdale, Ryan Fox would always be known in New Zealand as the son of Grant. Fox smiles when asked whetherthe claiming of the 154th Open Championshipmeans he has finally forged his own reputation for greatness. “I can plead a pretty good case for that,” he replies.“I have two Claret Jugs [one real, one replica] sitting at home so it is real but it certainly doesn’t feel that way yet. I can’t quite believe it. My wife and I have looked at each other quite a lot over the last few days and buzzed out a little bit saying: ‘What the hell just happened?’ It is crazy.”Fox’s journey has always been distinct. His grandfather Merv Wallace captained New Zealand at cricket. Grant’s fly-half performances and goal-kicking excellence as a World Cup-winning All Black mean he is revered. Ryan dabbled with both sports before landing on golf. “I didn’t have the mental strength to play cricket,” he says. “I was the guy who got to 30 really quickly then got out. If T20 was around back then, I would have been pretty good at it.”Crucially, he was always comfortable in his own skin and his own movie. Winning the Open, his first major, has elevated Fox’s own status in a land he still adores.Ryan Fox crowned Open champion as heavyweights wilt under pressureRead more“I grew up with Dad being stopped in the street,” he says. “When I played rugby it was hard because I was always directly compared to him. I was not very smart; played the same position and tried to kick goals. I didn’t help myself there.“I never had any pressure to succeed in sport. It was just what I wanted to do. I loved sport, grew up with sport, wanted to play sport. When I started to do well in amateur golf there was a little bit more attention because of who Dad was but that never bothered me.“I don’t know if it is genetic or learned but there has to be something there. Dad caddied for me a lot when I was an amateur and early in my professional career. Having someone who dealt with pressure like he did, kicking goals, translates pretty well into golf. Both are about routines, the ball not moving and starting everything yourself. I always had a sports psychologist on call 24/7. I wasn’t always great at listening but I think enough of it made it through.“Winning the inaugural World Cup, with how rugby-mad New Zealand is, still feels pretty hard to beat. You can’t really compare it all [to an Open win]. Playing cricket for New Zealand in the 1940s and 50s was a big deal, they didn’t play a lot of Test matches back then but my grandfather had an incredible career. Someone will try to debate all this. I just hope what happened last weekend is a pretty cool thing in general for sport in New Zealand.”View image in fullscreenRyan Fox celebrates his putt going in on the 72nd hole, making him the first New Zealander to win the Open since Bob Charles in 1963.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIndeed it is. This is Ryan’s own tale. We speak as Fox is about to board a flight from Florida back to Auckland, a surprise visit with the Claret Jug as hand luggage. “It will be a whirlwind trip and really sweet,” he says. “We didn’t even let New Zealand know we were flying back. I wasn’t going to play over the next couple of weeks and it would have seemed strange sitting in Florida when my peers were playing in different parts of the country. It felt like the ideal time to share this with friends, family and the media at home while it is still really fresh. I had planned to go home in late November but it would have been anticlimactic.“I have a big lineup of mates who are keen to drink something out of the Claret Jug. Dad is keen to do the same, a rugby tradition is drinking out of trophies. I may only get one chance with it so it feels like I should show it off and take it around. I want to enjoy this as much as possible. I think my life is going to be a bit different in New Zealand now but that is all part of this.“I vividly remember Michael Campbell winning the US Open in 2005. The whole country stopped. I was a golf fan and it was the greatest thing I ever saw. It is crazy to think a similar thing has happened to me now.”DeChambeau moves the dial for golf but is his posturing and pantomime worth the hassle? | Ewan MurrayRead moreBumps appeared on Fox’s path towards Open glory. Despite seeming a natural links player – he has competed at the Irish Open and won the Dunhill Links Championship – Fox’s record in the oldest major of all was average, until Birkdale. “I could never put four rounds together,” he explains. “You could argue I still haven’t together because Thursday was pretty average. But I am not complaining.” Fox sat two over par and seven from the lead after 18 holes.Fast forward to Sunday afternoon and the 15th, a treacherous par three. Fox’s iron shot rebounds from the bunker face to a horrible position under the sand trap’s back lip. The golfing gods were testing a player who had waded into uncharted territory.“It was a yard away from being perfect,” says Fox. “Links golf is funny like that. I knew before I got to the ball that it wasn’t any good. I could tell from the reaction of the on-course commentators. I was almost glad it was so close to the lip that I couldn’t even try to hit it out. You could make yourself look really silly if you try to take one of those shots on, on your knees under that pressure.”View image in fullscreenRyan Fox: ‘I have big lineup of mates who are keen to drink out of the Claret Jug.’Photograph: Tom Shaw/R&A/Getty ImagesFox hit his ball backwards, walking off with a bogey four that enhanced an already positive mindset. He was helped, perhaps, by the level of focus elsewhere. Bryson DeChambeau captured eyeballs.So, too, did Tommy Fleetwood. By the time crowds flocked to see Fox’s finish, he was so ensconced in a bubble, the size of the gallery did not matter.The 18th was the hole of Fox’s life. A 330-yard drive, an approach to just inside 12ft and a putt sunk with authority. Helookedso calm. “I remember everything, it just feels like I didn’t do it,” he says. “It doesn’t make sense if I try to put myself back there. It is like an out‑of-body experience.“I was a nervous wreck over the final putt. My hands were shaking and I almost had to talk myself down after getting to the green and realising I had a putt to win the Open. I am not quite sure how I did it.”Fox’s victory received widespread acclaim. His golf style is simple, his unfussy attitude so endearing. The surfing legend Kelly Slater has been in touch with congratulations. “I got a message from Ronan Keating, which my mum was pretty excited about,” Fox adds. “It has been surreal and I have not even got halfway through my emails. I reply to some people then check my phone again and have more messages than I started with. The support has been incredible.Fleetwood, Fox and fury: Tom Jenkins’ best images from the OpenRead more“The greatestinsight came from Justin Thomas. He congratulated me but also offered me advice about trying to remember every little detail because you never know when you will want to draw on it. I thought that was an awesome little nugget, from someone who has been through it.”A perhaps cruel but regular theme of elite golf is that when a player wins a major, coverage turns towards whether they can do it again. Winners of more than one earn extra kudos. “My caddie said it to me best on Sunday night after we had a few drinks. ‘Foxy, you may only ever have one putt to win a major and you holed it,’” Fox says. “I know I can do it and I would love to put myself in that position again. If I don’t, I am one from one.“I wouldn’t have thought in my wildest dreams I could achieve all this. Hopefully there is a little bit more left but if there isn’t, I can be incredibly proud.” As can his nation. Ryan Fox has etched his own name in the history books.Explore more on these topicsThe OpenEuropean TourGolfPGA TourinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World Cup | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Norway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdle
Author: Natalie Tan
Headline: Norway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdle
Content: Erling Haaland carries his raccoon, Vozinha enjoys the moment, Merlin the duck, Scotland supporters enjoy Boston and Wonderwall by Oasis.Composite: Getty Images, Guardian designView image in fullscreenErling Haaland carries his raccoon, Vozinha enjoys the moment, Merlin the duck, Scotland supporters enjoy Boston and Wonderwall by Oasis.Composite: Getty Images, Guardian designWorld Cup 2026From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World CupNorway’s striker left his mark, as did Scotland’s fans in Boston, but Turkey’s dark horses fell at the first hurdleNatalie TanandCalvin BurtonSat 25 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 15.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCuraçao’shistoric first goal“I played with him on my PlayStation, and now I’ve scored against him,” Livano Comenencia said after converting Curaçao’s first World Cup goal past Manuel Neuer in their opening match against Germany. The smallest nation ever to qualify for the World Cupwent on to lose 7-1but that goal – their only one of the tournament – will go down in history.‘Cablegate’Should Jude Bellingham’s first goal against Norway have been ruled out? Perhaps so given the ball appeared tohit an overhead cablein the buildup. Fifa insisted there had been no such intervention; Norway’s manager, Ståle Solbakken, was sure there had been. “Many on the bench reacted immediately … the ball fell down straight in front of us,” he said, furiously.Top 30: from half a million World Cup photos, why I love these the mostRead moreMarsch’s musings“I’d rather be us than them,” said Jesse Marschafter Canada were comprehensively beaten by Moroccoin the last 16. “It takes some nerve to say that when you lose 3-0,” said Morocco’s head coach, Mohamed Ouahbi, in response. Marsch also somewhat hilariously overestimated the capacity of BC Place after his side’s6–0 win over Qatar, saying: “There’ll be 60 million people that said they were here.”GlitteringGoldenBoot raceBetween 1978 and 2018, only the original Ronaldo had scored more than six goals at a single World Cup (eight in 2002). Lionel Messi and Kylian Mbappé had matched the Brazilian’s tally by the semi-finals this time around, with Mbappé winning the Golden Boot after scoring two goals against England inthe third-place playoff.Scotland fans take over BostonScottish supporters marked their return to football’s biggest stage in 28 years by taking over Boston, filling Fenway Park with songs and drinking their pubs dry. With the Tartan Army crowning some of the city’s most recognisable statues with bright orange traffic cones, the “Boston cone”was greeted byBoston’s mayor, Michelle Wu, upon its arrival from Glasgow last week. Scotland’s players may have made little impact in the US this summer, but their fans no doubt left a legacy.Ronaldo scores … andthen goes out with a whimper‘CR7’ finally ended his knockout goal droughtagainst Croatiaas Portugal squeezed into the last 16. However, joy soon turned to despair when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the next round. Ronaldo struggled to have any impact on proceedings, managing only 19 touches in what washis final World Cup match. “I gave it all, I gave it my best,” he said afterwards.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo scored against Croatia but could not prevent Portugal going out against Spain.Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockEmbolo’s mistaken identityThe mistaken identity rule was updated for this World Cup to cover situations where a player was booked but the offence was committed by the other team and well and truly took effectduring Argentina and Switzerland’s quarter-finalin Kansas City. The referee, João Pinheiro, initially issued Argentina’s Leandro Paredes a yellow card for his challenge on Switzerland’s Breel Embolo before the VAR called him to the monitor. Embolo was then ruled to have dived and was punished with a yellow card himself – it was the forward’s second of the game and he was duly sent off. “This rule destroyed the game today,” said Switzerland’s head coach, Murat Yakin, after his side’s 3-1 loss.Iran’s unprecedented tournamentCompeting against the backdrop of their country’s conflict with the US, Iran’s players faced incredible difficulties before a ball was kicked. With their training base abruptly switched from Arizona to Mexico before the tournament, the team were then only allowed to enter the US the day before their first two matches and had to leave immediately after. Despite that, they only narrowly missed out on the knockout rounds afterAustria and Algeria drew 3-3in the final round of the group stage to send them home on goal difference. “What these players have done should be written in history because the host country treated us very unfairly,” Iran’s head coach, Amir Ghalenoei, said.Erling Haaland: internet phenomenonSnapchat stories. Stuffed raccoons. Doing next to nothing against Brazil for 79 minutes and thenscoring twice in 11 minutes. It’s fair to say Erling Haaland made his mark at the World Cup. “When someone asks me what my biggest fear is but I can’t say being charged at by Haaland at full speed so I just say spiders,” reads a video that has racked up millions of views on Instagram, a reference to how Haaland chased down Iraq’s goalkeeper, Jalal Hassan, for his second goal of the tournament.Turkey are definitely not dark horsesTurkey were tipped to go far but, in the end, didn’t even make it out of the group stage. Indeed, they were the second country eliminated from the tournament following back-to-back losses to Australia and 10-man Paraguay. “We should have won these games … everybody’s sad, everybody’s crying,”said Arda Guler, Turkey’s wonderkid after his country’s less-than-wonderful showing.View image in fullscreenArda Guler (right) grimaces during Turkey’s defeat by Australia.Photograph: Lee Smith/ReutersEgypt outrage after controversial exit“I’m going home and won’t be watching any more games from the tournament,”said Egypt’s head coach, Hossam Hassan,after his side’s loss to Argentina in the last 16. “What happened to us wasn’t fair. We should have had a penalty, a goal was disallowed and I don’t know why.” Hassan was not alone in thinking crucial decisions had favoured the world champions in what was arguably the game of the tournament in Atlanta.The wonder of WonderwallIt started off as a standard submission for the World Cup’s official track list but was quickly adopted by England’s travelling support as the theme song of their tournament run, Oasis’s 1995 classic creating a genuinely uplifting bond between plays and fans. Harry Kane went as far as describing the post-match ritual of standing alongside his teammates, arms around each other’s shoulders, and facing a wall of happy, singing English faces as one of his “favourite ever moments in an England shirt”.Lamine Yamal’s brother becomes a starLamine Yamal had a great World Cup but not as great as his three-year-old brother, Keyne, whocaptured hearts worldwidewith his wide-eyed, big-grinned expressions of delight whenever his older sibling shone at the tournament. A young star was born on the back of another young star and both look here to stay.Mexico’s unofficial mascotMerlin the duck became a sensation after being spotted at Mexico’s post-game celebrations following their opening World Cup win over South Africa. Indeed, Merlin became so famous that he was granteda meeting with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. “We feel very honoured to be here with the president, it is an honour for us to stand before you and for the whole world to see the beautiful side of Mexico.” said Karla Gómez, Merlin’s owner. Sadly, Merlin wasunable to watch Mexico in the fleshdue to Fifa regulations.Death, taxesandMerino’s late winnersMessi, Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane … this has been a World Cup of goalscoring superstars well and truly coming to the fore, and thenthere has been Mikel Merino. The Spain midfielder came off the bench to score crucial winning goals against Portugal and Belgium in back-to-back knockout games. It was some contribution from the Arsenal player to his country’s World Cup triumph.View image in fullscreenMikel Merino races away after a late goal against Belgium.Photograph: Ringo Chiu/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAguirre meetsGordon“Gordon!” shouted Javier Aguirre at England’s left-sided forward during the first-half hydration break of an epic last-16 encounter at the Azteca, followed by something indistinguishable when Anthony Gordon turned back to look. Keen-eyed internet users later deciphered it as a very cheerful “fuck you!” from Mexico’s manager, with both men subsequently laughing with delight. “I’d just run the full-back down the line,” Gordon saidafter England’s 3-2 win. “So I took it as a bit of a compliment from him.”Vozinha’s star powerAfter being named player of the match in Cape Verde’sopening goalless draw with Spain, Vozinha teared up. “My mum didn’t manage to be here because of the visa,” said the 40-year-old goalkeeper. Two days later the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, announced that arrangements had been made to waive the cost of Ana Évora’s visa; she was subsequently in attendance as her son played in a2-2 draw with Uruguayand became one of the stars of the tournament.Penalty drama between Netherlands and MoroccoNeil El Aynaoui struck the crossbar. Justin Kluivert’s effort ricocheted off a post. Bart Verbruggen almost saved Soufiane Rahimi’s strike but helplessly watched it squirm under him and into the back of the net. At 2-2, Quinten Timber put his shot well wide, handing Morocco the advantage only for Achraf Hakimi to do the exact same thing. Standing bolt upright, Yassine Bounou saved from Crysencio Summerville before Ismael Saibari put an end to the rollercoaster of a trulyremarkable last-32 penalty shootout.Tuchel hits out at photographers“I’m begging Fifa to change the position of the photographers in the national anthem, because I could not see my team,” Thomas Tuchel said after England’sopening win against Croatia. “It was a very special moment, and I was standing in front of a wall of 50 photographers and I could not see one single player.” It wasn’t the first time at the tournament that England’s head coach made his frustrations clear.View image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel is not ready for his closeup.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesOpener smashes red-cardrecordMexico’s 2-0 win over South Africakicked off the World Cup and simultaneously almost equalled the 2022 tournament’s tally of red cards in a single match. Yaya Sithole capped off a terrible second half for South Africa by getting sent off just after the break before his teammate Themba Zwane and Mexican defender César Montes were shown red cards within eight minutes of each other.“Overturn this”With the vast majority of the football world rooting for them, Belgium reacted to the suspension of Folarin Balogun’s ban for the USA’s last-16 encounter with the Red Devils in Seattle with a ruthlessly commanding performance. Theybeat the co-hosts 4-1and marked the victory with a string of celebrations that made clear what they thought of thecontroversy surrounding’s Balogun’s presenceon the pitch, including an imitation of Donald Trump’s dance moves in the dressing room afterwards and a gleeful tweet from the team’s official account that simply read: “Overturn this.”Paraguay go from heroes to villainsThere was widespread delight whenParaguay eliminated Germany in the last 32with a show of togetherness and defiance but their popularity diminished during their subsequentdefeat by Franceon the back of a brutal display of the dark arts. Joe Hart brandished the South Americans an “absolute disgrace” while his fellow BBC pundit Micah Richards thought that the approach was wholly unnecessary, saying: “Paraguay are better than that. Defensively they were so good and they didn’t need to get into these antics.” The Uzbek referee, Ilgiz Tantashev, also faced intense criticism after inexplicably failing to book any Paraguay players.France players embrace DeschampsAfter Kylian Mbappé scored the first of his two goalsagainst Sweden, he and his teammates ran over to Didier Deschamps and hugged their head coach. The gesture was a response to Deschamps’ return to the touchline following the death of his mother. When asked about the embrace, Mbappé said: “That’s the DNA of this group. The coach has been through certain circumstances, and we’re all with him and will continue to support him.”View image in fullscreenDidier Deschamps is embraced by Kylian Mbappé as France take on Sweden.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesReferee stops play – with an injuryIn a bizarre twist, theUSA’s 2-0 victory over Australiain the group stages had to be stopped for, and not by, the referee, Felix Zwayer, after he collapsed with cramp in the dying minutes of the contest in Seattle. Australia’s midfielder Aiden O’Neill and the USA’s Balogun helped Zwayer stretch out the cramp amid ironic cheers from the crowd.Croatia goal disallowed by a hairCroatia had seemingly rescued their World Cup campaign from the jaws of defeat after Josko Gvardiol tapped in at the back post in the final stages of their last-32 encounter with Portugal in Toronto. But then VAR got involved and thegoal was ruled outafter Fifa’s sensor technology discovered that the cross to Gvardiol had taken the faintest touch off the head of Igor Matanovic. “It was very bad refereeing,” said Croatia’s manager, Zlatko Dalic. “I’m not saying that sometimes VAR can’t be of help, but it kills the emotions, it kills everything.”Jayden Adams tributesJayden Adams, who featured in all three of South Africa’s group games,passed away just days after returning homefrom North America. “Today, South African football mourn the loss of a talented player whose passion, dedication, and love for the beautiful game inspired many,” read a national team tribute. A minute’s silence was observed before all quarter-final matches, alongside an outpouring of touching tributes to the 25-year-old midfielder.Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: club-by-club guide to transfer business so far – and what they still need | Premier League | The Guardian
description: The English transfer record has been smashed, with Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers on the move during a busy summer of signings
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: The English transfer record has been smashed, with Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers on the move during a busy summer of signings
Content: Morgan Rogers of Chelsea; Elliot Anderson of Manchester City; Ipwich’s Emersonn; Jérémy Jacquet of Liverpool (from left).Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMorgan Rogers of Chelsea; Elliot Anderson of Manchester City; Ipwich’s Emersonn; Jérémy Jacquet of Liverpool (from left).Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesPremier LeaguePremier League: club-by-club guide to transfer business so far – and what they still needThe English transfer record has been smashed, with Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers on the move during a busy summer of signingsWill Unwin,Louise Taylor,Andy Hunter,Jamie JacksonandBilly MundaySat 25 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenalFor once, Mikel Arteta is not spending his summer looking for a No 9. Instead the champions have moved to strengthen out wide after the departure of Leandro Trossard withChristos Tzolis arriving for £34mhaving scored 33 league goals in his last two seasons from Club Brugge’s left wing. After missing out on Morgan Rogers to Chelsea, they will not want to be beaten to Alex Scott’s signature. Defensive cover will probably be necessary after the injury to William Saliba at the World Cup.Billy MundayMajor insPiero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m, after loan), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)Major outsLeandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m)Aston VillaIt is a very busy summer of comings and goings at Villa Park. Alejandro Garnacho is primed to swap places with Morgan Rogers and there is still scope for Emiliano Martínez to leave, forcing their hand in goal, and Arsenal’s interest in Ezri Konsa is not going away. Striker is another position without guarantees, with Nicolas Jackson one option, especially if Fenerbahce’s interest in Ollie Watkins becomes something more concrete. A left-back to replace the departing Lucas Digne is a must, while Leon Bailey is available for transfer and could head to Hull.Will UnwinMajor insJohan Manzambi (Freiburg, £51m), João Gomes (Wolves, £34m)Major outsMorgan Rogers (Chelsea, £117m), Youri Tielemans (Manchester United, £35m), Donyell Malen (Roma, £21.6m)BournemouthPlenty will depend on Alex Scott and whether he stays or goes, with interest in the midfielder, who has turned down a new contract, from Chelsea, Manchester United and Arsenal. Regardless of that, Benfica’s António Silva is lined up to replace Marcos Senesi, while the search is continuing for a right-back. With a first season in the Europa League ahead, planning accordingly to ensure the squad is sufficiently robust to cope with a more hectic schedule than usual is paramount.WUMajor insÁlvaro Rodríguez (Elche, £21.4m)Major outsLuis Sinisterra (Cruzeiro, £5.2m), Marcos Senesi (Tottenham, free)BrentfordUsually a big sale pushes the Bees into action but not this summer. Experience has been on the agenda, with Jaidon Anthony and Callum Wilson acquired, while the arrival of the young centre-back Jannik Schuster could mean the end of Ethan Pinnock’s time with the club. They are, as always, likely to look at bringing in players with potential. The Manchester United teenager Noah Ajayi falls into this category but whether a deal progresses remains to be seen.WUMajor insJaidon Anthony (Burnley, £15m), Jannik Schuster (Red Bull Salzburg, £14m), Callum Wilson (West Ham, free)BrightonInvesting in the defence early has freed up time to do other critical business, with a central midfield refresh potentially in the offing, while there is a desire to bolster the winger bullpen. Evan Ferguson is back at the club after a loan spell at Roma but whether he has a future at the club remains to be seen. If not, finding suitable support for the 35-year-old Danny Welbeck will be part of the strategy with the a Conference League campaign awaiting. Bart Verbruggen has attracted interest in Europe and a departure would call for a new No 1 to be found.WUMajor insLuka Vuskovic (Tottenham, £46m), Zadok Yohanna (AIK, £21.5m), Pascal Struijk (Leeds United, £18m), Costinha (Olympiakos, 11m)Major outsJan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham, £52m), Diego Coppola (Paris FC, £15.3m), James Milner (retired), Solly March (released)ChelseaMarc Cucurella’ssale has left a holeto fill at left-back. Options there include a return for Newcastle’s Lewis Hall or a move for Rayo Vallecano’s Pep Chavarría. The midfield is also looking light with Andrey Santos out the door and Enzo Fernández linked with a move away. The reluctance to sign a goalkeeper suggests 20-year-old Mike Penders is not far from competing for the No 1 spot. The capture of Morgan Rogers will excite supporters, but they still crave a top centre-back and striker.BMMajor insMorgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £117m), Marco Palestra (Atalanta, £47m), Geovany Quenda (Sporting, £40m), Emmanuel Emegha (Strasbourg, £21.6m)Major outsMarc Cucurella (Real Madrid, £52m), Andrey Santos (Manchester United, £50m), Tyrique George (Everton, £18m)View image in fullscreenEngland attacker Morgan Rogers is an exciting signing for Chelsea.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PACoventryWithout putting too fine a point on it, quality across the board is required. The club are still working on bringing the Brighton goalkeeper Carl Rushworth back after a successful loan in the Championship but price and competition for his signature will complicate matters. Finding strikers capable of converting chances will be integral to their chances of survival for Frank Lampard’s side. Norman Bassette has returned to Belgium after spending last season out of loan.WUMajor insLoum Tchaouna (Burnley, £20m), Aurèle Amenda (Eintracht Frankfurt, £15.4m), Frank Onyeka (Brentford, undisclosed fee)Crystal PalaceMaking sure Maxence Lacroix, Jean-Philippe Mateta and Adam Wharton are still at the club come kick-off is imperative. Chelsea’s interest in Lacroix and Wharton will cause the most concern, while extending Mateta’s deal beyond the end of the season will need to be addressed. The starting lineup is strong but greater depth, with another European campaign in the offing, is imperative for the club. Óscar Mingueza was a sensible signing on a free, especially after not replacing Marc Guéhi in January. Walter Benítez may leave in search of first-team football, which would leave a gap in the goalkeeping department.WUMajor insÓscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free)EvertonYoung, developing potential has been recruited so far in the form of Hayden Hackney – player of the season in the Championship with Middlesbrough in 2025-26 – Tyrique George and Merlin Röhl, the last two after loan spells with David Moyes’s side last season. But established players are still required to fill several weak spots, especially at right-back, a position that has needed strengthening for far too long now, and centre-forward. Left-back, central midfield and another wide player – the return of Jack Grealish possibly – would also be on the wishlist.Andy HunterMajor insTyrique George (Chelsea, £18m), Merlin Röhl (Freiburg, £17.3m), Hayden Hackney (Middlesbrough, £16.5m)Major outsSéamus Coleman (released)FulhamIt is a new era at Craven Cottage under Álvaro Arbeloa and there is much work to be done. The loss of Raúl Jiménez and, more important, the player of the season, Harry Wilson, means there are holes to fill. Like a year ago, it’s been a slow start to the window and things will need to speed up if they are to find a new striker, winger and a centre-back. Real Madrid’s Franco Mastantuono and Gonzalo García are under consideration, having previously worked with Arbeloa.WUMajor insJonah Kusi-Asare (Bayern Munich, £5.2m)Major outsIssa Diop (Ipswich, £8.5m), Harry Wilson (Leeds, free), Raúl Jiménez (Wolves, free)View image in fullscreenLeeds signing Harry Wilson excelled last season for Fulham.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAHullAfter avoiding an expected six-point deduction for breaching spending rules by selling the goalkeeper Ivor Pandur and the midfielder Aidon Shehu to Rangers and Panathinaikos respectively for a combined £8.5m at the end of June,the playoff winnersaim to make 10-12 new signings before September. Reinforcements are required all over the pitch, with central defence, central midfield and attack particular priorities. “Think about us like a volcano,” says Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Yet as much as the manager, Sergej Jakirovic, needs new faces he will be anxious to retain last season’s exceptionally powerful team spirit. Inspired loans and free transfer imports could prove crucial.Louise TaylorMajor insJack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m)Major outsIvor Pandur (Rangers, £6m)IpswichPromotion brings enough problems but doing so with a new manager brings added complexityas Gary O’Neilseeks to shape his squad. The aim is to be better prepared for the Premier League than last time by signing those with the physicality to compete in the top flight, preferably having done so before, hence the signing of Issa Diop. Inroads have been made but the spine of the team needs strengthening, especially in midfield and at centre-forward.WUMajor insEmersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m)Major outsArijanet Muric (Sassuolo, £6m)LeedsDaniel Farke has traditionally preferred to operate with a small, closely bonded, first-team squad but acknowledges a little expansion is required. As the defender Joe Rodon recently put it: “We want to make our squad bigger and better.” So far, though, the goalkeeping department has shrunk appreciably, with Karl Darlow and Illan Meslier having left while Lucas Perri is coveted by Torino. If new keepers currently top Farke’s shopping list – and Manchester City’s and England’s James Trafford in particular – the Southampton central midfielder Shea Charles is not far behind. Leeds seem determined to acquire the 22-year-old but the Champonship club are reluctant sellers who will demand top dollar. With Harry Wilson and Tarik Muharemovic having already arrived to reinforce attack and central defence respectively, considerable focus is on midfield where Julian Brandt, a free agent after leaving Borussia Dortmund, is also coveted.LTMajor insTarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free)Major outsPascal Struijk (Brighton, £18m), Karl Darlow (Manchester United, free)LiverpoolArne Slot wanted two new wingers and a right-back before he was sacked in May and the change of head coach has not changed Liverpool’s priorities.Victor Muñoz has been signedas a versatile forward but not as an immediate starter under Andoni Iraola, and the pursuit of top wide talent continues. Bradley Barcola and Yan Diomande are of interest, although Paris Saint-Germain may determine both their futures. Iraola is concerned at the thinness of his defensive options and, while in an ideal world he would consider Conor Bradley to be Liverpool’s first-choice right back, the Northern Irishman’s recovery from a serious knee injury is likely to force another transfer move. AH.AHMajor insJérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m)Major outsMohamed Salah (released), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)View image in fullscreenEngland midfielder Elliot Anderson has completed his move to Manchester City.Photograph: Nathan Ray Seebeck/Imagn Images/ReutersManchester CityElliot Anderson may alreadyhave joined for a British record transfer feebut City are still in the market for another midfielder, with the 18-year-old Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi being targeted for about £85m. Enzo Maresca also has Malo Gusto, one of his right-backs when he was Chelsea head coach, on the radar. A striker will be on the list, too, if Omar Marmoush leaves. And with Real Madrid retaining an interest, will Rodri sign on again? Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has a year left on his contract and his stock has rocketed. The incomings mean several players could leave, with Kalvin Phillips, Jack Grealish, Tijjani Reijnders, Nico González, Savinho and James Trafford among them.Jamie JacksonMajor insElliot Anderson (Nottingham Forest, £116m), Mathys Detourbet (Troyes, £21.6m), Jeremy Monga (Leicester, £12.5m)Major outsNathan Aké (Fenerbahce, £7m), Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free), John Stones (free agent)Manchester UnitedMichael Carrick is keen to add a third new midfielder after the arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, with Real Madrid’s Eduardo Camavinga, Bournemouth’s Alex Scott, Roma’s Manu Koné and Fulham’s Sander Berge on the list. He is also considering a move for a left-back: Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Fulham’s Antonee Robinson are being monitored. There will be outgoings too. At 28 Marcus Rashford is in his prime and available, surely for a fee in the same region as the £26m Barcelona balked at. Player and club want an exit yet at the moment he will start the new season at United. For the right deal this will change.JJMajor insAndrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m)Major outsRasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m)NewcastleMuch hinges on whether Bruno Guimarães stays or departs for Arsenal during a summer already featuring a significant changing of the St James’ Park guard. The adjustment tolife after Anthony Gordonand Sandro Tonali could be eased if Eddie Howe is able to attract a higher calibre central midfielder –Monaco’s Aladji Bamba has joined for £34m– and goalkeeper – Parma’s Zion Suzuki is one possibility. Most signings will be expected to conform to Newcastle’s new transfer policy of recruiting players aged 24 and under, with a valuation broadly between £20m and £40m. Meanwhile Nick Pope, Joe Willock and Jacob Murphy could depart. The club are operating under a three-year Uefa settlement agreement after breaching European spending rules but Howe’s overriding current priority is keeping Guimarães.LTMajor insBazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £34m)Major outsSandro Tonali (Tottenham, £92.5m), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona, £69.3m), Kieran Trippier (Wolves, free)Nottingham ForestSpending the money made from the Elliot Anderson sale is a top priority. Lucas Bergvall leads the list of replacements and the midfielder has told Tottenham his preference is to move to the City Ground but a deal needs to be agreed. If not, Monaco’s Lamine Camara could become part of the thinking. A new right-wingback and striker are also being plotted, with Sporting’s Ousmane Diomande a target in central defence. There is no requirement to sell any key players but the futures of some on the fringes are up in the air.WUMajor outsElliot Anderson (Manchester City, £116m)SunderlandRégis Le Bris says he is hoping to add “six or seven” new players this summer. Sunderland’s manager wants to ensure the squad is sufficiently robust to cope with the twin demands ofPremier Leagueand Europa League campaigns but has been bolstered by Granit Xhaka’s decision to recommit to the club amid interest in the captain from Chelsea. If recruiting holding midfield cover for Xhaka is one transfer priority, so too is providing Brian Brobbey with high-calibre attacking competition while also fortifying the right-winger and left-back positions. Le Bris is under no pressure to sell, so any attempts to acquire his increasingly influential attacking midfielder Enzo Le Fée will be strongly resisted.LTMajor insThomas Meunier (Lille, free)Major outsEliezer Mayenda (Rennes, £17.1m)TottenhamDespite acquiring a new central midfield and a new central defence, Roberto De Zerbi said Spurs are “not finished yet” in the transfer market. An upgrade on Richarlison up front should be a priority, while Marcus Rashford could be a blockbuster arrival out wide. As for outgoings, Cristian Romero and Lucas Bergvall could follow Luka Vuskovic and Will Lankshear through the door. Interest in Pedro Porro will be high after his outstanding World Cup and there is still uncertainty over Guglielmo Vicario’s future in goal.BMMajor insSandro Tonali (Newcastle, £92.5m), Mateus Fernandes (West Ham, £85m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Brighton, £52m), Andy Robertson (Liverpool, free), Marcos Senesi (Bournemouth, free), Martin Dubravka (Burnley, free)Major outsLuka Vuskovic (Brighton, £46m), Radu Dragusin (Fiorentina, loan)Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Defoe’s shock Woking exit came after ‘growing concerns’, says club | Jermain Defoe | The Guardian
description: Jermain Defoe’s departure from Woking came after ‘growing concerns’ at the club and the National League side’s football director claims the former Tottenham striker failed to turn up for training
Author: Andy Martin
Headline: Jermain Defoe’s departure from Woking came after ‘growing concerns’ at the club and the National League side’s football director claims the former Tottenham striker failed to turn up for training
Content: Jermain Defoe said it ‘impossible for me to continue’ at Woking.Photograph: Nigel French/PAView image in fullscreenJermain Defoe said it ‘impossible for me to continue’ at Woking.Photograph: Nigel French/PAJermain DefoeDefoe’s shock Woking exit came after ‘growing concerns’, says clubDirector of football claims manager failed to turn up for trainingFormer Spurs striker’s stint ended after four monthsAndy MartinSat 25 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 10.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJermain Defoe’s departure from Woking came after “growing concerns” at the club with Jody Brown, the National League side’s director of football, claiming the former Tottenham striker failed to turn up for training.Defoe’s contract at the National League club was mutually terminated on Thursday afterfour months in charge. In is first managerial job, the 43-year-old oversaw two wins and one defeat in six matches. The former England forward had said it was “impossible for me to continue” and described his time at the club as an “eye-opening” experience.But the club responded strongly on Saturday. “The recommendation to appoint Jermain as manager was mine, and I take full responsibility for it,” Brown said. “After meeting with him on several occasions, I believed he was the right person to lead the club into an exciting new era.”But he went on: “However, in recent weeks there had been feedback from across the club, including players, staff and other departments, regarding growing concerns.“To better understand the situation, I asked Jermain and Paul [Bracewell, the assistant manager] for a brief report outlining the squad’s current depth, recruitment targets and any operational challenges, so we could provide the support required and accelerate preparations for the season. That report was requested on more than one occasion but was never received.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A meeting was subsequently scheduled involving the directors, manager, assistant manager and head of operations to review preparations for the season. Neither Jermain nor his assistant attended that meeting or that day’s training session. Throughout his tenure, Jermain had never communicated any serious concerns directly to me, so I am not going to speculate on his reasons.”Defoe has not publicly responded to Woking’s claims.Explore more on these topicsJermain DefoenewsShareReuse this content

title: Missing a major football tournament? Fear not, Wafcon 2026 is about to start | Women's football | The Guardian
description: The Women’s Africa Cup of Nations starts in Morocco on Sunday, with Cape Verde and Egypt looking to continue feelgood factor from the men’s World Cup and Nigeria going for an 11th title
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Women’s Africa Cup of Nations starts in Morocco on Sunday, with Cape Verde and Egypt looking to continue feelgood factor from the men’s World Cup and Nigeria going for an 11th title
Content: (From left) Morocco’s Ghizlane Chebbak, Nigeria’s Chiamaka Nnadozie and Zambia’s Barbra Banda.Composite: Guardian Design; Xinhua/Alamy; Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen(From left) Morocco’s Ghizlane Chebbak, Nigeria’s Chiamaka Nnadozie and Zambia’s Barbra Banda.Composite: Guardian Design; Xinhua/Alamy; Fifa/Getty ImagesWomen's footballMissing a major football tournament? Fear not, Wafcon 2026 is about to startThe Women’s Africa Cup of Nations starts in Morocco on Sunday, with Cape Verde and Egypt looking to continue feelgood factor from the men’s World Cup and Nigeria going for an 11th titleFirdose MoondaSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe men’s World Cup may have finished but do not worry, the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) is ready to pick up where Spain and Argentina left off. The 34-match event will take place between 26 July and 16 August, which sandwiches it between football’s global showpiece and the start of the league season in Europe. Here’s your guide to one of the most underrated but interesting events on the sporting calendar.Why is it being played now?The tournament was scheduled to take place in three Moroccan cities – Rabat, Casablanca and Fes – between 17 March and 3 April. However, only 12 days before it was due to startit was postponedfor what the Confederation of African Football called “unforeseen circumstances”. Strangely, the conflict in the Middle East, which affected several travel routes, was never cited as one of them. Caf’s communications director, Luxolo September, said Morocco requested new dates “for a number of reasons”, none of which were disclosed.Putellas, Batlle and León are gone: what will be left of Barcelona after latest exodus?Read moreSouth Africa appeared to offer to host the tournament, before Morocco was reconfirmed and a new window was announced. A revised match list, which included only two of the three original host cities, Rabat and Casablanca, was revealed on 25 June. The draw remained the same.Several teams, including South Africa and Nigeria, expressed frustration at the late change, especially as they had already been playing warm-up matches in preparation for the tournament. Also, the change meant that, for many players, they will be out of season.What is the setup?This is the first time the tournament will be played with 16 teams – up from 12 in the past two editions – but the inclusion of the final four sides was unsatisfactory. They were added to the tournament only after the qualification process, which ran from February to October 2025, had been completed. The four sides – Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Mali and Egypt – were picked on rankings.While the Egypt midfielder Nadine Ghazi admitted that the team’s qualification was “different, if I can put it like that”, they hope to take inspiration from their men’s side, who reached the World Cup last 16 before losing to Argentina.Another team that will be looking to their male counterparts’ performances for motivation is Cape Verde, who are one of two tournament debutants. Malawi are the other first-timers.The teams are divided into four groups of four. The top two sides from each group will progress to the quarter-finals. All matches kick off at 6pm or later local time, unlike the 2025 edition, when some teams played at 3pm in extreme mid-summer heat.Who are the favourites?The competition’s most successful competitors, Nigeria,achieved “Mission X” and won their 10th Wafcon title in 2025, and it is difficult to look past them this time. They have retained the core of that squad, captained by Rasheedat Ajibade, but will be without the defender Ashleigh Plumptre because of a foot injury. The striker Asisat Oshoala and the goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie headline their squad.View image in fullscreenNigeria, who defeated Morocco in last year’s final, are aiming for a record-extending 11th Wafcon title.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesMorocco have been the runners-up in the past two editions and will be looking to go one better, especially as this could be the last in their trio of home tournaments. The 2028 Wafcon is set to be held elsewhere.Other strong candidates are the 2022 champions, South Africa, who have an experienced squad, and Zambia, who were bronze medallists in 2022 and quarter-finalists in 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho are the biggest stars?Malawi will make their first Wafcon appearance, with many eyes on sisters Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga. Tabitha, who will captain the side, plays at European powerhouse OL Lyonnes, while Temwa is at Kansas City Current, where she has been voted the NWSL’s MVP for two successive seasons. She was also the highest-ranked African player on theGuardian’s 100 best female footballers in the worldlast year in sixth place.Local fans will get behind the Morocco captain, Ghizlane Chebbak, who has won the Golden Boot at the past two Wafcons, scoring eight times across those tournaments. At 35 years old, this may be her last major tournament and she will not want to move on without a trophy.View image in fullscreenMalawi’s Tabitha Chawinga (left) and her sister Temwa will be making their Wafcon debuts.Zambia’s NWSL heavyweights Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji scored three goals each at the last tournament but could not take the team past the quarter-finals. Given their reputations the pair will be hoping to ensure Zambia can continue to enhance their reputation as serious continental challengers.Ghana were the most improved side last year, when they lost to Morocco on penalties in the semi-final. Their forward Princess Marfo, who recently signed for PSV Eindhoven, and Evelyn Badu, fresh off a hat-trick for Montreal Roses, are two to keep an eye on.What’s at stake?In short: money and major tournament qualification. Prize money at the last Wafcon increased by 45% in total, with each team earning at least $125,000 (£94,000) and the winners, Nigeria, pocketing $1m. This time there is something else at stake too: the four semi-finalists will qualify for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil, while the four losing quarter-finalists will play off to decide which two teams advance to the inter-confederation deciders.Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballNigeria women's football teamMorocco women's football teamZambia women's football teamSouth Africa women's football teamCameroon women's football teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Joshua gets up from two knockdowns to stop Kristian Prenga – as it happened | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Anthony Joshua recovered from two-first round knockdowns to stop Kristian Prenga in the second round of a wild heavyweight contest
Author: Alex Reid
Headline: Anthony Joshua recovered from two-first round knockdowns to stop Kristian Prenga in the second round of a wild heavyweight contest
Content: 2h ago19.38 EDTFight reportDonald McRaeAnthony Joshua cleared his final hurdle in the ring, before he fights Tyson Fury in November, after he was knocked down twice, shockingly, in the first round of his wild and chaotic bout with Kristian Prenga in the early hours of Sunday morning in Jeddah.
