title: Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronze | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty has hit out at his critics after he was beaten into third place in the Commonwealth Games 100m breaststroke
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty has hit out at his critics after he was beaten into third place in the Commonwealth Games 100m breaststroke
Content: England's Adam Ramsay-Peaty on his way to finishing third in the men's 100m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEngland's Adam Ramsay-Peaty on his way to finishing third in the men's 100m breaststroke final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Tearful Ramsay-Peaty tells critics ‘you can’t hurt me’ after shock Commonwealth bronzeRamsay-Peaty finishes third in 100m breaststroke‘People who comment … you don’t know who I am’Sean Ingleat Tollcross International Swimming CentreSat 25 Jul 2026 18.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 20.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdam Ramsay-Peaty has never been someone to mask his feelings. But defeat has never sounded as emotional or as raw as this. There were tears. Frustrations. Questions about why he kept putting himself through the 5.30am starts at the age of 31.And then came the crescendo in the form of a blistering attack on his critics on social media and the media. “You can’t hurt me,” he said, before telling them to “do better”. It was dramatic. It was powerful. And it was certainly heartfelt.This wasn’t the piece we came to the TollcrossSwimmingCentre to write. But then came a performance that no one – Ramsay-Peaty included – expected. He had believed he was in shape for gold after working hard in a heavy training block. Instead, at his best event, the 100m breaststroke, he had to settle for a bronze medal behind the Australian Sam Williamson and Jersey’s 18-year-old wunderkind Filip Nowicki.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead more“I’m not crying because it’s a bronze instead of a gold,” Ramsay-Peaty insisted. “I’m crying because I know that the swim could have been better, and I know I worked way better than that. Something isn’t hitting right. Whether it’s the pace, whether it’s the focus, I’m not sure. I feel like I couldn’t have really put more in.“And that’s where it hurts. I’m like: ‘What’s the point of all the 5.30am starts? What’s the point of being exhausted all the time? What’s the point of having to say no to family events because you’re training?’”Initially it seemed to be business as usual. Ramsay-Peaty arrived blowing kisses to the crowd. He then kept his rivals waiting as he took his pool coat off. Up to now this was classic Ramsay-Peaty. But when he launched into the pool, everything was off.At his best, the greatest breaststroke sprinter in history is able to power out of the blocks, establish a supreme dominance before the turn, and easily hold off any fast finishers. But he was in a fight from the start, and was only third at halfway.He scraped to the end, like all good fighters. But he was unable to catch Williamson, who won in 59.37sec, or Nowicki, who glided into second 0.17 back. Ramsay-Peaty’s finishing time of 59.65 was nearly three seconds off his world record.View image in fullscreenSam Williamson celebrates on the podium after winning the men’s 100m breaststroke final with Jersey’s Filip Nowicki and England’s Adam Ramsay-Peaty.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersAfter he collected his medal he kissed his wife, Holly, whose baby is due in December, on the belly. That recollection at least brought a smile. “She’s always going to be proud of me,” he said. “And as a father, it doesn’t matter if you come home with gold. As long as you come home with a teddy. That’s really what matters.“But I’m never going to be afraid to show weakness, because it’s so important for making stronger people, making stronger men, stronger fathers, husbands. And it’s a realisation of how much I do work. This cycle especially, I’m like: ‘Shit, how have I worked this hard at this age?’ And then you get a result like that, I’m like: ‘I’m better than that.’“And I can’t really put in where it went wrong. Maybe it’s just an off swim. Or maybe it is just because I’ve been two years out of the championships and heat semi-finals. But it does hurt.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThen came an attack on the media and snipers on social media, who have devoured every detail about the estrangement from one side of his family. Peaty said he had tried hard to focus hard on his job “without getting baited … and ignoring most of the rubbish you see online about me”, but then he addressed those who had attacked him directly.“You don’t know who I am,” he said. “And people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror. You can’t hurt me.“That hasn’t played a part in the sense of what I’ve experienced today, because I’m still happy with that result in some sense, but it has to stop. How many athletes, how many people, have to go through this until the media learn their lesson? You have to learn and do better.“I feel like I deserve more, to be honest. I know the shit I’ve been through. Which is no fault of my own, to be honest. But it does take a toll, you know?”Peaty still has another chance for a gold medal at these Commonwealths as he competes in the heats of the 50m on Sunday, with the final on Monday. But afterwards he suggested that maybe that 100m might no longer be on his longterm radar when it comes to the LA Olympics.“It’s too early to tell what I’m capable of at this age now,” he said. “But I’m a fighter. We’ve got two weeks until Europeans or just under, so we’ve got another opportunity to do it again. And yeah, I do enjoy a scrap, but I lost a scrap this time, and that is sport. But I feel like I deserve more, to be honest.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAdam Ramsay-PeatySwimmingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Abi Martin snatches Commonwealth bronze for England in gymnastics team final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: England edged out Wales by 0.900 in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final, won by Australia, while Gabriel Langton is out of hospital after his fall
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: England edged out Wales by 0.900 in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final, won by Australia, while Gabriel Langton is out of hospital after his fall
Content: England's Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Shanna-Kae Grant, Alia Leat, Abi Martin and Ruby Stacey are all smiles after winning a bronze medal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenEngland's Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Shanna-Kae Grant, Alia Leat, Abi Martin and Ruby Stacey are all smiles after winning a bronze medal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Abi Martin snatches Commonwealth bronze for England in gymnastics team finalEngland pip Wales to secure medal by just 0.900ptsGabriel Langton discharged from hospital after fallYara El-Shabouryat Glasgow International ArenaSat 25 Jul 2026 16.58 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland held their nerve to claim bronze in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final after a tense final rotation enabled them to edge Wales by less than a point in Glasgow. The defending champions finished with 154.300 points, just enough to snatch third place from Wales, while Australia delivered a dominant display to win gold ahead of Canada.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two in picturesRead moreAustralia set the tone from the opening rotation, with Kate McDonald posting the highest uneven bars score of the day at 14.200 as the silver medallists from Birmingham 2022 established an early lead they would never relinquish. England made a solid start on vault through Shantae-Eve Amankwaah, Ruby Stacey, Alia Leat and Abi Martin. However, the uneven bars proved costly. Amankwaah’s excellent 13.500 boosted England’s challenge, but Stacey fell during her routine and her score did not count, leaving England trailing Australia at the halfway stage.Heading into the final floor rotation, England trailed Canada by just 0.350 points in the battle for silver but also faced the threat of Wales, who watched on after they had set an impressive total earlier in the day.Amankwaah opened with a stylish routine before a music delay briefly interrupted Shanna-Kae Grant’sCommonwealth Gamesdebut, though that failed to unsettle her as she produced a superb routine, highlighted by a huge double Arabian, to keep England in medal contention. Leat’s 12.150 left England needing at least 12.350 from the final routine to overhaul Wales. Martin delivered under pressure, scoring 13.250 to spark celebrations as England secured bronze by just 0.900 points.Australia finished five points clear of Wales’ earlier total to reclaim Commonwealth gold, while Canada’s strong final vault rotation, led by Ellie Black’s impressive 13.950, secured silver. Wales were left agonisingly short of a first team medal since Glasgow 2014.Meanwhile, England’s Gabriel Langton has been discharged from hospital after scans determined no lasting damagefrom his fall during the men’s team finalon Friday. The 19-year-old landed head first off the high bar in the final apparatus. The competition was held up for 20 minutes as he was carried away from the arena on a stretcher.View image in fullscreenAbi Martin performs her floor routine which secured the bronze medal for England in the women’s artistic gymnastics team final.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA“Gabriel was transferred to the hospital as a precautionary measure overnight and underwent multiple scans today, with very positive results,” Team England said in a statement. “Thankfully, he has been cleared of any serious injury complications and will be discharged to return to the team hotel this evening.“He is in good spirits and hugely grateful for the many messages of support and the excellent care provided by the medical teams. He is looking forward to being reunited with the team to celebrate his silver medal.”Earlier in the day, before the medals were decided, one of the loudest cheers inside the Glasgow International Arena was reserved for a gymnast who would compete for less than two minutes. Two years ago, Tiana Sumanasekera was a United States Olympic alternate, training at the famed World Champions Centre in Houston alongside Simone Biles and Jordan Chiles. Now she is representing Sri Lanka – the country of her parents’ birth – with the aim of making the finals at Los Angeles in 2028.Sri Lanka achieved a milestone at the Tokyo Olympics when Milka Gehani became their first gymnast to compete at the Games. Sumanasekera’s arrival represents another significant step forward with the 18-year-old boasting the talent to challenge for world championship and Olympic finals on balance beam and floor exercise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCommonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead moreSumanasekera is a multiple Pan American Games medallist who finished third on balance beam at the 2024 US Olympic Trials; she has long been regarded as one of the sport’s most promising gymnasts.“I started competing at the elite level when I was 13 years old when I was with Team USA,” she said. “I had been with them for about five years and in 2024 I became an Olympic alternate. It really shifted my perspective on my capabilities.“From when I was a little girl, I’ve always wanted to compete at the Olympics, so I thought the best decision was to represent my parents’ home country of Sri Lanka. I’m so proud and honoured to be here and doing so.”But the Commonwealth Games arrived at the wrong time. A shoulder injury forced her to abandon plans to compete in the all-around event. Instead, she entered women’s qualification on one apparatus – balance beam – hoping to make the final despite limited preparation.View image in fullscreenTiana Sumanasekera’s originality has made her a fan favourite.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianHer routine opened with a back dive to chest stand mount, displaying the originality that has made her a fan favourite, but her trademark back handspring layout series came up just short. She lost her balance, the one-point fall deduction ending her hopes.Rather than unravel, Sumanasekera reeled off a beautifully connected front aerial into a split jump before finishing with perhaps the best moment of the routine – a stuck layout full-twisting dismount that drew applause from the crowd.It was not enough to secure a place in the final, but Sumanasekera hopes she can build on this before LA 2028. “It was absolutely amazing being out here representing Sri Lanka on one of the biggest stages in the world. I was so grateful to compete.“It didn’t go my way, but things happen. You live and you learn and you move on, so I’m excited for what’s to come next.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesGymnasticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Madeleine McCann’s younger brother Sean finishes eighth in Commonwealth Games final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The parents of Madeleine McCann cheered on as their son, Sean, finished eighth in the 400m freestyle final on his Commonwealth Games debut for Scotland
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The parents of Madeleine McCann cheered on as their son, Sean, finished eighth in the 400m freestyle final on his Commonwealth Games debut for Scotland
Content: Sean McCann finished in eighth place in the 400m freestyle final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSean McCann finished in eighth place in the 400m freestyle final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Madeleine McCann’s younger brother Sean finishes eighth in Commonwealth Games final400m freestyle swimmer cheered on in Games debut‘I was certainly nervous with so many people watching’Sean Ingleat Tollcross International Swimming CentreSat 25 Jul 2026 14.35 EDTFirst published on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe parents of Madeleine McCann cheered with pride as their son Sean finished eighth in the final of the men’s 400m freestyle on hisCommonwealth Gamesdebut for Scotland.The 21-year-old, who studies at Loughborough University, was given a huge roar when he was announced to the crowd. But he was unable to match the pace set by Australia’s Sam Short, the 2023 world champion, who took gold in 3 mins 41.25 as he finished 12 seconds back.Commonwealth Games 2026: day two updates – liveRead moreBut for McCann, reaching the final at all was a major achievement, especially as he was up against multiple Olympic and world medallists.“I’m buzzing,” said McCann, speaking after he qualified by finishing fourth in his morning heat. “It wasn’t really an expectation coming in, especially with how strong the field was, but I’m delighted to see I made it.“I wouldn’t say I felt the pressure but I was certainly nervous with so many people watching and I wanted to do well, not only for myself but Team Scotland as well. I was definitely nervous but I’m glad I produced a decent swim.“It was amazing, I could hear them the whole way through the race. They spurred me on to really give it my all down that last 100m.”McCann grew up in England, but qualifies for Scotland through his father, Gerry, who was at the Tollcross Swimming Centre, as was his mother, Kate, to support their son. He and his twin sister, Amelie, were two years old whenMadeleine, then aged three, went missingduring a family holiday in Praia Da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.View image in fullscreenKate and Gerry McCann (centre row), parents of Scotland’s Sean McCann, watch as he competes in the men’s 400m freestyle heats.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesMcCann started swimming seriously at Charnwood Triathlon Club when he was eight, and by the age of 10 had joined the high performance City of Leicester club. He has been part of the Scottish swimming programme since his teens.Asked about his motivation for wanting to swim, he said: “From a young age I really enjoyed competing. That makes all the hard hours in training worth it, coming out here in front of a crowd like this and swimming as well as I can really.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcCann is studying chemical engineering at Loughborough, where he is coached by Andi Manley, who is leading the England team in Glasgow. He will also compete in the 800m and 1500m freestyle and hopes it will be a launchpad to becoming an Olympian at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.“The Olympics is always that step even further so to be able to represent Scotland here is a good stepping stone,” he said. “Hopefully a couple of years of work will put my name in the mix.”Two other Australians completed the podium, with Elijah Winnington winning silver in 3:45.56, a hundredth of a second ahead of Benjamin Goedemans.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesSwimmingMadeleine McCannnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT | Family | The Guardian
description: Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
Author: Jenny Kleeman
Headline: Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?
Content: Video: Courtesy of Nicci Dhamu / Guardian DesignFamily‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPTAvtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. How did a chatbot bring them together?Jenny KleemanSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 10.45 EDTShareAs a small boy growing up in Amritsar, India, in the 1960s, Avtar Singh used to hear whispers.Your mum isn’t really your mum, the rumours would say.Your mum lives abroad.Avtar didn’t really pay any attention to it. “I thought, the neighbours are just making up stories.” But the stories were true: the woman raising Avtar was actually his grandmother. When he was too young to remember it, his father had emigrated to Canada to work as a teacher, leaving Avtar in the care of his paternal grandparents. His grandfather, a police officer, was a fearsome authoritarian, but his grandmother brought him up with tenderness, as if he were her own son. She called him by his nickname, Titu. He felt loved.When Avtar was around eight years old, he was told about his family in Canada: his dad, his mum and a little brother were waiting for him there, and he would soon travel to join them. Just after his ninth birthday, Avtar found himself sitting on a plane, dressed in a three‑piece suit and tie. He was travelling alone. He had never flown before. He didn’t speak a word of English. He landed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Christmas Eve, 1968; his family met him at the airport and took him home. “I didn’t know what to think,” Avtar, now 66, tells me in a video call from his home in Abbotsford, British Columbia. “Before I knew it, it was the first week of January, and I was put in school.”View image in fullscreenAvtar with his grandmother in the mid-60s in Amritsar, India (above), and (below) aged 10, in 1969, the year after he moved to Canada. Courtesy of Avtar SinghUnable to communicate with any of the other pupils, Avtar watched what they did and followed along, storing his snow boots in the cloakroom, standing up to sing the Canadian national anthem and God Save the Queen. But with his long hair tied in the topknot often worn by Sikh boys, he stood out. His parents offered to buy him a hockey stick and a pair of ice skates if he agreed to get his hair cut. He learned English. His nickname changed from Titu to the more Canadian “Tito”. He began to blend in.But Avtar didn’t fit in at home. He was much paler than everyone else – “the white sheep of the family,” he jokes. And they treated him like an outsider, an afterthought. When he was 14, his family went on holiday without him, leaving Avtar home alone for two weeks. He got on well enough with his father, but didn’t gel at all with his mother. “She didn’t have any of the warmth that my grandma had. She absolutely hated me.” She seemed much more like a stepmother than a mother.That feeling was confirmed when Avtar got married and his grandparents flew over to stay with him and his new wife, Rosey. His grandma “whispered into my wife’s ear” that Avtar was the product of his father’s first marriage. “She didn’t say what my mother’s name was. She just said, ‘Her family was from Africa, and she left the child with us and went back to Africa. She might have gone to live in the UK.’ That’s it.” It didn’t feel right to ask his grandparents for more information: this was clearly a family secret that no one wanted to discuss with Avtar.double quotation markThe thought of my mother didn’t leave my mind, everView image in fullscreenWhen his son was set a school assignment to complete his family tree, Avtar felt emboldened to approach his father. “I said, ‘Dad, you’ve got to tell me at least what my mother’s name was.’” His dad eventually relented: her first name was Savinder. But he would not give Avtar any more information, no matter how many times he asked. “I was stonewalled.” Avtar had no idea why his parents had split up. “All I really understood was that my mother’s family encouraged her to give up custody of me so it would be easier for them to remarry her.”He thought about his mother constantly. When Rosey was pregnant with their daughter, there were anomalies in some of the antenatal tests, and Rosey and Avtar were referred to a geneticist. Avtar was asked about his parents’ medical history. “I couldn’t tell them anything about my mother’s family history. It hit me right in the heart. That’s when I thought, I’ve got to do something.”He Googled and Facebooked, but there was almost nothing to go on; Savinder is a fairly common Punjabi Sikh name. In 2009, Avtar flew to London to visit the National Archives at Kew with the hope of finding immigration or marriage records that might lead him to his mother. “I couldn’t find anything at all.” On a later visit to London, he emailed Sunrise Radio, a British Asian station, asking if they could put out an appeal to find his mother, but they told Avtar they don’t do that kind of thing, out of respect for people’s privacy. That gave Avtar pause. “I thought, maybe I should just cool off. If my mother has some other family, I don’t want to disrupt her life.” Still, it niggled. Three or four years ago, he asked a British south Asian work colleague for advice; she suggested contacting the ITV show Long LostFamily. He watched a few episodes and decided it wasn’t for him. But he longed to know his mother. “The thought of her did not leave my mind, ever.”The one thing Avtar did not do was a DNA test. He is retired now, but he used to be a chartered accountant, and he knows enough about technology, data and privacy to be wary of giving up his genetic code to a corporation. “They can sell it. Not only that – if they see something in my DNA, that affects my kids. I don’t want that information up there.” He deactivated his Facebook account 12 years ago for similar reasons. “I don’t have faith that these companies have the proper safeguards.”double quotation markShe used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘my child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for herThen, on 8 May this year, Avtar and Rosey were on holiday in the south of France. Avtar had been battling cancer; their long-awaited trip to Europe came after he had finished his treatment. “It was early morning, and I had read all the news. I was bored. I had nothing else to do. I thought, I’ve tried Google and everything else, why don’t I give AI a shot?”View image in fullscreenSavinder Kaur in 1963. Courtesy of Nicci DhamuHe typed a prompt intoChatGPT, based on the little he knew, and what else he could infer. He assumed that his mother would be around the same age as his father (who died 10 years ago); he knew that Sikh women of her generation were generally given the middle name Kaur.AvtarCan you find any information about a Savinder Kaur?AvtarShe would be between 87 and 97 years old and would have lived in India and Africa and possibly in the UKChatGPTThe strongest match, based upon your clues, is this …ChatGPTSavinder Kaur Nagi, born in 1936 in Kisumu, Kenya, to Indian Sikh parents.ChatGPTThe article mentions family roots near Jammu and Kashmir in India and later migration connections to the UK.“I know that AI can just make up shit. So I thought, OK, that’snicesays Avtar. “But it actually referenced an article. I thought, I’ll look at that, at least. Just to see.”“I wrote it out of grief,” Nicci Dhamu tells me, in a cafe in west London. “Mummy never really had a voice, and that article was all about giving her one. I wanted to create a digital legacy for my mum.”Nicci is the jewellery designer behind the brand Sohavi. “Sohavi means beautiful in Gurmukhī, the Sikh script. I learned about making things beautiful from Mum.”Her article, published on both the Sohavi blog and the South Asian Heritage Month website, was a celebration of her mother’s creativity. “She suffered loss, and decisions were made for her when she young and wasn’t able to assert her own voice, like many south Asian women of her generation. But she lives on through me and the profound influences she had on me throughout my life,” Nicci wrote.Savinder Kaur Nagi died in her sleep in December 2024, aged 88. For the last five years of her life, she had dementia. Nicci, 58, had been her carer; they lived together and were very close. Nicci’s family moved to the UK from Kenya in 1973. She has an older sister and a younger brother, as well as three half-sisters from her dad’s first marriage; he was widowed before he met Savinder. “We grew up as one family. I didn’t know until I was about 10 or 11 years old that my sisters were my half‑sisters, and that was only because one of my sisters told me.” Theirs was a family that did not speak about the past.View image in fullscreenSavinder with Nicci Dhamu’s father, c1963. Courtesy of Nicci Dhamu“I remember once, Mum was in the kitchen making roti, and I asked her, ‘Mummy, you were, like, 25 years old when you got married to Dad. Wasn’t that a little old for somebody of your generation?’ I knew that something was different about our family, but I didn’t have the vocabulary to label it. My father never spoke to us about his wife who had died, and my mum never spoke about her life before him.”When Nicci was in her 40s, an older cousin casually revealed that Savinder had been married to another man before she met Nicci’s dad. “She was married off, very young. And it probably wasn’t what she wanted,” Nicci tells me. “My grandfather took her and her sisters out of school in Kenya and took them back to Punjab to a place called Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar.” Later in life, her mother would openly lament leaving school – she could read and write English, and loved studying – but never explained why she had been forced to give up her education. She did not discuss her first marriage. She never told her children they had an older half-brother.“My cousin told me in that conversation that she had a son.” Nicci’s eyes are bright at the memory. But she never felt able to ask her mother about him. “I couldn’t. There was intrinsic pain there.”There were times, Nicci says, when her mother would sink into a depression. “She would sit quietly, or take to bed because she was upset.” Nicci would bring Savinder her dinner, and encourage her to sit up and eat. “Towards the end of Mum’s life, she used to cry, ‘Mera bacha’ [‘My child’, in Punjabi]. The dementia was bringing up all these memories for her.”It was then – a couple of years before her mum’s death – that Nicci resolved to find the child her mother was crying for. But she did not know his name, and her mother was unwell so Nicci couldn’t ask her. Instead, she turned to her wider family.She began with her mother’s young brother, who lives in Birmingham. “He knew my mum’s child as a two- or three-year-old,” Nicci says. She picked his brains, and also her cousins’. She learned that her mother’s first husband was called Mohan Singh, a very educated man who taught at the Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school in Amritsar. Mohan’s father had been a police officer, and “quite a difficult man”. Savinder had told her father that her husband wasn’t treating her well. “I think my grandad thought, this is not a good place for my daughter to be. He went around and took his daughter back to his home, and she must have picked up her little boy, too.”Her mother raised the boy until he was three years old, Nicci was told. “As someone who is also divorced, I often reflect on the stigma my mother may have faced as a south Asian woman of her generation,” she tells me. “I think there was a lot of pressure from the family:let’s get her married. Somebody as young as her was going to have a very difficult life as a single mother. She was too young to be on her own. Her son’s family wanted him back. So they must have taken the child from her.”View image in fullscreenNicci Dhamu with Savinder in 2018. Courtesy of Nicci DhamuSavinder returned to Kenya, alone. At first, she stayed with her eldest brother. Nicci’s cousins have vivid memories of her time in their home. “She would take his baby clothes out and cry. She never forgot him.” She was soon introduced to Nicci’s father, a man 16 years her senior. “I think she carried that trauma throughout her life, but did a very good job of holding her head up high, making her life work, raising three more children.” Family in Kenya heard “through the grapevine” that Savinder’s first husband had moved to Canada, but they couldn’t tell Nicci when. And no one knew the name of Savinder’s little boy. They only knew his nickname: Titu.“No one’s going to call themselves Titu on LinkedIn, are they?” says Nicci with a deep laugh. That didn’t stop her trying to find him online, and his father and grandfather, too, Googling the names of teachers and police officers in Amritsar. “I didn’t capture anything. How do you find somebody without a name? It’s impossible.”Three or four months before her mother died, she submitted Savinder’s DNA to Ancestry.com. “I set up a profile for her, saying, ‘Profile managed by daughter, looking for her son, name is Titu, possibly living in Canada.’” She got some interesting titbits back about her mother’s ancestral roots in Kashmir, Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, which would explain her light complexion, but no useful matches.A month after her mother died, Nicci contacted friends who knew people who had worked for the magistrates court in Amritsar, in the hope of finding records of the divorce. “If there were divorce papers, there would be names – and maybe achild’sname.” But she was told that would be virtually impossible; a needle in a haystack.In April 2025, Nicci’s family took Savinder’s ashes to India. During her stay in Amritsar, Nicci hired a driver to take her to Sri Guru Ramdas Khalsa school, where Titu’s father had been a teacher. She spoke to the teachers and the security guard, but it was long after Mohan Singh’s time there, so no one knew of him or his son. All she wanted was a name for her half-brother, but no one could tell her. It felt hopeless.“I remember sitting there thinking, why doesn’t he just knock on the door? I knew that his father was an educated man – I was pretty sure that he must be educated, too. Why isn’t he looking for Mum?”Avtar blinked at the article ChatGPT had presented to him. Rosey was just waking up. He made her a coffee and showed her what he’d found, but she wasn’t convinced. After all, the article didn’t mention Savinder’s first marriage, divorce or long-lost son. “Rosey didn’t want me to be disappointed – she knows how hard I had looked for my mother.”Then he looked at the article again, and a picture stopped him in his tracks: not one of the many photos Nicci had posted of her mother – there was no flicker of instant recognition when he saw Savinder’s face – but an image of a certificate her mother had earned for dressmaking at a college in Dhariwal, just outside Amritsar, in 1962. (“She wassoproud of it,” Nicci beams. “She would talk about it quite often: ‘I went to college, I earned a certificate.’ I think that was her quiet victory.”)“This is two or three years after I was born, and it is in the exact city where I was born.” Avtar exhales deeply, as if he still can’t believe what he saw. He had to find out more. “This is the closest I’ve ever come. It would be a shame to just stop here.”At 8.36am that morning, he sent Nicci an email, thanking her for writing the tribute to her mother.AvtarWhat especially resonated with me was the part of her life connected to India. Reading about her journey raised many personal questions and reflections for me, and I found myself feeling there may be some distant family or community connections between us.AvtarI want to assure you that I am not reaching out for any business, financial, or other formal reason, only in the spirit of a friendly conversation.Nicci had spent the previous night praying at the gurdwara and watching Long Lost Familyon TV. Avtar’s email had arrived on the morning of what would have been her mother’s 90th birthday. “It waswild!” Nicci exclaims. “I just had a real sense of knowing. I can’t explain it. This is my mum’s son. It’sgotto be.”She agonised over how to reply, eventually adopting a similarly friendly but respectful tone.NicciI am equally intrigued to know if there might be a family connection. I would be happy to have a conversation with you.Her phone number was in her email signature. Avtar sent her a message on WhatsApp as soon as he saw it, asking when they could speak. Nicci scrutinised his WhatsApp profile picture. “He had a very distinctive nose. Everybody in my mother’s family has this prominent, distinguished nose.” She messaged back – she was free to talk there and then.It was barely two hours since Avtar had typed his prompt into ChatGPT. He was driving with Rosey to get some croissants for breakfast. He parked up, clicked on Nicci’s number and called her. There wasn’t much of a preamble. Avtar was too eager to have his questions finally answered.AvtarGood morning! This is Avtar SinghNicciHello AvtarAvtarHiNicciSo you live in CanadaAvtarWhen Is a good time to talkNicciI’m London based. As you probably know.NicciI’m free to talk nowAvtar 📞Voice call“Can you tell me a bit about your mother’s time in India?” he asked.“Mummy was married and divorced in India,” Nicci replied.“Did she have any children?”“Yes,” Nicci said. “She had a son.”Both Avtar and Rosey burst into tears.“Titu, is that you?” asked Nicci. “Are you Titu, my mother’s son?”“Yes,” Avtar replied. “That’s who I am. But I haven’t heard anyone pronounce my nickname that way since my grandma called me that, when I was a little boy.”“At that moment, time just froze,” Avtar remembers. “But I quickly recovered. I said, ‘You’re mysister. Holy shit – are there more of you out there?’ It had never occurred to me that my mother would have a family, and that I could actually meet them. That family, they knew aboutme– everybody knew about me, they just wouldn’t talk about it – but I had no knowledge aboutthemwhatsoever.”They spoke for two hours in that first phone call, until Avtar’s battery started to die. Nicci had assumed he must be in Canada; she couldn’t believe he was in France, so close by. “Why don’t you fly over?” she asked. Avtar’s head was spinning. They agreed to speak again later that evening, in a video call.AvtarThis was a dream of a lifetime!Nicci then gave Avtar a tour of the family photos displayed in the living room she used to share with their mother. “I was just sharing everything I could with him. And sobbing. And remembering Mum. All that grief about her yearning to see him again, and not meeting him. It’s like the universe just flung something at me – although I’ve lost my mum, I’ve gained a brother.”When Avtar told his son the news, he urged him to go to London and meet his newfound family. By the time he reached his daughter, she already knew: she had been using Avtar’s ChatGPT account and had seen his search history. “She said to me, ‘Dad, if you do not go see her now, you’re going to come back home and that’s all you’re going to think about. So go now.’”Within days, Avtar and Rosey were in London. Nicci shows me a picture of the first time they met, at a hotel near Heathrow. Their faces are flushed with joy. “I could see the raw emotion in her – she had been looking for me for so long,” Avtar says. “When I met her and hugged her tight, I thought, yes, this is my sister.” They went out for dinner and compared stories and timelines, piecing together the fragments that their families had given them.double quotation markEvery time I see Avtar, I just want to cry. That’s my brother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our livesView image in fullscreenNicci Dhamu.Photograph: Cian Oba Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAvtar Singh.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The GuardianThe following morning, Nicci took Avtar and Rosey to Birmingham, to meet their mother’s last-surviving sibling – their uncle – who had once shared a home with baby Titu. “He looked at me and said, ‘I remember you. I held you in my arms,’” Avtar tells me, his eyes awash with tears. “It was a great, great visit.”The next day, Avtar was introduced to his half‑brother – Nicci’s youngest sibling. He had been shocked when Nicci first told him she had found Avtar. “He said, ‘ButI’mMummy’s son,’” Nicci tells me, laughing. “I said, ‘Of course you are. Nothing’s going to change our family.’ When they finally met, Nicci says her younger brother shook Avtar’s hand. “I just knew it was going to be all right. My brother said, ‘I’ve always wanted a big brother.’”Avtar and Nicci both tell me they have no plans to confirm their relationship with a DNA test. There’s no need, they say.“I justknow,” Nicci tells me.“This world has a few billion people in it. And if somebody can randomly call me Titu … ” Avtar shakes his head. “I don’t think I need any more verification than that.”The joy at finally finding Titu is bittersweet for Nicci, because it came too late for her mother. “My biggest regret is that I didn’t talk to her about her son and let her cry about him, let her have a release,” she tells me. “It wasn’t her fault. It wasn’t anything that she did wrong. It just was a marriage that broke down.”“I grew up believing that she gave me up because it was the best thing to help her move on with her life. I was OK with that. I thought, I hope that she had a good life. I’m not the type of person to grieve or feel bad that I got abandoned or anything like that,” Avtar says. “Now I’ve heard from Nicci and other people in the family that my mum used to cry for me.That’s all I need to hear. It just feels so good to know that I was loved.”Plus, Avtar adds, there is “the treasure my mother left behind for me – I have all this family to get to know”. Word about Avtar is slowly spreading across the globe. He’s in a WhatsApp group for his maternal family, including cousins based in Kenya; they have seen each other on FaceTime. There’s discussion of a trip to Kenya so Avtar can meet them in the flesh, and see where Savinder once lived.double quotation markTechnology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be. There is a human touch to AI – look what happenedView image in fullscreenAvtar with Nicci in May during his first visit to the London home she shared with their mother.Photograph: courtesy of Avtar Singh“My cousins are so excited to meet him. He looks like them – same smiles, bald and bearded,” Nicci says with another throaty laugh. She whips out her phone to show me an AI-generated image Avtar has made of himself arm in arm with two cousins he’s yet to meet in person. Technology is bringing Savinder’s family together in ways she could never have envisaged, or even imagined.“We had a video call last night,” Nicci says. “Every time I see him, I look at him and I just want to cry. That’s mybrother. It’s so natural to want to have him in our lives.” She pauses. “Who would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.”Her half-brother sees things differently. “Right now, AI is still a glorified search engine. It is a piece of software that recognises a pattern in a string of characters, and it can look at millions of responses that match that character set and give you the highest probability best answer. What did it do? It looked at a couple of character strings that I typed in and found the best match. There’s no intelligence there.”Avtar remains as sceptical as ever about giving big tech his data, even though it was ChatGPT’s readiness to scrape blogs and give out personal information that led him to his maternal family. Had Avtar chosen to ask another AI, he might not have found Nicci at all. When he came back to Canada, he put the same prompt into Anthropic’s Claude, to see what it would say, just for fun. “It replied, ‘We don’t want to infringe on anybody’s privacy, so we don’t give out that information,” Avtar tells me. Then he shrugs. “I think that’s a good response.”

title: The AI jobs apocalypse probably isn’t coming anytime soon | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Artificial intelligence may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay
Content: ‘Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs.’Photograph: DragonImages/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs.’Photograph: DragonImages/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)The AI jobs apocalypse probably isn’t coming anytime soonEduardo PorterArtificial intelligence  may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to paySupported byAbout this contentSat 25 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 09.01 EDTShareIn March, Anthropic, the cutting-edge artificial intelligence business that gave us the chatbot Claude,published an analysison the impact of AI on employment, to help us assess the claim that intelligent robots were about to redefine human existence, ending demand for human labor.Last year in May, Anthropic’s co-founder, Dario Amodei, claimed AI could wipe out half of all entry-level jobs in one to five years. Last January,he told usAI would probably become a “general labor substitute for humans”. In Junehe saidwe risk “a world where the economic trade-off dial is stuck on the hypergrowth, hyper-inequality setting”.And yet, Anthropic’s report suggests that, so far, AI’s impact has fallen short of expectations: “We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022,” the report stated. Deployment of the technology “remains a fraction of what’s feasible”. Claude covers just 33% of all tasks in the computer and math category whereas theoretically it could take over nearly 100% of them.Forget the AI job apocalypse. AI’s real threat is worker control and surveillanceRead moreSpending on datacenters is going through the roof, for sure, butproductivityhas not been experiencing the galloping gains that the technorati’s epochal prognostications lead one to expect. Labor productivity was, in fact, slower in the first three years of our AI era than during the information technology boom that began in the mid 1990s.Even OpenAI’s Sam Altman, AI’s most public face, says he now doubts its job-killing potential. “I don’t think we’re going to have the kind ​of jobs apocalypse that some of the companies in our space advocate or talk about,”he said in May. As Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist David Autor noted: “A lot of people have noticed that the world is not changing as fast as they predicted.”This has opened the public conversation to a less cataclysmic narrative of the evolution of the technology. The emerging new story not only puts more emphasis on the complexity of the relationship between automation and human work across history. It is also raising doubts about the very feasibility of the threatened AI transformation of the universe. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index, which had been propelled almost exclusively by the rise of AI-related stocks, has fallen about 8% since its peak in early June.One strand of critique of the “AI-will-do-everything” story might be calledthe O-ring argument. It comes from the mid-flight explosion of the space shuttle Challenger 73 seconds into its flight on 28 January 1986. A lengthy investigation concluded that the demise of the multibillion dollar spaceship was causedby a rubber O-ringthat didn’t work at low temperatures.That cheap O-ring proved critical. The analogy suggests that as long as AI cannot perform every task perfectly, it will increase the value of the remaining tasks. Depending on whichthe AI takes over, it could increase the value of high skill workers who are relieved by AI of the low-end part of their job, or increase the opportunity of lower skilled workers by taking over the more expert tasks.Asone recent studynoted: “despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.”Things could change. As Jed Kolkopoints out, research on the labor market impact of artificial intelligence is still in its infancy. There are almost four years to go in Amodei’s one-to-five year window. And maybe devastation hits in year six. According to the Federal Reserve, adoption of AI isexpanding fastacross businesses.Moreover, Autor argues, AI is getting better. And its progress shows no sign that it will soon hit a ceiling. “Skepticism about thestochastic parrotis behind us,” he told me. The dystopian AI future – utopian, if you get to own and run the AI – is still on the cards.“Insiders are as gung ho as ever,” noted Daron Acemoglu, the Nobel prize-winning economist. “They still believe artificial general intelligence is around the corner.” Indeed, Elon Musk has not budged fromthe dream that“AI+Robots will be able to do everything, resulting in universal high income. Work will be optional.”One may recall the quip by Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Solow in the early years of the computer revolution: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in theproductivity statistics.” It took another 10 years or so, as businesses reorganized around the new technology. But computers did eventually show up in the stats.Clouds are nonetheless gathering on the AI horizon. It’s not just that AI may not end all human work. AI may not deliver on its promise of vast economic opportunity at a price that humanity is willing to pay.The politics have decidedly soured on the project.Seven in 10 Americansoppose building AI datacenters in their area. While this has to do with their insatiable demand for energy, which drives up local electricity costs, AI’s unpopularity is no doubt related to the proposition that it will destroy society as we know it.There are other bumps in the road. Despite its vast progress, big doubts remain on whether AI can do everything a modern economy needs. “Not everything is a computational problem,” notes Autor. AI is good at replicating language, but it cannot connect language to the reality around it. Despite its progress, it still makes plenty ofcritical mistakes.Gig workers are endlessly exploited. AI could make more of us share their fateRead moreAnd then there are the impossible economics. Even if AI could eventually solve all our problems, the solution looks expensive. How much of GDP are we willing to invest in AI datacenters, 20%? 30%? 40%? According to some estimates, that is where we are headed. The International Energy Agency estimates that powerdemand from datacenterswill more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, more than the energy consumption of Japan.The economics look more fragile considering how fast the investment in AI depreciates, as new models overtake those developed just a few months ago. Companies developing AI models “are never going to make money”, Acemoglu said. “They are losing hundreds of billions of dollars every year.”One may discount Altman’s new modesty as a PR feint. Somebody may have told him that equating the AI revolution with mass joblessness was not smart politics. But misgivings about AI’s vaunted capabilities are more than a marketing twist. The grand, epochal promise may be in trouble. Maybe artificial intelligence can’t deliver at a price society is willing to pay.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedAnthropicOpenAIElon MuskUS work & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: LeBron James’ final act in Philadelphia is about more than basketball. It’s about time | LeBron James | The Guardian
description: LeBron James’ move to Philadelphia isn’t about nostalgia or money. It’s about confronting basketball mortality and chasing one last meaningful title
Author: Claire de Lune
Headline: LeBron James’ move to Philadelphia isn’t about nostalgia or money. It’s about confronting basketball mortality and chasing one last meaningful title
Content: LeBron James said he seriously contemplated retirement after last season before deciding to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.Photograph: Joshua Gateley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeBron James said he seriously contemplated retirement after last season before deciding to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.Photograph: Joshua Gateley/Getty ImagesLeBron JamesLeBron James’ final act in Philadelphia is about more than basketball. It’s about timeClaire de LuneThe NBA superstar’s shock move to the Philadelphia 76ers isn’t about money or legacy. It’s about confronting the end of a career and making the most of whatever remainsSat 25 Jul 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 14.11 EDTShareThe most enormous celebrities, those larger-than-life characters with immense cultural impact, occupy a kind of hard-to-quantify space in the zeitgeist. They’re human, of course; that’s what makes them compelling. But they often come to represent something beyond themselves. In LeBron James’ case, for me, he’s become a measure of the passing of time. An aide-mémoire of my own mortality. Yes, his defiance of the aging process has been heartening proof that while Father Time comes for us all, the pace isn’t fixed. But the growing number of gray hairs in his beard, the players born after he was drafted who now meet him in transition, are persistent reminders that time marches on.LeBron James going to the Philadelphia 76ers is perfectly in characterRead moreOn the one hand, as anyone who has experienced it can attest, aging is exhausting. Battles once worth fighting no longer seem worth the effort. An extra 30 minutes of quiet solitude starts to feel like life’s greatest luxury. So perhaps that instinctive understanding clouded all of our assumptions about where LeBron would choose to finish his career. Surely,by now, he had to be tired. Why not golf with Stephen Curry in northern California while playing probably meaningless (but highly entertaining) basketball? Why not head back to Miami, where Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo could shoulder the defensive burden, allowing James to hand over the offensive keys and spend whatever time remained by the pool? Or why not end it in Cleveland, where he’s already beloved, where the stakes are lower, where the narrative is clean and tidy? Wouldn’t that beeasier?But something else comes with aging and the passing of time: the growing sharpness with which the fleeting nature of life comes into view. James may have served as a metaphor for time’s relentless forward march for everyone who watched him. But in his own life, it was moving just as fast, if not faster, as it does for the rest of us.That, it seems, was the real motivator of his decision to shock the league and sign with the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday. In a statement releasedvia his own X account, James said he was grappling with his basketball mortality at the end of his 2025-26 campaign, which marked the end of his eight-year stint with the Los Angeles Lakers – the longest continuous stint of his career. “I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game,” James said. “I was honest at that last press conference [after the Lakerswere eliminated by Oklahoma City] when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give.”James went on to explain that the decision wasn’t motivated by money – a claim easily corroborated by the two-year, $8m veteran’s minimum contract he signed – nor by family, who are currently split between Los Angeles, Tucson and Akron. The deciding factor? A new challenge, fresh excitement and one last good-faith shot at the ultimate prize. “What am I really playing for at this point?” James said in the statement. “I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning a championship.”View image in fullscreenLeBron James (left) talks with the 76ers’ VJ Edgecombe after a game last season in Philadelphia.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APAcquiring a player of LeBron James’ caliber – even at 41 years old – on a minimum contract simply doesn’t happen. But after seriously considering retirement, James’ freedom to choose virtually any destination came at the cost of a massive pay cut. Sticking it to his former employer was, of course, a fringe benefit: it’s been widely reported that James felt disrespected by the Lakers’ brass. Even to an outside observer, it was clear the franchise was eager to turn the page, building around 27-year-old Slovenian wunderkind Luka Dončić after pulling off thesports heist of the century. So even after James dragged an injury-depleted Lakers roster beyond the first round of the playoffs in April, the divorce felt inevitable. And like any middle-aged man going through a divorce, it appeared to elicit some genuine introspection.‘Maybe he’s a ‌racist’: Donald Trump takes bizarre swipe at NBA great LeBron JamesRead moreThe decision to sign withPhiladelphiamakes sense when viewed through that prism. That of a man who knows his time playing the game he loves, that which has defined his life, is rapidly coming to a close. A man forced to ask whether the juice is still worth the squeeze and, if it is, to what end. In some ways, signing with the Sixers is risky proposition: it’s a brand new city and team, with a lot of big names and personalities (in addition to Process™ holdover Joel Embiid, there’s All-NBA guard Tyrese Maxey, last season’s Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe and newly acquired Twitch-streaming NBA finals MVP Jaylen Brown). And then there’s the health issues, which have plagued Embiid and the franchise at large for years. But that’s also what makes the opportunity compelling. Delivering Philadelphia its first NBA championship in more than four decades would instantly become one of the defining achievements of James’ career. And with one of the league’s most talented starting lineups, the Sixers offer him the one thing he appears to have spent the summer searching for: a genuine chance to win one last title.One thing I often find myself pondering when considering the passing of time is the idea of alternate timelines – parallel realities where a single decision changes everything. The twilight of LeBron James’ career is full of them. What if he had stayed in Cleveland in 2018? What if the Lakers had never landed Dončić, extending James’ stay in Los Angeles? And perhaps most intriguing of all: what if the New York Knicks hadn’t won the championship this year? Had they fallen short, Madison Square Garden would have offered James perhaps the most irresistible final act in basketball. Win, and he’d deliver the Knicks the title they had chased for more than half a century. Lose, and he’d at least have the chance to write the ending himself. According to his agent, Rich Paul, that alternate reality came remarkably close to becoming this one. On the Game Over podcast, while reviewing anow-infamous whiteboardof potential destinations with co-host Max Kellerman, Paulpaused on New York. If they hadn’t hoisted the Larry O’Brien in 2026, Paul said, “there would be no board. He’d be going to the Knicks.”Instead, a different timeline prevails. One that’s intriguing, suspenseful and even bizarre: LeBron James, at age 41, is a 76er. In Philadelphia, he can attempt to do what no NBA player has ever done: win a championship with a fourth different team. He can have fun playing basketball, free from the enormous shadow the past version of himself casts in somewhere like Miami or Cleveland. He can grapple with his basketball mortality while trying, in equal measure, to stave it off. He can try and make the most of what’s left of his time.Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesPhiladelphia 76ersPhiladelphiaLos Angeles LakerscommentShareReuse this content

title: I tried so hard to become a salad eater. Now cyclospora is sending me back to burgers | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Between the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossible
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Between the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossible
Content: ‘The greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionFood safetyI tried so hard to become a salad eater. Now cyclospora is sending me back to burgersDave SchillingBetween the companies pushing junk food and the bacteria threatening our produce, eating right feels basically impossibleSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.43 EDTShareWhile war and conflict seem to be raging across the planet, the greatest weapon of mass destruction afflicting the United States today is, apparently, a salad – in the sense that fresh produce is now waging battle with our stomachs thanks to the cyclospora parasite. Cyclospora has infested an unknown amount of our food, causing thousands to suffer bowel movements that would make Pompeii look like a gender-reveal party.This is a tragedy for everyone except the fat cats at Big Toilet. Cyclospora may be spread through human feces getting into irrigation systems in the food supply due to poor worker hygiene. Itcan’t be killed through usual agricultural sanitation processes. The best we can do is throw all that cilantro away and start from scratch. The FDA is scrambling to find the source of the contamination as soon as possible, going as far as to finger the supplier Taylor Farms with a false positive test that they had to sloppily retract as fast as they declared it. I, for one, am trembling, and not because I’m seconds away from expelling parasitic eggs. I’m terrified because now I don’t know what to eat.A year-and-a-half ago, I was strongly recommended a diet by a kindly nutritionist that banished carbs and emphasized leafy greens. It brought down my cholesterol levels and blood pressure. I lost 40lbs. I’ve never felt less like a glistening slug, slithering through life trying to avoid getting stepped on by someone fitter than me during a vigorous jog.I’m not a healthy person, by nature. My son, who is addicted to McDonald’s chicken nuggets, caused me to indulge in fast food. If he’s going for yet another Happy Meal, why not a lovely Big Mac for Dad? When I wrote my first book, my only solace in the lonely days and nights of banging on a keyboard for hours was pizza delivery. Circumstances conspired to unlock my latent gluttony, causing every health marker on my chart to turn a sickly shade of red to denote “strong chance of every organ retiring from service all at once”. Personally, I’d like my body to keep working for another few years, so I took the advice from my nutritionist and gained all the benefits.Unfortunately, the very food I’m meant to eat to stay alive is now a potential threat. Sure, I could order a salad for lunch, but I also might have to move all my worldly possessions into the bathroom. I feel like I’ve stumbled into a Faustian bargain where, for the price of one prolonged bout of digestive emergency, I can have a summer beach body.I’d love to continue my journey toward dietary harmony, but as this outbreak continues, I’m starting to wonder if I should pivot back to my customary regimen of fried dough and cheese cones. If my food isn’t barbecued or dipped into hot grease, can I even trust it?Cuts to food safety programs at the federal levellast year certainly aren’t helping my belief in the propriety of what I put in my mouth. In 2025, a CDC program quietlytrimmed the number of foodborne illnesses it tracked from six to just two. One of the four illnesses axed from the program? Cyclosporiasis. Only salmonella andEcolisurvived the purge, which are at least two of the most famous illnesses. TheQ scorefor salmonella andEcolihas got to be Taylor-Swift-Rihanna levels at this point, making the term “going viral” almost literal.Yes, I know they are actually bacteria. But there’s an entire world of obscure microscopic bugs out there to contend with, and at least for now, we all need to eat food. Worse yet, we all need to eat good food, if such a thing even exists in our mass-produced, industrial culinary world. To match the voracious demand for sustenance and maximize profits, every step of the food-production process has been degraded. Who knows how many microplastics and pesticides are in my system right now, eager to wreak havoc on my internal systems at a moment’s notice? The answer to my food anxiety probably isn’t to subsist on Pop-Tarts and ranch dressing. The damage might be slower than bacteria would cause, but the bill will come due regardless.The problem isn’t with me or you or anyone else who relies on the safety of our food supply. It’s on the companies and the government agencies who manufacture and regulate what we eat. At this juncture, it feels less like my tax dollars go to securing our food and more like they’re going directly into my toilet.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsFood safetyOpinionHealthFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: Like Trump, Pauline Hanson plays the media and attacks the media simultaneously. Who’s using who?  | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: One Nation is borrowing heavily from the Maga playbook. But constant claims of being misquoted predate the US president’s
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: One Nation is borrowing heavily from the Maga playbook. But constant claims of being misquoted predate the US president’s
Content: Pauline Hanson is ‘making statements then walking them back or denying that she made them at all’, Zoe Daniel writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenPauline Hanson is ‘making statements then walking them back or denying that she made them at all’, Zoe Daniel writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionPauline HansonLike Trump, Pauline Hanson plays the media and attacks the media simultaneously. Who’s using who?Zoe DanielOne Nation is borrowing heavily from the Maga playbook. But constant claims of being misquoted predate the US president’sFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 25 Jul 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 22.22 EDTShareTime to call a spade a spade.One Nation’s rise is the media’s fault.AndPauline Hansonbeing misunderstood is also the media’s fault.Elements of the media haveamplified the rise of One Nation over three decades, with outsized coverage normalising what is now a populist machine.At the same time, Hanson treats the media as her enemy.Can both things be true?The first is a deliberately provocative statement. The second is an observation. Both lead to questions about the media’s role and responsibility in an era of information manipulation.The phrases “fake news” and “enemy of the people” come to mind in these times when it appears that whatever the question is for Hanson,Donald Trumpis the answer.The latest example relates to her comments about violence against women in which she makes excuses for violent men.“It is wrong but it’s also a two-way street,” she told the Brisbane radio station 4BC.“I’m not saying that it’s just men, women can lose their cool as well. Society is under so much pressure … Everyone is under so much pressure and it’s really hard.”The facts are thatintimate partner violence is overwhelmingly perpetrated by men.She went on to say that women who are being abused should just leave: “If these women are getting abused by men out there, then don’t put up with it.”The dataalso showsthat leaving is the most dangerous time for women and children.The remarks have caused an outcry which has provoked Hanson to again claim that her comments have been misrepresented.“Here’s exactly what I said on 4BC about domestic violence, so you don’t get it twisted by the media or the Labor Party,” she posted on social media. “There is a concerted effort by some in the media to constantly take my comments out of context.”Pauline Hanson blames ‘fake news’ media for her bad press. But serious leaders have to own their actionsRead moreIt could not be more Trumpian as she plays the media and attacks the media, simultaneously.In 2016, Trump was estimated to have receivedas much as US$5.9bnin free media coverage, more than doubling Hillary Clinton’s presence in the press, while underspending her official campaign on his way to victory in the 2016 presidential election.At the same time, he dominated social media, simultaneously vilifying and bypassing the mainstream media to build an audience he could communicate with directly, while sucking the legacy media into temptation chasing the ratings he could command.Sound familiar?When I was the US bureau chief for the ABC in 2016, US television networks hung on Trump’s every word, broadcasting hours of live, unchecked diatribes.By the time the factcheckers properly mobilised it was too late. The post-truth era was already upon us. Factchecking no longer landed with the average person.Trump had become all but untouchable. The media had become the enemy of the people and anything remotely critical was labelled fake news. Eroding trust in the media was crucial to his strategy.One Nation is now borrowing heavily from this playbook.Hanson’sgaslighting over the White Australia policy, “no good Muslims”, paid parental leave and now violence against women mirrors Trump’s tactics; making statements then walking them back or denying she made them at all.While she’s taken the predictable approach of arguing that the “left-wing media” has twisted her words in “false clickbait stories”, it’s not true.Her recent remarks follow a long pattern of behaviour.In her maiden parliamentary speech in 1996 she said: “I believe we are in danger of being swamped by Asians.”That was before she told the Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to “pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan”, which led to afederal court finding of unlawful racial discriminationand vilification under the Racial Discrimination Act.Yet parts of the media continue to facilitate her rise, while appearing surprised and disturbed that it’s happening.Channel Seven’s Spotlight program was snookered by Hanson’s team when iteither participated in or helped organise her trip around Europe, in which she met rightwingers and hung out in Italy with Gina Rinehart.Seven denies arranging the meetings while, surprise, surprise, Hanson has accused the program of misrepresenting its intentions.That said,the network got the ratings. Conspiracy theorists might suspect that the argy-bargy was confected to achieve that.Who knows?The mainstream media is losing influence as consumers increasingly get their news from social media, which is forcing legacy organisations to feed the algorithm to survive.But the more Hanson is freely platformed as clickbait rather than properly scrutinised, the more likely it is that One Nation will find its way to power.And who will take responsibility for that?Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and the former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsPauline HansonOpinionOne NationAustralian politicsAustralian mediaSeven NetworkSocial mediaDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Warning: Australian politicians are importing the British right’s visions of doom | Jack Jacobs | The Guardian
description: Having met Nigel Farage, Rupert Lowe and Tommy Robinson, Pauline Hanson is deploying their rhetoric in a country with a very different history of immigration, says doctoral researcher in history Jack Jacobs
Author: Jack Jacobs
Headline: Having met Nigel Farage, Rupert Lowe and Tommy Robinson, Pauline Hanson is deploying their rhetoric in a country with a very different history of immigration, says doctoral researcher in history Jack Jacobs
Content: One Nation leader Pauline Hanson during an anti-immigration rally in Canberra, in August 2025.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenOne Nation leader Pauline Hanson during an anti-immigration rally in Canberra, in August 2025.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOpinionPauline HansonWarning: Australian politicians are importing the British right’s visions of doomJack JacobsHaving met Nigel Farage, Rupert Lowe and Tommy Robinson, Pauline Hanson is deploying their rhetoric in a country with a very different history of immigrationSat 25 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 07.40 EDTShareIn a 1950 essay, the critic AA Phillipswrote of a “cultural cringe”in which insecure Australians looked to Britain for instruction. Today, some Australians are championing far-right British actors and importing their visions of doom to Australia.In June, the former Australian Liberalprime minister Tony Abbott spokeat the Alliance for Responsible Citizenship conference, which is organised around the idea of “renewing” western civilisation. “Sustained mass migration, especially from countries with quite different cultures,” said Abbott, “[is] the surest and swiftest way … to dilute and eventually to extinguish the Anglo-Celtic core culture and the Judeo-Christian foundational ethos (which is actually what attracts migrants to the Anglosphere).” Peta Credlin, his former chief of staff, now a Sky News Australia commentator,said: “You are a petri dish … [on] multiculturalism and radical Islam, you are where we don’t want to go.”Both are fighting a civil war for the command of Australia’s right, on terms set by the challenging party: One Nation, founded byPauline Hanson, a former fish-shop owner who became infamous in 1996 for claiming that Australia was “in danger of being swamped by Asians”.Now a Queensland senatorcalling for a “monocultural” Australia, Hanson’s enemy is Islam. Like Reform UK with the Tories, One Nation iscannibalising the Liberal party in polls, and is second onlyto the Australian Labor party, which is in government.Hanson is fresh off a “fact-finding mission” in the UK partlyshapedanddocumentedby Australia’s Channel Seven program Spotlight. She’s photographed with Nigel Farage at the Conservative Political Action Conference in London (a meeting fell through due to the Clacton byelection). She tours Tower Hamlets with recent Reform convert Robert Jenrick, to weirdly observe British Muslims going about their daily lives. She meets Restore Britain’s Rupert Lowe at the country house of Holly Valance, the Australian-British singer. Lowe gives Hanson a copy of his party’s policy paper Mass Deportations: Legitimacy, Legality, and Logistics, saying: “This is a jewel of what you need to do in Australia.”The reportpromises to remove“roughly 1.8 million illegals … living in our midst” in “exactly three years” through a “new hostile environment with voluntary returns and forced deportations”. Hanson later exclaims she “love[s]” the idea of mass deportations, clarifying that she means “for the ones that are [in Australia] illegally”. That despotic phrase, unnatural to the Australian tongue, is now parlayed on breakfast television.Hanson meets with Tommy Robinson; the meeting most preoccupying Australians. Ina podcast released on X, Robinson approaches Hanson with deference, even tenderness: “I have the great pleasure of meeting a lady I’ve looked up to for years.” Both see themselves as martyrs after serving jail time: Hanson for 11 weeks in 2003 for electoral fraudbefore her quashed conviction; Robinson, several times, including for fraud and contempt of court.She tells Robinson that the trouble started with the end of the White Australia policy under the Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam in 1973. The policy – introduced in the Federation of Australia’s states in 1901 – arbitrarily administered a near-impossible dictation test in European languages to preserve Australia’s white, mainly British, population. Contrary to Hanson’s claim, it was gradually dismantled by both Liberal and Labor governments from the 1950s onwards; Whitlam removed its final remnants in 1973 and introduced protections against racial discrimination in 1975. Hanson insists that European migrants assimilated better than more recent arrivals from the global south. (She nowdenies that she wants to revive the policy.) In footage cut from Robinson’s podcast but broadcast by Spotlight, Hanson says of Muslims: “They do breed.” She catches herself, in both versions: “They are having children … in the Qur’an it says Allah will provide, well, the Allah providing is the taxpayer.”Like Robinson, Hanson blames Islam for ruining western societies, disparaging an entire people while disregarding the unregulated markets that have torn up the old worlds they mourn. Robinson grew up in Luton, a deindustrialised car town whose working class feel abandoned; the Australians to whom Hanson appeals are breaking under cost of living pressure.Their visions contain shadows of truth, but their blind spots are black holes, sucking those who entertain them into a vortex of conspiracy that licenses hate. Britain suffers street violence and racial and religious tensions. Governments have failed to properly address the violence done to young women and girls by grooming gangs. But these scenes, consumed in frenzies on an X feed, are abstracted from British circumstances and sent by algorithms to scare Australians.Australians are already afraid. On 14 December 2025, a father and sonmurdered 15 people at a Hanukkah celebrationat Sydney’s Bondi beach. This was the worst terrorist attack on Jews globally since 7 October; the deadliest in Australian history. It spawned from a vengeful ideology imported on to Australian soil, with no defensible claim to being a faith. This attack and the politics practised by Hanson and Robinson are in no way equivalent. But both share the feature that they convert the countries they inhabit into a battleground for wars from elsewhere, endangering vulnerable minorities.Australia and the UK are different countries, with divergent immigration histories. Multicultural Britain was built by the postwar promises the empire made to its subject peoples. Since the dismantling of the White Australia policy, Australia has shown a powerful capacity to embrace successive waves of migrants; though not without a racism compounded by Indigenous dispossession.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a thoughtful and humane conversation to be had about how migration can be scaled in complex societies that sustains a shared sense of nationhood: one more capacious than the exclusive nostalgias to which Hanson and Robinson remain enslaved. Australia is well equipped to have it. White working-class Australians welcomed my family when they arrived from India in the 1960s and 1980s. Hanson refuses to accept that Australia’s multicultural way of life has grown up without her, resisting the monoculture not by government mandate, but through ordinary acts of decency that bind and make a society.Politicians like Hanson call themselves conservatives, even as they disavow that philosophy’s first commitment: to pay special attention to what is rare about one’s own country. By internalising British anxieties, we stop ourselves from seeing Australian problems – and our rare ability to solve them – with our own eyes.Jack Jacobs is an Australian doctoral researcher in history at the University of OxfordDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
