title: The hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownup | Jacq Kelly | The Guardian
description: There’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every time, says Toronto-based writer Jacq Kelly
Author: Jacq Kelly
Headline: There’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every time, says Toronto-based writer Jacq Kelly
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyThe hill I will die onSaladThe hill I will die on: Breakfast cereal is for babies – I eat salad in the mornings, like a grownupJacq KellyThere’s no way I could get by on a bowl of Coco Pops – give me sliced tomatoes and cucumber every timeSat 25 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 13.39 EDTShareIrecently got into a row on X about the unlikely subject of salad. I want to acknowledge that arguing with strangers on social media is definitely for babies and I should know better by now, but I’m a work in progress. And so I mentioned that I had enjoyed how readily available salads had been at breakfast buffets while I had been travelling in Denmark and Sweden this year compared with the UK.Saladhas been a part of my breakfast for about a decade now, and I think a lot of people would benefit from it. It’s a pretty easy way of getting a couple of portions of fruit and veg before you have even left the house.All hell broke loose. Salad for breakfast is “not normal in a northern European climate”, according to one agitated typer in a response to my post about its availability at breakfasts there. In one of the towns we visited,Luleå, we were just 100km south of the Arctic Circle and the sea was still frozen in April. The hotel had an excellent breakfast buffet–a rotating assortment of freshly prepared salad items with fruit that hadn’t even been poured from a can. Someone should alert the authorities.“Only freaks eat salad for breakfast,” another wordsmith reported. What really took the rice-crispy cake was the person who explained: “It’s the uk [sic], our food is heavy and warm here. Cold island nation that had to be out in the fields with constant rain”, which was presumably typed on a precariously balanced laptop by someone driving a tractor somewhere on Shetland. Obviously the people I worked with in UK offices who I witnessed spooning sugary snack foods into their faces while staring at their computer screens are the outliers here.Don’t misunderstand me – I love a bowl of Coco Pops. Not as a morning food option but as an after-lunch-and-too-early-for-dinnerhangry-managementsolution. There’s no way I could get through an entire morning on a bowl of crispy rice dusted with cocoa sloshing around in semi-skimmed cow juice.View image in fullscreenA selection of Danish smørrebrød: ‘a pretty easy way of getting a couple of portions of fruit and veg before you even leave the house’.Photograph: Sofiia Popovych/ShutterstockI need sliced salted tomatoes, a generous handful of fresh assorted leaves, the crunch of a cucumber and, if I am being fancy, thinly sliced mangetout with a handful of finely chopped dill, mint or parsley to set me up for the morning, and ideally I want to have it sitting at a breakfast table. Whatever curveballs might come my way throughout the day, I can start it knowing I have done something for me and by me that was not only healthy but also delicious, and that made me sit down with a knife and fork to actually make time for at least one civilised meal.So no thanks to the people who told me I could go into a supermarket or McDonald’s and buy salad whenever I like. That sort of misses the point – I want to eat breakfast in the place where I am staying. I don’t want to pick wilted leaves from a plastic bowl with my fingers in the middle of the high street.Complain all you like, but I’m eating salad as part of breakfast whenever I can. There’s a reason those Scandinavians have colour in their cheeks and live long and healthy lives, and I want in on that. As for the person who responded to the photo of my breakfast of salad, garlic mushrooms and boiled egg on toast with a sophisticated total of three “being sick” emojis, thanks for proving my point – cereal for breakfast really is for babies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJacq Kelly is a Toronto-based writer and disability rights campaignerExplore more on these topicsSaladThe hill I will die onBreakfastFoodCereals and grainscommentShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: ‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyChristopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epicCharlotte HigginsThere’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics?Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.42 EDTShareEveryone knows how dumb it is to be this person: the one who mourns the film adaptation of a favourite text because it misses out this scene, or misreads that particularly beloved character, or has a slightly “inauthentic” take on some detail. Of course I’m talking about Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of the Odyssey, a poem I have loved since I was a teenager. I enjoyed the movie, in common with a huge number of other people. It seems remarkable, even dizzying, that the adaptation of a nearly 3,000-year-old poemtook $264m(£196m) at the box office over its opening weekend, has sent translations of the Odysseysurging up the bestseller charts, and is sold out (for instance) at London’s BFI Imax screen deep into September. We are living in anOdyssey time, amid an Odyssey frenzy.There is no point trying to be a purist about a beloved classic text. Whoever reads the Odyssey, including Nolan, inescapably does so through the prism of their prejudices, informed by the conditions of their own place and time. Since the Odyssey is the result of decades, maybe centuries, of non-literate oral poets working with memory and improvisation, there’s no precise “original” place or time to return to, anyway. But what I can’t help doing is observe the choices Nolan has made and think about their consequences – because there are always divides in the road, paths not taken by any adapter.Nolan is brilliant at recreating one aspect of the original poem: its complicated structure. The poem tells the story of the decade-long return journey from the siege of Troy of its hero, Odysseus: the adventures he has along the way and how he reinstates himself as the head of his household once he’s home. There are monsters and witches and magic and storms at sea. And then he must infiltrate himself into his home disguised as a beggar, before a Tarantino-esque bloodbath of revenge. It is a story told not in sequence, but through parallel timelines and flashbacks. Nolan, as I had hoped of the creator ofInception,MementoandThe Prestige, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon (left, with bow) as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesBut his Odysseus, as filtered through Matt Damon’s performance, is a grim and agonised figure, not the loquacious, rhetorically able, charming liar that I see in the poem. Cinema is a visual medium – not a genre for wordy speeches – but nevertheless, Nolan’s hero is a notably laconic figure. He is also guilt-stricken and conscience-laden in a way that speaks more of a Judeo-Christian inheritance and Nolan’s sense of a war-weary world than anything in Homer. Where the poem has Odysseus inducting his son Telemachus into the life of a warrior, the pair fighting their domestic enemies together, the film finds a way to release the younger man from the burdens of a killer’s life.The Odyssey, though, is not an anti-war poem, though it is a post-war poem. Homer’s Odysseus is placed in a genealogy of warriors stretching back from the great veteran fighter Nestor and beyond (Nestor is absent from the film, so this layer of inheritance is lost) and forward to the next generation. War is, for the Odyssey, a fact of life – albeit one that is grievous and destructive. But the idea that Odysseus bears a moral burden for the destruction of Troy is pure Nolan. He has swamped the poem with his own preoccupations and anxieties, as all readers do in the end, and created an adaptation that is tamed and tuned to modern sensibilities. Had he cleaved closer to the source material, I’m not sure the movie accountants would be now totting up the money so gleefully. Would modern cinemagoers really queue up to see a row of enslaved women hanged, like doves caught in a trap (says the poem) their feet twitching as they are killed?Nolan has added, but of course he has also subtracted. He has removed not just dark and horrific moments like the hanging of the slaves, but also, by contrast, the epic’s lightness and wit. This is especially apparent in his treatment of female characters. Nolan’s resentful Helen, played by the excellent Lupita Nyong’o, is literally and metaphorically scarred, rather than poised and gleaming and elegant. His Circe is magnificent and strange (and given an extraordinary performance by Samantha Morton), but not funny or enticing. Because he has removed the Olympian gods from any meaningful role in the film, we miss a blissful moment in which the divine Calypso (played by Charlize Theron) rails to the god Hermes against the sexual double standard (it’s OK for gods to have sex with mortal women, she complains, but not for goddesses to sleep with men). The relationship between Zendaya’s Athena and Damon’s Odysseus lacks the flirtatious spark that’s so enjoyable in the poem.View image in fullscreenMia Goth as Melantho and Anne Hathaway as Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s adaptation.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesThere is no nervous young Nausicaa finding Odysseus battered and naked on the beach (a delicious scene), because Nolan has eradicated Nausicaa, and her enigmatic mother, Arete, too. Odysseus’s mother is also cut – and I would argue, his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), is also short of a couple of layers of complexity, her strange obliqueness gone. More or less removing the gods is an understandable decision, if you want to focus on human motivations and choices. It’s easier to imagine gods in a poem than to have them quivering awkwardly on a cloud in a film. I was reminded of novelist Colm Tóibíntelling mewhy there were no gods in his story House of Names, which also inhabits the world of the Trojan war: the novel is a deeply human form, he said, and the gods have no business in it. And for Nolan, at least, so is cinema. But why lose the sexual spark? I had a sneaking suspicion that by damping down Odysseus’s extramarital sexual adventures (and also Penelope’s ambivalence towards the men who are competing to marry her on Ithaca), Nolan has found another way to tame the Odyssey into modern moral acceptability.Read the poem. You won’t regret it. (If it feels forbidding, Mary Beard and I have apodcast seriesfor this.) And preorder Alice Oswald’s bookRhapsody: a Manifesto, which comes out in September and superbly draws out the qualities of Homer’s liquidness, the full wonder of his stories within stories, those Odyssean tales that peel back like layers of an onion to reveal further tales. She will show you the way the poem’s similes and apparently formulaic descriptions of characters are a form of time travel in which different, incompatible realities can coexist in a shimmering haze of poetic temporality that cinema, or at least this kind of cinema, cannot replicate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch things you will experience only if you engulf yourself in the poem. What you will learn in the film is about ourselves: about Nolan’s preoccupations, and about what modern sensibilities can stomach. Reading the poem turns the gaze outward – towards another reality that we recognise, but is at the same time foreign and wild and strange and delicious and disturbing and so different from our own. Watch the film, yes. Then open the pages of a book and disappear into a another world that no Imax cameras could ever summon.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyOpinionChristopher NolancommentShareReuse this content

title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
Content: ‘Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationStaff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious resultsArwa MahdawiA new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first termSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTShareDonald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates.According to anew reportcalled Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’snearly 150% higherthan the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”.High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretaryKristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as thePartnership for Public Servicenote in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far morestable.And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fuelinga power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king.“Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from thePartnership for Public Service writesin a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.”Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the presidentsaid in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,”he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.”Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helpedcreate, has been invaluable to him in this regard. InJuly 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme courtgave the president another gift:the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935rulingthat the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president.Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled inTrump v Cookthat the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile,wrote onTruth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”.I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who arebehind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there onpage 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere withelection administrationandweaponize the Department of Justiceagainst election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with.In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election.A bunch of losers are still complaining that the Odyssey isn’t white enoughElon Musk has been whining about Christopher Nolan casting Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy formonthsnow. This week, following rave reviews of the Odyssey, Muskannouncedthat his AI image and video generator Grok Imagine would create its own “historically accurate” version of the film. Perhaps Musk should listen to Colman Domingo, who recentlysaidon Jimmy Kimmel Live that he has a message for everyone upset about diversity in The Odyssey: “If you want to see a film with a cast of all white people who are cursed by the gods, the ‘Melania’ movie is currently streaming.”Record 384 World Cup-linked reports of domestic abuse in England and WalesThe data was collected as part of a strategy tobetter understand the linkbetween football tournaments and domestic abuse. A police chief citedextended pub opening hoursas one of the factors in the surge in violence.AOC is leading Kamala Harris in a new 2028 presidential poll by a long wayA University of New Hampshire poll has AOCleading the fieldwith 22% support while Pete Buttigieg has 21%. Harris only has 5%.Model scout for Jeffrey Epstein found dead at his home near ParisDaniel Siad, who was founddead at his home on Monday, compared his work trying to source women with fishing. “In This busyness I feel like fisherman some time I cache (sic) quick, some time no fish,”he wrotein an email to Epstein in 2014.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralian politician Pauline Hanson thinks domestic violence is a ‘two-way street’The senatoralso suggestedwomen experiencing abuse should simply “not put up with it”.Israeli rights groups warn of ‘mass pogroms’in occupied West BankWhile violence by Arabs is called “terrorism”, the media tends to downplay attacks by Jewish settlers in Israel by characterizing it as “settler violence”. This violence,enabledby the Israeli military and ignored by many in the US, has been intensifying. Following adeadly settler attack on Friday, Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem and 19 other Israeli human rights organisationscondemnedthe international community’s “silence and inaction” and called for “immediate action to stop Israel’s violence and prevent pogroms by settler militias”.Why middle-aged women are ravingWomen are putting the internalized ageism aside and realizing you’re never too old to go outclubbing.People are watching porn based on ICE raidsRule 34of the internet is that if something exists, there is porn of it. The dystopian machinations of the Trump administration are no exception. Wired has a disturbing pieceon the rise of Maga-themed porn.The week in pawtriarchyMeet Jimothy, who appears to be the internet’snew favourite racoon. Seattle-based Jimothy hasn’t won hearts and minds by passing outdrunk in a Virginia liquorstore like some of his compatriots. Rather, he has gone viral because of his distinctive body shape, which may be the result of a rare genetic condition called short spine syndrome. He looks a bit like afurry goblin, basically. I reckon Jimothy’s lack of a well-functioning backbone means he has a promising political career ahead of him. Perhaps Trump could make him Secretary of Trashury.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationThe Week in PatriarchyUS politicsDonald TrumpThe OdysseyElon MuskWorld CupAlexandria Ocasio-CortezcommentShareReuse this content

title: The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more | Fiction | The Guardian
description: From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny Colgan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny Colgan
Content: Illustration by Zara PickenFictionThe perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and moreFrom a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny ColganSat 25 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 04.05 EDTShareItis important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiographyA Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it:Whistlerby Ann Patchett.For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time:This Is Where the Serpent Livesby Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon:Glorious Exploitsby Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago,The Guest,a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’sStrangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m:The Impossible Fortuneby Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello.Bonnes vacances!View image in fullscreenFreida McFaddenauthor of The HousemaidOne of my favourite reads of the year has beenTheCalamity Clubby Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.Caro Claire Burkeauthor of YesteryearInThe Shampoo Effectby Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.View image in fullscreenTaffy Brodesser-Aknerauthor of Fleishman Is in TroubleI broughtHere in the Darkby my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.Alice Osemanauthor of HeartstopperConvenience Store Womanby Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.Mick Herronauthor of the Slough House seriesBeaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’sCountry Peopleis a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.Nita Proseauthor of The MaidThe Paper Palaceby Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.View image in fullscreenLisa Jewellauthor of None of This Is TrueThe best page-turner I’ve read this year isIt’s Not What You Thinkby Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.André Acimanauthor of Call Me by Your NameLondon Fallingby Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.View image in fullscreenLucy Foleyauthor of The Guest ListThe Wedding Peopleby Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.Erin Kellyauthor of The Night StairsThe Pinnacleby Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.Leigh Bardugoauthor of the Ninth House seriesThe Last Baronby Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.View image in fullscreenMatt Haigauthor of The Midnight LibraryThe Infinite Sadness of Small Appliancesby Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.Florence Knappauthor of The NamesA will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. InNora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.View image in fullscreenRobert Harrisauthor of ConclaveGraham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particularThe Power and the Glory,The Honorary ConsulandThe Quiet American–perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.Rebecca F Kuangauthor ofYellowfaceI recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’sCloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.View image in fullscreenMike Gayleauthor of On We GoAn MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So beginsBody of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.Bella Mackieauthor of Claws Out!The Enchanted Aprilby Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.View image in fullscreenCurtis Sittenfeldauthor of American WifeCrash Into Meby Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.View image in fullscreenHarriet Tyceauthor of Witch TrialNonesuchby Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation forTime to Burnby Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.View image in fullscreenAbir Mukherjeeauthor of The Burning GroundsMy choice isThe Shadow Stepby Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.Abigail Deanauthor of The Death of UsI’d recommendMain Charactersby Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.Jennie Godfreyauthor of The Barbecue at No9This year,Dead Heatby Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.View image in fullscreenShari Lapenaauthor of Getting Away With MurderInFiveby Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.Nick Harkawayauthor of Karla’s ChoiceIf Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d getThere Is No Antimemetics Divisionby qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?Paula Hawkinsauthor of The Girl on the TrainFour Terrible Parentsby Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.Kate Mosseauthor of The Map of BonesRecently reissued,Fennyby Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.Adele Parksauthor of Just My LuckMad Mabelby Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.Claire Powellauthor of All InI couldn’t get enough ofSome Bright Nowhereby Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.To support the Guardian, order your beach reads atguardianbookshop.com/beach-reads

title: Euphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re together  | Television | The Guardian
description: I was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s drama
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s drama
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningTelevisionEuphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re togetherI was uncertain about expressing my queerness, until I saw the way Zendaya and Hunter Schafer’s characters opened up to each other in HBO’s dramaRakel Clinton LucasSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t remember the exact moment when I started catching feelings for my friend Ellen. It might have been when she trusted me to cut her hair into a feathered bob, or when I noticed she’d taken to keeping my favourite tea at her parents’ house. But in the summer of 2019, a month before our final year of school together, I realised I was falling in love.We were 17 at the time and had been best friends since our first year of high school, both of us part of the same tight-knit group of girls. Ellen and I knew each other well and were quick to make each other laugh, but we were also very different. Whereas Ellen is reserved and gentle, I’m loud and loquacious. So my sudden attraction to her was confusing – especially since neither of us was openly queer.I had been raised in an accepting, liberal household in Stockholm, where queerness was never frowned upon. And yet, I had always assumed that I was straight. It was the default script that had been handed to me. So, each time Ellen greeted me with her one-dimpled smile, I tried to ignore the fluttering in my chest, thinking it would be too complicated, too daunting. Even as I sensed those feelings might be mutual, I didn’t dare act on them. I was worried it might damage our friendship.double quotation markIt was the first show I saw that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way tooThis all changed when I watched the first season of Sam Levinson’s television show Euphoria. Set in suburban California, the show (an adaptation of an Israeli series of the same name) follows a group of high-schoolers as they recklessly navigate adolescence. They abuse drugs, drink alcohol, have sex, watch porn and fall in and out of love.More specifically, it was the relationship between Rue (Zendaya), a recovering drug addict, and the town newcomer, a transgender girl named Jules (Hunter Schafer), that drew me in. The two meet after a party at the end of the first episode and quickly forge a connection. As their friendship deepens, Rue begins to fall for Jules.I recall watching the first few episodes at a friend’s house and being enthralled by Rue and Jules’s plotline, and how tender and complex it was. Even though my own world was far removed from the dark, gritty one of Euphoria, I related to the more innocuous parts of their story: the insecurities Rue has about her feelings toward Jules, that flicker of hope each time the line between platonic and romantic love is blurred. It all felt so similar to what I was experiencing.There was also something refreshing about the depiction of the characters’ sexuality. In the series, there are no major coming-out scenes, no need for Rue or Jules to explain their orientation. When Rue tells her mother she’s in a “relationship” with Jules, her mother simply responds by saying: “It may not matter what I think, but I really like her.” This is not to say that coming-out scenes in fiction aren’t important. But for me, Euphoria was the first show that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way too.Watching Rue and Jules open up to one another gave me the push I needed; when I finally did kiss Ellen, she kissed me right back. And as morning light filtered through the blinds of her bedroom, I knew I had made the right decision.We have been together for six years. We didn’t settle into a relationship right away; we needed time to figure out coupledom. But slowly, Ellen and I have managed to build a life, furnished with our mutual love of books, movie nights and laughter. She is my bulwark and the person who helps me decompress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI did try watching the later seasons of Euphoria. And while some viewers may have enjoyed thegrimmer tone, I couldn’t make it through the final run. Still, I’m grateful for that first season: it helped wash away my uncertainty and gave me the courage to make the first move. And truly, it was the greatest thing I ever did.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose.
