title: Treasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefacts  | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
Content: The artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe artefacts worn by Zendaya dated back almost 3,000 years and were loaned by a Mayfair dealer.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockHeritageTreasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefactsJewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological findsNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 25 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield.Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocallwearing earringsthat were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC.According to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer that owns the earrings, the gold medallion plaques are “attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-westIranin the late 1940s”. They were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, who mounted them with diamonds in yellow gold.View image in fullscreenGold plate showing a character fighting a lion from the Ziwiye Hoard exhibited at the Louvre Museum in Paris.Photograph: Lanmas/AlamyBut while the Mayfair retailer claims the jewellery celebrates “the remarkable artistry of ancient Persian goldsmiths” and encourages “wider appreciation of one of the world’s great artistic traditions”, academics take a different view.A petition has been launched calling for Barron London to publish the complete known provenance of the gold plaques, reveal the checks they undertook on the legality of the items, permit examination of the objects, and even suspend sale.Zendaya is used to the glare of camera lenses, but being the focus of academically qualified antiquarians is something else altogether.Dr Christos Tsirogiannis, an antiquities expert at the Swiss Federal Office of Culture, said: “Personally, after all these two and a half decades of continued scandals emerging everywhere about all sorts of illicit antiquities … I’m extremely surprised, negatively surprised, that no one among all these people that escort these celebrities said something to protect her.”‘Incredible’ Roman bathers’ gems lost 2,000 years ago found near Hadrian’s WallRead moreRomina Frohar, the founder of the Forensic Archive of Iran, an independent investigative archive documenting threats to Iran’s cultural heritage that set up the petition, said her concern was broader than Zendaya’s decision to wear the items.“Barron London has described the loan as a celebration of ancient Persian artistry, but cultural appreciation cannot substitute for provenance transparency,” she said. “If these objects are being publicly presented as Iranian cultural heritage, the evidence concerning their origin, export, ownership history and acquisition should be open to scrutiny.”Even if antiquities were authentic and lawfully possessed, ethical issues may still arise, said Frohar, a PhD researcher at the Glasgow School of Art. “Private custody can be responsible when it is transparent, conservation-led and attentive to public and scholarly access. But legal possession alone does not extinguish the cultural claims of the people whose history the object embodies.”The earrings’ odyssey from BC Iran to A-list actor involved a trip into the shadowy world of rare treasure trading – an industry in which priceless archeological finds are transformed into high-end luxury trinkets.Many of the collections of Mayfair dealers, auction houses and private homes would be at home in the glass cases of museums.Among items currently available to purchase from dealers online is an Egyptian mummy mask made of beads that dates from somewhere between 664BC to 332BC; Hellenistic gold earrings with garnet and agate dating back to the 3rd century BC, and a bronze dress pin with an end resembling an ibex that apparently comes from Iran and could be up to 3,000 years old. Their prices start at about £450.In parallel, auction houses have put astonishing antiquities under the hammer. In 2018, Christie’s sold a 3,000-year-old relief from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II, a neo-Assyrian king who ruled 800 years before the establishment of the Roman empire, fornearly $31m.Tsirogiannis is no stranger to such sales. His work has turned up evidence casting doubt on the provenance of numerous antiquities on the market. “About 90% of antiquities in the market one way or another, sooner or later, are proved to be illicit or lacking provenance, lacking documentation,” he said.If Zendaya’s earrings were authentic, they might also pose another moral conundrum: “Possibly they are coming from a burial. How does she feel that she is wearing an ancient dead woman’s earrings [that may have been] looted?” he said.View image in fullscreenThe Koh-i-noor diamond sits in a crown on the coffin of Britain’s late Queen Mother Elizabeth.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APProvenance and ownership of antiquities is an issue that has long passed beyond academia. Among the most notorious examplesis the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which was surrendered to Queen Victoria by the 10-year-old maharajah Duleep Singh in 1849 as part of the Treaty of Lahore, becoming part of the British crown jewels.The legalities around establishing who owns ancient items can be complex.“Most so-called source countries for antiquities now have state ownership laws in place to say that ancient objects discovered belong to the state,” said Simon Mackenzie, a professor of criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (Te Herenga Waka) in New Zealand. “So the act of discovery and looting is essentially a form of theft [from the government].”“In many countries, including Iran, these laws had been built up over time andwere not retroactive, so legal arguments could be made about what date exactly the theft rule applied from, he said.Despite the outrage, sprinkling some modern celebrity stardust on the treasures of millennia gone by is not always a bad thing. When bling attracts academic attention, a conversation about provenance can begin.When Kim Kardashian was snapped posing in a gold dress next to a gilded Egyptian coffin at the Met Gala in 2018, for example, experts in antiquities trafficking took notice.View image in fullscreenKim Kardashian’s appearance at the Met Gala in 2018 also sparked controversy.Photograph: Ian West/PAThe Met museum had acquired the 2,100-year-old coffin of a priest called Nedjemankh for $4m and made it the star of an exhibition. However,experts soon revealedit had been excavated by thieves in 2011 and smuggled out of Egypt to Dubai and then Europe, where it was restored and given false documents.The legal and ethical problems which came with Zendaya’s earrings may never be resolved, but there remains one conundrum that does not require a PhD to spot.As Tsirogiannis pointed out, the film star’s jewellery put the spotlight on Iran while promoting a film that had nothing to do with ancient Persia.Explore more on these topicsHeritageArchaeologyZendayaIranMiddle East and north AfricaCelebrityDisputed artnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epic | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: There’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics? asks the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: ‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘The director, as I had hoped, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.’Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyChristopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer’s epicCharlotte HigginsThere’s no denying the power of the film on the big screen. But how far should modern moral sensibilities influence adaptations of classics?Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 16.42 EDTShareEveryone knows how dumb it is to be this person: the one who mourns the film adaptation of a favourite text because it misses out this scene, or misreads that particularly beloved character, or has a slightly “inauthentic” take on some detail. Of course I’m talking about Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of the Odyssey, a poem I have loved since I was a teenager. I enjoyed the movie, in common with a huge number of other people. It seems remarkable, even dizzying, that the adaptation of a nearly 3,000-year-old poemtook $264m(£196m) at the box office over its opening weekend, has sent translations of the Odysseysurging up the bestseller charts, and is sold out (for instance) at London’s BFI Imax screen deep into September. We are living in anOdyssey time, amid an Odyssey frenzy.There is no point trying to be a purist about a beloved classic text. Whoever reads the Odyssey, including Nolan, inescapably does so through the prism of their prejudices, informed by the conditions of their own place and time. Since the Odyssey is the result of decades, maybe centuries, of non-literate oral poets working with memory and improvisation, there’s no precise “original” place or time to return to, anyway. But what I can’t help doing is observe the choices Nolan has made and think about their consequences – because there are always divides in the road, paths not taken by any adapter.Nolan is brilliant at recreating one aspect of the original poem: its complicated structure. The poem tells the story of the decade-long return journey from the siege of Troy of its hero, Odysseus: the adventures he has along the way and how he reinstates himself as the head of his household once he’s home. There are monsters and witches and magic and storms at sea. And then he must infiltrate himself into his home disguised as a beggar, before a Tarantino-esque bloodbath of revenge. It is a story told not in sequence, but through parallel timelines and flashbacks. Nolan, as I had hoped of the creator ofInception,MementoandThe Prestige, follows the spirit of the original poem’s twisted, coiling structure with his own complex design.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon (left, with bow) as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesBut his Odysseus, as filtered through Matt Damon’s performance, is a grim and agonised figure, not the loquacious, rhetorically able, charming liar that I see in the poem. Cinema is a visual medium – not a genre for wordy speeches – but nevertheless, Nolan’s hero is a notably laconic figure. He is also guilt-stricken and conscience-laden in a way that speaks more of a Judeo-Christian inheritance and Nolan’s sense of a war-weary world than anything in Homer. Where the poem has Odysseus inducting his son Telemachus into the life of a warrior, the pair fighting their domestic enemies together, the film finds a way to release the younger man from the burdens of a killer’s life.The Odyssey, though, is not an anti-war poem, though it is a post-war poem. Homer’s Odysseus is placed in a genealogy of warriors stretching back from the great veteran fighter Nestor and beyond (Nestor is absent from the film, so this layer of inheritance is lost) and forward to the next generation. War is, for the Odyssey, a fact of life – albeit one that is grievous and destructive. But the idea that Odysseus bears a moral burden for the destruction of Troy is pure Nolan. He has swamped the poem with his own preoccupations and anxieties, as all readers do in the end, and created an adaptation that is tamed and tuned to modern sensibilities. Had he cleaved closer to the source material, I’m not sure the movie accountants would be now totting up the money so gleefully. Would modern cinemagoers really queue up to see a row of enslaved women hanged, like doves caught in a trap (says the poem) their feet twitching as they are killed?Nolan has added, but of course he has also subtracted. He has removed not just dark and horrific moments like the hanging of the slaves, but also, by contrast, the epic’s lightness and wit. This is especially apparent in his treatment of female characters. Nolan’s resentful Helen, played by the excellent Lupita Nyong’o, is literally and metaphorically scarred, rather than poised and gleaming and elegant. His Circe is magnificent and strange (and given an extraordinary performance by Samantha Morton), but not funny or enticing. Because he has removed the Olympian gods from any meaningful role in the film, we miss a blissful moment in which the divine Calypso (played by Charlize Theron) rails to the god Hermes against the sexual double standard (it’s OK for gods to have sex with mortal women, she complains, but not for goddesses to sleep with men). The relationship between Zendaya’s Athena and Damon’s Odysseus lacks the flirtatious spark that’s so enjoyable in the poem.View image in fullscreenMia Goth as Melantho and Anne Hathaway as Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s adaptation.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesThere is no nervous young Nausicaa finding Odysseus battered and naked on the beach (a delicious scene), because Nolan has eradicated Nausicaa, and her enigmatic mother, Arete, too. Odysseus’s mother is also cut – and I would argue, his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), is also short of a couple of layers of complexity, her strange obliqueness gone. More or less removing the gods is an understandable decision, if you want to focus on human motivations and choices. It’s easier to imagine gods in a poem than to have them quivering awkwardly on a cloud in a film. I was reminded of novelist Colm Tóibíntelling mewhy there were no gods in his story House of Names, which also inhabits the world of the Trojan war: the novel is a deeply human form, he said, and the gods have no business in it. And for Nolan, at least, so is cinema. But why lose the sexual spark? I had a sneaking suspicion that by damping down Odysseus’s extramarital sexual adventures (and also Penelope’s ambivalence towards the men who are competing to marry her on Ithaca), Nolan has found another way to tame the Odyssey into modern moral acceptability.Read the poem. You won’t regret it. (If it feels forbidding, Mary Beard and I have apodcast seriesfor this.) And preorder Alice Oswald’s bookRhapsody: a Manifesto, which comes out in September and superbly draws out the qualities of Homer’s liquidness, the full wonder of his stories within stories, those Odyssean tales that peel back like layers of an onion to reveal further tales. She will show you the way the poem’s similes and apparently formulaic descriptions of characters are a form of time travel in which different, incompatible realities can coexist in a shimmering haze of poetic temporality that cinema, or at least this kind of cinema, cannot replicate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch things you will experience only if you engulf yourself in the poem. What you will learn in the film is about ourselves: about Nolan’s preoccupations, and about what modern sensibilities can stomach. Reading the poem turns the gaze outward – towards another reality that we recognise, but is at the same time foreign and wild and strange and delicious and disturbing and so different from our own. Watch the film, yes. Then open the pages of a book and disappear into a another world that no Imax cameras could ever summon.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyOpinionChristopher NolancommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘People who commit heinous crimes can be victims’: Michael Mann on the provocative power of Manhunter at 40 | Michael Mann | The Guardian
description: As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworld
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworld
Content: Tom Noonan as serial killer Francis Dolarhyde in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesView image in fullscreenTom Noonan as serial killer Francis Dolarhyde in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesMichael Mann‘People who commit heinous crimes can be victims’: Michael Mann on the provocative power of Manhunter at 40As a stunning 4K restoration arrives in theaters, the director and cast reflect on creating the disturbing descent into a criminal underworldMatthew AllanSat 25 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Mannhas shown time and again in films likeThief,Heat, Miami Vice andPublic Enemiesthat he is one of American film’s greatest explorers of the underworld. “It’s like a kind of cultural anthropology,” Mann tells me from his office in Los Angeles. “If you make films, you get to do that in a different place with a different subject every few years. For me, the exploration is the high.”With its unsettling atmosphere and soaring beauty, Mann’s 1986 film Manhunter reimagined how a thriller could look, sound and feel in an early high point for the director. To commemorate its 40th anniversaryManhunter: The Final Cut, a 4K restoration and director’s cut with three minutes of new footage, will see a theatrical release in New York and Los Angeles this weekend with a nationwide US rollout to follow.‘Maybe the best pumped-up sequel ever made’: James Cameron’s Aliens hits 40Read moreBased onThomas Harris’s bestselling horror novel Red Dragon, Manhunter follows FBI agent Will Graham (William Petersen), who has been lured out of retirement to hunt down an elusive serial killer before he performs another ritualistic killing on the night of the next full moon. Graham has been called on for his uncanny ability to access the methods and motives of killers by adopting their states of mind, though it has come with its own personal costs. When we meet Graham at his secluded beach house (rented to the film by pop artistRobert Rauschenberg) he’s recently returned from a stint in a psychiatric unit after a meltdown and a violent confrontation with the last prolific killer he captured but got too close to,Dr Hannibal Lecter(presented on screen for the first time here byBrian Cox).In a wounded and dreamlike fugue, Graham wanders through crime scenes late at night trying to psychically commune with the killer. Like the character he played, Petersen, who oscillates perfectly between dazed and hair-triggered here, had a hard time extricating himself from his work. “Your brain may know you’re acting, but your heart doesn’t,” Petersen said in a recent press release for The Final Cut. “Acting is a wonderful profession for giving you a rounded understanding of humanity. But you have to be careful not to get lost in it.” As soon as the film wrapped, Petersen shaved his beard and dyed his hair blonde to shake the role.Stephen Lang, who plays the ethically bankrupt tabloid reporter Freddie Lounds, remembers it as a challenging but rewarding shoot. “ I’ve worked with other directors who are considered within the business to be demanding,Jim [James] Cameronbeing one of them. And when asked the difference between the two, I have said that Jim and I discuss everything. We debate everything. When Michael says jump, I generally say: ‘How high?’ I don’t challenge Michael,” Lang says. “Michael could be tough and he could be short. But you also knew he was extremely generous as a director. He could be a lot of things. There’s a volatility to him, as there is in so many artists. Michael is not only a film-maker, he’s an artist. An auteur.”View image in fullscreenTom Noonan as Francis Dolarhyde with Stephen Lang as Freddie Lounds in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesIt’s hard not to see some of Mann himself in Graham. Known for an immersive pre-production process that leans heavy on investigation and research, Mann spent time with the FBI’s violent crimes and behavioral science units in preparation for Manhunter. He even corresponded for some time with an imprisoned murderer named Dennis Wayne Wallace, who would be the main inspiration for the film’s killer, Francis Dolarhyde (Tom Noonanin a career-defining role).“He’d write what he called ‘Jim Morrisonpsych-poetry’ to me, and tell me his whole story,” recalls Mann of Wallace. “ He had fantasized a love affair with Cinnamon Cindy, a go-go dancer at the Mellow Yellow in Gardena, California. Their song was In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida, which is why that’s used at the end of the picture. He also walked around wearing a hard hat with the Mad Magazine decal on it that said: ‘Support mental illness or I’ll kill you.’”In Wallace, Mann also saw how childhood abuse acted as a catalyst for brutality and used this insight to create a character that was at once evil and empathetic. “If Wallace soiled anything, shit was rubbed in his face,” says Mann. “He was literally leashed to a tree outside in the front yard. And that kind of abuse reduces self-esteem to some impossibly low level. You couple that with a strong ego and that’s how you get a Francis Dolarhyde.“I wanted to evoke that contradiction about killers. These people who commit heinous crimes who are at the same time victims themselves – how does one relate to that? Which is the dilemma for Graham.”View image in fullscreenJoan Allen in Manhunter: The Final Cut.Photograph: Courtesy Rialto PicturesWe come to empathize most with Dolarhyde when he falls for Reba (Joan Allen), a blind woman he works with at a photolab in St Louis. Back at Dolarhyde’s place, they drink gin and tonics and, unbeknown to Reba, watch home movies of the family he plans to kill next. His eyes float between Reba and the bikini-clad woman in the home movie, a smiling mother playing with her child in a pool. There’s some shared humanity between this stranger on screen and the woman next to him that Dolarhyde appears to register. Later, they lie naked in bed together and Dolarhyde kisses sleeping Reba’s hand and weeps. You begin to see that maybe beneath the madness of this man, beneath his sense of godlike superiority over his victims, is some bottomless need for a love he never had. “To me that was evoking the Dolarhyde that had been there as an innocent child,” Mann says. “The person he could have evolved into had he not been the victim of such abuse.”Heat at 30: Michael Mann’s electric crime thriller is a film of fire and sadnessRead moreDespite the macabre content, Manhunter comes in as glossy and delectable a package as you can imagine. It’s got just enough juicy 80s B-movie DNA to offset everything vile unfolding on screen. Manhunter’s greatest achievement is its marriage of visual splendor and psychological depth. There’s a heightened, swooning quality to the look of the film that has never been replicated: all hypermodern, minimalist spaces flooded with alien light.The juxtaposition of Mann’s commitment to authenticity in research and writing with his complete disregard for it visually makes for a satisfying and hyper-real combination. Despite initial disappointment at the box office, Manhunter has continued to dig its claws into culture and has had a lasting influence few could have seen coming. Its icy synth-dominated score set the table for modern crime scores, particularly Cliff Martinez’s collaborations withNicolas Winding Refn. It’s hard to imagine the myriad of films and shows about criminal profiling existing without it.“It influenced a lot,” agrees Mann. “I was trying to find how I could push the medium forward, that was very much on my mind. How do I make it so expressive that you really feel you are in this place?”Manhunter: The Final Cut is out in the US now with a UK release on 25 September and an Australian release to be announcedExplore more on these topicsMichael MannBrian CoxHannibal LecterThomas HarrisCrime filmsThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail
Content: Photograph: Olivia RichardsonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Olivia RichardsonGoing out, staying inCultureFrom A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trailSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaA Useful GhostOut nowWinner of best film at Cannes Critics’ Week, this tale of a woman reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner takes you to plenty of unexpected places, even when you discount the sort of unexpectedness suggested by the premise. Part Marxist thriller, part supernatural romance, and taking in foul-mouthed monks and drama with the in-laws along the way, Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke’s directorial debut is an oddball treat.On the SeaOut nowMade mostly outside the traditional funding mechanisms for UK film, this independent second feature from Helen Walsh is a lovely, graceful depiction of repression and queer desire in a Welsh mussel-harvesting community. Barry Ward gives a fine performance as the married man who finds himself drawn to a younger itinerant worker (Lorne MacFadyen).Aardman RetrospectiveCinemas nationwideIn the run-up to the release of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, look out for summer holiday rereleases of a plethora of Aardman classics in cinemas, including A Matter of Loaf and Death, The Curse of the Were-Rabbit and the film that first introduced woolly hero Shaun, A Close Shave.Pinocchio UnstrungOut nowDirector Rhys Frake-Waterfield was also behind Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey and its sequel. This new instalment in what the film-makers call The Twisted Childhood Universe features Robert Englund (Freddy Krueger) as the voice of Jiminy Cricket.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenBig country … Luke Combs goes next-level.Photograph: Dingena Mol/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesCamp BestivalLulworth Castle, nr Wareham,30 Julyto 2 AugustRob da Bank’s enduring family-friendly festival returns with its mix of kids’ activities – bee-keeping has been added this year, alongside skateboard ramp lessons and trampolining – and music from Bastille, Fatboy Slim, Self Esteem and more.Michael CraggElgar’s FirstRoyal Albert Hall, London,29 JulyThe English composer’s magnificent Symphony No 1 gets top billing, but this concert also features the first major world premiere of the BBC Proms season. The World’s Wife by Brett Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry and is performed by soprano Claire Booth and BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth.Flora WillsonLuke CombsEdinburgh,25 July; London,31 Julyto 2 AugustTheUS country music superstar, who scored a UK hit with his cover of Fast Car in 2023, steps up to stadiums. With six albums under his belt, including this year’s deeply personal The Way I Am, expect a setlist brimming with crowd-pleasing self-reflection.MCEdinburgh Jazz & Blues festivalVarious venues, 25 & 26 JulyThis event consistently embraces international and Scottish artists. Its closing weekend includes folk-inflected sax-led quartet Harben Kay (25 July), Joni Mitchell-inspired singer Michelle Willis (25 July) and multi award-winning jazz/hip-hop sax star Soweto Kinch (26 July).John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenBack to bedlam … Richard Dadd’s Bacchanalian Scene, 1862.Photograph: Oliver Cowling & RodTidnam/Tate ImagesRichard DaddRoyal Academy of Arts, London,25 Julyto 25 OctoberStep into a world of fairies and folklore in Beyond Bedlam, a look at the work of the Victorian artist. He remained forgotten by history until the 1960s, when his life in Victorian asylums became a source of inspiration for countless artists.Michael PinskyMidlands Arts Centre, Birmingham,25 Julyto 4 OctoberFor The Final Bid, Pinksy has filled this gallery with secondhand chairs, all hung from the ceiling, which visitors are invited to bid on. Each bid drives the chair higher up towards the ceiling, in a strange capitalistic ballet about value and detritus.Clare WoodsPitzthanger Manor, London,29 Julyto 8 NovemberThe exhibition, called Garden Without Seasons, sees meditative paintings and collages of the natural world in this Sir John Soane-designed country house, each work pushing the boundary between abstraction and figuration and asking viewers to slow down and contemplate.Susan HughesMAC, Belfast,30 Julyto 18 OctoberThis Belfast-based artist and fiddle player travelled around Ireland collecting stories about the mysteries, myths and collective power of traditional music. The result is this show filled with objects, songs and a stage for ad-hoc performances.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenDolly, pardon? … The World Is Full of Married Men.Photograph: Emmalisa PaulyThe World Is Full of Married MenThe Yard theatre, London,to 1 AugustThe great Yard theatre opens its doors after a huge refurb. Its opening season includes a reimagined King Lear with Ian McKellen as well as this brilliantly bizarre adaptation of Jackie Collins’s racy novel, set amid a series of doll’s houses – and performed by dolls.Miriam GillinsonMike Reiss25 July to 6 August; tour starts LondonAs part of The Simpsons’ original writing team – and co-showrunner during the programme’s early 1990s glory years – nobody is better placed to unpick the seminal cartoon’s ingenious comic tapestry than Reiss. This tour sees him spill all his Springfield-related secrets and take audience questions.Rachel AroestiMatthew Bourne’s The Car ManSheffieldLyceum,25 July;Sadler’s Wells,London,28 Julyto 29 AugustOne of Bourne’s steamiest dance shows is also one of his best dramas. Loosely based on Bizet’s Carmen, but transported to small-town 50s US, a gang of macho mechanics have their close-knit, closed-minded world interrupted when a stranger comes to town. Lust, betrayal, revenge, it’s all here.Lyndsey WinshipCherry OrchardThe Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon,to 29 AugustHelen Hunt, Bill Pullman and Kenneth Branagh star in Chekhov’s exquisite final play. The new version has been written by Laura Wade (Posh, Rivals) whose work always manages to be brilliantly entertaining but shot through with real darkness and political bite.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenMaking a killing … Scoot McNairy and Emmy Rossum in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyFuriousDisney+,27 JulyElizabeth Meriwether (New Girl, Dying for Sex) helms this thriller about an FBI agent whose first case happens to feature that rarest of beasts: a female serial killer. Emmy Rossum – who also came up with the show’s concept – stars as the detective who finds empathy for a devilish criminal.The RaptureiPlayer & BBC One, 26 July, 9pmAdapted by the performance artist Bryony Kimmings from Liz Jensen’s novel, this drama centres on a forensic psychologist treating a teenage girl with the ability to predict catastrophic events. If that doesn’t sound stressful enough, the whole thing takes place in a heatwave. Ruth Madeley, Iwan Rheon and Ruth Jones star.Ghosts AustraliaiPlayer & BBC Three,25 July, 10.30pmMost British comedies get lost in translation when franchised abroad, but this wildly original format is the exception. Following US, French, Greek and German versions, this Aussie spin sees a young couple haunted by an aerobics instructor, a biker, a gold rush miner and a socialite.Gomorrah: The OriginsNow & Sky Atlantic,28 July, 9pmRoberto Saviano’s acclaimed Italian mafia drama was described as a darker alternative to The Sopranos when it aired a decade ago. This similarly gritty prequel returns to the mean streets of 1970s Naples to recount the origin story of Camorra boss Pietro Savastano.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenChief concern … Halo: Campaign Evolved.Photograph: MicrosoftHalo: Campaign EvolvedPC, Xbox, out28 JulyA quarter-century on from the first Halo, the game has been revitalised with new visuals and the original voice actors re-recorded. No competitive multiplayer but you can play cooperatively with one local friend on console, or up to three online.Mistfall HunterPC, PS5, Xbox, out29 JulyTime to learn some new terminology, Gyldhunter. This dark fantasy PvPvE (player-v-player-v-environment) extraction ARPG (action role-playing game) has you (and optional friends) perfecting your weapon stances and combos to kill monsters in an ever-shifting battlefield beneath the Gyldenmist. Gyld luck!Jordan Erica WebberStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenWelcome to the Junglist … Nia Archives.Photograph: Iris LuzNia Archives – Emotional JunglistOut nowThe Brit-nominated “darling of jungle” follows up 2024’s Top 20 debut Silence Is Loud. Co-produced by her alongside James Ford (Arctic Monkeys) and Ethan P Flynn (FKA twigs), songs such as Boys in Blue expand on her sonic palette, pushing towards 90s electronica and indie.Baby Queen – I Hope You Don’t Remember MeOut nowInspired by a whirlwind relationship that ended with a ghosting, South Africa-born, London-based alt-pop star Bella Latham returns with a second album that channels emotional turbulence into galloping synthpop on Feel Something, and something far knottier on the frantic Word Vomit.The Strokes – Reality AwaitsOut nowHaving pulled off a surprising creative and commercial rebirth on 2020’s The New Abnormal, the Strokes return with this seventh album. Produced once again by bearded Zen master Rick Rubin, confounding recent single Going Shopping continues frontman Julian Casablancas’s obsession with Auto-Tune.Charli xcx – Music, Fashion, FilmOut nowDespite a recent pivot to acting, Charli returns with her second album of 2026. The follow-up to February’s excellent Wuthering Heights soundtrack dials up the guitars – see snarky lead single Rock Music – while keeping Brat’s potent mix of hedonism and existential dread.MCStaying in:Brain foodArmchair ExplorerPodcastJust in time for the summer holidays, this beloved travel documentary series features deep dives into global cultures and dream itineraries. Highlights include a road trip through Australia’s Northern Territory and a safari in Botswana wilderness.60 Second DocsInstagramPacking engrossing narrative and fascinating detail into one-minute shorts, this Instagram page is a treasure trove of bite-size curios. Topics range from spoon-playing musical maestros to the art of clay “hug pots” and green-screen tattoos.James Turrell: Master of LightBBC World Service,28 July, 4.32amAmerican artist James Turrell’s Skyspaces are large installations that play with natural light. For this edition of In the Studio, Julian May meets Turrell in Denmark as he prepares one of his most ambitious ones to date.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Furious: this serial killer thriller is the most staggeringly feminist TV you’ll ever watch  | Television | The Guardian
description: The new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fans
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: The new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fans
Content: Murderess on the loose … Lola Petticrew as Catherine in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyView image in fullscreenMurderess on the loose … Lola Petticrew as Catherine in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyThe watcherTelevisionFurious: this serial killer thriller is the most staggeringly feminist TV you’ll ever watchThe new detective series with Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine chasing a female serial killer is a must-see for Killing Eve fansRhik SamadderSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmale friend recently attended a Lily Allen show, and shakily described the experience to me. “I felt like a vegetarian fox at an armed chicken convention,” he said. An overwhelmingly female crowd were experiencing powerful catharsis, united in their anger at men and joy of bangers. I told him chickens couldn’t handle firearms, but I don’t think he heard me. He had tinnitus from the screaming.There isn’t much screaming in Furious, Disney+’s new detective series (from Monday, 27 July). Also missing are the standard tropes of murder dramas: mutilated female bodies, an absence of women’s agency generally. Furious is the cat and mouse story between junior FBI agent Alice Black (Emmy Rossum) and Catherine (Lola Petticrew), a serial killer who is bumping off male victims with calculated sadism. Catherine might be the least serial killer name imaginable, but that’s just one way this show rewrites the rule book. I’d say it’s the most feminist show I’ve ever seen – except that might lead some to write it off.The show’s ethos goes beyond having female leads. You can see it in the way Black and her FBI sex-crimes squad mentor Nora, played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine, interview victims. The clues and tells they notice, their knowledge of a system that fails women. Grimly fitted to Epstein-aware times, the show is interested in the way wealthy men buy legal immunity. Trafficking charges are hard to make stick, notes Nora, thanks to the vulnerability of female witnesses. “Once you accept money for sex, you are a criminal.”View image in fullscreenPsychology of killing … Emmy Rossum and Scoot McNairy in Furious.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyInjustice does not sit solely on the upper rungs of the social ladder. Black is forced to work the case alongside an abusive ex-partner from the NYPD. She never made a formal complaint against him, choosing to simply leave her police job. He’s brilliantly played by Jake Lacy, an actor I feel for. There’s something about his handsome, preppy face, instantly hateable in The White Lotus, that suits villainy. Something that screams “bro” louder than a reunion at a rowing club. Something about it that makes you think: “I want someone to punch you.” Can’t be easy.This isn’t a punching show, though. It’s more sophisticated, more weary. There is sisterhood, but it’s fraught. Black and Catherine share traumatic pasts; only one of them skilfully manipulates women and men alike to work through a kill list. Black chooses to swallow her PTSD, emotionally cauterising herself. Nora is jaded by decades of working in the dark. As part of her job, she has to watch child sexual abuse images, which she does in a locked room she compares to the entrance of Hades. “Why do you want to work in the basement on sex crimes, and crimes against children? Do you hate yourself?” she asks Black at their first meeting.In the half of the series I’ve watched, there are perhaps two men who aren’t at best chauvinists, and often coercive hypocrites. People might grumble about this. But it seems fair enough, given TV’s history of female representation. Plus you can’t critique a patriarchy-omelette without breaking some legs. I mean eggs. There’s no such thing as a vegetarian fox.One of the few nice ones is Black’s former partner Danny, played by Scoot McNairy. (He’s a work partner, not the violent romantic partner. The NYPD here clearly employ a good cop, bad cop, bad cop, bad cop strategy.) Danny believed Black’s story of domestic abuse and spoke out. His allyship has cost him the support of his male colleagues. Yet in an excruciating scene, we learn that Black has also stopped speaking to Danny; he reminds her of the past, her need to be rescued. This is a rare crime show equally interested in the psychology of victimhood as killing, and which values nuance and complexity over catharsis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFurious acknowledges its dark attraction to the damaged Catherine, whom Nora describes as “our avenging angel, our evil Fury, our murderess”, as she enacts a justice that otherwise never comes. Is it Catherine’s fury to which the show’s title refers? Nora herself, or Black? The childish anger of its weak men? Almost certainly, it speaks to its female audience. For fans ofKilling Eve,Promising Young WomanandLily Allen, it’s a must-see. I’m less sure if men will watch. Even the good ones, who know they should.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #253: ​Once the season of surprise breakout hits, this summer’s TV has lost its heat | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited about
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited about
Content: Hot fail … Will Angus, Nicholas Duvernay and Jack Martin in Not Suitable For Work.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenHot fail … Will Angus, Nicholas Duvernay and Jack Martin in Not Suitable For Work.Photograph: DisneyThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #253: ​Once the season of surprise breakout hits, this summer’s TV has lost its heatIn this week’s newsletter: The release calendar is more shaped by award seasons than what viewers might be looking for, with even the big platforms offering little to get excited aboutGwilym MumfordSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in 2015, when I worked on the old print version of the Guide, weran a covercalling on readers to “Stay inside this summer”. Our argument went that, such was theamount of great TVairing in the months from June to August that year (True Detective,My Mad Fat Diary,Veepand, err, a show about Abz from the boyband 5ive’s new career in farming), you’d be a fool to head outside for some vitamin D.This wasn’t a contrarian viewpoint. Streaming’s sudden rise had broken down the walls that had previously left the summer a parched, desolate wasteland and kept the good TV penned into the more viewer-friendly periods of spring and autumn. Now, great new shows would arrive all year round. In the years that followed, some of the most talked-about scripted TV would debut around or after the solstice: Stranger Things, Yellowstone, Euphoria, I May Destroy You, The Bear, and plenty more besides.But, if the Guide magazine still existed in 2026, its equivalent cover would be very different.“Touch grass, not your TV remote”.This year’s summer televisual offering, in the UK and the US, has rarely been worth eschewing the sun for. There may have been a few big returnees (The Bear for its final season, Silo, House of the Dragon) and a couple of interesting curios (the BBC’s delicious premium trash series Two Weeks in August, or Apple TV’s fantastic For All Mankind spin-off Star City), but buzzy, agenda-setting new shows have failed to materialise. If you were feeling generous you might stretch the criteria to includeWidow’s Bay, which finished its much raved-about debut season on 17 June, but I’m not feeling generous: that was inarguably a spring sensation; its shivery, low-lit charms incompatible with a June heatwave. And, discounting that show, the cupboard is severely bare.There’s a major mitigating factor here, of course: a bigger-than-ever World Cup, one that, as well as taking over the TV schedules of BBC and ITV in the UK, had by virtue of happening in North American timezones, eaten into the US primetime period where you’d usually encounter big new summer series too. Still, I’m not sure that alone is enough to excuse the dearth of shows this summer, especially when plenty will have been seeking some non-football counter-programming. And the situation hardly seems to be improving now that the World Cup is over. I can see only two upcoming series in the entirety of August that might fall into the “big new show” bucket: Lanterns, an HBO superhero series that is mainly interesting for being Damon Lindelof’s first show since the excellent Watchmen; and The Shards, an FX Bret Easton Ellis adaptation from Ryan Murphy (and given Murphy’srecenttrack record, that has a more than slim chance of being a major disappointment).View image in fullscreenMaking the effort … Apple TV’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed.Photograph: Zach Dilgard/AppleWhere have the streamers – who don’t have to worry about such notions as “primetime” and “schedules” – been? Netflix, in particular, has endured a rotten summer so far, following on from a similarly miserable spring. Can you remember the last truly conversation-starting Netflix series? That inability to mint major new shows is said to be of serious concern to its higher-ups, according to Vulture’s TVindustry columnist, Joe Adalian. Amazon has hardly fared any better – its most-discussed show, the Legally Blonde prequelElle, has mainly prompted conversations over how wretched it is. Disney+ can only really point to the final season of The Bear as a qualified success this summer (Mindy Kaling’sNot Suitable For Workhaving been swiftly memory-holed), while HBO have produced little aside from the dreary House of the Dragon and a Larry David historical sketch show that landed with a thump. Only Apple TV seem to be at least making an effort this summer, with a regular drip-drip of programming: Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed, Star City, Lucky,Cape Fear, Silo,Sugar, and, next month, the returning Ted Lasso.Moreover, this isn’t a one-off aberration, 2025’s summer season was also something of a washout. The only debuting series that hasn’t been swiftly forgotten from that period was Alien: Earth. That suggests a larger tectonic shift away from the summer, and perhaps that’s the result of a greater emphasis on Emmy awards, which streaming services in particular are keen to hoover. Voting for the Emmys closes on 31 May, and in recent years there has been increasing eagerness to launch the best new series right before that cut off point. And why drop new shows in June, July and August when most viewers will still be catching up with the deluge delivered in late spring? (Something similar could be said to happen the UK, where the Bafta TV awards cut off point is 31 December, causing an autumnal glut of series.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt all means that TV-wise, summer is likely to be a washout for a while yet. Yes, you might have to go outside and enjoy the sunshine. Ghastly, I know.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterTelevisionnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: hit British comedy Ghosts gets a fun new twist  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Scream for help … Ghosts Australia on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/© BBC Studios Productions Australia Pty Ltd, Network Ten Pty Limited, Network Ten All Access Pty Limited, Screenwest (Australia) Ltd 2024View image in fullscreenScream for help … Ghosts Australia on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/© BBC Studios Productions Australia Pty Ltd, Network Ten Pty Limited, Network Ten All Access Pty Limited, Screenwest (Australia) Ltd 2024TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: hit British comedy Ghosts gets a fun new twistThe Australian version of the sitcom is every bit as entertaining! Plus, get ready to belt out Bonnie Tyler’s best hits. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Graeme Virtue,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 25 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGhosts Australia10.30pm, BBC ThreeBuy a mouldy flat with a toilet in the kitchen or move into the rundown mansion of a dead great-uncle? It’s a no-brainer for couple Kate and Sean in this Oz version of the hit British sitcom. But as fans of the original show already know, their home is riddled with ghosts, which only Kate can see after a near-death experience. A new batch of ghost characters add a fresh spin on a firm comedy favourite.Hollie RichardsonAlan Carr’s Picture Slam6.40pm, BBC OneThe new series of the picture quiz where contestants have to identify a range of snaps continues. Three teams are competing for the cash prize of £10k, including Alan Carr superfans Lucy and Sharon. They tell the comedian to “check the bins” when he gets home after the show. He looks scared.Priya ElanBonnie Tyler at the BBC8.30pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenI really need you tonight! … Bonnie Tyler at the BBC on BBC Two.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAThe husky-voiced powerhouse died earlier this month, so here are the belting songs that made her a Welsh legend over a five-decade career. Sing along to archive performances of hits from Lost in France to Loving You Is a Dirty Job and Holding Out for a Hero. But save your lungs for the Total Eclipse of the Heart finale.HRThe Sentinels9pm, BBC FourA double bill of the sombre French world war one drama about super-soldiers forced to put country over family. After losing a comrade, the remaining three Sentinels are ready to blow off some steam. Meanwhile, Irène’s investigations into dodgy military dealings point her toward the fleshpots of northern Paris.Graeme VirtueThe Staircase9.15pm, ITV1Colin Firth and Toni Collette’s true-crime drama first aired on Sky back in 2022. Michael Peterson called 911 to report finding his wife Kathleen’s body at the bottom of their stairs at home. But he immediately became a suspect, and the first episode shows flashbacks to what their relationship was really like.HRSchitt’s Creek11.45pm, BBC ThreeA triple bill of the much-loved Canadian sitcom that gave the late, great Catherine O’Hara a second wind. First up, Moira (O’Hara) and Johnny (Eugene Levy) go bargain hunting at an estate sale, while Alexis (Annie Murphy) tries to hide the fact that she can’t ride a bike.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceLurker, 6.15pm, Sky Cinema PremiereAt first sight, Alex Russell’s intense drama is about a pop singer stalked by an obsessive fan. Théodore Pellerin’s LA clothes shop worker Matthew talks himself into the entourage of the apparently easy-going Oliver (Archie Madekwe), a British musician on the up. As he sidles from obsequious gofer to would-be documentary profiler, Matthew’s neediness is embarrassing going on excruciating – but it also flatters Oliver. And as their relationship develops over weeks, the power balance between them shifts drastically.Simon WardellMonster, 10.25pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenHeartbreaking … Monster on BBC Four.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyJapanese film-maker Hirokazu Kore-eda has long been a brilliant illuminator of children’s fractured, often inarticulated lives. This 2023 Cannes winner is another compelling look into their inner worlds, framed as an episodic mystery. First, we see events from the point of view of Sakura Ando’s single mother Saori, who thinks her son Minato (Sōya Kurokawa) is being bullied by his teacher, Mr Hori (Eita Nagayama). But then we get Hori’s side of the story and, crucially, Minato’s; what emerges is a heartbreaking tale of friendship and difference.SWLive sportCommonwealth Games, 8.30am, TNT Sports 2Day two includes netball, boxing, artistic gymnastics and bowls.Men’s Tour de France , 10am, TNT Sports 1The penultimate stage, from Le Bourg-d’Oisans to Alpe d’Huez.World Matchplay Darts, 9pm, Sky Sports Main EventThe semi-finals in Blackpool.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We can see the boats that supply the restaurant’s lobsters from our seats’: a culinary tour of Gower, Wales | Wales holidays | The Guardian
description: On a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning scenery
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: On a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning scenery
Content: A selection of summer dishes at the View Rhossili on the Gower peninsula in south Wales.View image in fullscreenA selection of summer dishes at the View Rhossili on the Gower peninsula in south Wales.Wales holidays‘We can see the boats that supply the restaurant’s lobsters from our seats’: a culinary tour of Gower, WalesOn a coastline brimming with seafood shacks, crab sandwiches and hyperlocal flavour, our food writer is happy to be distracted from the stunning sceneryFelicity CloakeSat 25 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 25 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf we take it as read that the better the view, the worse the cooking, then by rights south Wales’s Gower peninsula should be a culinary desert. The first time I visited almost 15 years ago, I was unprepared for its loveliness – back in 1956, Gower (nevertheGower, as locals were quick to correct me) was thefirst place in the UK to be designated an area of outstanding natural beauty, and though the peninsula abuts the country’s second city, Swansea, it still feels profoundly rural. Crisscrossed by narrow lanes flanked by towering hedges and ancient churches, it’s a great place to cycle, to drive, and above all to walk up an appetite.Indeed, it’s been a long-held ambition of mine to hike the 43 miles of the Welsh Coast Path from Mumbles to Loughor. Sadly, it remains just that because on this latest trip I spent considerably more time chomping than yomping … though in fairness I was on a research mission for a walking trip with a friend here later in the summer, because as a food writer and semi-professional glutton, I never like to head anywhere unprepared.View image in fullscreenWith this in mind, and another friend on hand as a chauffeur, Wilf the dog and I began our investigations in Mumbles, where Swansea thins into a pretty seaside village of colourful Victorian villas culminating in a magnificent, privately owned pier. (A few years ago, a visiting Prince William observed to owner Bert Bollom, the third generation of his family to run it, that this was an unusual career choice. Bert shrugged that he’d inherited the job from his dad. “Tell me about it,” he recalls the prince sighing.)Though the pier is undergoing restoration work, there’s a good view of the “crown of the Bristol Channel” from another Bollom enterprise,On the Rocks, a steak restaurant with a terrace jutting over the foreshore that’s no doubt a terrific place for a sundowner. But, I tell myself sternly, when you’re starting a walk you need to put one foot in front of the other, not sit around drinking, especially as the friend I plan to come back with later in the summer is happily, if rather inconveniently, pregnant.View image in fullscreenCrab sandwich at the Gower Seafood Hut in Mumbles.There’s thus not much point in returning to theGower Brewery Taproom, despite the warm welcome and dog biscuits we receive on this occasion – I’ll probably suggest we stop instead atJoe’s, the local cult masquerading as an ice-cream parlour. (Vanilla, freshly churned in-house daily, is the only move here. Unless you’re under the age of 10, do not waste your time on other flavours.) Thankfully, the expectant one is past the nauseous stage, so I can also steer her in the direction of the crab sandwiches (local sourdough and deliciously saltyShirgar butter) at theGower Seafood Hutwith a clear conscience – depending on the time of day, it might also feel appropriate to fortify ourselves with a helping of fried whitebait or cockle popcorn before joining the coast path, particularly as Chris Price, who mans the stoves, has, according to co-owner Sarah Kift, already walked much of it himself.That said, I reckon I’ve got the fuelling part of the route covered; for a start, there’s another ice-cream parlour,Fortes, just round the headland in Limeslade Bay. From the neat beach huts of Langland to the golden sands of Three Cliffs Bay, however, the sites are more prehistoric than edible (tasty as theBacon Hole cavesounds, the nearest it gets to cured meat is its hoard of ancient narrow-nosed rhinoceros and straight-tusked elephant bones, now 200 miles away in the British Museum). Take a brief detour into the village of Southgate though, and you’ll happen upon a brilliant Greek cafe – I didn’t anticipate tucking into a sugar-dustedbougatsacustard pie and a punchy little coffee inThe Gower Deli, but this place is full of surprises.double quotation markI didn’t anticipate tucking into a sugar-dusted bougatsa custard pie in The Gower Deli, but this place is full of surprisesSometimes they come too thick and fast even for my boundless appetite: just 20 minutes inland from Three Cliffs, if you follow the lazy meandering waters of the Pennard Pill past the ruins of a Norman castle, sits theGower Heritage Centre. Clustered around a 12th-century water mill, it boasts a cider press, organic community agriculture project, sauerkraut producer, jewellery designer and bike shop plus – and the jewel in its crown as far as I’m concerned – the superbLittle Valley bakery, whose traditional Gower loaf is produced using the mill’s barley flour. They also make ridiculously flaky pasties, focaccia sandwiches, huge cookies and excellent viennoiserie – in short, a rambler’s dream.View image in fullscreenThe Beach House restaurant in Oxwich on the Gower.From Three Cliffs, it’s about another five miles along the coast to Oxwich. If you make one reservation for your Gower trip, make it at theBeach Housethere. Admittedly, given its Michelin star, one might not want to wander in directly from the path in quick-dry hiking sandals, but our welcome couldn’t be warmer, despite Wilf’s rather over-effusive manner (the terrace is dog-friendly, as is one table inside, which you can bet your boots I will be booking well in advance).View image in fullscreenA Michelin-star dish at the Beach House restaurant in Oxwich.From our seats, we can see the two boats that supply the restaurant with lobster. “They belong to Paul and Jim,” says chef Hywel Griffith. “Every morning, I text them what we need that day.” The lamb is from the North Gower salt marsh; the seaweed in the laverbread rolls (a clever play on the traditional puree) from Selwyn’s in Pen-clawdd; and the dessert, a malted mousse with wood sorrel and fermented pine syrup, is the single most delicious thing I’ve eaten since Sarah Kift’s crab sandwich.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFive more miles brings us to Port Eynon, whose chief attraction on this visit is the tiny, genuinely artisanGower Gin Company– having enjoyed one solo guided tasting with my designated driver and the teetotal terrier, I’ll pass on another with a reluctant abstainer. It’s six more miles to Rhossili, once, somewhat absurdly, declared the “ninth best beach in the world” by TripAdvisor. What’s not up for debate is that it’s 3 miles long and stunning.View image in fullscreenSunrise over Mumbles lighthouse and privately owned pier.Photograph: leighcol/Getty ImagesThanks to the National Trust, it’s also untouched by the grubby hand of commercialism, so should you be peckish, pause at the aptly namedView cafebefore you descend the cliff. Offering colourful vegan “power bowls” (popular with the surfing crowd apparently) and homemade falafel alongside the rarebit and bara brith, the only packaged food in sight is a bag of locally produced dog treats I’m bullied into buying for my elderly companion who, despite a brisk trot down to the Worms Head Coastwatch station beforehand, is in no mood to obey the house rule that “shouting is not permitted”.The key to an unforgettable holiday? Just focus on the food | Felicity CloakeRead moreTurn the corner on to the north coast, and you’re faced with Whiteford Sands, yet another broad expanse of golden gorgeousness with great cooking attached in the form of theBritannia Innin Llanmadoc, where the salt marsh lamb croquettes at the bar drive the tiny diner under the table to distraction.Fortunately, I don’t have to test Wilf’s restraint on the living, bleating thing on this occasion, as the remaining seven miles of the route – through the marshes to Pen-clawdd, – will have to wait till next month. When we finally get there, however, I will insist on stopping at the Gower Brewery to toast our achievement. I’ve even road-tested their Zero beer in preparation. As I said, I like to plan ahead.Explore more on these topicsWales holidaysEurope holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysFood and drinkFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Out of this world’: the best supermarket chocolate ice-cream, tasted and rated | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Who makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for you
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Who makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for you
Content: Simple pleasures: higher quality with fewer additives is the order of the day.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenSimple pleasures: higher quality with fewer additives is the order of the day.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.The FilterIce-cream and sorbetReview‘Out of this world’: the best supermarket chocolate ice-cream, tasted and ratedWho makes the smoothest, creamiest, chocolatiest tub? We have the inside scoop for youThe best supermarket dark chocolateTom HuntSat 25 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.There’s been a marked shift towards less-processed ice-cream sinceI tested vanilla ice-cream for this column last summer. Most ice-cream on the market used to be a cocktail of gums and emulsifiers, but now they’re of much higher quality and with fewer additives.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.All today’s chocolate ice-creams are sophisticated, rich and complex, with deep, dark flavours, and I scored them on taste and texture first (I favour denser, French-style, custard-based ice-creams). I also prioritised smoothness and mouthfeel.I awarded extra marks to products that are rich in cream, as well as for provenance and lower processing. Fewer additives were a plus, too. After all, a short and recognisable ingredients list rarely lies, and usually means more cream, better chocolate and a cleaner finish.The best supermarket chocolate ice-creamBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Santo Domingo chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£4.50 for 480ml at Waitrose (94p/100ml)★★★★☆Voluminous, super-rich, smooth and creamy (35% West Country whipping cream). Dark and deeply chocolatey, with complex flavour notes; quite sweet, though. Rainforest Alliance-certified Dominican Republic chocolate and free-range egg. Great Taste one-star award. Remarkably good, and no stabilisers.Best bargain:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 480ml at Sainsbury’s (73p/100ml)★★★★☆Rich, dense and very creamy, with a medium intensity. Made with British cow’s milk and (27%) double cream, while the Rainforest Alliance-certified cocoa produces a medium-dark chocolate custard with a sugary, toffee flavour. No stabilisers or emulsifiers beyond the soya lecithin in the chocolate.And the rest …Brickell’s all-natural craft chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£7.50 for 475ml at Brickell’s (£1.58/100ml)★★★★☆Out of this world: fudgy, rich and satiating. Very smooth and characterful, with a bittersweet, nutty, complex and strong caramel-molasses flavour from the dark brown sugar. Made with British milk from the family farm,Westcombe Dairy,Pump Street85%-cocoa Ecuadorian chocolate and free-range eggs. Additive-free, too, and this week’s best splurge.M&S 85% dark chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£5 for 500ml at Ocado (£1/100ml)★★★★☆Mousse-like, soft, silky and super-smooth. Clean but rich with West Country double cream and honey. The 85% chocolate is subtle and subdued by the milk and cream, but it still provides a bittersweet complexity. No stabilisers or emulsifiers.Häagen-Dazs Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£5.75 for 460ml at Tesco (£1.25/100ml)£6 for 460ml at Waitrose (£1.30/100ml)★★★★☆Interestingly textural, with 72%-cocoa dark chocolate shards dotted throughout the chocolate custard. Intensely rich (27.4% cream) and sweet, with a strong caramel flavour. Excellent quality, and the benchmark with which to compare other traditional ice creams.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesco Finest Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 480ml at Tesco (73p/100ml)★★★★☆Light, mousse-like and rich, and made with West Country whole milk, 24% double cream and small chocolate chips for textural crunch. Hits the sweet spot of sugar and fat, and dangerously addictive – it’s a bit like eating whipped frozen chocolate bars. Preservative and stabiliser free, bar the soya and sunflower lecithins in the chocolate.Morrisons the Best Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3 for 480ml at Morrisons (63p/100ml)★★★★☆Sophisticated and intensely chocolatey, with bitter cocoa notes dominating. Very sweet, with a smooth, mousse-like, airy texture. Made with Cornish milk and 26% cream. Refreshingly simple ingredients list.Lidl Deluxe Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£2.69 for 500ml at Lidl (54p/100ml), in store only★★★☆☆Luxuriously rich (24% British double cream), smooth, light and airy. Intensely chocolatey, with textural chunks of Rainforest Alliance chocolate. Contains several additives.Carte D’Or Indulgent chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.74 for 900ml at Asda (42p/100ml)£3.90 for 900ml at Tesco (43p/100ml)★★☆☆☆Airy and light, and made with a base of reconstituted skimmed milk, rather than whole milk or cream. Even so, surprisingly good, with a rich, bitter cocoa flavour (though it leaves a greasy feeling on the tongue and has a soya taste, too). Rainforest Alliance-certified milk chocolate pieces add texture. Contains several additives.Jude’s Belgian chocolate ice-creamView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 460ml at Ocado (76p/100ml)★★☆☆☆Very airy and light, yet still rich and chewy. At 9.6% cream, it has less than you’d expect in a premium product, and coconut oil is used to boost the fat content. Very scoopable straight from the freezer, and smooth with no ice crystals. A dark and intense bitter cocoa flavour with added depth from vanilla, but a slightly synthetic flavour. Free-range eggs and Great Taste one star. Contains additives.For more, read thebest supermarket dark chocolateand thebest supermarket coffeeExplore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe FilterFoodChocolatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegan recipe for cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and lime | Noodles | The Guardian
description: This globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kick
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: This globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kick
Content: Meera Sodha's cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut coriander and lime.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha's cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut coriander and lime.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.The new veganNoodlesMeera Sodha’s vegan recipe for cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and limeThis globetrotting cold fusion dish boasts south-east Asian, Middle-Eastern and even Italian influences, producing sweet and sour notes and a chilli kickMeera SodhaSat 25 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan a person in a heatwave ever have too many cold noodle dishes? I’d wager no – hence today’s recipe. It started life as one of my favourite meals, the mighty spaghetti pomodoro, but then packed its bags and travelled through the Middle East, picking up some tahini along the way, then on to Indonesia for some heat (sambal oelek), and then hopped over to Vietnam for a final hurrah of fresh lime, coriander and peanuts. The result is a creamy but perky tomato sauce that can live in the fridge for up to a week for the too-hot-to-cook days.Cold tomato and tahini noodles with peanut, coriander and limeI’ve said “light” tahini and agave syrup (over “dark”), but if the jar or bottle doesn’t say which it is, don’t worry. Ramen noodles are available in larger supermarkets; you’ll need to go farther afield (or online) for sambal oelek, a bright Indonesian chilli sauce, but it’s worthwhile. It’s a very easy-to-use and versatile condiment. You can make the tomato sauce ahead of time and add the cooked noodles and topping when you’re ready to serve.Prep10 minCook30 minServes4250g ramen noodles3½ tbsp neutral oil(eg, rapeseed or sunflower)3 garlic cloves, peeled and finely minced1½cm x 2cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated400g tin finely chopped tomatoes(AKA “polpa”)1¼ tsp fine sea salt1 tbsp sambal oelek2 tbsp light tahini1½ tbsp light soy sauce1½ tbsp toasted sesame oil2 tsp light agave syrup75g roasted salted peanuts, finely chopped to breadcrumb size1 lime, zest finely grated, then juiced to get 1 tbsp15g fresh coriander, finely choppedCook the noodles according to the packet instructions. Just before the end of the cooking time, take out a small mug of the cooking water, then drain the noodles and rinse them under the cold tap until cold. Gently and with clean hands, mix in a tablespoon of oil, then leave to drain.To make the sauce, put two tablespoons of oil in a large saucepan or deep saute pan on a medium heat. When hot, add the garlic and ginger, cook for a couple of minutes until sticky and golden, then add the tinned tomatoes. Fill the empty tin a quarter-full of water (to get the last bits), then tip this into the pan, too, along with a teaspoon of salt and the sambal oelek.Cook for eight to 10 minutes, until the bubbles are thick and the sauce reduced. Mash away any lumps of tomato with a potato masher, then take off the heat and stir through the tahini, soy sauce, sesame oil and agave.For the topping, put the peanuts, lime zest, a quarter-teaspoon of salt and half a tablespoon of oil in a small pan on a medium to low heat, and stir frequently until the peanuts take on a deep, brown colour. Stir in the tablespoon of lime juice, leave that to dry off, then take off the heat and leave to cool for five minutes.Stir the coriander through the topping mix. Add the noodles to the cooled sauce, toss to coat, then tip on to a platter and sprinkle over the topping.Explore more on these topicsNoodlesThe new veganVegetablesFoodTomatoesSummer food and drinkSauces and graviesMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
